3.1.2 Operational criteria
PICO is a framework for thinking; inclusion criteria are its operational expression, specific enough that two reviewers working independently reach the same decision on the same record (7). Table 3.3 contrasts vague and operational versions for a review of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure.



Table 3.3: From PICO to operational criteria.










Element
Vague
Operational




Population
Adults with heart disease
Adults aged 18 years or more with physician-diagnosed heart failure and ejection fraction below 40%


Intervention
SGLT2 inhibitor
Any licensed SGLT2 inhibitor at an approved dose for at least 12 weeks


Comparator
Placebo or usual care
Placebo, or standard care without an SGLT2 inhibitor


Outcome
Heart failure outcomes
Composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure; all-cause death; KCCQ score


Time
Not stated
Outcomes assessed at 12 months or later






The vague versions fail in predictable ways. “Heart disease” mixes myocardial infarction, heart failure and arrhythmia, which cannot sensibly be pooled. “Beta-blockers” includes drugs that are not interchangeable. “Mortality” could mean all-cause or cardiovascular, in hospital or at five years. “Long-term” is not a criterion at all. Each ambiguity is a researcher degree of freedom, and each one resolved after seeing the data inflates the chance of a false-positive conclusion (8).


3.1.3 Time, and intercurrent events
Time is not a footnote to PICO; it is part of what makes the estimand estimable (Section 1.3). A pre-specified time does two jobs. It says when an outcome counts, so “outcomes at 12 months or later” is a criterion, not a preference. And it fixes when the clock starts relative to eligibility and treatment assignment; misalign these and immortal time bias follows (Section 3.2.1).
Time alone does not complete the estimand. It also needs a pre-specified strategy for intercurrent events: participants who stop treatment, switch, or need rescue medication before follow-up ends (9). An intention-to-treat analysis, which analyses everyone as randomised, corresponds to the treatment-policy strategy. A per-protocol analysis, restricted to adherent participants, roughly targets a hypothetical strategy: what would have happened had everyone adhered? Applied to the same trial, the two answer different questions. A review that takes the intention-to-treat result from one trial and the per-protocol result from another pools two estimands as if they were one, which is why the choice belongs in the protocol and is checked at extraction (Section 3.4.3).


3.1.4 Types of review question
The type of question determines the eligible designs, the effect measure, the main threats to validity and the risk-of-bias tool (Table 3.4).



Table 3.4: Types of review question.












Question type
Example
Designs
Effect measures
Risk-of-bias tool




Effectiveness
Do SGLT2 inhibitors reduce cardiovascular death in heart failure?
Randomised trials; observational studies under pre-specified conditions
RR, OR, HR, RD
RoB 2; ROBINS-I (Chapter 5)


Aetiology
Is exposure E associated with outcome O?
Cohort, case–control
RR, OR, HR
ROBINS-E


Diagnostic accuracy
How well does test T identify condition C?
Cross-sectional comparison with a reference standard
Sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios
QUADAS-3


Prognosis
What happens to patients with condition C, and can we predict it?
Prospective cohort
Absolute risk, discrimination, calibration
PROBAST (models), QUIPS (factors)






For aetiology the exposure often cannot be randomised (smoking, genes, poverty), so confounding and selection bias are the main threats. Diagnostic questions replace PICO with population, index test, reference standard and target condition. Prognostic questions add setting and time (PICOTS).

Diagnostic accuracy: QUADAS-3
QUADAS-3 (10,11) replaced QUADAS-2 in 2026. It assesses risk of bias in four domains: participants (was recruitment free of selection bias?), index test (was it conducted and interpreted blind to the reference result, with a pre-specified threshold?), target condition (formerly “reference standard”: does it correctly classify who has the condition?) and analysis (formerly “flow and timing”: were all participants accounted for, and indeterminate or missing results handled appropriately?). Applicability to the review question is judged for the first three domains.
Three changes matter most. Reviewers first define the ideal test accuracy trial for their question and judge real studies against it. Judgements are made for each accuracy estimate, not each study, since one paper may report accuracy in several subgroups. And signalling questions are answered on a five-point scale (yes, probably yes, probably no, no, no information) rather than yes, no or unclear.


Prognostic models: PROBAST
PROBAST assesses studies that develop, validate or update multivariable prediction models (12,13). Its 20 signalling questions, phrased so that “yes” indicates absence of bias, fall into four domains: participants (appropriate data source and inclusions), predictors (defined and assessed the same way for everyone, without knowledge of the outcome, and available when the model would be used), outcome (pre-specified, determined the same way for everyone and blind to predictors, with an appropriate interval) and analysis (enough events per candidate predictor, no univariable pre-selection, appropriate handling of missing data, censoring and competing risks, and correction for overfitting). A study is at low risk of bias only if all four domains are at low risk; a model developed without any external validation is usually rated high risk, unless the development sample was very large and internally validated.



3.1.5 Principles for inclusion and exclusion criteria
Whatever the question type, the criteria are written into the protocol before a single record is screened.
Inclusion criteria should be pre-specified in the registered protocol; derived from the estimand, so that each criterion maps to a component of P, I, C, O or T; no more restrictive than the question requires, since each one reduces generalisability; explicit about partial information (what if a trial reports outcomes at 6 and 24 months but not 12?); and applied to studies, not reports.
Exclusion criteria should be justified by the estimand rather than by convenience, kept to a minimum, and explicit about studies that partly meet the criteria. Legitimate exclusions include non-human studies and studies whose outcome data cannot be obtained even after contacting the authors. Illegitimate exclusions include studies with unwelcome results, studies in languages the reviewers do not read (use translation), and older studies, unless the intervention did not exist.


3.1.6 Which studies can be pooled?
Not every included study should be pooled with every other. The Cochrane Handbook asks reviewers to pre-specify how studies will be grouped for synthesis (7). In practice, “can these be pooled?” means “do these studies share the same estimand?”: the same operationally defined P, I, C and O, and a compatible T. Pooling is reasonable when populations are clinically similar, the effect measure is the same (or transformable to the same scale), and outcome definitions and timing are compatible.
Studies should be analysed separately when interventions differ in mechanism, populations differ fundamentally (children and adults, say), outcome definitions are incompatible, or designs are too heterogeneous. A structured narrative synthesis is then the right output.






Computable is not meaningful



Any set of numbers can be averaged. The question is whether the pooled estimate answers a clinically meaningful question. A forest plot that should not exist is worse than no forest plot.

title: 3  From Question to Data
text:
3.2 When eligible studies are observational
Effectiveness reviews increasingly include observational studies, especially when trials are few or short. Two recent studies show why their eligibility, and their design, must be scrutinised rather than assumed.

3.2.1 The promise of target trial emulation
Target trial emulation (TTE) asks investigators to specify the randomised trial they would ideally run (eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment, time zero, outcomes, analysis) and then emulate it as closely as possible with observational data (14). It is now widely cited in cardiology, oncology and pharmacoepidemiology as a remedy for confounding and immortal time bias.
The key feature of a randomised trial that an emulation must copy is that eligibility, treatment assignment and the start of follow-up (time zero) coincide. When they do not, bias follows even if every other step is done well. Figure 3.1, adapted from (15), catalogues the ways alignment can fail.






Figure 3.1: Failure modes when eligibility (E), treatment assignment (A) and time zero (T0) are not aligned. In panels 1 and 2, assignment is resolved before time zero: selection bias without immortal time. In panel 3, time zero precedes both eligibility and assignment: selection bias with immortal time, since no one can die before completing eligibility. In panels 4 and 5, time zero coincides with eligibility but assignment is confirmed later: classic immortal time bias, in which deaths during the immortal window are either excluded (selection) or counted as unexposed (misclassification). Adapted from (15).





3.2.2 Example: GLP-1 RAs and breast cancer survival
A 2026 cohort study in a high-impact journal used a US electronic health record network to compare women with breast cancer who did or did not use GLP-1 RAs (16). Of more than 840 000 eligible patients, propensity-score-matched cohorts were formed among women with obesity (users versus non-users) and with type 2 diabetes (GLP-1 RAs versus insulin or metformin, and versus SGLT2 inhibitors). The reported hazard ratios for 10-year all-cause mortality were 0.35 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.58) in the obesity cohort and 0.09 (0.06 to 0.15) against insulin or metformin, a 91% reduction in the risk of death.
The design explains the size of these effects. Exposure was defined as at least two prescriptions, but follow-up started at diagnosis. A woman could only be classified as exposed if she survived long enough to fill a second prescription; deaths before that point counted against the unexposed group. This is the arrangement of panels 4 and 5 in Figure 3.1.
How large can the resulting bias be? A simulation answers the question directly. We generate breast cancer patients whose survival is completely unaffected by the drug (true HR = 1). A fraction of them start a GLP-1 RA at some point after diagnosis and fill a second prescription one to three months later. We then analyse the same data three ways:

As in the paper: exposure fixed at baseline (“ever had two prescriptions”), clock starting at diagnosis.
Landmark analysis: patients who died before 6 months are excluded and the clock restarts there, but exposure is still defined by any later second prescription. This was the paper’s sensitivity analysis.
Time zero aligned: exposure is time-varying, so each patient contributes unexposed person-time until her second prescription and exposed person-time afterwards.



Code
# One simulated cohort, analysed three ways. The drug has NO effect on survival.
simulate_itb <- function(n = 5000,           # patients per cohort
                         median_start = 18,  # median months from diagnosis to 1st Rx
                         p_user = 0.3,       # proportion who ever start the drug
                         median_surv = 60,   # median survival, months
                         max_fu = 120,       # administrative censoring, months
                         lm_time = 6) {      # landmark, months
  t_death <- rexp(n, log(2) / median_surv)
  user    <- runif(n) < p_user
  t_rx1   <- ifelse(user, rexp(n, log(2) / median_start), Inf)
  t_rx2   <- t_rx1 + runif(n, 1, 3)          # 2nd prescription 1-3 months later
  time    <- pmin(t_death, max_fu)
  status  <- as.integer(t_death <= max_fu)
  exposed <- t_rx2 < time                    # survived to fill a 2nd prescription
  d <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n), time, status, exposed, t_rx2)

  # 1. Paper's design: exposure fixed at baseline, clock starts at diagnosis
  hr_naive <- exp(coef(coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ exposed, data = d)))

  # 2. Landmark: exclude deaths before lm_time, restart the clock there
  dl <- subset(d, time > lm_time)
  hr_lm <- exp(coef(coxph(Surv(time - lm_time, status) ~ exposed, data = dl)))

  # 3. Aligned: unexposed until the 2nd prescription, exposed afterwards
  pre  <- data.frame(id = d$id, start = 0, stop = pmin(d$time, d$t_rx2),
                     event = ifelse(d$exposed, 0L, d$status), x = 0L)
  de   <- subset(d, exposed)
  post <- data.frame(id = de$id, start = de$t_rx2, stop = de$time,
                     event = de$status, x = 1L)
  hr_tv <- exp(coef(coxph(Surv(start, stop, event) ~ x,
                          data = rbind(pre, post), timefix = FALSE)))

  c(paper = unname(hr_naive), landmark = unname(hr_lm),
    aligned = unname(hr_tv))
}


We repeat the simulation 200 times for each of three scenarios in which patients start the drug, on average, 6, 18 or 36 months after diagnosis.


Code
set.seed(2026)
scenarios <- c(6, 18, 36)
itb <- do.call(rbind, lapply(scenarios, function(m) {
  r <- t(replicate(200, simulate_itb(median_start = m)))
  data.frame(delay = m, r)
}))

itb_summary <- itb |>
  group_by(delay) |>
  summarise(across(c(paper, landmark, aligned), median))
kable(itb_summary, digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Median delay to 1st Rx (months)",
                    "As in the paper", "Landmark", "Time zero aligned"))











Median delay to 1st Rx (months)
As in the paper
Landmark
Time zero aligned




6
0.81
0.90
1.00


18
0.66
0.72
1.00


36
0.57
0.62
1.01







Code
itb |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(paper, landmark, aligned),
                      names_to = "analysis", values_to = "hr") |>
  mutate(analysis = factor(analysis, c("paper", "landmark", "aligned"),
                           c("As in the paper", "Landmark", "Time zero aligned")),
         delay = factor(paste("Median delay", delay, "months"),
                        levels = paste("Median delay", scenarios, "months"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hr, fill = analysis)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6, colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ delay, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("firebrick", "darkorange", "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "Estimated hazard ratio", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.y = element_blank())








Figure 3.2: Hazard ratios from 200 simulated cohorts per scenario in which the drug has no effect (true HR = 1, dashed line). The longer patients wait before starting treatment, the more immortal time is credited to the exposed group.





With a drug that does nothing, the paper’s design produces median hazard ratios of 0.81, 0.66 and 0.57 as the delay to treatment lengthens. The landmark analysis reduces the bias only slightly, because immortal time after the landmark is still credited to the exposed group. Only the time-aligned analysis recovers the truth. The simulated bias is smaller than the published effects, but the simulation is deliberately simple: it ignores confounding by indication, and the real comparison against insulin or metformin adds differences in disease severity.
The paper also contained an unrecognised clue. Against SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 RAs showed no difference (HR 0.97, 0.82 to 1.14). Both groups had to survive long enough to fill two prescriptions, so immortal time was roughly symmetrical and cancelled out. Attenuation towards the null when the comparator shares the same bias is exactly what immortal time bias predicts.


3.2.3 Example: GLP-1 RAs and obesity-associated cancers
A second 2026 study, in an oncology journal of even higher impact, explicitly described itself as a target trial emulation (17). In a database of 113 million US patients it matched about 81 000 adults with obesity, but without diabetes, who were prescribed a GLP-1 RA to the same number who received diet or exercise counselling, and reported a hazard ratio for 13 obesity-associated cancers of 0.59 (0.53 to 0.67) over a median follow-up of only two years.
Again the exposure was confirmed by a prescription after the index date. And again the results contained a clue. The hazard ratio was about 0.8 for semaglutide but about 0.3 for tirzepatide, a 70% reduction in cancer incidence within two years. A biological explanation for so large and so fast an effect is implausible. A design explanation is not: tirzepatide was launched in 2022, semaglutide for diabetes in 2017, so the two drugs had very different patterns of initiation relative to the index date, and therefore different amounts of immortal time.


3.2.4 TTE is a framework, not a credential
Properly implemented, target trial emulation increases transparency and eliminates self-inflicted biases such as immortal time. But citing the framework is not the same as implementing it. Even when it is implemented correctly, TTE does not guarantee the right model, high-quality data or the absence of residual confounding, and it does not justify the choice of estimand.






Two over-corrections to avoid



“Observational studies are unreliable” was too pessimistic; “well-done causal inference from observational data approximates a trial” is too optimistic. Causal inference remains an exercise in critical judgement, not the assured output of a design label. For a systematic reviewer, this means that a study’s claim to be a target trial emulation is a reason to check the alignment of eligibility, assignment and time zero, not a reason to skip the check.

title: 3  From Question to Data
text:
3.3 Randomised trials can mislead too
Randomisation protects against confounding, not against misinterpretation. The INCEPTION trial randomised 134 patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest to extracorporeal or conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) (18). At 30 days, 14 of 70 patients in the extracorporeal group (20%) and 10 of 62 in the conventional group (16%) had a favourable neurological outcome (OR 1.4, 95% CI 0.5 to 3.5; P = 0.52). The authors concluded that the two strategies had similar effects.
That conclusion confuses absence of evidence with evidence of absence (Section 1.4). A Bayesian reanalysis makes the point concrete. With independent, flat Beta(1, 1) priors on the probability of a good outcome in each arm, the posterior for each arm is also a beta distribution, so the posterior of the odds ratio can be simulated exactly in a few lines.


Code
set.seed(123)
n_draws <- 200000
p_conv  <- rbeta(n_draws, 1 + 10, 1 + 62 - 10)   # conventional CPR: 10/62
p_ecpr  <- rbeta(n_draws, 1 + 14, 1 + 70 - 14)   # extracorporeal CPR: 14/70
or_post <- (p_ecpr / (1 - p_ecpr)) / (p_conv / (1 - p_conv))

inception <- c(
  median    = median(or_post),
  lower95   = unname(quantile(or_post, 0.025)),
  upper95   = unname(quantile(or_post, 0.975)),
  p_benefit = mean(or_post > 1),                     # any benefit
  p_clin    = mean(or_post > 1.1),                   # clinically meaningful benefit
  p_equiv   = mean(or_post > 0.9 & or_post < 1.1))   # practical equivalence
round(inception, 2)


   median   lower95   upper95 p_benefit    p_clin   p_equiv 
     1.28      0.54      3.12      0.71      0.63      0.15 




Code
dens <- density(or_post, from = 0, to = 6, n = 2048)
dd   <- data.frame(x = dens$x, y = dens$y)
ggplot(dd, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(dd, x <= 0.9), fill = "#f4a6b0") +
  geom_area(data = subset(dd, x >= 1.1), fill = "#3fbfbf") +
  geom_line(colour = "grey20") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.9, 1.1)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 5)) +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio (extracorporeal vs conventional CPR)", y = "Density")








Figure 3.3: Posterior distribution of the odds ratio for a favourable outcome with extracorporeal versus conventional CPR in the INCEPTION trial (flat priors). The vertical lines bound a range of practical equivalence (0.9 to 1.1); the shaded areas show the probability of meaningful harm (left) and meaningful benefit (right).





The posterior median odds ratio is 1.28 (95% credible interval 0.54 to 3.12). The probability that extracorporeal CPR improves outcomes is 71%, and the probability of a clinically meaningful benefit (OR above 1.1) is 63%, whereas the probability that the two strategies are practically equivalent is only 15%. The data do not show “similar effects”; they show that the trial was too small to tell.
The same model can be fitted with brms, the interface to Stan used for Bayesian models throughout this book; Bayesian methods are developed fully in Chapter 13. With an identity link and no intercept, each coefficient is the probability of a good outcome in one arm, and the posterior draws reproduce the beta distributions above.


Code
library(brms)
d_inc <- data.frame(arm = factor(c("conventional", "extracorporeal")),
                    y = c(10, 14), n = c(62, 70))
fit_inc <- brm(y | trials(n) ~ 0 + arm, data = d_inc,
               family = binomial(link = "identity"),
               prior  = prior(beta(1, 1), class = b, lb = 0, ub = 1),
               seed = 123, refresh = 0)
draws <- as_draws_df(fit_inc)
p_c <- draws$b_armconventional; p_e <- draws$b_armextracorporeal
quantile((p_e / (1 - p_e)) / (p_c / (1 - p_c)), c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))


For a systematic reviewer the lesson is practical: extract the numbers, not the authors’ verbal conclusion. “No difference” in an abstract may describe a trial that is entirely compatible with an important benefit.

title: 3  From Question to Data
text:
3.4 Data extraction

3.4.1 What to extract, and who extracts it
Data extraction transfers information from the included studies into a structured form that allows synthesis (19). Four groups of items are extracted:

study characteristics: design, setting, country, dates, funding source and conflicts of interest;
participants: numbers randomised or enrolled, age, sex, disease severity, baseline risk;
interventions: drug, dose, duration, route, co-interventions, and the comparator;
outcomes: definition, timing, scale, and the data needed for the effect estimate and its precision (events and totals; means, SDs and numbers; or an estimate with its confidence interval).

Two reviewers extract independently and then reconcile. This is a methodological requirement, not a courtesy: transcription errors are common even among careful reviewers, ambiguous data are read differently by different people, and unconscious selective extraction is a form of bias. Disagreements are resolved by discussion, by returning to the paper and, if necessary, by a third reviewer. Report agreement for extraction as well as for screening (Section 2.5.4).


3.4.2 Designing the extraction form
The form is designed during the protocol stage, before the data are seen. It has one row per study (or per study and outcome); categorical items are pre-coded rather than left as free text; a notes field records ambiguities instead of resolving them silently. Pilot the form on three to five studies, revise it where reviewers disagree, and keep it under version control so that any later change is documented.
Purpose-built tools include Covidence, which integrates screening and extraction, and the free SRDR+ from the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, which allows extraction forms and data to be shared publicly. REDCap or a spreadsheet will do for a small review, with care. Whatever the tool, export the raw extraction data and keep them with the analysis: they are part of the reproducible record.
In R, an extraction form is naturally a schema defined once in the protocol and joined to a record for each study. Adding a study means adding a record; the schema and the code that displays it never change.


Code
# Fixed once, in the protocol
schema <- tribble(
  ~key,             ~Field,               ~Type,
  "study_id",       "Study ID",           "Text",

  "followup_mo",    "Follow-up (months)", "Numeric",

  "events_C",       "Events, control",      "Integer",

  "ci_hi",          "95% CI upper",       "Numeric",

)

  study_id = "EMPEROR-Reduced", first_author = "Packer", year = 2020,
  design = "RCT", n_rand = 3730, mean_age = "66.9 (10.8)", pct_female = 24,

3.4.3 Common extraction errors
Numerical errors include extracting an odds ratio when the paper reports a risk ratio; transcription errors (0.75 recorded as 0.57, which is more common than you think); swapping the bounds of a confidence interval; entering intervention data in the comparator columns; reading a value from a figure when the table gives it exactly; and mixing intention-to-treat and per-protocol results, which, as Section 3.1.3 explained, are different estimands.
Conceptual errors include taking adjusted estimates from some studies and unadjusted from others without a pre-specified rule; treating imputed data as observed; extracting one component (cardiovascular death) when the outcome was a composite (cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure); choosing, among many reported outcomes, the most significant one; and failing to notice that the published primary outcome differs from the registered one (Section 3.6.1).






Invisible in the forest plot



None of these errors is visible in the final meta-analysis. They are found only by returning to the source, which is why extraction is duplicated and the sheet is validated before analysis (Section 3.7.1).




3.4.4 Missing and ambiguous data
Missing data at extraction are the rule, not the exception. Standard deviations, unadjusted estimates, subgroup results, specific adverse event counts and even the duration of follow-up are often missing. Pre-specify how missing data will be handled; do not decide case by case during extraction.
First check the supplementary material, the trial register, the published protocol and other reports of the same trial. Then contact the authors, especially of recent trials, and document the attempt whatever the response. Some statistics can be recovered from others (Section 3.5.3). Finally, run sensitivity analyses with and without studies that lacked key data; if the conclusions change, the missing data matter. Missing data are developed further in Chapter 14.

title: 3  From Question to Data
text:
3.5 Effect measures: what to extract

3.5.1 Binary outcomes
The effect measure is part of the estimand and must be pre-specified (21). For binary outcomes the main options are summarised in Table 3.6; they are developed fully in Chapter 8.



Table 3.6: Effect measures for binary outcomes.










Measure
Definition
Properties




Risk ratio (RR)
\(p_I / p_C\)
Relative; intuitive


Odds ratio (OR)
\(\dfrac{p_I/(1-p_I)}{p_C/(1-p_C)}\)
Relative; used in logistic regression; exaggerates the RR when events are common


Risk difference (RD)
\(p_I - p_C\)
Absolute; most relevant to decisions


Number needed to treat (NNT)
\(1/\lvert RD \rvert\)
Absolute; depends on baseline risk and follow-up time


Hazard ratio (HR)
Ratio of instantaneous event rates
Time-to-event; summarises a possibly changing effect as one number






The choice matters. The RR and OR are similar for rare outcomes but diverge when events are common. Absolute effects depend on baseline risk: an RR of 0.75 means an NNT of 40 when the baseline risk is 10% but 400 when it is 1%. Extract both relative and absolute information where possible; if only a relative effect is reported, the control-arm risk lets you compute the absolute one.
Papers rarely report everything a meta-analysis needs, so it is worth computing the measures once from first principles. For EMPEROR-Reduced:


Code
events_I <- 361; n_I <- 1863   # empagliflozin
events_C <- 462; n_C <- 1867   # placebo

p_I <- events_I / n_I
p_C <- events_C / n_C
RR  <- p_I / p_C
OR  <- (p_I / (1 - p_I)) / (p_C / (1 - p_C))
RD  <- p_I - p_C

# Standard errors on the log scale, used by meta-analysis
se_log_RR <- sqrt(1/events_I - 1/n_I + 1/events_C - 1/n_C)
se_log_OR <- sqrt(1/events_I + 1/(n_I - events_I) + 1/events_C + 1/(n_C - events_C))
se_RD     <- sqrt(p_I * (1 - p_I) / n_I + p_C * (1 - p_C) / n_C)

ci <- function(est, se, log = TRUE) {
  if (log) exp(log(est) + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se) else est + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se
}
rbind(RR = c(RR, ci(RR, se_log_RR)),
      OR = c(OR, ci(OR, se_log_OR)),
      RD = c(RD, ci(RD, se_RD, log = FALSE))) |>
  round(3)


     [,1]   [,2]   [,3]
RR  0.783  0.693  0.884
OR  0.731  0.626  0.854
RD -0.054 -0.080 -0.027


The risk ratio is 0.78 and the odds ratio 0.73: with a control-arm risk of 25%, the two already differ noticeably. The risk difference of -5.4 percentage points corresponds to an NNT of about 19 over the trial’s 16 months.
Hand-written formulas are worth understanding, but they are also how sign and transcription errors enter an analysis. For routine work, a function that takes the raw counts and returns every measure with its confidence interval is safer. epiR::epi.2by2() does this:


Code
tab <- matrix(c(events_I, n_I - events_I,
                events_C, n_C - events_C),
              nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
              dimnames = list(Group = c("Empagliflozin", "Placebo"),
                              Outcome = c("Event", "No event")))
epiR::epi.2by2(as.table(tab), method = "cohort.count")

3.5.2 The number needed to treat
The NNT is popular because it incorporates baseline risk in a single, apparently intuitive number. Its calculation is not error-free. An NNT is the reciprocal of a difference in cumulative incidence over a stated period. When follow-up differs between patients, simple proportions of patients with an event, or incidence rates per patient-time, are not cumulative incidences, and the NNT derived from them can be badly misleading; Kaplan–Meier estimates at a fixed time are needed instead (22). Always report an NNT with its time horizon.
The NNT also frames results favourably. An NNT of 250 could equally be described as 249 patients treated needlessly for each one who benefits; that is, 99.6% of treated patients gain nothing from treatment (22).


3.5.3 Continuous outcomes
For continuous outcomes (blood pressure, a symptom score, lung function) extract the mean, standard deviation and number of participants in each arm, and the timing of the measurement. The mean difference is the natural effect measure when all studies use the same scale; the standardised mean difference (SMD), the difference divided by the pooled SD, is used when studies measure the same construct on different scales.
Papers often report a standard error, a confidence interval or a P value instead of the SD. The SD can then be recovered (21). Two situations must be distinguished.
A confidence interval for one group’s mean. The interval is the mean ± \(t \times SE\), and \(SD = SE \times \sqrt{n}\).
A confidence interval (or P value) for the difference between two groups. Now \(SE = SD_{pooled}\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}\), so \(SD_{pooled} = SE / \sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}\). Using \(\sqrt{n}\) here, a common mistake, gives the wrong answer.


Code
# (a) One arm reports its mean with a 95% CI: 24.1 (21.7 to 26.5), n = 60
n1 <- 60
se_arm <- (26.5 - 21.7) / (2 * qt(0.975, df = n1 - 1))
sd_arm <- se_arm * sqrt(n1)

# (b) A paper reports only the mean difference between arms, -5.0,
#     with 95% CI -8.5 to -1.5, and 60 participants per arm
n_I2 <- 60; n_C2 <- 60
df   <- n_I2 + n_C2 - 2
se_diff_ci <- (-1.5 - -8.5) / (2 * qt(0.975, df))
sd_pooled_ci <- se_diff_ci / sqrt(1/n_I2 + 1/n_C2)

# (c) ... or only the mean difference and its P value, P = 0.006
se_diff_p <- abs(-5.0) / qt(1 - 0.006/2, df)
sd_pooled_p <- se_diff_p / sqrt(1/n_I2 + 1/n_C2)

round(c(sd_one_arm = sd_arm,
        sd_pooled_from_ci = sd_pooled_ci,
        sd_pooled_from_p  = sd_pooled_p), 2)


       sd_one_arm sd_pooled_from_ci  sd_pooled_from_p 
             9.29              9.68              9.79 


The three recovered SDs are about 9.3, 9.7 and 9.8. Had the \(\sqrt{n}\) formula been misapplied to the difference in (b), the result would have been 19.4, wrong by a factor of two. Document every recovered value, and run a sensitivity analysis excluding studies that needed it.
Once each arm has a mean, SD and number, let metafor::escalc() compute the effect size and its variance, consistently, for every study in the sheet:


Code
cont_dat <- data.frame(
  study = "Example trial",
  m1i = 24.1, sd1i = sd_arm, n1i = 60,   # intervention arm (SD recovered above)
  m2i = 28.6, sd2i = 9.2,    n2i = 60)   # control arm (SD reported)

escalc(measure = "SMD",
       m1i = m1i, sd1i = sd1i, n1i = n1i,
       m2i = m2i, sd2i = sd2i, n2i = n2i,
       data = cont_dat)

title: 3  From Question to Data
text:
3.6 The same study, many reports
A single trial often generates many publications: the primary efficacy paper, secondary outcomes, long-term follow-up, subgroups, safety, cost-effectiveness, a protocol paper and several conference abstracts. EMPEROR-Reduced, for example, produced a primary paper in 2020 and further papers on renal outcomes, biomarkers and safety, all from the same 3730 participants. Treating these as separate studies double-counts participants and is one of the most consequential, and least recognised, errors in systematic reviews.
Reports are linked to studies by the trial registration number (the most reliable link), by overlapping authors and institutions, by identical or nested numbers of participants, by recruitment dates and sites, and by explicit cross-references to “companion papers”. At extraction, create one record per study, list every linked report, take each item from the most complete source, and record which report supplied each value.






One study, one row



Never enter data from two reports of the same study as separate rows of the extraction sheet.



3.6.1 Extraction as an audit of outcome reporting
Every extraction is also a comparison with the registered protocol. Open the register entry (ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN, the EU Clinical Trials Register) alongside the paper and compare the primary outcome, the secondary outcomes, the analysis population and the statistical analysis. Typical discrepancies are a primary outcome changed after randomisation, pre-specified secondary outcomes not reported, outcomes reported that were never registered, and an analysis population narrowed to exclude unfavourable participants. Such discrepancies are common in leading journals (23). They are direct evidence of selective reporting and are recorded in the risk-of-bias assessment (Chapter 5).


3.6.2 Living reviews and continuous extraction
A living systematic review is updated as new evidence appears rather than every few years (24). It needs automated search alerts, pre-specified triggers for an update (for example, any new trial with more than 500 participants), a version-controlled extraction form and pre-specified rules for adding new evidence to the analysis. Bayesian meta-analysis accommodates sequential updating naturally.
In a scripted review, an update is a short pipeline. The search function is the one built in Section 2.6.4; the file names stand for wherever your own project keeps its extraction sheet and analysis script.


Code
# 1. Search for records added since the last update
last_update <- as.Date(readLines("data/last_update.txt"))
new_records <- fetch_rcts(mesh_terms = "heart failure",
                          start = format(last_update, "%Y/%m/%d"),
                          end   = format(Sys.Date(), "%Y/%m/%d"))

# 2. Screen new records against the inclusion criteria (in duplicate)
# 3. Extract eligible studies (in duplicate) into new_extraction

# 4. Append to the existing extraction sheet, validate, and save
extraction <- bind_rows(read.csv("data/extraction.csv"), new_extraction)
validate_extraction(extraction)
write.csv(extraction, "data/extraction.csv", row.names = FALSE)
writeLines(format(Sys.Date()), "data/last_update.txt")

# 5. Rerun the analysis
source("analysis/meta_analysis.R")


Adding a study means rerunning one script, not rebuilding the analysis.

3.7 From extraction to synthesis
Everything downstream of extraction (forest plots, heterogeneity, subgroup analyses, certainty ratings) is only as good as the extracted data. Table 3.7 shows the extraction sheet for four large trials of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure: the primary composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure, as reported in each trial’s main publication (20,25–27).

  study    = c("EMPEROR-Reduced 2020", "DAPA-HF 2019",
               "EMPEROR-Preserved 2021", "DELIVER 2022"),
  events_I = c(361, 386, 415, 512),
  n_I      = c(1863, 2373, 2997, 3131),
  events_C = c(462, 502, 511, 610),

From here, escalc() computes log risk ratios and their variances, and rma() fits a random-effects model (Section 9.3). Figure 3.4 previews the result; forest plots are the subject of Chapter 4.


Code
sglt2_es <- escalc(measure = "RR",
                   ai = events_I, n1i = n_I, ci = events_C, n2i = n_C,
                   data = sglt2, slab = study)
res_sglt2 <- rma(yi, vi, data = sglt2_es, method = "REML")
forest(res_sglt2, atransf = exp, at = log(c(0.6, 0.8, 1, 1.25)),
       xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)", header = "Trial")








Figure 3.4: Random-effects meta-analysis of four SGLT2 inhibitor trials.





The pooled risk ratio is 0.80 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.85).

3.7.1 Validating the extraction sheet
Before any analysis, check that every included study has exactly one record; that effect measures are on a consistent scale; that outcome definitions and timing windows are compatible; that the pre-specified primary outcome was the one extracted; and that the missing-data strategy has been applied consistently. Then look for red flags that call for re-extraction: events exceeding totals, standard errors of zero or less, confidence intervals that exclude their own point estimate, implausibly large effects, and a direction of effect that contradicts the paper’s abstract.
Many of these checks can be automated. The function below checks four of them and should be run on the extraction sheet before every analysis.


Code
validate_extraction <- function(df) {
  issues <- list()
  # Events cannot exceed totals, or be negative
  bad_I <- with(df, events_I > n_I | events_I < 0)
  bad_C <- with(df, events_C > n_C | events_C < 0)
  if (any(bad_I, na.rm = TRUE)) issues$impossible_counts_I <- df$study[which(bad_I)]
  if (any(bad_C, na.rm = TRUE)) issues$impossible_counts_C <- df$study[which(bad_C)]
  # Log risk ratio and its standard error
  log_rr <- with(df, log((events_I / n_I) / (events_C / n_C)))
  se     <- with(df, sqrt(1/events_I - 1/n_I + 1/events_C - 1/n_C))
  if (any(!is.finite(se) | se <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))
    issues$invalid_se <- df$study[which(!is.finite(se) | se <= 0)]
  # Implausibly large effects (|log RR| > 3, i.e. RR < 0.05 or > 20)
  if (any(abs(log_rr) > 3, na.rm = TRUE))
    issues$large_effect <- df$study[which(abs(log_rr) > 3)]
  # Duplicate studies
  if (any(duplicated(df$study)))
    issues$duplicates <- df$study[duplicated(df$study)]

  if (length(issues) == 0) message("All checks passed.") else print(issues)
  invisible(issues)
}

validate_extraction(sglt2)


The real sheet passes. To see the function at work, introduce two typical errors: a duplicated row and a transposed number.


Code
broken <- rbind(sglt2, sglt2[2, ])        # DAPA-HF entered twice
broken$events_C[4] <- 6100                # 610 mistyped as 6100
validate_extraction(broken)


$impossible_counts_C
[1] "DELIVER 2022"

$duplicates
[1] "DAPA-HF 2019"


Writing such a function takes half an hour; finding the same errors after the analysis has been written up takes much longer.

title: 3  From Question to Data
text:
Key points

Inclusion criteria are the operational definition of the estimand; every ambiguity left to be resolved later is a researcher degree of freedom.
Time, and the strategy for intercurrent events, are part of the estimand: intention-to-treat and per-protocol results are not interchangeable.
The question type determines the eligible designs, the effect measures and the risk-of-bias tool.
In observational studies, check that eligibility, treatment assignment and time zero coincide; a claim of target trial emulation is a reason to check, not a guarantee.
Extract numbers, not conclusions: “no significant difference” is not evidence of no difference.
Extraction is done in duplicate, on a pre-specified, piloted form; disagreements are resolved, not averaged.
One study is one record; multiple reports are linked, and the trial register is used to audit outcome reporting.
Validate the extraction sheet in code before every analysis.

title: 3  From Question to Data
text:
Exercises

For the GLP-1 RA question in Section 3.1.1, write operational inclusion criteria that decide, in advance, whether SELECT and PIONEER 6 are eligible. Justify each decision in terms of the estimand.
Download the EMPEROR-Reduced paper (20) and its registration (NCT03057977). Extract the primary outcome into the form in Section 3.4.2, and note any discrepancies between the registered and published outcomes.
Using simulate_itb(), explore how the bias depends on the proportion of patients who ever start the drug (p_user) and on the landmark time (lm_time). When does the landmark analysis come closest to the truth, and why?
Rerun the INCEPTION analysis with the range of practical equivalence widened to 0.8–1.25. How do the probabilities change, and does your interpretation?
Add two checks to validate_extraction(): that the reported confidence interval contains the reported point estimate, and that the direction of the computed risk ratio agrees with the reported one.

title: 4  Visualising Evidence
text:
4.1 A pattern-recognition test
A meta-analysis is usually summarised by a single figure, the forest plot, and many readers look at nothing else. That makes visualisation a methodological step in its own right. A good figure shows the reader what the data can and cannot support; a poor one, or a misleading one, can persuade them of something the data do not show. This chapter starts with a figure of the second kind.
Figure 4.1 shows the association between a prenatal exposure to chemical X and eight neurodevelopmental outcomes in young children, each estimated as a log hazard ratio with its 95% confidence interval. The idea for the exercise comes from (1).
Code
n   <- 400                       # number of comparisons made
se  <- 1                         # standard error of each log(HR)
yi_all <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = se)   # true log(HR) = 0 for every comparison

# Show 8: the most extreme positive, the most extreme negative, and 6 others at random
idx_pos  <- which.max(yi_all)
idx_neg  <- which.min(yi_all)
idx_6    <- sample(setdiff(seq_len(n), c(idx_pos, idx_neg)), 6)
idx_pick <- c(idx_6[1:3], idx_pos, idx_neg, idx_6[4:6])

outcomes <- c("ADHD", "ASD composite", "Asperger syndrome", "Atypical autism",
              "Autistic disorder", "Developmental delay", "Language disorder",
              "Other PDD")
df <- tibble(
  outcome   = outcomes,
  yi        = yi_all[idx_pick],
  ci_lo     = yi - 1.96 * se,
  ci_hi     = yi + 1.96 * se,
  outcome_f = factor(outcome, levels = rev(outcomes)))
Code
df |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", yi, ci_lo, ci_hi)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = yi, y = outcome_f)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = ci_lo, xmax = ci_hi), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_text(aes(x = max(ci_hi) + 0.4, label = label), hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(min(df$ci_lo) - 0.5, max(df$ci_hi) + 3.5)) +
  labs(x = "log(hazard ratio)", y = NULL)








Figure 4.1: Association between exposure to chemical X and eight neurodevelopmental outcomes.
We return to this figure in Section 4.4. The code above already shows how it was made, so you may have guessed. Most readers who see only the figure do not.

title: 4  Visualising Evidence
text:
Before reading on, write down your answers




Is the exposure associated with the outcomes?
Which outcome has the strongest association?
How would you summarise the pattern?
Would you conclude that the exposure is harmful?

title: 4  Visualising Evidence
section: 4.2 Why visualisation is a methodological step
text:
4.2 Why visualisation is a methodological step
Before analysis, plots help you understand the evidence base: tables of study characteristics reveal clinical heterogeneity before any statistical test; scatter plots of effects against study characteristics suggest moderators; dot plots of the raw estimates show outliers and the shape of their distribution; plotting effects against publication year shows temporal trends; and risk-of-bias displays show patterns that affect interpretation. You should look at the data before fitting a single model.
After analysis, each standard plot encodes different information and has different blind spots. Forest plots communicate the individual and pooled estimates and the heterogeneity between them. Funnel plots examine small-study effects, including possible publication bias. Galbraith plots identify studies that contribute disproportionately to heterogeneity. L’Abbé plots show whether the effect depends on baseline risk. Summary-of-findings tables communicate certainty (Chapter 5). Knowing what each plot cannot show is as important as knowing what it can.
Good figures help readers understand concepts and data, emphasise the message, build trust and inform decisions. Poor figures do the opposite, and readers rightly discount the authors’ other work when a figure is careless or misleading.

title: 4  Visualising Evidence
text:
4.3 Building forest plots
Three R tools draw forest plots: ggplot2, which gives complete control; metafor, the most comprehensive meta-analysis package; and meta, which has the most accessible syntax for clinicians. Figure 4.1 was drawn with ggplot2. To compare the three on a real meta-analysis we use a classic data set, distributed with metafor: 13 trials of BCG vaccine against tuberculosis (2).


Code
bcg <- escalc(measure = "RR",
              ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg,
              data = dat.bcg,
              slab = paste(author, year))
# Fitting from the raw counts (rather than yi and vi) keeps the arm-level
# data in the model object, which labbe() needs later
res_bcg <- rma(measure = "RR", ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg,
               data = dat.bcg, slab = paste(author, year), method = "REML")



4.3.1 ggplot2
ggplot2 needs more code, but every element can be changed. The pooled diamond must be drawn as a polygon from the model’s estimate and confidence limits. Here studies whose confidence interval excludes 1 are highlighted, and the dotted line below the diamond shows the 95% prediction interval, the range in which the effect in a new study is expected to lie (Section 9.4.1).


Code
pred <- predict(res_bcg)
k    <- nrow(bcg)
plot_df <- data.frame(study = attr(bcg$yi, "slab"),
                      yi = bcg$yi, se = sqrt(bcg$vi)) |>
  mutate(lo = yi - 1.96 * se, hi = yi + 1.96 * se,
         sig = hi < 0 | lo > 0,
         row = rev(seq_len(k)) + 1)          # leave rows 0-1 for the summary

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = yi, y = row)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, colour = sig)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = sig, size = 1 / se^2), shape = 15) +
  annotate("polygon",
           x = c(pred$ci.lb, pred$pred, pred$ci.ub, pred$pred),
           y = c(0.5, 0.85, 0.5, 0.15), fill = "#041E42") +
  annotate("segment", x = pred$pi.lb, xend = pred$pi.ub, y = 0.5, yend = 0.5,
           linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey40", `TRUE` = "#C8102E"),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 5), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(plot_df$row, 0.5),
                     labels = c(plot_df$study, "Random-effects pooled")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = log(c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)),
                     labels = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())








Figure 4.2: Forest plot of the BCG trials drawn with ggplot2. Red: confidence interval excludes no effect. Dotted line: 95% prediction interval.





Use ggplot2 when you need a non-standard forest plot: coloured by risk of bias, split into subgroups, or combined with other panels. The price is more code, and the geometry of the diamond and any text columns must be built by hand.


4.3.2 metafor
metafor::forest() takes the fitted model and adds weights, the confidence intervals, the diamond and, optionally, the prediction interval automatically.


Code
forest(res_bcg, atransf = exp, at = log(c(0.05, 0.25, 1, 4)),
       showweights = TRUE, addpred = TRUE,
       xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)", header = "Trial")








Figure 4.3: The same meta-analysis drawn by metafor.





metafor computes effect sizes (escalc()), supports subgroup headings and prediction intervals, and produces a layout reviewers recognise. Its plots are base R graphics, so they are less flexible than ggplot2 and cannot be combined with ggplot2 panels. It is the natural choice when metafor is already being used for the analysis.


4.3.3 meta
meta (3) fits the model and draws the plot from the raw counts in two short calls.


Code
library(meta)
m_bcg <- metabin(event.e = tpos, n.e = tpos + tneg,
                 event.c = cpos, n.c = cpos + cneg,
                 studlab = paste(author, year), data = dat.bcg,
                 sm = "RR", method.tau = "REML",
                 common = FALSE, random = TRUE, prediction = TRUE)
forest(m_bcg)








Figure 4.4: The same meta-analysis drawn by meta.





meta has good defaults for binary and continuous outcomes and functions such as metabind() for displaying several analyses together, at the cost of less fine control.



Table 4.1: Which package to use for forest plots.









Situation
Package




Custom layout, publication figure, combined panels
ggplot2


Standard meta-analysis with heterogeneity statistics and prediction intervals
metafor


Quick analysis, teaching, shorthand for common outcomes
meta


Network meta-analysis
netmeta (Chapters 17–18)


Bayesian meta-analysis
brms, bayesmeta (Chapter 13)






All three appear in this book. Being able to read and adapt code written with any of them is more useful than mastering only one.

title: 4  Visualising Evidence
text:
4.4 What forest plots hide

4.4.1 The reveal
Every one of the 400 effects simulated in Section 4.1 was generated under the null hypothesis: the true log hazard ratio was zero for every comparison. The eight in Figure 4.1 were chosen after seeing the results. Rows 4 and 5 are the most extreme effects in either direction; the other six were picked at random from the remaining 398 (Figure 4.5). The striking pattern is entirely noise, produced by selective presentation.


Code
tibble(yi = yi_all, picked = seq_len(n) %in% idx_pick) |>
  mutate(jitter = runif(n, -0.1, 0.1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = yi, y = jitter, colour = picked)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "#C8102E"),
                      labels = c("Not shown", "Shown in the forest plot"),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "log(hazard ratio)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 4.5: All 400 simulated log hazard ratios. Every true effect is zero; red points are the eight shown in the forest plot.











What is not shown matters



This is what selective outcome reporting and publication bias look like from the inside. A compelling forest plot can be built entirely from null effects. Always ask what was measured but not shown.




4.4.2 Expected extremes: Blom’s formula
How large should the most extreme of 400 null estimates be? Let \(Z_1, \dots, Z_n\) be independent standard normal variables, and sort them; \(Z_{(k)}\) is the \(k\)-th smallest. Its expected value is well approximated by Blom’s formula (4):
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[Z_{(k)}\right] \approx \Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{k - 0.375}{n + 0.25}\right),
\]
a small correction to the naive plotting position \(k/n\) that matters most at the extremes. For the maximum of \(n = 400\) values, \(k = n\):


Code
blom_max <- qnorm((n - 0.375) / (n + 0.25))
blom     <- qnorm((seq_len(n) - 0.375) / (n + 0.25))   # every order statistic
blom_max


[1] 2.95536


Because our simulated log hazard ratios have standard error 1, they are on the z scale, and the expected largest log hazard ratio is about 2.96: a hazard ratio of about 19, produced entirely by chance.


4.4.3 Checking by simulation
The maximum is itself a random variable, with a right-skewed sampling distribution. Simulation shows both its mean and its range.


Code
maxima <- replicate(5000, max(rnorm(n)))
mc <- c(mean = mean(maxima), quantile(maxima, c(0.025, 0.975)))
round(mc, 2)


 mean  2.5% 97.5% 
 2.97  2.35  3.86 




Code
ggplot(data.frame(maxima), aes(maxima)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60,
                 fill = "grey80", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mc[2:3], linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = blom_max, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#C8102E", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Largest z value in each simulation", y = "Density")








Figure 4.6: Distribution of the largest of 400 standard normal values, in 5000 simulations. Red dashed line: Blom’s approximation. Dotted lines: empirical 95% range.





The simulated mean, 2.97, agrees closely with Blom’s 2.96, and in 95% of simulations the largest value lay between 2.35 and 3.86.
Blom’s formula is also the basis of the normal Q–Q plot. If the 400 simulated values really are independent draws from a standard normal distribution, their sorted values should lie along the line of identity when plotted against the Blom-expected order statistics (Figure 4.7). A systematic departure would indicate an error in the simulation.


Code
ggplot(tibble(expected = blom, observed = sort(yi_all)),
       aes(expected, observed)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.9, alpha = 0.6, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "#C8102E") +
  labs(x = "Blom-expected normal order statistic", y = "Observed log(HR)")








Figure 4.7: Normal Q–Q plot: the sorted simulated values against the Blom-expected order statistics.











Key point



Whenever a paper reports results for many outcomes, subgroups, time points or tests, the largest apparent effect is expected to be large, whatever the true effects. Pre-specifying primary outcomes, and correcting for multiple comparisons, are methodological requirements, not optional refinements.

title: 4  Visualising Evidence
text:
4.5 Multiple comparisons

4.5.1 The family-wise error rate
If \(m\) independent hypotheses, all truly null, are each tested at \(\alpha = 0.05\), the probability of at least one false-positive result, the family-wise error rate (FWER), is
\[
P(\text{at least one false positive}) = 1 - (1 - 0.05)^m .
\]


Code
m <- c(1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 400)
kable(data.frame(m = m, fwer = 1 - 0.95^m), digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Tests (m)", "P(at least one false positive)"))




Table 4.2: Probability of at least one false-positive result among m independent tests of true null hypotheses.






Tests (m)
P(at least one false positive)




1
0.05


5
0.23


10
0.40


20
0.64


50
0.92


400
1.00








With 400 tests we expect 20 false-positive results at \(\alpha = 0.05\).


4.5.2 Corrections
Base R’s p.adjust() implements the common corrections. We apply three of them to the 400 null comparisons.


Code
pvals <- tibble(z = yi_all / se,
                p = 2 * pnorm(abs(z), lower.tail = FALSE)) |>
  mutate(Bonferroni = p.adjust(p, "bonferroni"),
         Holm       = p.adjust(p, "holm"),
         BH         = p.adjust(p, "BH"))

n_sig <- pvals |>
  summarise(Uncorrected = sum(p < 0.05),
            Bonferroni  = sum(Bonferroni < 0.05),
            Holm        = sum(Holm < 0.05),
            `Benjamini-Hochberg` = sum(BH < 0.05))
kable(pivot_longer(n_sig, everything(), names_to = "Method",
                   values_to = "Significant (of 400)"))





Method
Significant (of 400)




Uncorrected
22


Bonferroni
0


Holm
0


Benjamini-Hochberg
0





Without correction, 22 of the 400 null comparisons are “significant”, close to the 20 expected; every one is a false positive. All three corrections remove them in this example.
The corrections control different error rates:

Bonferroni tests each hypothesis at \(\alpha/m\) (here 0.05/400 = 0.000125). It controls the FWER and is very conservative.
Holm’s step-down method orders the P values from smallest to largest and rejects \(p_{(i)}\) while \(p_{(i)} < \alpha/(m - i + 1)\), stopping at the first that fails (5). It also controls the FWER and is uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni.
Benjamini–Hochberg finds the largest \(i\) with \(p_{(i)} \le (i/m)\,\alpha\) and rejects \(p_{(1)}, \dots, p_{(i)}\) (6). It controls the false discovery rate, the expected proportion of false positives among the results declared positive. It is much more powerful, accepting some false positives in exchange for more true discoveries.

FWER control suits a single pre-specified primary outcome, where even one false positive is costly. FDR control suits many exploratory secondary or subgroup outcomes, where findings will be replicated before anyone acts on them. In a systematic review, both choices must be pre-specified.


Code
pvals |>
  arrange(p) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  select(rank, Uncorrected = p, `Benjamini-Hochberg` = BH, Holm, Bonferroni) |>
  pivot_longer(-rank, names_to = "method", values_to = "adj_p") |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, c("Uncorrected", "Benjamini-Hochberg",
                                   "Holm", "Bonferroni"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(rank, adj_p, colour = method, linetype = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1", name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid", "solid", "22"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Rank (smallest to largest P value)", y = "Adjusted P value (log scale)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 4.8: Adjusted P values against rank for the 400 null comparisons. With so many tests, Bonferroni and Holm adjusted values reach 1 for almost every rank and their lines coincide. Dashed line: 0.05.

title: 4  Visualising Evidence
text:
4.6 Funnel plots
A funnel plot shows each study’s effect estimate against a measure of its precision, usually the standard error, with the axis inverted so that large studies are at the top. In the absence of bias, small studies scatter widely and large studies narrowly around the true effect, forming a symmetrical inverted funnel; the pseudo-confidence limits mark where 95% of studies should fall. Publication bias, and the other causes of small-study effects, are examined in detail in Chapter 15. Here we concentrate on building and reading the plots.
To see what bias looks like, we simulate 30 studies of an intervention with a true log risk ratio of −0.25, then “lose” the small studies (standard error above 0.25) that happened to show harm, as if they had never been published.


Code
set.seed(42)
n_studies <- 30
se_s  <- runif(n_studies, 0.05, 0.5)
eff_s <- rnorm(n_studies, mean = -0.25, sd = se_s)
published <- !(eff_s > 0 & se_s > 0.25)        # small studies showing harm vanish
df_funnel <- tibble(yi = eff_s[published], sei = se_s[published])

res_f <- rma(yi, sei = sei, data = df_funnel, method = "REML")
egger <- regtest(res_f, model = "lm")
begg  <- ranktest(res_f)




Code
funnel(res_f, xlab = "log(risk ratio)", back = "grey95")








Figure 4.9: Funnel plot of the published studies. Small studies with unfavourable results are missing from the lower right.





Of the 30 studies, 24 were “published”, and the gap in the lower right of Figure 4.9 is visible. Two tests formalise the impression. Egger’s test regresses the standardised effect on precision (7); here it gives P = 0.001. Begg’s test uses the rank correlation between effects and their variances (8); here P = 0.013. Both tests have low power when there are fewer than 10 to 15 studies, which is the usual situation in practice, so a non-significant result is weak reassurance, and visual inspection and knowledge of the field are always needed (9). Exercise 3 explores how quickly the tests lose their power as studies are removed.
Asymmetry has several causes besides publication bias:

publication bias: small studies with unfavourable results are not published;
true heterogeneity: small studies are done in different populations or settings, where the effect really differs;
selective outcome reporting within studies;
poorer methodological quality, and so exaggerated effects, in small studies;
chance, especially when there are few studies.







Asymmetry is not proof of publication bias



A funnel plot shows that small studies differ from large ones. It does not say why.



4.6.1 Contour-enhanced funnel plots
Shading the regions of conventional statistical significance helps distinguish the explanations (9). If the missing studies would have fallen in the region of non-significance, publication bias is plausible; if they would have fallen in regions of significance, other explanations are more likely.


Code
funnel(res_f, level = c(90, 95, 99), shade = c("white", "grey75", "grey55"),
       refline = 0, legend = TRUE, xlab = "log(risk ratio)")








Figure 4.10: Contour-enhanced funnel plot. Studies in the white region are not statistically significant (P > 0.10).







4.6.2 Trim and fill
The trim-and-fill method (10) removes the most extreme small studies from the crowded side of the funnel until it is symmetrical, counts how many it removed, then adds back that many mirror-image “missing” studies on the sparse side and re-estimates the pooled effect.


Code
tf <- trimfill(res_f)




Code
funnel(tf, xlab = "log(risk ratio)", back = "grey95")








Figure 4.11: Trim and fill. Open circles are imputed studies, not data.





Trim and fill imputed 8 studies and moved the pooled risk ratio from 0.70 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.77) to 0.76 (0.67 to 0.87), compared with the true value of 0.78.






A sensitivity analysis, not a correction



The imputed studies are assumptions, not data. Trim and fill gives an adjusted estimate under one particular model of why studies are missing. Report it as a sensitivity analysis, alongside, never instead of, the unadjusted estimate.

title: 4  Visualising Evidence
text:
4.7 Other essential plots

4.7.1 L’Abbé plots
A L’Abbé plot shows the event rate in the treatment arm of each trial against the rate in its control arm (11). Points below the diagonal favour treatment; points on it show no effect. If the risk ratio is constant, the points scatter around a straight line through the origin whose slope is the risk ratio. If the points bow away from that line, the treatment effect depends on baseline risk.


Code
labbe(res_bcg, transf = exp, xlab = "Risk in control arm",
      ylab = "Risk in vaccine arm")








Figure 4.12: L’Abbé plot of the BCG trials. Point area is proportional to trial size. Dashed line: no effect. Solid line: the pooled random-effects risk ratio.





In Figure 4.12 the trials with the highest control-group risks lie well below the diagonal, whereas several trials with low baseline risk lie close to it. Baseline risk in these trials is closely tied to latitude, the best-known moderator of BCG’s effect (2). A single pooled risk ratio describes these trials poorly, which the forest plots also suggested through the wide prediction interval.






Key point



L’Abbé plots are underused. They reveal clinically important effect modification by baseline risk that a single heterogeneity statistic such as \(I^2\) cannot show.




4.7.2 Galbraith (radial) plots
A Galbraith plot shows each study’s standardised effect (\(\hat\theta_i / SE_i\), a z score) against its precision (\(1/SE_i\)) (12). The slope of the line through the origin is the common-effect (fixed-effect) pooled estimate, and studies outside the 95% bounds around it are those that contribute most to heterogeneity. Because the plot asks which studies are inconsistent with a single common effect, it is drawn from a common-effect model.


Code
res_bcg_ce <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg, method = "EE")   # common-effect model
radial(res_bcg_ce)








Figure 4.13: Galbraith (radial) plot of the BCG trials.







Code
z_resid <- rstandard(res_bcg_ce)$z
outside <- attr(bcg$yi, "slab")[abs(z_resid) > 1.96]


The BCG trials are strongly heterogeneous (\(I^2\) = 92%), and 6 of the 13 trials (Ferguson & Simes 1949; Hart & Sutherland 1977; Stein & Aronson 1953; Vandiviere et al 1973; TPT Madras 1980; Rosenthal et al 1961) have standardised residuals beyond ±1.96. These are the trials whose methods and populations deserve the closest inspection. By contrast, a Galbraith plot of the four SGLT2 inhibitor trials of Section 3.7, which show almost no heterogeneity, has every trial close to the central line: a plot with nothing unusual to report is informative too.






Outliers that forest plots hide



A study can be an outlier on the Galbraith plot without standing out on the forest plot, because large, precise studies with modest deviations are visually unremarkable among wide confidence intervals.




4.7.3 Risk-of-bias plots
The robvis package (13) draws the two standard risk-of-bias displays from a data frame with one row per study and one column per domain: the “traffic light” plot of individual judgements and a summary bar chart. It includes example data for RoB 2 (randomised trials) and ROBINS-I (non-randomised studies); the tools themselves are covered in Chapter 5.


Code
library(robvis)
rob_traffic_light(data_rob2[1:5, ], tool = "ROB2")








Figure 4.14: Traffic-light plot of RoB 2 judgements for five example trials.







Code
rob_summary(data_rob2, tool = "ROB2")








Figure 4.15: Summary of RoB 2 judgements across the example trials.





If the extraction sheet stores risk-of-bias judgements in this format from the start, the figure is a single function call.

title: 4  Visualising Evidence
text:
Key points

Visualisation is a methodological step: look at the data before modelling, not only after.
A compelling forest plot can be built entirely from null effects. Always ask what was not shown.
When many outcomes or subgroups are examined, large apparent effects are expected; pre-specify primary outcomes and correct for multiplicity, using FWER control for confirmatory and FDR control for exploratory questions.
Funnel asymmetry has many causes; do not equate it with publication bias, and treat trim and fill as a sensitivity analysis.
L’Abbé and Galbraith plots reveal effect modification and influential studies that forest plots and \(I^2\) conceal.
Choose the tool to suit the figure: ggplot2 for control, metafor for standard output, meta for speed.

title: 4  Visualising Evidence
text:
Exercises

Repeat the simulation in Section 4.1 with 200 null effects, select the five most extreme, and draw a forest plot. What would a reader conclude without knowing how the five were chosen?
Using Blom’s formula, how large would you expect the largest of 20 null z statistics to be? Of 10 000? Check your answers by simulation.
Rerun the funnel plot simulation with n_studies <- 12. How often, over repeated simulations, do Egger’s and Begg’s tests detect the asymmetry that was built in? Then change the simulation so that all small studies with \(P > 0.05\) go unpublished: how do the funnel plot and trim and fill change?
Add absolute latitude (ablat) to the BCG data as a moderator with rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = bcg). How much of the heterogeneity does it explain? Relate your answer to Figure 4.12.
Redraw Figure 4.2 with the trials ordered by latitude and coloured by the allocation method (alloc).

title: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE
text:
5.1 Bias and imprecision
Chapters 2 to 4 dealt with finding, selecting and displaying the evidence. Before the evidence is combined, each study must be appraised: how far can its result be trusted? This chapter introduces the tools for appraising individual studies (risk-of-bias assessment) and the framework for rating a whole body of evidence (GRADE). Chapter 6 applies GRADE domain by domain.
A study’s estimate can be wrong for two reasons. Imprecision, or random error, makes estimates scatter around the truth; it shrinks as studies grow and is quantified by the standard error and confidence interval. Bias, or systematic error, makes estimates deviate from the truth in a consistent direction. Bias arises from flaws in a study’s design, conduct, analysis or reporting, and more data do not remove it: they only narrow the confidence interval around the wrong value (2).
The two are independent. A large trial can be precise and seriously biased; a small one can be imprecise but unbiased. This matters for synthesis: pooling biased studies in a meta-analysis produces an estimate that is precise but wrong.
Assessments of bias are expressed in words — “low”, “some concerns”, “high” — and words are slippery. People attach very different probabilities to phrases such as “likely”, “a realistic possibility” or “little chance”. In an online survey, more than 5000 respondents assigned a percentage to each of 19 such phrases (1). Figure 5.1 summarises their answers.
Code
phrases <- readr::read_csv("data/ch05/absolute_judgements.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

phrase_summary <- phrases |>
  group_by(term) |>
  summarise(q10 = quantile(probability, 0.10), q25 = quantile(probability, 0.25),
            median = median(probability),
            q75 = quantile(probability, 0.75), q90 = quantile(probability, 0.90)) |>
  mutate(iqr = q75 - q25) |>
  arrange(median, q25) |>
  mutate(term = factor(term, levels = term))

ggplot(phrase_summary, aes(y = term)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = q10, xmax = q90), linewidth = 3, colour = "grey85") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = q25, xmax = q75, colour = iqr), linewidth = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = median), shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#2C4A7E", high = "#C8102E",
                        name = "Interquartile range (percentage points)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 20), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Probability assigned", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 5.1: Probability assigned to 19 verbal phrases by more than 5000 respondents: median (circle), interquartile range (coloured bar, darker red for wider ranges) and 10th to 90th percentiles (grey). Adapted from J. Lopes’ TidyTuesday visualisation ‘The Scale of Chaos’ (3); data from the CAPphrase dataset (1).
Half of respondents placed “realistic possibility” somewhere between 40% and 75%, and “might happen”, “may happen” and “could happen” were almost as diffuse. Risk-of-bias tools address this partly by fixing the categories and the rules for reaching them, but each judgement should still be accompanied by its reasons.
