title: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE
text:
Precisely wrong



A meta-analysis of biased trials is not high-quality evidence. It is a precise estimate of a biased quantity.
crumbs: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE

title: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE
text:
5.2 Where bias enters a trial
Bias can enter at each stage of a randomised trial:

Design. Inadequate generation of the random sequence or concealment of allocation lets investigators influence who receives which treatment, producing groups that differ at baseline (selection bias).
Conduct. If participants or personnel know the allocation, they may behave differently, for example by adding co-interventions (performance bias). If outcome assessors know it, they may measure or classify outcomes differently (detection bias). Losses to follow-up that differ between groups, or are related to the outcome, break the comparability created by randomisation (attrition bias).
Analysis. Analysing participants other than as randomised, choosing among several analyses after seeing the data, or using an analysis vulnerable to chance baseline imbalance (Section 5.6.1).
Reporting. Reporting only some outcomes or analyses, or not publishing at all, depending on the results (Section 5.4).

Figure 5.2 summarises these entry points and the tools that address each.


Code
stages <- tibble::tibble(
  x     = 1:4,
  stage = c("Design", "Conduct", "Analysis", "Reporting"),
  what  = c("sequence generation\nallocation concealment",
            "blinding, co-interventions\nlosses to follow-up",
            "not as randomised\nchoice among analyses",
            "selective outcomes\nnon-publication"),
  tool  = c("RoB 2 domain 1", "RoB 2 domains 2-4",
            "RoB 2 domains 2 and 5", "RoB 2 domain 5; ROB-ME;\nregisters, funnel plots"))
ggplot(stages) +
  geom_tile(aes(x, 2, fill = stage), width = 0.92, height = 0.9, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(x, 2.25, label = stage), colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  geom_text(aes(x, 1.85, label = what), colour = "white", size = 3.3, lineheight = 0.9) +
  geom_text(aes(x, 1.38, label = tool), size = 3.3, lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1:3 + 0.47, xend = 1:3 + 0.53, y = 2, yend = 2,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#041E42", "#2C4A7E", "#5B7DB1", "#C8102E")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1.2, 2.5)) +
  theme_void()








Figure 5.2: Where bias enters a trial, and the main tools that detect it.





Other recognised sources are stopping a trial early for benefit, which selects an extreme interim result; multiple testing without pre-specification (“p-hacking”) and hypothesising after the results are known; and conflicts of interest, which can operate through any of the mechanisms above.






Poor reporting is not the same as poor conduct



A well-conducted trial may be poorly reported, and a well-reported trial may have been badly conducted. Where a report is silent, look for the protocol, the register entry and, if necessary, ask the authors before judging.
crumbs: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE

title: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE
text:
5.3 Empirical evidence that bias matters
Meta-epidemiological studies compare trials with and without a given methodological flaw within the same meta-analyses, so that differences in clinical question do not explain the results. The result is a ratio of odds ratios (ROR): the odds ratio in flawed trials divided by that in sound trials. For outcomes coded so that an odds ratio below 1 favours the intervention, a ratio below 1 means that flawed trials show more benefit.
The first large study of this kind examined 250 trials from 33 meta-analyses in pregnancy and childbirth (4). Trials with inadequate allocation concealment had odds ratios 41% lower, that is, more beneficial, than adequately concealed trials (ROR 0.59), and trials that were not double blind 17% lower (ROR 0.83). Later and larger studies found smaller average biases but confirmed the direction, and showed that the bias is concentrated in trials with subjectively assessed outcomes (5,6). Combining seven meta-epidemiological studies (1973 trials in 234 meta-analyses), (6) estimated RORs of 0.89 for inadequate or unclear sequence generation, 0.93 for allocation concealment and 0.87 for lack of double blinding. Figure 5.3 shows these estimates together.


Code
meta_epi <- tibble::tribble(
  ~source,                ~flaw,                                        ~ror, ~lo,  ~hi,
  "Schulz 1995",          "Allocation concealment inadequate",          0.59, 0.48, 0.73,
  "Schulz 1995",          "Allocation concealment unclear",             0.67, 0.60, 0.75,
  "Schulz 1995",          "Not double blind",                           0.83, 0.71, 0.96,
  "Wood 2008",            "Concealment inadequate/unclear: subjective", 0.69, 0.59, 0.82,
  "Wood 2008",            "Concealment inadequate/unclear: objective",  0.91, 0.80, 1.03,
  "Wood 2008",            "No blinding: subjective outcomes",           0.75, 0.61, 0.93,
  "Wood 2008",            "No blinding: objective outcomes",            1.01, 0.92, 1.10,
  "Savovi\u0107 2012",    "Sequence generation inadequate/unclear",     0.89, 0.82, 0.96,
  "Savovi\u0107 2012",    "Concealment inadequate/unclear",             0.93, 0.87, 0.99,
  "Savovi\u0107 2012",    "Lack of double blinding",                    0.87, 0.79, 0.96) |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, unique(source)),
         flaw = factor(flaw, rev(unique(flaw))))

ggplot(meta_epi, aes(ror, flaw)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), colour = "#041E42") +
  facet_grid(source ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1, 1.1)) +
  labs(x = "Ratio of odds ratios (log scale): < 1 = flawed trials show more benefit", y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0))








Figure 5.3: Ratios of odds ratios comparing trials with and without each flaw, from three meta-epidemiological studies. Values below 1 mean that flawed trials report more benefit. Data from (4) (adapted from its Table 2), (5) and (6) (95% credible intervals).





Two other sources of bias are well documented.
Funding. In a systematic review of 30 studies, industry-sponsored research was about four times as likely as other research to report outcomes favourable to the sponsor (odds ratio 4.05, 95% CI 2.98 to 5.51) (7). A later Cochrane methodology review of 75 papers estimated more modest but consistent associations, expressed as risk ratios: favourable efficacy results 1.27 (1.17 to 1.37) and favourable conclusions 1.34 (1.19 to 1.51), with no clear difference for harms (8) (Figure 5.4). Notably, industry-sponsored studies were not at higher risk of bias on the standard domains, so the usual tools do not capture this influence. Many mechanisms can contribute without any dishonesty: choice of comparator and dose, selection of outcomes and patients, selective publication, framing (“spin”) and stopping early.


Code
sponsor <- tibble::tribble(
  ~label,                                                ~est, ~lo,  ~hi,
  "Lexchin 2003: outcome favours sponsor (OR)",          4.05, 2.98, 5.51,
  "Lundh 2017: favourable efficacy results (RR)",        1.27, 1.17, 1.37,
  "Lundh 2017: favourable conclusions (RR)",             1.34, 1.19, 1.51,
  "Lundh 2017: favourable harms results (RR)",           1.37, 0.64, 2.93) |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, rev(label)))
ggplot(sponsor, aes(est, label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), colour = "#C8102E") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", est, lo, hi)), x = log10(7),
            hjust = 0, size = 3.3) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4), limits = c(0.5, 16)) +
  labs(x = "Industry vs other sponsorship (log scale)", y = NULL)








Figure 5.4: Association between industry sponsorship and favourable results. Data from (7) (odds ratio) and (8) (risk ratios); the two measures are not directly comparable.





Stopping early for benefit. Comparing 91 trials stopped early for benefit with 424 trials of the same questions that were not, (9) found a pooled ratio of relative risks of 0.71 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.77): stopped trials reported effects roughly 30% more extreme. The difference was largest when fewer than 500 events had accrued, and it was present whether or not a formal stopping rule had been used. The mechanism is selection. A trial is stopped when an interim estimate crosses a boundary, and interim estimates cross it most easily when chance has pushed them towards benefit. A simulation reproduces the pattern (Figure 5.5).


Code
# Normal approximation on the log RR scale: with D events, var(log RR) is about 4 / D
one_sequential_trial <- function(true_rr = 0.8, looks = seq(50, 1000, by = 50),
                                 z_stop = -2.96) {
  info  <- looks / 4                                   # statistical information
  inc   <- rnorm(length(looks), log(true_rr) * diff(c(0, info)), sqrt(diff(c(0, info))))
  score <- cumsum(inc)
  z     <- score / sqrt(info)
  k     <- which(z < z_stop)[1]                       # first look crossing the boundary
  stopped <- !is.na(k)
  if (!stopped) k <- length(looks)
  c(events = looks[k], stopped = stopped, rr_hat = exp(score[k] / info[k]))
}
set.seed(2010)
seq_trials <- as.data.frame(t(replicate(5000, one_sequential_trial()))) |>
  mutate(ratio = rr_hat / 0.8,
         group = case_when(!stopped ~ "Ran to 1000 events",
                           events < 200 ~ "Stopped, < 200 events",
                           events < 500 ~ "Stopped, 200-499 events",
                           TRUE ~ "Stopped, 500+ events"),
         group = factor(group, c("Stopped, < 200 events", "Stopped, 200-499 events",
                                 "Stopped, 500+ events", "Ran to 1000 events")))

ggplot(seq_trials, aes(group, ratio)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 0.65, ymax = 0.77,
           fill = "#C8102E", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2, fill = "#B9C6DE") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimated / true relative risk (log scale)")








Figure 5.5: Simulated trials with a true relative risk of 0.80, analysed after every 50 events and stopped for benefit if Z < -2.96 (two-sided P < 0.003), with a maximum of 1000 events. Each box shows the ratio of the estimated to the true relative risk. The shaded band is the pooled ratio (95% CI) reported by (9) for truncated trials.







Code
early_gm <- seq_trials |> group_by(group) |>
  summarise(n = n(), geo_mean_ratio = exp(mean(log(ratio))))
early_gm |> kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("", "Trials", "Geometric mean ratio"))

Trials stopped with fewer than 200 events overestimated the benefit by about 36% on average, close to the empirical estimate, while trials stopped late were nearly unbiased. Note that every trial in the simulation was impeccably randomised and blinded: the bias is produced by the stopping decision alone. Trials that continue to their planned end are slightly less favourable than the truth, because the most favourable sequences were removed by stopping; pooled with weights proportional to their information, as a fixed-effect meta-analysis does, all 5000 simulated trials give a ratio of 0.999. This is one reason not to exclude stopped trials from a meta-analysis, but to check whether they dominate it.






Key point



Flaws in design and conduct exaggerate treatment effects on average, especially for subjective outcomes. Risk-of-bias assessment is therefore not a formality: it identifies the studies whose results are most likely to be inflated.

title: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE
text:
5.4 Non-reporting biases
A second layer of bias acts before any study is appraised: the selective availability of results. Table 5.1 summarises the main types (10).



Table 5.1: Non-reporting biases.










Bias
Definition
Main defences




Publication bias
Whether results are published depends on their direction or significance
Trial registers; funnel plots (Section 4.6)


Time-lag bias
Favourable results are published sooner
Trial registers with dates; updating searches


Language bias
Favourable results are more likely to appear in English-language journals
Searching without language restrictions


Citation bias
Favourable studies are cited more often, and so found more easily
Systematic database searching, not citation chasing alone


Multiple publication bias
Favourable results are published more than once
Linking reports to studies by registration number (Section 3.6)


Location bias
Favourable results appear in more accessible, better-indexed journals
Searching several databases and the grey literature


Selective outcome reporting
Within a published study, only favourable outcomes or analyses are reported
Comparing paper with register and protocol (Section 3.6.1)






These biases distort the evidence base independently of how well the included studies were conducted. Comprehensive searching (Chapter 2) is the main defence; the ROB-ME tool provides a structured way to assess the risk of bias due to missing evidence in a synthesis (11).
crumbs: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE

title: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE
text:
5.5 Assessing risk of bias

5.5.1 RoB 2 for randomised trials
The Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials, RoB 2, assesses bias in five domains (12,13):

bias arising from the randomisation process (sequence generation, allocation concealment, baseline imbalances);
bias due to deviations from intended interventions (blinding, co-interventions, and whether an appropriate analysis was used to estimate the effect of assignment);
bias due to missing outcome data;
bias in measurement of the outcome (including whether assessors knew the allocation);
bias in selection of the reported result (from multiple outcome measurements or analyses).

Each domain contains signalling questions (answered yes, probably yes, probably no, no or no information) that lead, through an algorithm, to a judgement of low risk, some concerns or high risk. The overall judgement is low only if every domain is low; it is high if any domain is high, or if several domains raise some concerns that together substantially lower confidence in the result.
Three features of RoB 2 are easy to forget:

It assesses a result, not a study. The same trial can be at low risk of bias for mortality and high risk for a patient-reported outcome.
It requires the reviewer to state the effect of interest: the effect of assignment to the intervention (intention to treat) or of adhering to it. The appropriate analyses differ.
It is about bias, not reporting quality or imprecision. “Some concerns” should reflect genuine doubt about how the trial was conducted, not merely an omitted detail that could have been found in the protocol.



5.5.2 ROBINS-I for non-randomised studies
For non-randomised studies of interventions, ROBINS-I compares each study with a hypothetical target trial (Section 3.2.1) across seven domains: confounding, selection of participants, classification of interventions, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, measurement of outcomes and selection of the reported result (14). Judgements are low, moderate, serious or critical risk of bias. ROBINS-I is not simply RoB 2 for observational studies: confounding has its own domain because, without randomisation, it is the main threat to validity, and misaligned time zero is assessed under the selection and classification domains.


5.5.3 Displaying the judgements in R
The robvis package draws the standard displays from a data frame with one row per study and one column per domain (15). It includes example data for both tools. Figure 5.6 shows the “traffic-light” plot of individual judgements and Figure 5.7 the summary across studies, in which each bar shows the proportion of studies (optionally weighted) at each level of risk.


Code
rob_traffic_light(data_rob2[1:4, ], tool = "ROB2")








Figure 5.6: RoB 2 judgements for four example trials (robvis example data).







Code
rob_summary(data_rob2, tool = "ROB2")








Figure 5.7: Summary of RoB 2 judgements across the example trials.





The same functions work for ROBINS-I with tool = "ROBINS-I" and the seven ROBINS-I domains (Figure 5.8).


Code
# The example data are called data_robins in robvis 0.3.0 (CRAN), data_robins_i in later versions
robins_example <- if (exists("data_robins_i")) data_robins_i else data_robins
rob_traffic_light(robins_example[1:3, ], tool = "ROBINS-I")








Figure 5.8: ROBINS-I judgements for three example non-randomised studies.





If the extraction sheet (Section 3.4.2) stores the domain judgements in this format, the figure is a single line of code.

title: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE
text:
5.6 Case study: the STRIDE trial
STRIDE randomised 792 adults with type 2 diabetes and symptomatic peripheral artery disease (intermittent claudication) to weekly semaglutide or placebo for 52 weeks (16). The primary outcome was the ratio of maximum walking distance on a treadmill at week 52 to its value at baseline. The trial was double blind, funded by the manufacturer, and reported as positive (Table 5.2).


Code
stride_tab <- data.frame(
  ` ` = "Maximum walking distance at week 52, ratio to baseline",
  Semaglutide = "n = 338; 1.21 (0.95 to 1.55)",
  Placebo     = "n = 345; 1.08 (0.86 to 1.36)",
  `ETR (95% CI)` = "1.13 (1.06 to 1.21)",
  P = "0.0004", check.names = FALSE)
kable(stride_tab)




Table 5.2: STRIDE primary endpoint. Adapted from Table 2 of (16). Medians (IQR) are observed; the estimated treatment ratio (ETR) is from the trial’s model.














Semaglutide
Placebo
ETR (95% CI)
P




Maximum walking distance at week 52, ratio to baseline
n = 338; 1.21 (0.95 to 1.55)
n = 345; 1.08 (0.86 to 1.36)
1.13 (1.06 to 1.21)
0.0004








Two features deserve a closer look: an outcome expressed relative to each participant’s baseline, and the participants who are missing from the table (396 were randomised to each arm).

5.6.1 Change from baseline and regression to the mean
Any measurement made once contains measurement error and day-to-day variation. Participants whose baseline value happened to be unusually low will, on average, score higher when measured again even if nothing has changed: regression to the mean (17). In a randomised trial this matters through chance baseline imbalance. Randomisation makes the arms comparable on average, but in any one trial their baseline means differ a little. (18) show what follows:

An analysis of follow-up values only ignores the imbalance. If the treated arm happened to start worse, the treatment effect is underestimated.
An analysis of change from baseline (or of a ratio to baseline) over-corrects. The arm that started worse is expected to improve more by regression to the mean alone, so the treatment effect is overestimated. Analysing change does not control for baseline imbalance, because of regression to the mean.
Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), which regresses the follow-up value on treatment and baseline, adjusts by the amount the data indicate and is unaffected by the imbalance. It is also the most precise of the three.

Each analysis is unbiased when averaged over all possible randomisations; the difference is in how each behaves given the imbalance that actually occurred, which is the trial that readers see. (19) gives further reasons to avoid change scores: subtracting the baseline assumes that follow-up and baseline are on the same scale with a slope of exactly 1, that the change is unrelated to the baseline value, and that there are no floor or ceiling effects.
A simulation shows all three behaviours. We generate many trials with a true treatment effect of 10 m on walking distance, with baseline and follow-up both measured with error, and analyse each trial three ways.


Code
one_trial <- function(n = 396, effect = 10) {
  true_bl  <- rnorm(2 * n, mean = 185, sd = 40)       # true walking capacity
  obs_bl   <- true_bl + rnorm(2 * n, sd = 30)         # baseline measured with error
  treat    <- rep(0:1, each = n)
  followup <- true_bl + effect * treat + rnorm(2 * n, sd = 30)
  change   <- followup - obs_bl
  c(followup  = unname(diff(tapply(followup, treat, mean))),
    change    = unname(diff(tapply(change, treat, mean))),
    ancova    = unname(coef(lm(followup ~ treat + obs_bl))["treat"]),
    imbalance = unname(diff(tapply(obs_bl, treat, mean))))   # treated - control baseline
}
set.seed(2027)
sims <- as.data.frame(t(replicate(2000, one_trial())))

sims |>
  summarise(across(c(followup, change, ancova), list(mean = mean, sd = sd))) |>
  round(1)

All three analyses are unbiased on average: the mean estimates are close to the true 10 m. ANCOVA is the most precise (standard deviation of the estimates 2.7 m, against 3.0 m for change scores and 3.6 m for follow-up values), so it needs the fewest participants for the same power. More important for the reader of a single trial, the follow-up and change-score estimates depend on the chance baseline imbalance, in opposite directions (Figure 5.9).


Code
sims |>
  pivot_longer(c(followup, change, ancova), names_to = "analysis", values_to = "estimate") |>
  mutate(analysis = factor(analysis, c("followup", "change", "ancova"),
                           c("Follow-up only", "Change from baseline", "ANCOVA"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(imbalance, estimate)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#C8102E") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ analysis) +
  labs(x = "Chance baseline imbalance (m)", y = "Estimated effect (m)")








Figure 5.9: Estimated treatment effect against the chance difference in observed baseline means (treated minus control), in 2000 simulated trials with a true effect of 10 m (dashed line). Follow-up-only estimates rise and change-score estimates fall as the treated arm’s baseline rises; ANCOVA estimates do not depend on it.







Code
slopes <- sapply(c(followup = "followup", change = "change", ancova = "ancova"),
                 function(a) unname(coef(lm(sims[[a]] ~ sims$imbalance))[2]))
reliability <- 40^2 / (40^2 + 30^2)   # var(true baseline) / var(observed baseline)
round(c(slopes, reliability = reliability), 2)


   followup      change      ancova reliability 
       0.65       -0.35        0.01        0.64 


The slopes have a simple explanation. Follow-up values depend on true baseline, and only a fraction of an observed baseline difference is real: the reliability of the baseline measurement, here 0.64. The follow-up-only analysis ignores the baseline (it implicitly multiplies it by 0) and so inherits a slope of about 0.65. The change-score analysis subtracts the whole observed baseline (it multiplies it by 1), over-correcting by the unreliable part, and inherits a slope of about -0.35: in a trial whose treated arm happened to start 5 m lower, it overstates the effect by about 1.8 m. ANCOVA estimates the multiplier from the data, close to the reliability, and its estimates do not drift with the imbalance. The over-correction of the change score is regression to the mean: the arm with the lower observed baseline regresses upwards.


5.6.2 Did STRIDE analyse change?
A ratio to baseline sounds like a change score, so one might conclude that STRIDE’s result is vulnerable to regression to the mean. The protocol and the paper say otherwise. Walking distances were log-transformed and analysed with a mixed model for repeated measures that included the log baseline distance as a covariate (16,20). On the log scale a ratio to baseline is a difference, \(\log(Y/B) = \log Y - \log B\), and once \(\log B\) is in the model as a covariate, analysing \(\log(Y/B)\) or \(\log Y\) gives the same treatment estimate; only the coefficient of \(\log B\) changes, by exactly 1. The estimated treatment ratio is therefore an ANCOVA-type, baseline-adjusted estimate. We can check the identity on one simulated trial:


Code
set.seed(2025)
n <- 396
trial_rtb <- tibble::tibble(
  treat    = rep(0:1, each = n),
  true_bl  = rlnorm(2 * n, log(185), 0.4),
  baseline = true_bl * exp(rnorm(2 * n, sd = 0.2))) |>
  mutate(week52 = true_bl * exp(log(1.13) * treat + rnorm(2 * n, sd = 0.2)))

fit_ratio <- lm(log(week52 / baseline) ~ treat + log(baseline), data = trial_rtb)
fit_level <- lm(log(week52)            ~ treat + log(baseline), data = trial_rtb)
rbind(ratio_outcome = coef(fit_ratio), level_outcome = coef(fit_level)) |> round(4)


              (Intercept) treat log(baseline)
ratio_outcome      1.0712 0.132       -0.2071
level_outcome      1.0712 0.132        0.7929


The treatment coefficients are identical (exponentiated, an estimated ratio of 1.14); only the baseline coefficients differ, by 1. The medians in Table 5.2, by contrast, are unadjusted summaries of each arm and should not be compared directly. The lesson is general: the label of an outcome does not tell you how it was analysed. Before judging an analysis, read the statistical methods and, where available, the protocol and analysis plan.


5.6.3 Missing outcome data
The primary outcome at week 52 was available for 338 of 396 participants (85%) in the semaglutide arm and 345 of 396 (87%) in the placebo arm (Table 5.2). Losses of this size are common, but they matter if the reasons for missing data are related to the outcome, for example if participants whose claudication worsened, or who could not tolerate the drug, were less likely to attend the final treadmill test.
How much could that change the result? A simple sensitivity analysis removes the 15% of participants with the least favourable results in one arm and the most favourable in the other, the worst pattern for an honest comparison.


Code
set.seed(2028)
n <- 396
trial <- tibble(
  treat    = rep(0:1, each = n),
  baseline = rnorm(2 * n, 185, 40) + rnorm(2 * n, sd = 30)) |>
  mutate(followup = baseline + 10 * treat + rnorm(2 * n, sd = 35))
fit_full <- coef(lm(followup ~ treat + baseline, data = trial))["treat"]

# Extreme scenario: the worst 15% of treated and the best 15% of controls go missing
trial_obs <- trial |>
  mutate(gain = followup - baseline) |>
  group_by(treat) |>
  arrange(if_else(treat == 1, -gain, gain), .by_group = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(prop = 0.85) |>
  ungroup()
fit_miss <- coef(lm(followup ~ treat + baseline, data = trial_obs))["treat"]
round(c(complete_data = fit_full, after_selective_loss = fit_miss), 1)


       complete_data.treat after_selective_loss.treat 
                       8.2                       27.8 


With complete data the estimate is close to the true 10 m. If 15% of each arm were lost in the most unfavourable way, the estimate would be 28 m. This extreme scenario is not a claim about what happened in STRIDE; it is a bound on what could have happened, and it shows why RoB 2 asks whether missingness could depend on the true value of the outcome. Methods for handling missing data are developed in Chapter 14.


5.6.4 A RoB 2 assessment
Figure 5.10 summarises one reviewer’s RoB 2 assessment of the primary outcome. Randomisation was well conducted and the trial was double blind, so neither participants nor those supervising the treadmill test knew the allocation (domains 1, 2 and 4 at low risk). About 15% of outcome data were missing, and withdrawal could plausibly be related to walking capacity (domain 3, high risk). A reviewer persuaded by the trial’s sensitivity analyses for missing data could reasonably judge this domain “some concerns” instead; the reasons matter more than the label. The primary outcome and its baseline-adjusted analysis were pre-specified in the protocol, but walking distance was analysed under several estimands and time points (domain 5, some concerns).


Code
stride_rob <- data.frame(
  Study = "STRIDE (2025)",
  D1 = "Low", D2 = "Low", D3 = "High", D4 = "Low", D5 = "Some concerns",
  Overall = "High")
rob_traffic_light(stride_rob, tool = "ROB2")








Figure 5.10: An illustrative RoB 2 assessment of STRIDE’s primary outcome.





Note what the assessment does not capture. Had STRIDE analysed unadjusted change scores, the resulting sensitivity to chance baseline imbalance (Section 5.6.1) would not fit neatly into any RoB 2 domain (it is a matter of precision and conditional bias rather than systematic error); it would be raised under domain 5 only if a baseline-adjusted analysis had been performed and not reported. Otherwise it is a weakness the reviewer must flag in the text. STRIDE avoided it by adjusting for baseline (Section 5.6.2). Risk-of-bias tools structure judgement; they do not replace it.






Key point



Assess risk of bias for each result, give reasons for each judgement, and report weaknesses that the tool’s domains do not capture.

title: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE
text:
5.7 Introduction to GRADE

5.7.1 From study-level bias to outcome-level certainty
Risk-of-bias tools judge individual results. Decisions need a judgement about a body of evidence: how confident can we be in the pooled effect on a given outcome? The GRADE approach (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) provides that judgement in a structured, transparent way, and is used by Cochrane, the WHO and most guideline developers (21,22).



Table 5.3: Risk-of-bias tools and GRADE.











Risk-of-bias tool
GRADE




Assesses
Bias in a study’s result
Certainty in a body of evidence


Level
Each study, for each result
Each outcome, across studies


Considers
Internal validity
Risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias


Output
Low / some concerns / high
High / moderate / low / very low






The two are complementary, not alternatives: risk-of-bias judgements are the input to the first GRADE domain. In a culinary analogy, the risk-of-bias tool inspects each ingredient; GRADE judges whether the finished dish can be trusted.


5.7.2 Certainty levels and the GRADE workflow
GRADE rates certainty at four levels (23):



Table 5.4: GRADE certainty levels.










Level
Symbol
Meaning




High
⊕⊕⊕⊕
We are very confident that the true effect lies close to the estimate


Moderate
⊕⊕⊕◯
The true effect is likely to be close to the estimate, but may be substantially different


Low
⊕⊕◯◯
The true effect may be substantially different from the estimate


Very low
⊕◯◯◯
The true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimate






The workflow, for each outcome:

Assess risk of bias in each study’s result (RoB 2 or ROBINS-I).
Synthesise the results (meta-analysis or structured narrative synthesis).
Start at high certainty for randomised trials, low for observational studies.
Rate down by one level (serious concern) or two (very serious) for each of five domains: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias.
Rate up observational evidence, if no reason to rate down remains, for a large effect, a dose–response gradient, or plausible residual confounding that would have reduced the observed effect.
Report the final certainty with an explicit reason for every change.

Ratings are made per outcome: the same review can provide high-certainty evidence for mortality and very low certainty for quality of life. Downgrades in different domains accumulate, but the same problem should not be counted twice. Chapter 6 works through each domain with real data and shows how the results are presented in a summary-of-findings table.






Study design is a starting point, not a verdict



Starting randomised trials at high certainty does not mean that every trial result is trustworthy, and starting observational studies at low does not mean they are uninformative. The rest of GRADE exists to move the rating to where the evidence actually belongs.


The traditional “evidence pyramid” ranks study designs from expert opinion at the bottom to systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top (Figure 5.11, left). It is a useful mnemonic for where GRADE starts, but it is a poor guide to where it ends. (24) proposed redrawing it with wavy boundaries between designs, to show that a design’s position can move with its risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, and with systematic reviews removed from the top and used as a lens through which the other designs are viewed. Others have been blunter (Figure 5.11, right).


Code
levels_trad <- c("Expert opinion",
                 "Case reports and case series", "Case-control studies",
                 "Cohort studies", "Non-randomised controlled trials",
                 "Randomised controlled trials",
                 "Systematic reviews and meta-analyses")
band <- function(i, n) {               # trapezium i (1 = bottom) of a pyramid of n bands
  y0 <- (i - 1) / n; y1 <- i / n
  data.frame(x = c(-(1 - y0), 1 - y0, 1 - y1, -(1 - y1)) / 2, y = c(y0, y0, y1, y1))
}
trad <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(levels_trad), function(i)
  cbind(band(i, length(levels_trad)), id = i, panel = "Traditional hierarchy")))
labs_trad <- data.frame(y = (seq_along(levels_trad) - 0.5) / length(levels_trad),
                        label = levels_trad, panel = "Traditional hierarchy") |>
  mutate(x = (1 - y) / 2 + 0.03)      # just right of each band
alt <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = c(-0.5, 0.5, 0.15, -0.15), y = c(0, 0, 0.7, 0.7), id = 1),
  data.frame(x = c(-0.15, 0.15, 0, 0), y = c(0.7, 0.7, 1, 1), id = 2)) |>
  mutate(panel = "An alternative view")
labs_alt <- data.frame(x = 0, y = c(0.3, 0.78),
                       label = c("The other garbage",
                                 "Thoughtful,\nwell-conducted\nstudies of\nany design"),
                       panel = "An alternative view")
pyr <- rbind(trad, alt) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, c("Traditional hierarchy", "An alternative view")),
         fill = case_when(panel == "An alternative view" & id == 1 ~ "#E05A55",
                          panel == "An alternative view" ~ "#87C8F5",
                          TRUE ~ colorRampPalette(c("#C8102E", "#F2C14E", "#5B9B5B",
                                                    "#2C4A7E", "#6A3D9A"))(7)[id]))
ggplot(pyr, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_polygon(aes(group = id, fill = fill), colour = "white") +
  geom_text(data = rbind(labs_trad, labs_alt) |>
              mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels(pyr$panel))),
            aes(label = label, hjust = ifelse(panel == "Traditional hierarchy", 0, 0.5)),
            size = 3.2, lineheight = 0.85, fontface = "bold", colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(add = c(0.02, 0.02))) +
  geom_blank(data = data.frame(x = c(-0.5, 1.3), y = 0, panel = "Traditional hierarchy") |>
               mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels(pyr$panel)))) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"))








Figure 5.11: Left: a traditional hierarchy of evidence by study design. Right: an alternative pyramid, adapted from a post by Darren Dahly (25). GRADE sits between the two: design sets the starting point, and the quality of the specific studies decides the rating.

title: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE
text:
Key points

Bias is systematic error: more data narrow the confidence interval around the wrong value.
Inadequate randomisation, allocation concealment and blinding exaggerate treatment effects, especially for subjective outcomes; industry funding and early stopping are also associated with more favourable results, and early stopping does so even in impeccably conducted trials.
Non-reporting biases shape the evidence base before any study is appraised.
RoB 2 and ROBINS-I assess the risk of bias in each result, domain by domain, with explicit reasons; robvis displays the judgements.
Analyses of change from baseline over-correct for chance baseline imbalance, because of regression to the mean; analyses of follow-up alone under-correct. ANCOVA adjusts correctly and is the most precise. Check how a trial actually analysed its outcome before judging it: STRIDE’s ratio to baseline was analysed with baseline adjustment.
GRADE rates the certainty of a body of evidence for each outcome, using risk-of-bias judgements as one of five domains.

title: 5  Risk of Bias and GRADE
text:
Exercises

Using the RoB 2 signalling questions (12), assess the risk of bias in the primary outcome of EMPEROR-Reduced (26) (registration NCT03057977). Record a reason for each domain judgement. A worked answer is given in Section 6.1.
Change the measurement error in one_trial() (the sd of the baseline error) to 0, then to 60. How do the precision of the three analyses and the slopes in Figure 5.9 change? Relate your answer to the reliability of the baseline measurement.
In stride-identity, drop log(baseline) from both models. Do the treatment estimates still agree? Which analysis does each model now correspond to?
In the missing-data example, how large would the losses have to be for the estimated effect to disappear?
Find a published trial with a subjective primary outcome that was not blinded. Which RoB 2 domains are affected, and how would you judge them?

title: 6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
text:
6.1 A worked RoB 2 assessment: EMPEROR-Reduced
Chapter 5 introduced risk-of-bias tools and the GRADE framework. This chapter applies GRADE domain by domain to a real body of evidence and shows how the result is presented in a summary-of-findings table. Chapter 7 turns from the evidence to the review itself: how it is reported (PRISMA 2020), how it was conducted (AMSTAR 2), whether its conclusions are at risk of bias (ROBIS), and whether they say more than the evidence allows (spin).
The exercise at the end of Chapter 5 asked for a RoB 2 assessment of the primary outcome of EMPEROR-Reduced, which randomised 3730 patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction to empagliflozin or placebo (1). One reasonable assessment, domain by domain:
Code
rob_traffic_light(data.frame(Study = "EMPEROR-Reduced", D1 = "Low", D2 = "Low",
                             D3 = "Low", D4 = "Low", D5 = "Low", Overall = "Low"),
                  tool = "ROB2")








Figure 6.1: RoB 2 assessment of the primary outcome of EMPEROR-Reduced.
The contrast with STRIDE (Section 5.6.4) is instructive. Both trials were industry funded and double blind; the difference lies in the outcome. Adjudicated clinical events, ascertained in almost everyone, are much less vulnerable than a performance test that a sixth of participants did not complete. Funding source is recorded, but is not by itself a reason to judge a result at high risk of bias.

title: 6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
text:
Randomisation process: low. Central, computer-generated randomisation with concealed allocation; no important baseline imbalances.
Deviations from intended interventions: low. Double blind with matching placebo; background therapy not differential; analysis by intention to treat.
Missing outcome data: low. Vital status and the primary outcome were ascertained for almost all patients. Treatment discontinuation differed slightly between arms, but discontinuation is not missing outcome data.
Measurement of the outcome: low. Cardiovascular death and hospitalisation for heart failure were adjudicated by a committee blind to allocation.
Selection of the reported result: low. The trial was registered, the primary outcome was pre-specified and the trial ran to its planned number of events; secondary outcomes were tested in a pre-specified hierarchy.

title: 6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
text:
6.3 Domain 1: risk of bias
The risk-of-bias domain is judged for each outcome across all the studies contributing to it, and by their weight in the analysis rather than their number (5). Three small trials at high risk contributing 5% of the weight matter far less than one large trial at high risk contributing 60%. A practical rule: if studies carrying most of the weight are at high risk, or at some concerns in a way that plausibly affects the result, rate down by one level; rate down by two only if the limitations are severe and dominate the evidence.
Common errors are to rate down for lack of blinding regardless of the outcome (it matters far more for subjective outcomes than for death), to rate down because a trial was open label without asking whether this plausibly affected the result, to confuse study-level and outcome-level risk of bias, and to penalise the same weakness twice in different domains.
All four SGLT2 inhibitor trials were large, double blind and placebo controlled, with adjudicated outcomes and near-complete follow-up: no serious risk of bias for either outcome.

title: 6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
text:
6.4 Fixed-effect and random-effects models
Judging inconsistency requires the two basic models for pooling, which are developed fully in Chapter 9. Under the fixed-effect (or common-effect) model, every study estimates the same true effect, and differences between studies are due to sampling error alone; each study is weighted by the inverse of its variance, \(w_i = 1/v_i\). Under the random-effects model, each study estimates its own true effect, and these effects vary around a mean with between-study variance τ²; the weights become \(w_i = 1/(v_i + \tau^2)\), so large studies dominate less, and the confidence interval for the mean widens to reflect the heterogeneity.
Figure 6.2 fits both models to five hypothetical studies whose results differ more than chance would explain.


Code
toy <- data.frame(study = paste("Study", LETTERS[1:5]),
                  yi = c(0.10, 0.85, 0.30, 1.05, 0.55),
                  vi = c(0.015, 0.020, 0.018, 0.022, 0.016))
fe_toy <- rma(yi, vi, data = toy, method = "FE",   slab = study)
re_toy <- rma(yi, vi, data = toy, method = "REML", slab = study)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
forest(fe_toy, header = "Study", xlab = "Effect size", mlab = "Fixed effect",
       xlim = c(-1.8, 2.7), alim = c(-0.5, 1.5))
forest(re_toy, header = "Study", xlab = "Effect size", mlab = "Random effects",
       xlim = c(-1.8, 2.7), alim = c(-0.5, 1.5))








Figure 6.2: The same five studies summarised by a fixed-effect model (left) and a random-effects model (right).





The individual studies are identical in both panels; only the summary changes, from 0.53 (0.41 to 0.65) to 0.56 (0.23 to 0.90). The fixed-effect interval answers a question these studies cannot honestly answer: what is the one effect they all share?
When τ² is estimated as zero, the random-effects model reduces exactly to the fixed-effect model. Defaulting to random effects therefore costs little when heterogeneity is absent, whereas defaulting to fixed effect understates uncertainty when it is present. Random effects (with REML estimation) is the usual default; the fixed-effect model needs a specific justification.






How studies are combined can reverse a conclusion



A 1999 meta-analysis of circumcision and HIV infection simply added up events and participants across 29 studies of very different sizes and designs, and found circumcised men at slightly higher risk (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.12) (6). Reanalysing the same studies by comparing men within each study and then pooling reversed the direction (7), and a systematic review of 27 studies in sub-Saharan Africa found circumcised men at about half the risk (RR 0.52, 0.40 to 0.68) (8). Three later randomised trials confirmed a protective effect of about 50% to 60%. Pooling raw counts across studies discards the comparison within each study and invites Simpson’s paradox.

title: 6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
text:
6.5 Domain 2: inconsistency
Inconsistency means unexplained heterogeneity in the results (9). If the variation can be explained by a pre-specified effect modifier, it is reported as such, not penalised.

6.5.1 Measuring heterogeneity
Four statistics are commonly reported:

Cochran’s Q, \(Q = \sum_i w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta)^2\) with fixed-effect weights, tests whether the results vary more than chance would predict. It has low power when there are few studies.
I² \(= \max\{0, (Q - df)/Q\} \times 100\%\) is the proportion of the variation in estimates due to heterogeneity rather than chance. It depends on the precision of the studies, not only on how much the true effects vary.
τ² is the between-study variance of the true effects, on the scale of the analysis (here log risk ratios).
The prediction interval is the range in which the true effect in a new study similar to those included is expected to lie (10):

\[
\hat\mu \pm t_{k-2,\,0.975}\sqrt{\hat\tau^2 + \text{SE}(\hat\mu)^2}.
\]
The prediction interval is the most clinically useful of the four, because it is on the scale of the effect: it tells a reader what to expect in their own setting.


Code
pi_comp <- predict(res_comp, transf = exp)
pi_acm  <- predict(res_acm,  transf = exp)
het <- data.frame(
  Outcome = c("CV death or HF hospitalisation", "Death from any cause"),
  RR      = c(pi_comp$pred, pi_acm$pred),
  CI      = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", c(pi_comp$ci.lb, pi_acm$ci.lb), c(pi_comp$ci.ub, pi_acm$ci.ub)),
  PI      = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", c(pi_comp$pi.lb, pi_acm$pi.lb), c(pi_comp$pi.ub, pi_acm$pi.ub)),
  Q_p     = c(res_comp$QEp, res_acm$QEp),
  I2      = c(res_comp$I2, res_acm$I2),
  tau2    = c(res_comp$tau2, res_acm$tau2))
kable(het, digits = c(0, 2, 0, 0, 2, 0, 4),
      col.names = c("Outcome", "Pooled RR", "95% CI", "95% PI", "P (Q)", "I² (%)", "τ²"))

For both outcomes the results of the four trials are compatible with a single effect: τ² is estimated as zero, so the random-effects model has reduced to the fixed-effect model, and metafor’s prediction interval coincides with the confidence interval. (By default metafor uses the normal distribution; the formula above, with a t distribution on k − 2 = 2 degrees of freedom, would give a much wider interval with so few studies, an honest reminder of how little four studies say about heterogeneity.) Figure 6.3 shows the composite outcome with its prediction interval, drawn by addpred = TRUE.


Code
forest(res_comp, atransf = exp, addpred = TRUE, header = "Trial",
       at = log(c(0.6, 0.8, 1, 1.25)), xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)")








Figure 6.3: Cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure. The line beneath the diamond is the 95% prediction interval.











No evidence of heterogeneity is not evidence of none



With four studies, Q has very little power. τ² = 0 is the best estimate, but a modest true heterogeneity cannot be excluded. This is one reason to report the prediction interval rather than rely on the P value for Q.




6.5.2 When the prediction interval tells a different story
For a contrast, return to the BCG vaccine trials of Section 4.3.


Code
bcg <- rma(measure = "RR", ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg,
           data = dat.bcg, method = "REML")
pi_bcg <- predict(bcg, transf = exp)


Here the pooled risk ratio is 0.49 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.70), clearly favouring vaccination, but I² = 92% and the 95% prediction interval runs from 0.15 to 1.55. The average effect is real, but in a new setting the vaccine might do little or nothing. Three situations are worth distinguishing:

The prediction interval excludes no effect (the SGLT2 inhibitor trials): the benefit is consistent across settings; no reason to rate down.
The pooled estimate excludes no effect but the prediction interval does not (the BCG trials): the average effect is real but varies importantly; rate down by one level unless the heterogeneity is explained (for BCG, largely by latitude).
The prediction interval spans important benefit and important harm: the direction of effect depends on the setting; rate down by two levels, and question whether a single pooled estimate is meaningful.

There is no fixed I² threshold for rating down. GRADE asks whether point estimates vary widely, whether confidence intervals overlap, whether results fall on both sides of a decision threshold, and whether the heterogeneity is unexplained (9). Conventional bands (I² below 40% might not be important, 30% to 60% moderate, 50% to 90% substantial, above 75% considerable) overlap deliberately (11).
Judgement for the SGLT2 inhibitor trials: no serious inconsistency for either outcome.

title: 6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
text:
6.7 Domain 4: imprecision
Imprecision is judged from the confidence interval in relation to a decision threshold, supplemented by the optimal information size (OIS) (14).
The confidence interval. If the 95% CI includes values that would lead to different decisions — typically both an important benefit and no effect, or a threshold of minimal importance — rate down. An RR of 0.88 (95% CI 0.70 to 1.10) is imprecise for most purposes; 0.88 (0.81 to 0.96) usually is not. Conversely, a wide interval need not be penalised if every value in it would lead to the same decision.
The optimal information size. Even when the CI excludes no effect, a small body of evidence can produce implausibly large and unstable estimates. The OIS is the number of participants a single adequately powered trial would need to detect a plausible effect. For a binary outcome, with control-group risk \(p_C\) and intervention-group risk \(p_I\), the number per arm is
\[
n = \frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2\,[p_C(1-p_C) + p_I(1-p_I)]}{(p_C - p_I)^2}.
\]
If the total number of participants in the meta-analysis is well below the OIS, rate down, whatever the confidence interval shows.


Code
ois_binary <- function(p_C, RR, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80) {
  p_I <- p_C * RR
  z   <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(power)
  ceiling(z^2 * (p_C * (1 - p_C) + p_I * (1 - p_I)) / (p_C - p_I)^2)   # per arm
}

p_C_comp <- sum(sglt2$comp_C) / sum(sglt2$n_C)    # pooled control-group risk
p_C_acm  <- sum(sglt2$acm_C)  / sum(sglt2$n_C)
n_total  <- sum(sglt2$n_I + sglt2$n_C)

ois <- data.frame(
  Outcome  = c("CV death or HF hospitalisation", "Death from any cause"),
  p_C      = c(p_C_comp, p_C_acm),
  RR       = c(pi_comp$pred, pi_acm$pred),
  OIS      = 2 * c(ois_binary(p_C_comp, pi_comp$pred), ois_binary(p_C_acm, pi_acm$pred)),
  N        = n_total)
kable(ois, digits = c(0, 3, 2, 0, 0),
      col.names = c("Outcome", "Control risk", "Pooled RR", "OIS (total)", "N in review"),
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

For the composite outcome the review includes 20,725 patients against an OIS of 2,944, and the confidence interval is narrow: no serious imprecision. For death from any cause, the OIS for an effect as small as the one observed (RR 0.93) is 38,830, more than the number of patients available, and the confidence interval runs from 0.87 to 1.00, close to no effect at its upper limit. Whether to rate down depends on the decision threshold: if any reduction in mortality would change practice, the evidence is reasonably precise; if only a reduction of, say, 10% or more would, the interval includes both important and unimportant effects, and rating down by one level for serious imprecision is justified.






Key point



The OIS asks whether there is enough information that a new trial would be unlikely to overturn the conclusion. A statistically significant result below the OIS is a preliminary result.

title: 6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
section: 6.9 Biases specific to bodies of randomised evidence
text:
6.9 Biases specific to bodies of randomised evidence
Two problems deserve emphasis because they can affect a whole body of randomised evidence rather than a single trial.
Attrition. Randomisation makes the groups comparable at baseline; it does not keep them comparable if participants drop out for reasons related to treatment or prognosis. With substantial, differential or outcome-related losses, the comparison at follow-up is no longer between randomised groups, and imputation cannot fully restore it. When reading a meta-analysis, check the losses in each arm of each trial, whether the reasons are reported, whether heterogeneity tracks the attrition rate, and whether a sensitivity analysis restricted to trials with little missing data agrees with the main result (16).
Sponsorship and selective reporting. Industry-sponsored studies are more likely to reach conclusions favourable to the sponsor (OR 3.60, 95% CI 2.63 to 4.91, in one systematic review) (17). When antidepressant trials submitted to the US Food and Drug Administration were compared with the published literature, 94% of published trials appeared positive, against 51% according to the FDA’s own analyses, and the apparent effect size was inflated by about a third (18). In a cohort of trials, 62% had at least one primary outcome changed, introduced or omitted between protocol and publication (19). None of this requires fabrication: comparator choice, run-in periods that exclude poor responders, composite outcomes, the analysis population and selective publication are enough. Record each trial’s funding, compare registered and reported outcomes, and search registers for trials that were never published.

title: 6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
text:
6.10 Summary-of-findings tables
A summary-of-findings (SoF) table is the main output of GRADE: for each important outcome it shows the number of studies and participants, the relative effect, the absolute effect, the certainty of the evidence and the reasons for any rating down (20). Absolute effects require an assumed baseline risk, ideally that of the population to whom the review will be applied:
\[
\text{Risk difference} = p_C \times (\text{RR} - 1).
\]
The same relative effect implies very different absolute benefits in high-risk and low-risk populations, so SoF tables often show more than one baseline risk.


Code
per1000 <- function(p_C, rr) round(1000 * p_C * (rr - 1))
sof <- data.frame(
  Outcome = c("CV death or HF hospitalisation", "Death from any cause"),
  Studies = sprintf("4 RCTs; %s patients", format(n_total, big.mark = ",")),
  Relative = sprintf("RR %.2f (%.2f to %.2f)",
                     c(pi_comp$pred, pi_acm$pred), c(pi_comp$ci.lb, pi_acm$ci.lb),
                     c(pi_comp$ci.ub, pi_acm$ci.ub)),
  Control = sprintf("%.0f per 1000", 1000 * c(p_C_comp, p_C_acm)),
  Absolute = sprintf("%d per 1000 (%d to %d)",
                     c(per1000(p_C_comp, pi_comp$pred), per1000(p_C_acm, pi_acm$pred)),
                     c(per1000(p_C_comp, pi_comp$ci.lb), per1000(p_C_acm, pi_acm$ci.lb)),
                     c(per1000(p_C_comp, pi_comp$ci.ub), per1000(p_C_acm, pi_acm$ci.ub))),
  Certainty = c("⊕⊕⊕⊕ High", "⊕⊕⊕◯ Moderate"),
  Reason = c("", "Rated down once for imprecision: CI includes effects too small to matter"))
kable(sof, col.names = c("Outcome", "Studies and participants", "Relative effect (95% CI)",
                         "Risk with placebo", "Difference with SGLT2i", "Certainty", "Comments"))

A summary-of-findings table answers two separate questions for each outcome: how large is the effect? and how sure are we? A cartoon by Leo Garel, often shown in GRADE workshops, makes the point with a weather forecaster who gives the chance of showers and, separately, the chance that he knows what he is talking about. Figure 6.4 shows both answers for the SGLT2 inhibitor outcomes.


Code
sof_plot <- data.frame(
  outcome = factor(c("CV death or HF hospitalisation", "Death from any cause"),
                   levels = rev(c("CV death or HF hospitalisation", "Death from any cause"))),
  est = c(per1000(p_C_comp, pi_comp$pred),  per1000(p_C_acm, pi_acm$pred)),
  lo  = c(per1000(p_C_comp, pi_comp$ci.lb), per1000(p_C_acm, pi_acm$ci.lb)),
  hi  = c(per1000(p_C_comp, pi_comp$ci.ub), per1000(p_C_acm, pi_acm$ci.ub)),
  certainty = c("\u2295\u2295\u2295\u2295  High", "\u2295\u2295\u2295\u25ef  Moderate"))
xmax <- max(sof_plot$hi) + 25
ggplot(sof_plot, aes(est, outcome)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_text(aes(x = xmax, label = certainty), hjust = 0, size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(min(sof_plot$lo) - 5, xmax + 40),
                     breaks = seq(-50, 10, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Difference with SGLT2 inhibitor, events per 1000 patients", y = NULL)








Figure 6.4: Two answers for each outcome: the absolute effect per 1000 patients (point and 95% CI, left) and the certainty of the evidence (right). The idea of separating the two is captured in a cartoon by Leo Garel.





Negative differences are fewer events with an SGLT2 inhibitor. The absolute effects use the pooled control-group risks of the trials; in a population at lower risk the same relative effects would prevent fewer events. Packages such as gt produce more elaborately formatted tables, and GRADEpro GDT builds SoF tables interactively, but the content is what matters: every outcome, absolute as well as relative effects, and the reason for every rating.

title: 6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
text:
Key points

GRADE domains are judged per outcome, with explicit reasons; risk of bias is weighted by the studies’ contribution to the estimate, not by their number.
Random effects is the usual default; when τ² is zero it reduces to the fixed-effect model.
Report the prediction interval: it translates heterogeneity into the range of effects to expect in a new setting.
A plausible surrogate is not a validated one; CAST is the standing warning.
Imprecision is judged from the confidence interval against a decision threshold, and from the optimal information size.
Funnel plots need at least 10 studies; with fewer, judge publication bias from the search and the registers.
Summary-of-findings tables must give absolute as well as relative effects.

title: 6  Rating Certainty with GRADE
text:
Exercises

Re-run the analyses of Section 6.2 with a fixed-effect model. Which results change, and why?
Using ois_binary(), compute the OIS for detecting a 10% relative reduction in all-cause mortality, with the control-group risk of these trials. How does your judgement of imprecision change?
Recompute the SoF table for a population whose annual risk of the composite outcome is half that of the trials. What happens to the absolute effects and to the number needed to treat?

title: 7  Reporting and Appraising Systematic Reviews
text:
7.1 Is the review completely reported? PRISMA 2020
Chapter 5 and Chapter 6 were about the evidence: the risk of bias in each study, and the certainty of the body of evidence for each outcome. This chapter is about the review itself. Most readers meet the evidence through someone else’s systematic review, and a review can fail at several levels independently of the studies it contains. Four questions organise the chapter:
Reviews of observational studies need extra care at every step, and we deal with them before the appraisal tools.
crumbs: 7  Reporting and Appraising Systematic Reviews

title: 7  Reporting and Appraising Systematic Reviews
text:
7.1.1 Why reporting standards exist
A review that does not report what was done cannot be appraised, reproduced or updated. Reporting guidelines list the minimum information a report should contain; the EQUATOR Network maintains hundreds of them. For systematic reviews the core guideline is PRISMA 2020 (2), with extensions for particular kinds of review:



Table 7.1: Reporting guidelines for evidence syntheses.





Review type
Guideline




Any systematic review, with or without meta-analysis
PRISMA 2020


Protocol
PRISMA-P


Network meta-analysis
PRISMA-NMA


Diagnostic test accuracy
PRISMA-DTA


Individual participant data
PRISMA-IPD


Scoping review
PRISMA-ScR


Meta-analysis of observational studies
MOOSE (Section 7.2.5)












Complete reporting is not good methods



PRISMA asks whether something is reported, not whether it was done well. A perfectly reported review of biased trials is still a review of biased trials. Methodological quality is appraised with AMSTAR 2 and ROBIS, later in this chapter.




7.1.2 Structure of PRISMA 2020
PRISMA 2020 has 27 items, several with sub-items, in seven sections (Table 7.2) (2,3).



Table 7.2: Sections and items of PRISMA 2020.










Section
Items
Content




Title
1
Identify the report as a systematic review


Abstract
2
Structured summary (PRISMA 2020 for Abstracts)


Introduction
3–4
Rationale; objectives


Methods
5–15
Eligibility criteria, information sources, search strategy, selection process, data collection, data items, risk of bias, effect measures, synthesis methods, reporting bias assessment, certainty assessment


Results
16–22
Study selection (flow diagram), study characteristics, risk of bias in studies, results of individual studies, results of syntheses, reporting biases, certainty of evidence

23
Interpretation, limitations of the evidence and of the review, implications


Other information
24–27
Registration and protocol, support, competing interests, availability of data, code and other materials






Compared with PRISMA 2009, the 2020 statement requires the full search strategy for every database, a description of any automation tools used in screening, reporting of certainty assessments, and the availability of data and analytic code (item 27). The flow diagram (Section 2.5.3) separates records identified from databases and registers from those identified by other methods, such as citation searching.


7.1.3 Items that reviews often fail
Adherence to PRISMA is incomplete even in journals that endorse it (4). In appraising a review, check particularly:

Registration and protocol (item 24): was a protocol registered before the search, and are deviations from it explained?
Search strategy (item 7): is the full strategy given for every database, or only paraphrased?
Selection and data collection (items 8–9): were screening and extraction done in duplicate, and were automation tools described?
Risk of bias (items 11 and 18): is risk of bias assessed per outcome and used in the synthesis, or only displayed?
Synthesis methods (item 13): is the choice of model justified, and are heterogeneity and its exploration described?
Reporting biases (items 14 and 21): are funnel plots used with fewer than 10 studies?
Certainty (items 15 and 22): is certainty rated per outcome?
Interpretation (item 23): do the conclusions match the certainty of the evidence?

The last is the most consequential: conclusions that overstate low-certainty evidence are a form of spin (Section 7.5).

title: 7  Reporting and Appraising Systematic Reviews
text:
7.2 Reviews of observational studies
For long-term harms, rare outcomes and exposures that cannot be randomised, observational studies are often the only evidence. The question is not whether to use them but how to use them critically. Chapter 19 treats the synthesis of observational studies in detail; here we cover what an appraiser needs to know.

7.2.1 What is different
Every bias that threatens a review of trials (selective reporting, publication bias, sponsorship, Section 5.4) also threatens a review of observational studies. Observational studies add three structural problems:

Confounding. Without randomisation, exposed and unexposed people may differ in ways that also affect the outcome: confounding by indication, the healthy-user effect (people who take preventive treatments tend to be healthier in other ways) and protopathic bias (a drug prescribed for early symptoms of the outcome under study). Adjustment removes only the confounding that was measured and modelled correctly.
Selection. Who enters the study, or the analysis, can itself depend on exposure and outcome (Section 7.2.2).
Misclassification of exposure or time. Immortal time bias, the most common self-inflicted error in pharmacoepidemiology, is a combination of misclassification and selection; it was dissected with a simulation in Section 3.2.

Two further problems arise at the synthesis stage. Studies adjust for different sets of confounders, so a pooled “adjusted” estimate averages estimates of different quantities, and they may report odds ratios, risk ratios and hazard ratios over different time horizons (Chapter 8). And because the studies differ so much in populations, exposure definitions and outcome ascertainment, heterogeneity is usually large.
How different are observational and randomised estimates of the same effect? A Cochrane methodology review combined 14 methodological reviews and found no systematic difference on average: the ratio of odds ratios comparing trials with observational studies was 1.08 (95% CI 0.96 to 1.22) (5). That average conceals large disagreements on particular questions; hormone therapy and coronary disease (Section 8.4.3) is a famous example. The lesson for appraisal is that observational evidence is neither reliably biased in one direction nor reliably trustworthy: each study’s design has to be examined.






No pooling model repairs a biased input



In a review of observational studies, the design choices made in the primary studies (time zero, exposure definition, new-user versus prevalent-user cohorts, the adjustment set) constrain validity far more than the choice of meta-analytic model. Pooling biased studies produces a precise estimate of the wrong quantity.




7.2.2 Two meanings of selection bias
“Selection bias” is used for two different problems (6):

Failure to generalise (external validity). The sample is not representative of the target population. This does not by itself bias the comparison within the sample. If the effect differs across subgroups and their distribution in the target population is known, the estimate can be standardised to that population; otherwise its applicability is a limitation to state.
Bias within the sample (internal validity). Whether someone ends up in the analysed sample depends on, or shares causes with, both the exposure and the outcome. The comparison is then biased even among the people studied, and no reweighting to a target population fixes it.

The second kind has a single structure: conditioning on a common effect, or collider (7). A collider is a variable caused by two others; two arrows point into it. Conditioning on it, whether by restriction, stratification, matching, regression adjustment, or simply because a study can only enrol people with a certain value of it, creates an association between its causes even when they are independent.
A simulation makes the mechanism visible. Income and blood pressure are generated independently. Both raise the chance of a medical visit, and the study samples only people who had a visit.


Code
set.seed(123)
n <- 5000
population <- tibble::tibble(
  income = rnorm(n),                       # standardised; independent of BP
  bp     = rnorm(n)) |>
  mutate(visit = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2 + 2 * income + 2 * bp)))   # the collider
sampled <- filter(population, visit == 1)

rbind(
  population = coef(summary(lm(bp ~ income, data = population)))["income", c(1, 4)],
  visited    = coef(summary(lm(bp ~ income, data = sampled)))["income", c(1, 4)]) |>
  round(3)


           Estimate Pr(>|t|)
population   -0.006    0.672
visited      -0.362    0.000




Code
ggplot(population, aes(income, bp)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = factor(visit)), alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_smooth(data = sampled, method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#C8102E") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("0" = "grey75", "1" = "#C8102E"),
                      labels = c("No visit", "Visit"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Income (standardised)", y = "Blood pressure (standardised)")








Figure 7.1: Income and blood pressure are independent in the population (grey line), but negatively associated among the people who had a medical visit (red line), because a visit is a common effect of both.





Among people with a visit, those with low income must, on average, have had high blood pressure to have been sampled, and vice versa. The slope of -0.36 is entirely an artefact of selection. Hospital-based case-control studies are vulnerable to the same structure when both the exposure and the disease independently lead to admission (Berkson’s bias).
Table 7.3 summarises the difference between a confounder and a collider.



Table 7.3: Confounders and colliders.











Confounder
Collider




Structure
Common cause of exposure and outcome
Common effect of two variables


Path through it, unconditioned
Open: creates a spurious association
Blocked: creates none


Effect of conditioning on it
Blocks the path; removes bias
Opens the path; creates bias








7.2.3 Adjustment can create bias: M-bias
Because conditioning on a collider opens a path, “adjust for everything available” is not a safe default. The clearest case is M-bias, named for the shape of its diagram: a variable is caused both by a cause of the exposure and by a cause of the outcome, without being a confounder. Adjusting for it opens a path from exposure to outcome that was previously closed.
An example from my own work shows how easily this can happen. In a study of oral fluoroquinolones and retinal detachment, we adjusted for myopia, among other variables, on the reasoning in Figure 7.2 (A): myopia is associated with fluoroquinolone use through socioeconomic factors and is a strong risk factor for detachment, so it looked like a confounder (8). Years later another causal model was put to me, Figure 7.2 (B). There, low socioeconomic status leads to both fluoroquinolone use and myopia, and unknown factors (genetic predisposition, axial elongation of the eye) lead to both myopia and detachment. Myopia is then a collider, and adjusting for it opens the path fluoroquinolone ← SES → myopia ← unknown → detachment.


Code
nodes <- tibble::tribble(
  ~panel, ~node,    ~x,  ~y,
  "A",    "FQ",     0,   1,
  "A",    "RD",     2,   1,
  "A",    "Myopia", 1,   0,
  "B",    "SES",    0,   2,
  "B",    "U",      2,   2,
  "B",    "Myopia", 1,   1.2,
  "B",    "FQ",     0,   0,
  "B",    "RD",     2,   0)
edges <- tibble::tribble(
  ~panel, ~from,    ~to,
  "A",    "FQ",     "RD",
  "A",    "Myopia", "FQ",
  "A",    "Myopia", "RD",
  "B",    "SES",    "FQ",
  "B",    "SES",    "Myopia",
  "B",    "U",      "Myopia",
  "B",    "U",      "RD",
  "B",    "FQ",     "RD") |>
  left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", from = "node")) |>
  left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", to = "node"), suffix = c("", "end")) |>
  mutate(shrink = 0.12,
         dx = xend - x, dy = yend - y, len = sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2),
         x = x + shrink * dx / len, y = y + shrink * dy / len,
         xend = xend - shrink * dx / len, yend = yend - shrink * dy / len)
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(2.5, "mm"), type = "closed"),
               colour = "grey35") +
  geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = node,
                               fill = node == "Myopia"),
             size = 3.6, label.size = 0, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#F2C14E", "FALSE" = "#DCE3EE")) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, labeller = as_labeller(c(A = "(A) Myopia as confounder",
                                               B = "(B) Myopia as collider"))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.3, 2.3), ylim = c(-0.3, 2.3)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))








Figure 7.2: Two causal models for fluoroquinolone (FQ) use, myopia and retinal detachment (RD). (A) Myopia as a confounder. (B) Myopia as a collider of low socioeconomic status (SES) and unknown causes of detachment (U): an M-structure. The FQ to RD arrow is the effect under study.





Which model is right is a question of subject-matter knowledge, not of the data. What a simulation can show is what each analysis does if (B) is true. We generate data in which fluoroquinolones have no effect on detachment, and estimate the odds ratio with and without adjustment for myopia, once with strong arrows into myopia and once with modest ones.


Code
one_mbias <- function(n = 20000, strength = 1.5) {
  ses    <- rnorm(n)                                    # low SES (standardised)
  u      <- rnorm(n)                                    # unknown causes of RD
  myopia <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + strength * ses + strength * u))
  fq     <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.5 + strength * ses))
  rd     <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-3 + strength * u))     # no effect of fq
  c(crude    = exp(coef(glm(rd ~ fq, family = binomial))[["fq"]]),
    adjusted = exp(coef(glm(rd ~ fq + myopia, family = binomial))[["fq"]]))
}
set.seed(2012)
mbias <- rbind(
  data.frame(arrows = "Strong (log OR 1.5)", t(replicate(200, one_mbias(strength = 1.5)))),
  data.frame(arrows = "Modest (log OR 0.5)", t(replicate(200, one_mbias(strength = 0.5)))))
mbias_summary <- mbias |>
  group_by(arrows) |>
  summarise(across(c(crude, adjusted), median))
kable(mbias_summary, digits = 3,
      col.names = c("Arrows into myopia", "Crude OR (median)", "Adjusted for myopia (median)"))





Arrows into myopia
Crude OR (median)
Adjusted for myopia (median)




Modest (log OR 0.5)
1.003
0.994


Strong (log OR 1.5)
1.003
0.755





The crude odds ratio is correct (close to 1) under model (B); adjusting for myopia biases it, to about 0.76 when the arrows into myopia are strong and to about 0.99 when they are modest. M-bias is real, but with modest arrows it is negligible; it could not have produced the 4.5-fold association we reported. The broader point stands: before adjusting for or restricting on a variable, ask whether it could be a consequence of both the exposure (or its causes) and the outcome (or its causes). Draw the causal diagram before choosing the adjustment set, not after.


7.2.4 Recognising selection bias in included studies
When appraising a study or a review, ask: could whether someone was enrolled, retained or analysed have depended on both their exposure and their outcome, or on causes of each? Table 7.4 maps common named biases onto that question.



Table 7.4: Named selection biases and how to recognise them.











Named bias
Typical setting
Red flag
Design or analytic remedy




Differential loss to follow-up
Cohorts with dropout related to exposure and prognosis
Attrition that differs between groups, without sensitivity analysis
Inverse probability of censoring weights; sensitivity analyses


Berkson’s bias
Hospital-based case-control studies
Exposure and disease both independently lead to admission
Population-based controls


Prevalent-user bias
Pharmacoepidemiology cohorts including existing users
Cohort entry is not treatment initiation
New-user (incident-user) design


Immortal time bias
Exposure defined by events after time zero
“Ever used”, or a second prescription, required for exposure
Align time zero, eligibility and treatment assignment (Section 3.2)


Over-adjustment and M-bias
Adjustment for a mediator or a collider
Variables measured after exposure, or adjusted “just in case”
Choose the adjustment set from a causal diagram


Control-selection bias
Case-control studies
Controls from a different setting or period from the cases
Sample controls from the population that produced the cases


Non-response and volunteer bias
Surveys, registries, voluntary participation
Low or unreported response rate
Non-response weighting; compare responders with non-responders








7.2.5 Reporting: MOOSE
MOOSE (Meta-analysis Of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) is a 35-item reporting checklist for meta-analyses of observational studies, organised under background, search strategy, methods, results, discussion and conclusions (9). Beyond what PRISMA 2020 asks, it requires reviews to list the confounders considered in the included studies, to justify the use of adjusted or unadjusted estimates, to describe how different effect measures were combined, and to report sensitivity analyses by study design. MOOSE dates from 2000 and has not been updated; reviews of observational studies should report against PRISMA 2020 and use MOOSE for these additional items.


7.2.6 Risk-of-bias tools for non-randomised studies
The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) awards up to nine stars for selection (four), comparability (two) and outcome (three) in cohort studies, with a parallel version for case-control studies. It remains popular because it is quick, but it has well-documented problems. Its items score what a paper reports, so it partly measures reporting; it is not outcome specific; it has no items for missing data or selective reporting; its stars are often summed and treated as a continuous “quality score”; and agreement between reviewers is poor. In 131 cohort studies, agreement ranged from substantial for length of follow-up to poor for selection of the non-exposed cohort, and the NOS score was not associated with effect estimates (10). Agreement between reviewers and the studies’ own authors was poorer still (11).
ROBINS-I judges a non-randomised study of an intervention against the target trial it is trying to emulate, in domains that parallel RoB 2: confounding, selection of participants, classification of interventions, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, measurement of outcomes and selection of the reported result, with overall judgements of low, moderate, serious or critical risk of bias (12) (see Section 5.5.2). Version 2, released in 2025, adds algorithms that map signalling questions to domain judgements and explicitly addresses immortal time bias, which the 2016 version did not; it has six domains (13). ROBINS-E applies the same approach to observational studies of exposures, such as environmental or occupational exposures, rather than interventions (14).
ROBINS-I and ROBINS-E take much longer than the NOS, but they ask the right question: how far is this estimate likely to be from the causal effect it claims to estimate?
