title: 7  Reporting and Appraising Systematic Reviews
section: 7.3 Was the review well conducted? AMSTAR 2
text:
7.3 Was the review well conducted? AMSTAR 2
AMSTAR 2 (A MeaSurement Tool to Assess systematic Reviews) appraises the conduct of a systematic review of healthcare interventions that includes randomised or non-randomised studies, or both (15). It has 16 items, seven of them designated critical because a flaw in them can invalidate a review’s results (Table 7.5). Items are answered “yes”, “partial yes” (for some items) or “no”; items 11, 12 and 15 also allow “no meta-analysis conducted”.



Table 7.5: The 16 items of AMSTAR 2; critical items marked.










Item
Content
Critical




1
Research question and inclusion criteria include the PICO components



2
Protocol established before the review, deviations justified
✓


3
Selection of study designs for inclusion explained



4
Comprehensive literature search
✓


5
Study selection performed in duplicate



6
Data extraction performed in duplicate



7
List of excluded studies, with reasons for exclusion
✓


8
Included studies described in adequate detail



9
Satisfactory technique for assessing risk of bias in individual studies
✓


10
Sources of funding of the included studies reported



11
Appropriate methods for statistical combination of results
✓


12
Impact of risk of bias in individual studies on the meta-analysis assessed



13
Risk of bias accounted for when interpreting or discussing the results
✓


14
Heterogeneity explained and discussed satisfactorily



15
Publication bias (small-study bias) investigated and its likely impact discussed
✓


16
Conflicts of interest, including funding of the review, reported







AMSTAR 2 deliberately does not produce a score. Instead, the pattern of flaws determines an overall confidence rating (15):

High: no or one non-critical weakness;
Moderate: more than one non-critical weakness (and no critical flaw);
Low: one critical flaw, with or without non-critical weaknesses;
Critically low: more than one critical flaw.

The rule is simple enough to write as a function, which makes it transparent and applies it identically to every review:


Code
critical_items <- c(2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15)

amstar2_rating <- function(ratings) {
  # ratings: character vector of 16 responses ("Yes", "Partial Yes", "No", "No MA")
  flaw <- ratings == "No"                 # "Partial Yes" and "No MA" are not flaws
  n_critical     <- sum(flaw[critical_items])
  n_noncritical  <- sum(flaw[-critical_items])
  if (n_critical > 1) "Critically low"
  else if (n_critical == 1) "Low"
  else if (n_noncritical > 1) "Moderate"
  else "High"
}



7.3.1 Profiles, not scores
Two reviews can receive the same rating for completely different reasons, and the reasons determine what a reader should do. Consider two constructed reviews:


Code
review_a <- rep("Yes", 16); review_a[c(2, 4)] <- "No"       # no protocol; narrow search
review_b <- rep("Yes", 16); review_b[c(11, 13)] <- "No"     # wrong model; RoB ignored
c(A = amstar2_rating(review_a), B = amstar2_rating(review_b))


               A                B 
"Critically low" "Critically low" 


Both are critically low. Review A was not registered and searched a single database, but assessed risk of bias properly, used appropriate methods and stated its conclusions with appropriate caution. Its main threat is missed studies: a targeted search of trial registers may show whether anything important is missing, and its estimate may be roughly right. Review B was registered and searched comprehensively, but pooled substantially heterogeneous trials with a fixed-effect model and drew conclusions that ignored its own risk-of-bias assessment. Its pooled estimate should not be used as it stands, although its extracted study-level data may support a reanalysis. Read the item profile, not just the overall rating.
A critically low rating means that safeguards protecting the validity of the review are missing, so confidence in its results is limited. It does not mean that the conclusions are wrong, that the underlying evidence is weak, or that the review should be ignored. Whether the missing safeguards actually distorted the conclusions is a separate judgement, which is what ROBIS adds.


7.3.2 How published reviews fare
The amstar2Vis package, which produces tables and figures of AMSTAR 2 appraisals, is distributed with ratings of 495 systematic reviews (1). Applying our function to them:


Code
amstar_reviews <- readr::read_csv("data/ch07/amstar2vis_reviews.csv",
                                  show_col_types = FALSE)
item_cols <- paste0("Item", 1:16)
amstar_reviews$overall <- apply(amstar_reviews[, item_cols], 1, amstar2_rating)
overall_tab <- table(factor(amstar_reviews$overall,
                            levels = c("High", "Moderate", "Low", "Critically low")))
overall_tab



          High       Moderate            Low Critically low 
            19              7             87            382 


Code
pct_no <- round(100 * colMeans(amstar_reviews[, item_cols] == "No"))   # % rated "No", by item




Code
amstar_reviews |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(item_cols), names_to = "item", values_to = "rating") |>
  mutate(item_no = as.integer(sub("Item", "", item)),
         item = paste0(item_no, ifelse(item_no %in% critical_items, "*", "")),
         item = factor(item, levels = rev(unique(item[order(item_no)]))),
         rating = factor(rating, levels = c("No", "Partial Yes", "Yes", "No MA"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = item, fill = rating)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No" = "#C8102E", "Partial Yes" = "#F2C14E",
                               "Yes" = "#2E7D32", "No MA" = "grey70"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Percentage of reviews", y = "AMSTAR 2 item") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 7.3: AMSTAR 2 item ratings across 495 systematic reviews; critical items are marked with an asterisk. Data distributed with the amstar2Vis package (1).





Only 26 of the 495 reviews (5%) reach moderate or high confidence. The failures are concentrated in a few items: no list of excluded studies with reasons (item 7, 84% of reviews), no report of the included studies’ funding (item 10, 73%), no protocol established in advance (item 2, 65%) and no explanation of the choice of study designs (item 3, 65%). Because items 2 and 7 are critical, these two failures alone make most reviews critically low. The package documentation describes the ratings only as data from a published paper, so the sample’s representativeness is unknown; but low ratings for most published reviews are the usual finding.






Using AMSTAR 2 efficiently



Start with the critical items most likely to change your view: was there a protocol (item 2), was the search comprehensive (item 4), was risk of bias assessed and used (items 9 and 13), were the methods appropriate (item 11), was publication bias considered (item 15)? Rate the rest afterwards, and keep the rating sheet as you go rather than reconstructing it at the end.

title: 7  Reporting and Appraising Systematic Reviews
section: 7.4 Are the conclusions at risk of bias? ROBIS
text:
7.4 Are the conclusions at risk of bias? ROBIS
ROBIS (Risk Of Bias In Systematic reviews) asks a different question from AMSTAR 2: not whether the safeguards were in place, but whether the review’s process plausibly distorted its results and conclusions (16). It applies to reviews of interventions, diagnosis, prognosis and aetiology, and has three phases:

Relevance (optional): does the question addressed by the review match the user’s target question?
Concerns with the review process, in four domains: (1) study eligibility criteria; (2) identification and selection of studies; (3) data collection and study appraisal; (4) synthesis and findings. Signalling questions (yes, probably yes, probably no, no, no information) lead to a judgement of low, high or unclear concern for each domain.
Risk of bias in the review: low, high or unclear, judged by asking whether the interpretation of the findings addressed the concerns from phase 2, whether the relevance of the included studies was considered, and whether the reviewers avoided emphasising results on the basis of their statistical significance.

Phase 3 is not a sum of the domains. A review whose included trials are all at high risk of bias can still be at low risk of bias itself, if it assessed that risk properly and took it into account in its conclusions (16).

7.4.1 ROBIS in practice
Suppose you are advising on statins for adults aged 75 or older without cardiovascular disease, and you find this (constructed) review: Statins and all-cause mortality in older adults.

Eligibility: adults aged 60 or older, with or without cardiovascular disease; randomised trials and cohort studies; statin versus placebo or no statin; outcome all-cause mortality. Protocol registered before the search, no changes reported.
Search: MEDLINE, Embase and the Cochrane Library; no trial registers or grey literature. Titles and abstracts screened by one reviewer.
Appraisal: the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale applied to all studies, trials included, with one global score per study; the scores were not used in the synthesis.
Synthesis: 12 trials and cohorts pooled in a single random-effects model; I² = 58%, described as “moderate, not clinically important”; heterogeneity not explored; no prediction interval, absolute effects or GRADE.
Conclusion: “Statins significantly reduce all-cause mortality in older adults.”




Table 7.6: ROBIS assessment of a constructed review.










ROBIS
Judgement
Reason




Phase 1: relevance
Partly relevant
Includes ages 60 and over, with and without CVD, and does not report results by age or by prior CVD


Domain 1: eligibility
Low concern
Criteria specified in a protocol registered before the search


Domain 2: identification and selection
High concern
No registers or grey literature, so unpublished trials may be missing; single screener


Domain 3: data collection and appraisal
High concern
A tool designed for cohort studies applied to trials; one global score per study; not linked to conclusions


Domain 4: synthesis and findings
High concern
Trials and cohorts pooled together; substantial heterogeneity dismissed and unexplored; no certainty assessment


Phase 3: risk of bias in the review
High
The interpretation addresses none of these concerns, and the conclusion rests on statistical significance






The review is at high risk of bias and only partly answers the question. Its conclusion should not be used to support a recommendation for adults over 75 without primary prevention trials in that group, or a better review.


7.4.2 AMSTAR 2 and ROBIS compared
The two tools examine much the same features of a review but make different judgements (Table 7.7). AMSTAR 2 is a checklist: a missing safeguard is a flaw, whatever its consequences. ROBIS asks whether the flaws could have changed the findings. A review with no registered protocol and no list of excluded studies may be critically low on AMSTAR 2 yet at low risk of bias on ROBIS if neither omission plausibly affected its conclusions; a review that satisfies most AMSTAR 2 items can still be at high risk on ROBIS if its synthesis misrepresents the evidence.



Table 7.7: AMSTAR 2 and ROBIS.











AMSTAR 2
ROBIS




Question
Were the safeguards of a rigorous review in place?
Are the review’s results and conclusions likely to be biased?


Approach
16 items, 7 critical; a missing item is a flaw
Signalling questions; judgement of likely impact in 4 domains


Output
Confidence: high, moderate, low, critically low
Risk of bias: low, high, unclear


Content found only here
Protocol, PICO, list of excluded studies, funding of included studies, conflicts of interest
Relevance to the user’s question; whether the interpretation addressed the concerns


Scope
Reviews of healthcare interventions
Interventions, diagnosis, prognosis, aetiology






Use AMSTAR 2 to document how a review was conducted; use ROBIS when you must decide whether to act on its conclusions.

title: 7  Reporting and Appraising Systematic Reviews
section: 7.5 Do the conclusions outrun the evidence? Spin
text:
7.5 Do the conclusions outrun the evidence? Spin
Spin is reporting that makes results look more favourable than they are, whatever the motive. In a study of 72 randomised trials with statistically nonsignificant primary outcomes, spin appeared in the conclusions of 58% of abstracts and in the main-text conclusions of 50% of reports (17). Spin also changes how readers interpret results. In the SPIIN trial, 300 clinicians were randomised to read cancer trial abstracts with or without spin; those who read the spun versions rated the experimental treatment as more beneficial (18). A systematic review of 35 studies of spin found it in more than a quarter of systematic reviews and meta-analyses that had been assessed for it (19).
Systematic reviews have their own forms of spin. A classification developed with members of Cochrane identified 39 types, grouped as misleading reporting, misleading interpretation and inappropriate extrapolation; the three judged most severe were recommendations for practice not supported by the findings, a misleading title, and selective reporting (20).
Common forms of spin in reviews include:

emphasising a significant secondary outcome or subgroup when the primary outcome is null;
reporting relative effects without absolute effects, or without the baseline risk;
describing a nonsignificant result as “a trend towards benefit”;
making recommendations stronger than the GRADE certainty allows;
giving harms less prominence than benefits.

The last point connects spin to Chapter 6: spin is the gap between the certainty of the evidence and the confidence of the conclusions, and GRADE, applied honestly, is the best protection against it.

7.5.1 Spotting and correcting spin
Here is a constructed abstract conclusion, followed by the facts it summarises.

Conclusion: Drug X significantly reduces hospitalisation and should be considered for all patients with condition Y.

Results: six trials. Primary outcome, all-cause mortality: RR 0.94 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.08). Secondary outcome, hospitalisation: RR 0.85 (0.74 to 0.98); control-group risk 8% per year. GRADE: low certainty for hospitalisation (risk of bias, imprecision). Serious adverse events reported only in the supplement.
The conclusion promotes a secondary outcome over a null primary outcome, omits the absolute effect, ignores the low certainty, extrapolates to “all patients” and leaves out harms. A conclusion consistent with the evidence would read:

Conclusion: Drug X did not clearly reduce mortality (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.08). It may reduce hospitalisation (about 12 fewer per 1000 patients per year), but the certainty of this evidence is low. Serious adverse events are summarised in the supplement. Better-conducted trials are needed before the drug can be recommended.

section: 7.6 A sequence for appraising a published review
text:
7.6 A sequence for appraising a published review
The tools of this and the previous chapters fit together into a structured first pass (Table 7.8). It surfaces the most consequential flaws efficiently, but it is a floor, not a ceiling: a borderline or methodologically complex review can take much longer to appraise properly.



Table 7.8: A seven-step sequence for appraising a systematic review.











Step
Tool
Question
Red flags




1
PRISMA 2020
Is the review completely reported?
Missing items 7, 13, 16, 22, 24


2
ROBIS phase 1
Does it address my question?
PICO mismatch with the decision at hand


3
AMSTAR 2 items 2, 4, 7
Protocol, comprehensive search, justified exclusions?
No registration; one database; no list of exclusions


4
AMSTAR 2 items 9, 11, 13, 15
Risk of bias assessed and used? Appropriate methods? Publication bias considered?
One global quality score; heterogeneity ignored; risk of bias absent from the conclusions


5
ROBIS phase 2 and 3
Are the conclusions at risk of bias?
High concern for synthesis and findings, not addressed in the interpretation


6
GRADE
What is the certainty for each outcome?
No certainty ratings; no summary-of-findings table


7
Spin
Do the conclusions match the certainty?
Strong recommendations from low-certainty evidence; no absolute effects; abstract contradicts primary outcome

title: 7  Reporting and Appraising Systematic Reviews
text:
Key points

A review can fail in its reporting, its conduct or its interpretation, independently of the quality of the studies it includes; each needs its own tool.
PRISMA 2020 checks reporting; complete reporting is necessary but not sufficient.
In reviews of observational studies, the design of the primary studies matters more than the pooling model. Selection bias within a sample is conditioning on a collider, and adjustment can create bias as well as remove it.
Prefer ROBINS-I (version 2) or ROBINS-E to the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.
AMSTAR 2 gives a confidence rating from the pattern of critical and non-critical flaws; read the profile, not just the rating.
ROBIS judges whether the review’s conclusions are at risk of bias, and whether the review answers your question.
Spin is common, influences readers, and is the gap between the certainty of the evidence and the confidence of the conclusions.

title: 7  Reporting and Appraising Systematic Reviews
text:
Exercises

Choose a published systematic review in your field. Check PRISMA 2020 items 7, 13, 22, 23 and 24, and compare the date of registration with the date of the search.
Rate the same review with AMSTAR 2, record your answers as a vector, and compute the overall rating with amstar2_rating(). Then apply ROBIS. Do the two tools agree? If not, which matters more for your purpose?
In mbias-sim, make fluoroquinolones truly harmful by adding + 1 * fq to the linear predictor for rd, so that the odds ratio conditional on u is 2.72. How do the crude and myopia-adjusted odds ratios compare with it? Why would neither be expected to equal it exactly? (Hint: the odds ratio is not collapsible, Section 8.2.3.)
Modify collider-sim so that only income affects the chance of a visit. Is there still a spurious association? Explain using Table 7.3.
Find one sentence of spin in the abstract or conclusions of your chosen review, and rewrite it to match the GRADE certainty.

20. Yavchitz A, Ravaud P, Altman DG, Moher D, Hróbjartsson A, Lasserson T, et al. A new classification of spin in systematic reviews and meta-analyses was developed and ranked according to the severity. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. 2016;75:56–65.

title: 8  Effect Measures
text:
8.1 What a meta-analysis needs from each study
Before results can be combined across studies they need a common currency: a statistic that captures the direction and size of the effect and can be computed from every study. Section 3.5 showed what to extract. This chapter develops the measures themselves: how they are computed, how precisely they are estimated, how they behave, and how to choose among them. Chapter 9 shows how they are pooled.
Most meta-analytic methods need just two numbers from each study: an estimate of the effect and its variance (or standard error). Everything else about a study, its size, its design, its raw data, enters only through these two quantities, and the variance determines the study’s weight. This “two-stage” approach treats each study’s estimate as normally distributed with a known variance. That works well for large studies and is approximate for small studies, rare events and zero cells; methods that work directly from the counts (Mantel-Haenszel, Peto, binomial likelihoods) are covered in Section 9.6.
The choice of measure is not a technicality. It determines what question the meta-analysis answers, whether pooling across studies is coherent, and how the result can be communicated.

title: 8  Effect Measures
text:
8.1.1 Estimates, not P values
A P value mixes two things: the size of an effect and the precision with which it was measured. For an estimate \(d\) with standard error \(SE_d\), the test statistic is \(Z = d/SE_d\), and \(|Z| > 1.96\) exactly when the 95% confidence interval \(d \pm 1.96\,SE_d\) excludes the null. Testing and estimation answer the same question, but only the estimate keeps the size and the precision apart.


Code
two_studies <- data.frame(study = c("A", "B"), effect = c(0.50, 0.50), se = c(0.20, 0.05)) |>
  mutate(z = effect / se, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)))
kable(two_studies, digits = c(0, 2, 2, 1, 4))

title: 8  Effect Measures
text:
8.2 Binary outcomes
All binary effect measures come from the same 2×2 table (Table 8.1).



Table 8.1: Notation for a two-arm trial with a binary outcome.






Event
No event
Total




Treated
\(a\)

\(n_1 = a + b\)


Control
\(c\)
\(d\)
\(n_0 = c + d\)






With risks \(p_1 = a/n_1\) and \(p_0 = c/n_0\):
\[
RD = p_1 - p_0, \qquad RR = \frac{p_1}{p_0}, \qquad OR = \frac{p_1/(1-p_1)}{p_0/(1-p_0)} = \frac{ad}{bc}.
\]

8.2.1 Computing the measures and their precision
Ratio measures are skewed, so they are analysed on the log scale, where their sampling distributions are approximately normal. Their variances come from the delta method, which approximates the variance of a function \(g(X)\) by \([g'(E[X])]^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)\):
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\log RR) \approx \frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{c} - \frac{1}{n_0}, \qquad
\mathrm{Var}(\log OR) \approx \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} + \frac{1}{d},
\]
\[
\mathrm{Var}(RD) = \frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n_0}.
\]
The approximations are good when no cell is small. For a trial in which 15 of 100 treated and 30 of 100 control patients have an event:


Code
a <- 15; b <- 85; c <- 30; d <- 70
n1 <- a + b; n0 <- c + d
p1 <- a / n1; p0 <- c / n0

rd    <- p1 - p0
se_rd <- sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n1 + p0 * (1 - p0) / n0)
log_rr    <- log(p1 / p0)
se_log_rr <- sqrt(1/a - 1/n1 + 1/c - 1/n0)
log_or    <- log((a * d) / (b * c))
se_log_or <- sqrt(1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d)

binary_ex <- tibble::tibble(
  measure  = c("Risk difference", "Risk ratio", "Odds ratio"),
  estimate = c(rd, exp(log_rr), exp(log_or)),
  lower    = c(rd - 1.96 * se_rd, exp(log_rr - 1.96 * se_log_rr), exp(log_or - 1.96 * se_log_or)),
  upper    = c(rd + 1.96 * se_rd, exp(log_rr + 1.96 * se_log_rr), exp(log_or + 1.96 * se_log_or)))
kable(binary_ex, digits = 3)

Hand calculation builds intuition and lets you check a package’s output, for example when its default continuity correction for zero cells differs from what you expected.


8.2.2 Risk ratio or odds ratio?
In the example the risk falls from 30% to 15%: the RR is 0.50, a 50% reduction in risk, while the OR is 0.41, a 59% reduction in odds. Both are correct, but they describe different quantities, and an OR read as if it were an RR overstates the effect. The two are close only when the outcome is rare in both groups; as a rule of thumb, they diverge noticeably once risks exceed about 10% (1). Given the control risk \(p_0\), an OR can be converted to the corresponding RR:
\[ RR = \frac{OR}{1 - p_0 + p_0 \times OR}. \]
The OR has properties that explain its popularity in meta-analysis:

It is symmetric in the outcome. The OR for “event” is the reciprocal of the OR for “no event”, so it does not matter which way the outcome is coded. The RR lacks this property: here the RR for an event is 0.50, but the RR for remaining event-free is 1.21, not 2.00, and a meta-analysis of RRs can give different conclusions depending on which outcome is analysed (2).
It is bounded sensibly. Any OR is compatible with any baseline risk, whereas an RR of 2 is impossible if the control risk exceeds 50%.
It is what case-control studies and logistic regression estimate.

The RR is easier to interpret and more often what readers think they are being told. Either is defensible; the choice should be pre-specified, and the result should always be translated into absolute terms.


8.2.3 The odds ratio is not collapsible
A less familiar property of the OR matters for meta-analysis. Suppose a trial enrols equal numbers of low-risk and high-risk patients, with control risks of 20% and 60%, and treatment doubles the odds of the event in both groups. There is no confounding: risk group is balanced by randomisation.


Code
risk_from_or <- function(p0, or) { odds <- p0 / (1 - p0) * or; odds / (1 + odds) }
p0_strata <- c(low = 0.2, high = 0.6)
p1_strata <- risk_from_or(p0_strata, or = 2)
p0_all <- mean(p0_strata); p1_all <- mean(p1_strata)

collapse <- rbind(
  "Within each stratum" = c(OR = 2, RR_low = p1_strata[[1]] / p0_strata[[1]],
                            RR_high = p1_strata[[2]] / p0_strata[[2]]),
  "Whole trial"         = c(OR = (p1_all / (1 - p1_all)) / (p0_all / (1 - p0_all)),
                            RR_low = p1_all / p0_all, RR_high = p1_all / p0_all))
round(collapse, 2)


                      OR RR_low RR_high
Within each stratum 2.00   1.67    1.25
Whole trial         1.77   1.35    1.35


The OR is 2 in each stratum but 1.77 in the trial as a whole, even though nothing is confounded. The OR is non-collapsible: the marginal (unadjusted) OR is not an average of the conditional ones. The RR is collapsible: the whole-trial RR of 1.35 lies between the stratum RRs. Hazard ratios are also non-collapsible. Two practical consequences follow. First, in a randomised trial, adjusting an OR or HR for prognostic covariates changes the estimate even without confounding, because the adjusted and unadjusted analyses estimate different quantities; the adjusted estimate is further from 1. Second, a meta-analysis that mixes adjusted and unadjusted ORs or HRs combines estimates of different quantities, and the review should say which it used and why.


8.2.4 Absolute effects: risk difference and NNT
The risk difference is the measure that matters for decisions: how many events a treatment prevents (or causes) per 100 or 1000 people treated. Its reciprocal is the number needed to treat (NNT), here 1/0.15 ≈ 7. Conventionally the NNT is rounded up. Two cautions apply. The NNT refers to a specific follow-up period, which must be stated. And when the confidence interval for the RD includes zero, the interval for the NNT runs through infinity, from a number needed to treat to benefit to a number needed to harm, so it should be reported with care, or the RD reported instead.
The absolute effect depends on baseline risk. With the same RR of 0.5:


Code
nnt_tab <- tibble::tibble(baseline_risk = c(0.30, 0.10, 0.02)) |>
  mutate(rd = baseline_risk * (0.5 - 1), nnt = ceiling(1 / abs(rd)))
kable(nnt_tab, digits = 3, col.names = c("Baseline risk", "Risk difference", "NNT"))





Baseline risk
Risk difference

8.2.5 Which measure is stable across studies?
If a treatment’s effect were constant on the RR scale, studies in populations with different baseline risks would show different RDs and ORs (Figure 8.1). The RD would then appear heterogeneous across studies purely because baseline risks differ.


Code
tibble::tibble(p0 = seq(0.01, 0.6, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(`Risk ratio` = 0.5,
         `Odds ratio` = (0.5 * p0 / (1 - 0.5 * p0)) / (p0 / (1 - p0)),
         `Risk difference` = p0 * (0.5 - 1)) |>
  pivot_longer(-p0, names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(p0, value, colour = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Risk ratio" = "#041E42", "Odds ratio" = "#F28E2B",
                                 "Risk difference" = "#C8102E"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Baseline (control) risk", y = "Value of the measure") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 8.1: Risk difference and odds ratio when the risk ratio is constant at 0.50, as baseline (control) risk varies.





Which measure is actually constant is an empirical question. In an empirical comparison across meta-analyses from 551 systematic reviews, the RR and OR were on average more consistent across trials than the RD, with no difference on average between the RR and the OR (2). This supports the standard workflow, which the summary-of-findings tables of Section 6.10 follow:

pool on a relative scale (RR or OR);
choose a baseline risk that represents the population of interest, which need not be the trials’ average;
convert: \(RD = p_0 \times (RR - 1)\), and report the NNT for a stated period;
report both: the relative effect for the synthesis, the absolute effect for the decision.







A relative effect alone is not an answer



A pooled RR or OR without a baseline risk tells clinicians the direction of an effect but not its size for their patients. An RR of 0.5 means an NNT of 4 or of 100, depending on whom you treat.

title: 8  Effect Measures
text:
8.3 Continuous outcomes

8.3.1 Mean difference
When all studies measure the outcome on the same scale (blood pressure in mmHg, HbA1c in %), the mean difference (MD), \(\bar X_1 - \bar X_2\), is the natural measure: its units are clinically meaningful. Its variance can be estimated allowing different SDs in the two groups, \(S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2\), or from a pooled SD, \(S_p^2(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)\), which assumes equal population SDs. metafor::escalc() uses the first by default. The two coincide when the groups are the same size and differ otherwise:


Code
md_ex <- data.frame(m1i = 103, sd1i = 5.5, n1i = 40, m2i = 100, sd2i = 4.5, n2i = 60)
sp2   <- with(md_ex, ((n1i - 1) * sd1i^2 + (n2i - 1) * sd2i^2) / (n1i + n2i - 2))
c(escalc_default  = escalc(measure = "MD", m1i = m1i, sd1i = sd1i, n1i = n1i,
                           m2i = m2i, sd2i = sd2i, n2i = n2i, data = md_ex)$vi,
  unequal_by_hand = with(md_ex, sd1i^2 / n1i + sd2i^2 / n2i),
  pooled_sd       = with(md_ex, sp2 * (1 / n1i + 1 / n2i))) |> round(3)


 escalc_default unequal_by_hand       pooled_sd 
          1.094           1.094           1.010 


Paired designs. In crossover trials and before-after comparisons, each participant contributes both measurements. The SD of the within-person differences is \(S_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{S_1^2 + S_2^2 - 2rS_1S_2}\), where \(r\) is the correlation between the two measurements, and \(SE = S_{\text{diff}}/\sqrt n\):


Code
paired <- tibble::tibble(r = c(0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99)) |>
  mutate(sd_diff = sqrt(10^2 + 10^2 - 2 * r * 10 * 10), se_md = sd_diff / sqrt(50))
kable(paired, digits = 2, col.names = c("Correlation r", "SD of differences", "SE of MD"),
      caption = "Standard error of a paired mean difference with SDs of 10 and n = 50.")

The stronger the correlation, the more between-person variation the pairing removes. Papers often report the two means and SDs but not the correlation; treating paired data as independent (\(r = 0\)) overstates the uncertainty, giving the study too little weight. If \(r\) is unknown, borrow it from a similar study and check the sensitivity of the results.


8.3.2 Standardised mean difference
When studies measure the same construct on different scales (different depression questionnaires or pain scales), the MDs cannot be pooled. The standardised mean difference (SMD) divides each by a standard deviation, putting all studies in SD units:

Cohen’s d uses the pooled SD: \(d = (\bar X_1 - \bar X_2)/S_p\), with \(\mathrm{Var}(d) \approx \frac{n_1 + n_2}{n_1 n_2} + \frac{d^2}{2(n_1 + n_2)}\).
Hedges’ g corrects the small-sample upward bias of d: \(g = d \times \left(1 - \frac{3}{4(n_1 + n_2) - 9}\right)\). This is the usual choice in meta-analysis and what escalc(measure = "SMD") returns.
Glass’s Δ divides by the control-group SD alone, appropriate when the intervention may change the variability of the outcome.



Code
escalc(measure = "SMD", m1i = m1i, sd1i = sd1i, n1i = n1i,
       m2i = m2i, sd2i = sd2i, n2i = n2i, data = md_ex)

Cohen’s benchmarks of 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 for small, medium and large effects (3) were offered as rough guides for the behavioural sciences and are no substitute for clinical judgement. The SMD has other drawbacks. It depends on how variable the study population is, so the same treatment effect gives a larger SMD in a homogeneous trial population than in a diverse one. It is hard to interpret clinically. And it should not be used when all studies share a scale. A pooled SMD can be translated back into the units of a familiar instrument by multiplying it by a typical SD of that instrument in the relevant population.


8.3.3 Correlations: Fisher’s z
Correlations have a skewed sampling distribution whose variance depends on the true correlation, so they are pooled on Fisher’s z scale, \(z = \tfrac12 \ln\frac{1+r}{1-r}\), with variance approximately \(1/(n-3)\), and back-transformed for presentation. The dat.molloy2014 dataset in metafor contains the correlations between conscientiousness and medication adherence in 16 studies (4):


Code
molloy <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR", ri = ri, ni = ni, data = dat.molloy2014,
                 slab = paste(authors, year, sep = ", "))
res_molloy <- rma(yi, vi, data = molloy)
predict(res_molloy, transf = transf.ztor)



   pred  ci.lb  ci.ub   pi.lb  pi.ub 
 0.1488 0.0878 0.2087 -0.0371 0.3248 




Code
forest(res_molloy, atransf = transf.ztor,
       at = transf.rtoz(c(-0.4, -0.2, 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6)),
       xlab = "Correlation (r)", header = "Study")








Figure 8.2: Correlation between conscientiousness and medication adherence in 16 studies, pooled on Fisher’s z scale and back-transformed (4).





The pooled correlation is 0.15 (95% CI 0.09 to 0.21), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 62%): the prediction interval, -0.04 to 0.32, includes no association at all.

title: 8  Effect Measures
text:
8.4 Time-to-event outcomes

8.4.1 The hazard ratio
The hazard at time \(t\) is the instantaneous event rate among those still event-free at \(t\). The hazard ratio (HR) compares the hazards in two groups, \(HR(t) = h_1(t)/h_0(t)\). Its advantages over a risk ratio at a fixed time are that it uses all the follow-up and handles censoring. Reporting a single HR, however, assumes proportional hazards: that the ratio is constant over time.
The veteran dataset in the survival package comes from a randomised trial of standard versus test chemotherapy in advanced lung cancer (5). We fit Cox models without and with adjustment for performance status (Karnofsky score) and age:


Code
vet <- survival::veteran |>
  mutate(trt = factor(trt, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Standard", "Test")))
fit_unadj <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ trt, data = vet)
fit_adj   <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + karno + age, data = vet)
rbind(unadjusted = summary(fit_unadj)$conf.int["trtTest", c(1, 3, 4)],
      adjusted   = summary(fit_adj)$conf.int["trtTest", c(1, 3, 4)]) |> round(2)


           exp(coef) lower .95 upper .95
unadjusted      1.02      0.71      1.45
adjusted        1.21      0.84      1.74


The HR moves from 1.02 to 1.21 with adjustment. In a randomised trial this is not removal of confounding: partly it reflects chance imbalance in performance status, and partly the non-collapsibility of the HR (Section 8.2.3). Neither estimate is statistically significant.


8.4.2 Checking proportional hazards
Kaplan-Meier curves make no assumption about proportionality and should be examined before any HR is trusted (Figure 8.3).


Code
km <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ trt, data = vet)
tibble::tibble(time = km$time, surv = km$surv,
               arm = rep(sub("trt=", "", names(km$strata)), km$strata)) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, surv, colour = arm)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Standard = "#C8102E", Test = "#041E42"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Days", y = "Survival probability") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 8.3: Kaplan-Meier survival curves for standard and test chemotherapy in the veteran lung cancer trial. The curves cross.





The test arm does worse early and better late, so the curves cross between about 150 and 200 days. A formal check uses scaled Schoenfeld residuals: at each event time, the difference between the covariate value of the person who had the event and its expected value among those at risk. Under proportional hazards these show no trend with time.


Code
zph <- cox.zph(fit_adj)
zph


        chisq df       p
trt     0.284  1 0.59439
karno  12.003  1 0.00053
age     2.100  1 0.14735
GLOBAL 19.102  3 0.00026




Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(zph)








Figure 8.4: Scaled Schoenfeld residuals against time for each covariate in the adjusted Cox model, with a smoothed trend and ±2 SE band. A trend indicates a non-proportional effect.





There is no evidence against proportional hazards for treatment (P = 0.59), but strong evidence for Karnofsky score (P < 0.001): the prognostic effect of performance status fades with time. A model that assumes it is constant is misspecified, and the treatment HR from it should be interpreted with that in mind. The test is not perfectly sensitive, and the crossing curves are a warning that a single treatment HR summarises an effect that changes sign.
When hazards are not proportional, alternatives include reporting HRs for separate periods, survival curves, or the restricted mean survival time (RMST), the area under the survival curve up to a chosen time, which is the average event-free time over that period (6):


Code
rmst <- summary(km, rmean = 400)$table[, c("rmean", "se(rmean)")]
rmst


                rmean se(rmean)
trt=Standard 121.0250   13.6685
trt=Test     115.6425   15.7712


Over 400 days, patients on standard chemotherapy lived on average 121 days and those on the test drug 116 days, a difference of 5 days, which is easy to interpret and does not depend on proportional hazards.


8.4.3 The hazards of hazard ratios
The Women’s Health Initiative randomised trial of combined hormone therapy reported an overall HR for coronary heart disease of 1.24 after an average of 5.2 years (7). (8) used the trial’s year-by-year results (Figure 8.5) to show two problems with HRs, even in a randomised trial with no confounding.


Code
whi <- tibble::tibble(
  year = factor(c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6+"), levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6+")),
  cases_ht = c(42, 38, 19, 32, 29, 28), rate_ht = c(0.50, 0.45, 0.23, 0.39, 0.41, 0.37),
  cases_pl = c(23, 28, 15, 25, 19, 37), rate_pl = c(0.29, 0.35, 0.19, 0.32, 0.28, 0.56),
  hr = c(1.81, 1.34, 1.27, 1.25, 1.45, 0.70),
  lo = c(1.09, 0.82, 0.64, 0.74, 0.81, 0.42),
  hi = c(3.01, 2.18, 2.50, 2.12, 2.59, 1.14))
ggplot(whi, aes(year, hr)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1.24, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#C8102E") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = "#041E42") +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Year of follow-up", y = "Hazard ratio (log scale)")








Figure 8.5: Hazard ratios for coronary heart disease by year of follow-up in the Women’s Health Initiative trial of estrogen plus progestin. Data from Table 2 of (7); the dashed line is the overall HR of 1.24.





First, the overall HR depends on the length of follow-up. It is a weighted average of period-specific HRs that fall from 1.81 in year 1 to 0.7 after year 5. A trial stopped after one year would have reported an 80% increase in risk; a much longer trial might have reported almost none.
Second, the period-specific HRs carry a built-in selection bias. The HR in year 6 is computed only among women who were still free of coronary disease at the start of year 6. If women vary in their susceptibility, hormone therapy removes the most susceptible women from the treated arm early, so the survivors in that arm are less susceptible than those in the placebo arm. This differential depletion of susceptibles can push later HRs below 1 even if the treatment is never protective for anyone.
Hernán’s recommendation is to report survival (or cumulative risk) curves, with adjustment where needed, which also give absolute risks directly. In year 1 the annual rates were 0.50% and 0.29%: an HR of 1.8, but an absolute difference of about two events per 1000 women per year.


8.4.4 Other time-to-event measures
For rare events over short periods the HR, RR and OR are close; with common events and long follow-up they diverge. When participants can have the outcome more than once (hospitalisations, exacerbations, seizures), an analysis of time to first event discards information, and a rate ratio, events per person-time in each group, modelled with Poisson or negative binomial regression to allow for overdispersion, is more appropriate. Heart failure trials increasingly report total (first and recurrent) hospitalisations this way. Rate ratios and hazard ratios estimate different quantities and should not be pooled together.

Good practice in reporting:

Pre-specify the primary effect measure in the protocol, and justify it rather than adopting whatever the studies reported.
For binary outcomes, report both relative and absolute effects, with the baseline risk on which the absolute effect is based and the time period of the NNT.
Report confidence intervals, and back-transform log-scale estimates for presentation.
Say whether adjusted or unadjusted estimates were pooled, and why.
For time-to-event outcomes, check proportional hazards, state the follow-up period, and show survival curves where possible.

title: 8  Effect Measures
text:
Key points

A meta-analysis combines, for each study, an estimate and its variance; effect sizes, not P values, are the currency.
Ratio measures are analysed on the log scale; their variances come from the delta method.
The OR approximates the RR only for rare outcomes; it is symmetric in the outcome coding but not collapsible, so adjusted and unadjusted ORs (and HRs) estimate different quantities.
Relative effects are usually more consistent across studies than risk differences; pool on a relative scale and convert to absolute effects for a stated baseline risk.
Use the MD when studies share a scale and the SMD only when they do not; account for pairing in paired designs.
A single HR assumes proportional hazards and depends on the length of follow-up; check the assumption, and prefer survival curves or RMST when it fails.

title: 8  Effect Measures
text:
Exercises

For the four SGLT2 inhibitor trials of Section 6.2, compute the RR, OR and RD for the composite outcome in each trial with escalc(). Which measure varies most across trials, relative to its standard error?
Using the OR-to-RR conversion, find the control risk at which an OR of 0.5 corresponds to an RR of 0.6.
Extend noncollapsible to a trial with three equally sized strata with control risks of 10%, 40% and 70%. What is the marginal OR when the conditional OR is 3?
In paired-r, how large must r be for the paired SE to be half the unpaired SE?
For the veteran trial, compute the RMST at 200 and at 600 days. How and why does the difference between arms change?
Read the WHI report and recompute the absolute difference in coronary events per 1000 women for each year of follow-up from Figure 8.5. Does the absolute picture tell the same story as the HRs?

title: 9  Meta-Analysis Models
text:
9.1 Should the studies be combined?
Chapter 8 developed the effect measures that are the currency of meta-analysis: for each study, an estimate and its variance. This chapter shows how those estimates are combined. The arithmetic is simple, and metafor::rma() does it in one line. The judgements are not: whether to combine at all, what model to assume, how to estimate the between-study variance, how to build the interval, and how to describe what remains unexplained. Each choice can change the answer, and the second half of the chapter shows by how much, using a published meta-analysis whose conclusion turns out to rest on them.
Every model in this chapter starts from the same decomposition:
\[\text{Observed effect}_i = \text{True effect}_i + \text{Sampling error}_i .\]
The models differ in what they assume about the true effects (one common value, or a distribution of values) and about the sampling error (normal with a known variance, or modelled exactly from the counts).
Pooling is a scientific judgement, not a default. The question is not “can these studies be pooled?” (any set of numbers can be averaged) but “what would the pooled estimate estimate, and is that a meaningful quantity?” Before any statistics, compare the studies’ populations, interventions, comparators and outcomes, the PICO elements of Section 3.1 (see also Section 3.1.6). A summary of trials in heart failure with reduced and with preserved ejection fraction, or of placebo-controlled and active-controlled trials, is an average over different questions. If the studies are clinically too different, a stratified analysis or a structured narrative synthesis is more honest than a single number. A statistically significant pooled estimate from clinically incompatible studies is still misleading.

title: 9  Meta-Analysis Models
text:
9.1.1 Why vote counting fails
The traditional alternative to pooling is to count how many studies were “positive” (statistically significant) and how many were not. Vote counting discards the direction, size and precision of every estimate, gives every study the same vote whatever its size, and treats “not significant” as “no effect” (1). When the studies are individually underpowered, it reaches the wrong answer, and adding more studies makes it more confidently wrong.
Figure 9.1 simulates 33 trials of a treatment that truly reduces risk by 20% (RR 0.80) in a population with a 10% control risk. The trials are of typical size for many fields, between 100 and 800 patients per arm.


Code
set.seed(629)
k      <- 33
p0     <- 0.10                                # control risk
rr     <- 0.80                                # true risk ratio
n_arm  <- round(runif(k, 100, 800))           # patients per arm
ev_c   <- rbinom(k, n_arm, p0)
ev_t   <- rbinom(k, n_arm, p0 * rr)

vote <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = ev_t, n1i = n_arm, ci = ev_c, n2i = n_arm,
               data = data.frame(trial = 1:k, n_arm, ev_t, ev_c))
vote <- summary(vote) |>                      # adds ci.lb, ci.ub and the z test
  mutate(signif = ci.ub < 0)                  # CI excludes 1, in favour of treatment
fit_vote <- rma(yi, vi, data = vote, method = "REML")

n_sig  <- sum(vote$signif)
n_harm <- sum(vote$ci.lb > 0)
power  <- mean(map_lgl(n_arm, \(n) power.prop.test(n = n, p1 = p0, p2 = p0 * rr)$power > 0.8))




Code
vote_plot <- vote |>
  mutate(rr = exp(yi), lo = exp(ci.lb), hi = exp(ci.ub),
         trial = reorder(factor(trial), n_arm))
pooled <- with(fit_vote, c(est = exp(b[1]), lo = exp(ci.lb), hi = exp(ci.ub)))

ggplot(vote_plot, aes(y = trial)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rr, colour = "#B22222", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_point(aes(x = rr, shape = signif, size = n_arm), colour = "#041E42") +
  annotate("polygon", x = pooled[c("lo", "est", "hi", "est")],
           y = c(-1, -0.4, -1, -1.6), fill = "#E69F00") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 1, `TRUE` = 16),
                     labels = c("Not significant", "Significant"), name = NULL) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3.5, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.8, 1, 2, 4)) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(2.2, 0.6))) +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio (log scale); trials ordered by size", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())








Figure 9.1: Thirty-three simulated trials of a treatment with a true risk ratio of 0.80. Filled points: confidence interval excludes 1. The diamond is the random-effects pooled estimate.





Only 2 of the 33 trials are statistically significant, and none significantly favours control. A vote count reads this as “conflicting evidence, mostly negative”. Yet the point estimates of 26 trials favour treatment, and the pooled estimate, RR 0.84 (0.78 to 0.91), recovers the true effect with good precision. The “negative” trials are not evidence against the treatment; they are too small to detect it. Here, not one of the trials had 80% power for the true effect. Doubling the number of trials would leave the proportion of significant results about the same, so the vote count would still say “mostly negative”, while the pooled interval would narrow around the truth. Vote counting is not a conservative alternative to meta-analysis but a biased one.

title: 9  Meta-Analysis Models
text:
9.2 The fixed-effect model
The fixed-effect (or common-effect) model assumes that every study estimates the same true effect θ, so that all differences between the study estimates \(\hat\theta_i\) are sampling error. The best combination of estimates with variances \(v_i\) is then the inverse-variance weighted mean:
\[w_i = \frac{1}{v_i}, \qquad \hat\theta_{IV} = \frac{\sum w_i \hat\theta_i}{\sum w_i}, \qquad \text{Var}(\hat\theta_{IV}) = \frac{1}{\sum w_i}.\]
Precise studies have small variances and large weights. The weighted mean is the minimum-variance unbiased combination when the assumption holds, and inverse-variance weighting is the backbone of every model in this chapter: what changes between models is the weight, not the principle.


Code
logRR <- c(-0.35, -0.28, -0.41)               # three studies, log risk ratios
se    <- c(0.12, 0.08, 0.15)
w     <- 1 / se^2
theta <- sum(w * logRR) / sum(w)
se_th <- sqrt(1 / sum(w))

fe_check <- rma(yi = logRR, sei = se, method = "EE")   # metafor's "equal effects" model
tibble::tibble(
  Study  = c("1", "2", "3", "Pooled (by hand)", "Pooled (rma)"),
  Weight = c(sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * w / sum(w)), "", ""),
  RR     = sprintf("%.2f", exp(c(logRR, theta, fe_check$b[1]))),
  `95% CI` = c(sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", exp(logRR - 1.96 * se), exp(logRR + 1.96 * se)),
               sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", exp(theta - 1.96 * se_th), exp(theta + 1.96 * se_th)),
               sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", exp(fe_check$ci.lb), exp(fe_check$ci.ub)))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")

Study 2 has the smallest standard error and carries more than half the weight. In a forest plot the area of each square is proportional to this weight.
The fixed-effect assumption is plausible when the studies are near-identical replications, and its answer is narrow: the best estimate of the effect in these studies. It is implausible when populations, doses, durations or comparators differ, and it gives no basis for generalising beyond the studies included. metafor calls it the equal-effects model (method = "EE"); the label “fixed effects” (method = "FE") is used for a subtly different model, in which the true effects may differ but inference is confined to their weighted average in the included studies. The point estimates and intervals are identical.

title: 9  Meta-Analysis Models
text:
9.3 The random-effects model
The random-effects model lets each study have its own true effect, drawn from a distribution with mean μ and variance τ²:
\[\hat\theta_i = \mu + u_i + e_i, \qquad u_i \sim N(0, \tau^2), \qquad e_i \sim N(0, v_i).\]
There are now two sources of variation: the within-study sampling error \(v_i\), and the between-study variance τ² in the true effects. The weights become
\[w_i^* = \frac{1}{v_i + \hat\tau^2},\]
with four consequences:

The interval for μ is wider, because each study is now less informative about the mean.
The weights are more equal. When τ² is large relative to the \(v_i\), every study receives similar weight, and a single large trial no longer dominates. This is not always desirable: small studies are more prone to bias (Chapter 15), and the random-effects model gives them relatively more influence.
The estimand changes. \(\hat\mu\) is the average of a distribution of true effects, not a single true effect. If the trials of a drug enrolled different populations, μ describes the average population studied, which may correspond to no real patient group.
The prediction interval becomes essential, because the spread of true effects, not just the uncertainty in their mean, is now part of the answer (Section 9.4.1).

The choice between the models is a substantive claim about the evidence, not a statistical convenience, and it should be made before seeing the results. When the two give very different answers, usually because small studies differ systematically from large ones, that is a finding to explain rather than a nuisance to resolve by picking one.

9.3.1 Estimating τ²
τ² is not observed and has to be estimated from the scatter of the study estimates, which with a handful of studies is very imprecise. Many estimators exist (2). The oldest and best known, from (3), is a moment estimator built on Cochran’s Q:
\[Q = \sum w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_{IV})^2, \qquad \hat\tau^2_{DL} = \max\left(0,\; \frac{Q - (k-1)}{\sum w_i - \sum w_i^2/\sum w_i}\right), \qquad w_i = 1/v_i.\]
If the studies share one effect, Q has expectation \(k - 1\); any excess is attributed to τ², truncated at zero. The estimator is simple and closed-form, but it tends to underestimate τ² when heterogeneity is substantial, which makes intervals for μ too narrow.



Table 9.1: Estimators of the between-study variance τ².











Estimator
metafor

Performs well in simulations

The ML estimator is biased low for the same reason that a sample variance divided by \(n\) rather than \(n-1\) is: it measures spread around an estimated mean as if it were the true one. REML corrects for this, as DL does through the \(k-1\) in its formula. Simulation studies show no estimator best in all conditions, but favour REML and Paule-Mandel over DL (2,4). DL was for decades the only option in Cochrane’s RevMan software, so most published meta-analyses use it. Since 2024, the Cochrane Handbook recommends REML as the default, and RevMan now uses it (5). metafor’s default has always been REML.


9.3.2 The confidence interval for μ
The standard (Wald) interval for μ is
\[\hat\mu \pm 1.96\,\sqrt{\text{Var}(\hat\mu)}, \qquad \text{Var}(\hat\mu) = \frac{1}{\sum w_i^*},\]
which treats the weights, and therefore \(\hat\tau^2\), as if they were known. With few studies they are not, and the interval is too narrow: its coverage can fall well below 95%. The Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) interval (6,7) makes two changes. It replaces 1.96 by a t quantile with \(k-1\) degrees of freedom (2.78 for five studies, 2.57 for six), and it rescales the variance by how much the studies actually scatter around \(\hat\mu\):
\[\hat\mu \pm t_{k-1,\,0.975}\sqrt{\text{Var}^*(\hat\mu)}, \qquad \text{Var}^*(\hat\mu) = \frac{\sum w_i^*(\hat\theta_i - \hat\mu)^2}{(k-1)\sum w_i^*}.\]
In simulations the HKSJ interval keeps close to its nominal coverage where the Wald interval does not (8). In metafor it is test = "knha", after Knapp and Hartung, who extended it to meta-regression (9); in meta it is method.random.ci = "HK".
The rescaling has a catch. When the studies scatter less than their variances predict, the rescaling factor is below 1, and the HKSJ interval can be narrower than the Wald interval, which is not a sensible correction for uncertainty (10). The usual fix is to use the larger of the two variances, test = "adhoc" in metafor (adhoc.hakn.ci = "se" in meta). Current Cochrane Handbook guidance is to consider HKSJ when \(\hat\tau^2 > 0\) and there are more than two studies, and to check that it is not narrower than the Wald interval (5). With very few studies, two or three, the HKSJ interval can be so wide as to be uninformative, which is an honest statement of how little a few studies say about a variance.

title: 9  Meta-Analysis Models
text:
9.4 Quantifying heterogeneity
Four statistics describe heterogeneity. They answer different questions, and no one of them is sufficient. The BCG vaccine trials, whose forest plots were drawn in Section 4.3, are a good illustration: their results are scattered far more widely than sampling error can explain.


Code
bcg <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg,
              data = dat.bcg, slab = paste(author, year))
m_bcg  <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg, method = "REML")
ci_het <- confint(m_bcg)$random                 # Q-profile intervals for tau^2, I^2
pr_bcg <- predict(m_bcg, transf = exp)





Table 9.2: Four ways of describing the heterogeneity of the BCG trials (REML; ranges are 95% confidence intervals).











Statistic
BCG trials
What it answers
Limitations




Cochran’s Q
152 on 12 df, P < 0.001
Is there more variation than chance predicts?
A test, not a measure; low power with few studies, too much with many large ones


I²

Relative: depends on study size as much as on heterogeneity


τ² (τ)

Prediction interval
RR 0.15 to 1.55

Relies on normally distributed true effects; unstable with few studies






Cochran’s Q is a test of the hypothesis that all studies share one effect. Because it has little power when there are few studies, a threshold of P < 0.10 is often used; with many large studies it detects trivial differences. A non-significant Q is not evidence of homogeneity.
I² is the proportion of the total variation in the estimates that is due to between-study variation rather than chance (11). In its original form, \(I^2 = (Q - (k-1))/Q\), truncated at zero; metafor and the current RevMan compute it from \(\hat\tau^2\) instead. I² is the most reported and most misread of the four. It is not an absolute measure of heterogeneity: because sampling error shrinks as studies get larger, the same τ² gives a higher I² in a meta-analysis of large trials than of small ones (12). An I² of 90% can describe heterogeneity too small to matter clinically, and an I² of 30% heterogeneity large enough to reverse a decision. Its confidence interval, rarely reported, is usually wide; for the BCG trials it is 82% to 98% even with 13 trials.
τ² is the variance of the true effects, so τ is their standard deviation on the scale of analysis. For the BCG trials τ = 0.56 on the log RR scale: even if μ were known exactly, 95% of true RRs would lie between about 0.16 and 1.47. Turner and colleagues collected τ² from thousands of Cochrane meta-analyses, which gives a sense of what is typical for different outcomes and comparisons (13); Chapter 13 uses these as prior distributions.

9.4.1 The prediction interval
The prediction interval combines τ² with the uncertainty in \(\hat\mu\) to describe where the true effect in a new study, or a new setting, is likely to lie (14,15):
\[\hat\mu \pm t_{k-2,\,0.975}\sqrt{\hat\tau^2 + \text{Var}(\hat\mu)}.\]
The t distribution with \(k-2\) degrees of freedom is the convention proposed by (14) and used by the meta package. Software differs: metafor’s predict() uses the normal quantile after a standard (Wald) fit and a t quantile with \(k-1\) degrees of freedom after test = "knha", and RevMan offers both. With few studies the choice matters, and the method should be stated.
For the BCG trials the average effect is clear, RR 0.49 (0.34 to 0.70): BCG roughly halves the risk of tuberculosis on average. The prediction interval, 0.15 to 1.55, says that in a new setting the vaccine could be anything from highly protective to useless. The confidence interval and the prediction interval answer different questions, and they behave differently as evidence accumulates. Figure 9.2 simulates meta-analyses of increasing size from a population of true effects like the BCG trials’.


Code
sim_width <- function(k, tau = 0.56, mu = log(0.5)) {
  se  <- runif(k, 0.15, 0.6)
  yi  <- rnorm(k, mu, tau) + rnorm(k, 0, se)
  fit <- rma(yi, sei = se, method = "REML", test = "knha", control = ctl)
  p   <- predict(fit)
  c(ci = fit$ci.ub - fit$ci.lb, pi = p$pi.ub - p$pi.lb)
}
set.seed(2026)
widths <- map_dfr(c(5, 10, 20, 40, 80), \(k) {
  w <- replicate(500, tryCatch(sim_width(k), error = \(e) c(ci = NA, pi = NA)))
  tibble::tibble(k = k, `Confidence interval for the mean` = median(w["ci", ], na.rm = TRUE),
                 `Prediction interval` = median(w["pi", ], na.rm = TRUE))
}) |>
  pivot_longer(-k, names_to = "interval", values_to = "width")

ggplot(widths, aes(k, width, colour = interval)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2 * 1.96 * 0.56, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(5, 10, 20, 40, 80)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#041E42", "#B22222"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Number of studies (log scale)", y = "Width on the log RR scale") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 9.2: Width of the 95% confidence interval for the mean and of the 95% prediction interval, as studies are added. Simulated trials with true log risk ratios drawn from N(log 0.5, 0.56²) and within-study standard errors of 0.15 to 0.6; median of 500 simulations at each size. The dashed line is the width of the true 95% range of effects.





The confidence interval for the mean narrows roughly as \(1/\sqrt{k}\). The prediction interval narrows at first, as τ² and μ become better estimated, and then levels off at the true spread of effects: more trials like these would pin down the average, but not the effect in any particular setting. “BCG halves the risk of tuberculosis on average” is well supported; “BCG will halve the risk in your population” is not. Chapter 10 asks why the BCG trials differ.
Prediction intervals are not a cure-all. They assume normally distributed true effects, they are unreliable when there are few studies, and the Cochrane Handbook urges caution in reporting them for small meta-analyses (5). But a meta-analysis that reports only the confidence interval for μ, with substantial heterogeneity, describes the average and leaves readers to assume that it applies to them.


9.4.2 Statistical and clinical importance
Neither a significant pooled estimate nor a low I² says whether an effect matters. Figure 9.3 shows five hypothetical results against both the null (RR 1.0) and a minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of a 15% relative reduction (RR 0.85).


Code
scen <- tibble::tibble(
  id    = LETTERS[1:5],
  label = c("Not significant; important effect unlikely",
            "Not significant; important effect possible",
            "Significant; not clinically important",
            "Significant; important effect possible",
            "Significant and clinically important"),
  lo = c(0.884, 0.712, 0.865, 0.757, 0.609),
  hi = c(1.118, 1.074, 0.989, 0.926, 0.777)) |>
  mutate(est = sqrt(lo * hi), y = factor(id, levels = rev(LETTERS[1:5])))

ggplot(scen, aes(y = y)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.85, colour = "#E69F00", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.2, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_point(aes(x = est), size = 2.4, colour = "#B22222") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 1.17, label = label), hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.84, y = 5.6, label = "MCID", hjust = 1, colour = "#b07800") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.01, y = 5.6, label = "No effect", hjust = 0) +
  scale_x_log10(limits = c(0.58, 2.3), breaks = c(0.6, 0.7, 0.85, 1, 1.15)) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.5, 0.9))) +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio (95% CI), log scale", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())








Figure 9.3: Five hypothetical risk ratios (95% CI) compared with no effect (RR 1.0) and a minimal clinically important difference (RR 0.85).





A result is statistically significant if its interval excludes 1.0, and clearly clinically important only if the whole interval lies beyond the MCID. Neither implies the other. The same reading applies to a meta-analysis, with one addition: compare the prediction interval, not only the confidence interval, with the MCID. The relation between P values, intervals and decisions is taken up in Chapter 11.

title: 9  Meta-Analysis Models
text:
9.5 A published meta-analysis, reproduced
In 1996 JAMA published a meta-analysis of six small randomised trials that added unfractionated heparin to aspirin in unstable angina (16). The primary outcome was myocardial infarction or death during randomised treatment. The authors pooled the trials with a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model, reported a summary of 0.67 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.02), and concluded that their findings were “consistent with a 33% reduction in risk” and that most patients with unstable angina should receive both drugs.


Code
heparin <- tibble::tribble(
  ~study,           ~ev_asa, ~n_asa, ~ev_hep, ~n_hep,
  "Theroux 1988",        4,    121,       2,    122,

hep_rr <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = ev_hep, n1i = n_hep, ci = ev_asa, n2i = n_asa,
                 data = heparin, slab = study)

9.5.1 What was actually pooled?
The article’s tables label the summary a risk ratio, but its methods say odds ratios were pooled with 0.5 added to zero cells. Reproducing the summary settles which.


Code
dl_rr <- rma(yi, vi, data = hep_rr, method = "DL")
dl_or <- rma(yi, vi, data = hep_or, method = "DL")
f_ci  <- \(m) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(m$b[1]), exp(m$ci.lb), exp(m$ci.ub))
tibble::tibble(Analysis = c("As published", "DerSimonian-Laird, risk ratio",
                            "DerSimonian-Laird, odds ratio"),
               `Summary (95% CI)` = c("0.67 (0.44 to 1.02)", f_ci(dl_rr), f_ci(dl_or))) |>
  kable()





Analysis

The odds ratio reproduces the published result; the risk ratio does not. The summary is an odds ratio labelled as a risk ratio. With control risks up to 30%, the two diverge (Section 8.2.2), and the labelled “33% reduction in risk” is a 33% reduction in the odds. Only by trying to reproduce the analysis does the inconsistency come to light.


9.5.2 How much do the analytic choices matter?
The published analysis made three choices: the odds ratio, the DL estimator of τ², and a Wald interval. Figure 9.4 repeats the analysis with each of the seven estimators of Table 9.1, on both scales, with Wald and HKSJ intervals and a prediction interval.


Code
ests <- c("DL", "HE", "PM", "ML", "REML", "EB", "SJ")
fit_one <- function(method, dat) {
  z  <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = method, control = ctl)
  hk <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = method, test = "adhoc", control = ctl)
  pk <- predict(hk, transf = exp)
  tibble::tibble(method, tau2 = z$tau2, est = exp(z$b[1]),
                 wald_lo = exp(z$ci.lb), wald_hi = exp(z$ci.ub),
                 hk_lo = exp(hk$ci.lb), hk_hi = exp(hk$ci.ub),
                 pi_lo = pk$pi.lb, pi_hi = pk$pi.ub)
}
grid <- bind_rows(
  map_dfr(ests, fit_one, dat = hep_or) |> mutate(scale = "Odds ratio"),
  map_dfr(ests, fit_one, dat = hep_rr) |> mutate(scale = "Risk ratio"))
g <- \(m, s = "Odds ratio") filter(grid, method == m, scale == s)




Code
grid |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = rev(ests))) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = pi_lo, xmax = pi_hi), height = 0, colour = "#B22222",
                 linewidth = 0.6, position = position_nudge(y = -0.25)) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = hk_lo, xmax = hk_hi), height = 0, colour = "#041E42",
                 linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = wald_lo, xmax = wald_hi), height = 0, colour = "#041E42",
                 linewidth = 2.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = est), shape = 21, fill = "#E69F00", size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 4.2, label = sprintf("tau^2 == '%.3f'", tau2)), parse = TRUE,
            hjust = 1, size = 3.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale) +
  scale_x_log10(limits = c(0.25, 4.2), breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Summary (aspirin + heparin vs aspirin), log scale",
       y = "Estimator of the between-study variance")








Figure 9.4: The heparin meta-analysis repeated with seven estimators of τ², on the odds ratio and risk ratio scales. Thick bar: Wald 95% CI. Thin bar: HKSJ 95% CI (never narrower than Wald). Red: 95% prediction interval. Labels give the estimated τ².





Three things stand out.

Five of seven estimators find τ² = 0 on both scales, including DL, so the published “random-effects” analysis is the fixed-effect analysis. REML and SJ find some heterogeneity (on the odds ratio scale τ² = 0.013 and 0.035). With six small trials, “τ² = 0” means only that the trials cannot detect heterogeneity, not that there is none: the REML confidence interval for τ² runs from 0 to 0.37.
The interval never excludes 1. The published Wald interval, 0.44 to 1.02, already included no effect. With HKSJ intervals the upper limit rises to between 1.15 and 1.18, because with six trials the t multiplier is 2.57 rather than 1.96.
The prediction interval is wide. Under REML on the odds ratio scale it runs from 0.35 to 1.25: a new trial could plausibly show a large reduction in the odds of MI or death, or an increase.

The evidence amounted to 68 events among 655 patients on aspirin and 55 among 698 on aspirin and heparin, a difference of 13 events in more than 1300 patients, with no reduction in mortality, mostly unblinded trials, and a composite outcome in which a small infarction counted as much as a death. Writing about it at the time, I argued that these data were consistent with no additional benefit from heparin, that further trials were needed, and that for lower-risk patients the bleeding risk might outweigh an uncertain benefit. The point is not that the authors were wrong to pool, but that “consistent with a 33% reduction” describes one point in a range of results that is equally consistent with none, and that the range widens with every defensible change to the analysis.

title: 9  Meta-Analysis Models
text:
9.6 Methods for binary outcomes
The inverse-variance methods above treat each study’s log odds ratio as normally distributed with a known variance. With small trials and few events, both approximations are poor, and a trial with a zero cell has no finite log odds ratio unless something is added to the cells. Two older methods work directly from the 2×2 tables.

9.6.1 Mantel-Haenszel
For trial \(i\) with \(a_i\) events among \(n_{1i}\) treated patients, \(c_i\) among \(n_{0i}\) controls, and \(b_i\), \(d_i\) the corresponding non-events, the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio is
\[\widehat{OR}_{MH} = \frac{\sum_i a_i d_i / n_i}{\sum_i b_i c_i / n_i}.\]
Each trial adds its own within-trial products to the numerator and the denominator. Nothing is logged or inverted, so a trial with no events in one arm still contributes (it adds zero to one sum and a positive amount to the other), and a trial with no events in either arm drops out, correctly, because it says nothing about the relative effect. The method has equivalents for the RR and RD, is a fixed-effect method, and performs well with sparse data (17). In metafor it is rma.mh(); in meta, metabin(method = "MH").


9.6.2 Peto
Peto’s one-step method compares the observed events in the treated arm, \(O_i = a_i\), with those expected if treatment had no effect, \(E_i = n_{1i}(a_i + c_i)/n_i\):
\[\widehat{OR}_{Peto} = \exp\left(\frac{\sum_i (O_i - E_i)}{\sum_i V_i}\right),\]
where \(V_i\) is the hypergeometric variance of \(O_i\). It handles single zero cells without correction and performs well when events are rare, arms are balanced and the effect is modest. It is biased when the odds ratio is far from 1 or the arms are very unequal in size (17). In metafor it is rma.peto().


Code
iv   <- rma(yi, vi, data = hep_or, method = "EE")
mh   <- rma.mh(measure = "OR", ai = ev_hep, n1i = n_hep, ci = ev_asa, n2i = n_asa, data = heparin)
peto <- rma.peto(ai = ev_hep, n1i = n_hep, ci = ev_asa, n2i = n_asa, data = heparin)
tibble::tibble(Method = c("Inverse variance (0.5 added to Cohen 1990)", "Mantel-Haenszel", "Peto"),
               `Odds ratio (95% CI)` = c(f_ci(iv), f_ci(mh), f_ci(peto))) |>
  kable(caption = "Fixed-effect odds ratio for the heparin trials, three ways.")



Fixed-effect odds ratio for the heparin trials, three ways.


Method
Odds ratio (95% CI)




Inverse variance (0.5 added to Cohen 1990)
0.67 (0.45 to 1.01)


Mantel-Haenszel
0.66 (0.44 to 0.99)


Peto
0.67 (0.45 to 0.99)





The three agree closely here, because events are not very rare, arms are balanced and only one trial has a zero cell. Yet the Mantel-Haenszel and Peto intervals just exclude 1 and the inverse-variance interval just includes it, another reminder that a result this close to the boundary should not be summarised by which side of 0.05 it falls on.


9.6.3 Never add up the tables
A tempting shortcut is to add the events and patients across trials into a single 2×2 table. This breaks randomisation, which guarantees comparable arms only within each trial. When trials differ in their baseline risk and in their allocation ratio, the shortcut produces Simpson’s paradox.


Code
toy <- tibble::tibble(trial = c("A (high risk, 4:1 allocation)", "B (low risk, 1:4 allocation)"),
                      ev_t = c(160, 8), n_t = c(400, 100), ev_c = c(50, 40), n_c = c(100, 400))
toy_or <- escalc(measure = "OR", ai = ev_t, n1i = n_t, ci = ev_c, n2i = n_c, data = toy)
odds   <- \(e, n) e / (n - e)
added  <- with(toy, odds(sum(ev_t), sum(n_t)) / odds(sum(ev_c), sum(n_c)))
mh_toy <- rma.mh(measure = "OR", ai = ev_t, n1i = n_t, ci = ev_c, n2i = n_c, data = toy)
tibble::tibble(Analysis = c(toy$trial, "Both trials added into one table", "Mantel-Haenszel, by trial"),
               `Odds ratio` = sprintf("%.2f", c(exp(toy_or$yi), added, exp(mh_toy$b[1])))) |>
  kable(align = "lr")





Analysis
Odds ratio




A (high risk, 4:1 allocation)
0.67


B (low risk, 1:4 allocation)
0.78


Both trials added into one table
2.31


Mantel-Haenszel, by trial
0.69





Both trials show benefit, but the added table shows harm, because most treated patients come from the high-risk trial and most controls from the low-risk one. The comparison across trials is confounded by trial. Stratifying by trial, as Mantel-Haenszel and every other method in this chapter does, recovers the benefit. The same error appeared in a published meta-analysis of male circumcision and HIV infection (Section 6.4), and Chapter 10 shows a subtler version of the paradox that affects meta-regression.


9.6.4 Zero cells and rare events
Safety outcomes are often rare, and many trials record no events at all in one or both arms. The options are:

A continuity correction, conventionally 0.5 added to every cell of a trial with a zero. Simple, but arbitrary, and it biases the estimate towards no effect, more so when the arms are unbalanced. Alternatives that scale the correction to the size of the opposite arm perform better (18).
Mantel-Haenszel or Peto, which need no correction for single-zero trials. Both drop trials with no events in either arm.
Exact or likelihood-based methods that model the counts with binomial or hypergeometric distributions, including logistic random-effects models (rma.glmm() in metafor).
Bayesian models, which model the counts directly and can keep double-zero trials (Chapter 13).

The choice can matter. In 2007 Nissen and Wolski pooled 42 trials of rosiglitazone with Peto’s method and found an increased risk of myocardial infarction, OR 1.43 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.98), P = 0.03 (19). Many trials had no infarctions in either arm and so contributed nothing. Reanalyses of the same trials with other methods and other handling of the zero-event trials gave estimates that were often no longer statistically significant (20). The result shaped regulatory action on both sides of the Atlantic, and the controversy was partly about statistical method rather than data. For rare events, report how zero cells were handled and show that the conclusion survives other reasonable choices.

title: 9  Meta-Analysis Models
section: 9.7 A first look at Bayesian meta-analysis
text:
9.7 A first look at Bayesian meta-analysis
The random-effects model has a natural Bayesian form: the same structure, with prior distributions placed on μ and τ, updated by the data into posterior distributions. Two features make it attractive for meta-analysis. First, τ is poorly estimated from a few studies, and an informed prior, such as the empirical distributions of (13), stabilises it and carries its uncertainty through to the estimate of μ, which the frequentist plug-in approach ignores. Second, the posterior answers questions that clinicians actually ask, such as the probability that the treatment reduces risk by more than the MCID. Chapter 12 fits a first Bayesian model to a real example, and Chapter 13 develops the approach.

title: 9  Meta-Analysis Models
text:
Key points

Decide whether to pool on clinical grounds first. Vote counting is not an alternative: it confuses “not significant” with “no effect” and becomes more wrong as underpowered studies accumulate.
Every standard method is an inverse-variance weighted mean; the fixed-effect and random-effects models differ in the weights and in what the summary estimates.
The random-effects mean is the average of a distribution of true effects. Estimate τ² with REML or Paule-Mandel rather than DerSimonian-Laird, and recognise that with few studies every estimate of τ² is imprecise.
With few studies, the Wald interval for μ is too narrow; use the HKSJ interval, guarded so that it is never narrower than Wald, and report the choice.
Report Q, I², τ² and a prediction interval. I² is relative, not an absolute measure of heterogeneity; the prediction interval is the most clinically meaningful.
Reproduce before you trust: the heparin meta-analysis pooled odds ratios labelled as risk ratios, and its conclusion depended on choices that no one would notice from the abstract.
For sparse binary data, use Mantel-Haenszel or likelihood-based methods, show sensitivity to the handling of zero cells, and never pool by adding 2×2 tables.

title: 9  Meta-Analysis Models
text:
Exercises

Rerun vote-sim with 330 trials instead of 33. What proportion are significant? What happens to the pooled interval?
Compute \(\hat\tau^2_{DL}\) for the BCG trials by hand from Q and the fixed-effect weights, and check it against rma(method = "DL").
For the BCG trials, compare the Wald and HKSJ intervals and the prediction intervals from metafor’s predict() with one built by hand with \(t_{k-2}\). How different are they with 13 trials? Repeat with the first five trials only.
In the heparin analysis, remove Holdright 1994, the largest trial. How do the summary, τ² and the prediction interval change under DL and REML?
Construct a pair of trials, like simpson-toy, in which both trials show harm but the added table shows benefit.
Fit rma.glmm(measure = "OR", model = "UM.FS") to the heparin trials. How does it compare with the inverse-variance and Mantel-Haenszel results?
