title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
10.1 Explaining heterogeneity: meta-regression
Chapter 9 described heterogeneity: how much the true effects vary, and what that means for a new setting. This chapter asks two further questions. Can the heterogeneity be explained? And how robust is the pooled result to the studies included and the methods chosen? The first is answered, cautiously, by meta-regression; the second by a set of sensitivity analyses that every meta-analysis should plan in advance.
The 13 BCG vaccine trials of Section 9.4 disagree far more than chance allows: I² is over 90%, and the prediction interval runs from strong protection to none. Rather than stop at “the pooled effect is unreliable”, we can ask why the trials differ. The hypothesis of long standing, put forward before these trials were assembled, is geographic: BCG protects less near the equator (1).
Code
bcg   <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg,
                data = dat.bcg, slab = paste(author, year))
m_bcg <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg, method = "REML", test = "knha")

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
10.1.1 The model
The random-effects model of Section 9.3 has two layers: each observed log RR \(y_i\) is the trial’s true effect plus sampling error, and the true effects scatter around a mean μ:
\[y_i = \theta_i + \varepsilon_i,\quad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, v_i); \qquad \theta_i = \mu + u_i,\quad u_i \sim N(0, \tau^2).\]
Meta-regression replaces the single mean by a line in a study-level covariate, here the trial’s absolute latitude:
\[\theta_i = \alpha + \beta\,\text{latitude}_i + u_i, \qquad u_i \sim N(0, \tau^2_{\text{res}}).\]
\(\alpha\) is the predicted log RR at the equator, \(\beta\) the change in log RR per degree of latitude, and \(\tau^2_{\text{res}}\) the heterogeneity left over once latitude is accounted for. The model is a weighted regression in which each trial’s weight is \(1/(v_i + \tau^2_{\text{res}})\) (2,3).


Code
m_reg <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = bcg, method = "REML", test = "knha")
m_reg



Mixed-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of residual heterogeneity):     0.0764 (SE = 0.0591)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):             0.2763
I^2 (residual heterogeneity / unaccounted variability): 68.39%
H^2 (unaccounted variability / sampling variability):   3.16
R^2 (amount of heterogeneity accounted for):            75.62%

Test for Residual Heterogeneity:
QE(df = 11) = 30.7331, p-val = 0.0012

Test of Moderators (coefficient 2):
F(df1 = 1, df2 = 11) = 12.5905, p-val = 0.0046

Model Results:

         estimate      se     tval  df    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub     
intrcpt    0.2515  0.2839   0.8857  11  0.3948  -0.3735   0.8764     
ablat     -0.0291  0.0082  -3.5483  11  0.0046  -0.0472  -0.0111  ** 

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Each degree of latitude away from the equator multiplies the RR by 0.971 (95% CI 0.954 to 0.989), a further relative reduction in risk of about 2.9% per degree. The predicted RR is 1.29 at the equator, no protection at all, and 0.30 at 50°. Figure 10.1 shows the fit.


Code
regplot(m_reg, mod = "ablat", pi = TRUE, shade = c("grey80", "grey92"),
        xlab = "Absolute latitude (degrees from the equator)",
        ylab = "Log risk ratio (BCG vs control)", bg = "#B22222")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey40")








Figure 10.1: Meta-regression of the BCG trials on absolute latitude. Point area is proportional to the trial’s weight. Inner band: 95% confidence interval for the mean log RR at each latitude. Outer band: 95% prediction interval for a new trial.







10.1.2 R² and residual I²
The output reports R² = 76% and a residual I² of 68%. Both are correct, because they measure different things.
R² is the proportional reduction in τ² when latitude is added: from 0.313 to 0.076, \((\tau^2 - \tau^2_{\text{res}})/\tau^2\) = 76%. I² compares the remaining τ² with the trials’ sampling variances. These are mostly large trials with small sampling variances (a typical value is about 0.035), so even the reduced τ² dominates and I² stays high. The residual τ of 0.28 means that at any given latitude the true RRs still vary by a factor of about 1.7 either way. Latitude explains much of the heterogeneity, not all of it.


10.1.3 The Knapp-Hartung adjustment in meta-regression
By default, rma() treats the standard errors of the coefficients as known and tests the moderator with a χ² statistic. Those standard errors depend on \(\hat\tau^2\), estimated from 13 trials, so the default tests are too liberal. test = "knha" applies the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman logic of Section 9.3.2: it rescales the standard errors by the scatter of the trials around the regression line and uses t and F distributions with \(k - p\) degrees of freedom (4). Here the moderator test becomes F(1, 11) = 12.6, P = 0.005, compared with χ²(1) = 16.4, P = 5.2e-05 by default. The evidence for latitude survives the adjustment; weaker moderators often do not. REML is preferable to ML for τ² in meta-regression for the reason given in Section 9.3.1: ML ignores the degrees of freedom used by the coefficients, and each moderator uses one more.


10.1.4 A moderator is not a confounder
Latitude here is an effect modifier: a characteristic that changes the size of the treatment effect. It is not a confounder of the BCG effect, because within each trial the vaccine was randomised. Figure 10.2 makes the distinction.


Code
nodes <- tibble::tibble(x = c(0, 3, 1.5), y = c(0, 0, 2),
                        lab = c("BCG\n(randomised)", "Tuberculosis", "Latitude\n(mycobacterial\nexposure)"))
ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.6, y = 0, xend = 2.35, yend = 0, linewidth = 1.2,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), colour = "#041E42") +
  annotate("segment", x = 1.95, y = 1.6, xend = 2.8, yend = 0.35, linewidth = 0.8,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")), colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("segment", x = 1.5, y = 1.45, xend = 1.5, yend = 0.1, linewidth = 1,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), type = "closed"), colour = "#B22222") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.6, y = 0.8, label = "effect\nmodification", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.6, colour = "#B22222", lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.55, y = 1.15, label = "baseline\nrisk", size = 3.4,
           colour = "grey35", lineheight = 0.9) +
  geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = lab), size = 4, fill = "#F4F6F8", lineheight = 0.9) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.5, 3.5), ylim = c(-0.4, 2.5)) +
  theme_void()








Figure 10.2: Latitude affects the baseline risk of tuberculosis (grey), which randomisation balances between arms, and modifies the effect of BCG (red, an arrow into the BCG-to-TB arrow). There is no arrow from latitude to BCG within a trial.





Within a trial everyone shares the same latitude, so there is nothing to “adjust for”. The question “does the BCG effect change with latitude?” is a question about the treatment effect across trials, with the effect estimate as the outcome and latitude as the covariate. Meta-regression is the study-level analogue of a treatment-by-latitude interaction.
A plausible mechanism, stated before the analysis, is what distinguishes a credible moderator from a lucky one. For latitude there are two. Non-tuberculous mycobacteria in soil and water are more common in warm, humid regions, and childhood exposure to them may give partial immunity, so that BCG adds little, or may block the replication of the live vaccine; and BCG, a live vaccine, may lose viability in tropical conditions (1). Latitude is a proxy for these mechanisms, not the mechanism itself.


10.1.5 But study-level covariates can be confounded
Although the vaccine was randomised within each trial, latitude was not randomised across trials. Trials at different latitudes also differ in when they were done, how they allocated participants, which BCG strain they used and how they diagnosed tuberculosis. Any of these can masquerade as a latitude effect, or hide one. The BCG data record two such characteristics, year of publication and method of allocation.


Code
fit_mod <- function(f) {
  m <- rma(yi, vi, mods = f, data = bcg, method = "REML", test = "knha")
  tibble::tibble(Moderators = deparse(f[[2]]) |> sub(pattern = "ablat", replacement = "latitude") |>
                   sub(pattern = "alloc", replacement = "allocation method"), `R² (%)` = sprintf("%.0f", m$R2),
                 `Residual I² (%)` = sprintf("%.0f", m$I2),
                 `Moderator test P` = sprintf("%.3f", m$QMp))
}
map_dfr(list(~ ablat, ~ year, ~ alloc, ~ ablat + year), fit_mod) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr",
        caption = sprintf("Meta-regressions of the BCG trials (REML, Knapp-Hartung tests). Latitude and year are correlated (r = %.2f).",
                          cor(bcg$ablat, bcg$year)))



Meta-regressions of the BCG trials (REML, Knapp-Hartung tests). Latitude and year are correlated (r = -0.66).


Moderators

Year alone explains some heterogeneity, because the later trials were done nearer the equator. With both in the model, latitude still carries most of the explanatory power. (R² is lower with both covariates than with latitude alone; R² is computed from two separately estimated values of τ², and with 13 trials it is itself imprecise.) With only 13 trials, though, that is as far as the data can go: they cannot separate latitude from everything that travels with it. A meta-regression association is observational evidence about effect modification, and is subject to the confounding and bias of any observational study (3).
Two further problems follow from analysing studies rather than patients.

The ecological fallacy. A study-level covariate need not describe the patients within the study. A meta-regression on the mean age of trial participants can find an association that does not exist among individual patients, or miss one that does. Patient-level characteristics are best examined with individual patient data (Chapter 16).
Aggregation bias. When a study-level characteristic is related both to the outcome and to the covariate, the association across studies can differ in direction from the association within them (Section 10.2).



10.1.6 Data dredging
Meta-regressions usually have few studies and many candidate moderators: dose, duration, year, setting, risk of bias, mean age, proportion of women. Testing them one at a time, and reporting the “significant” ones, produces false positives. Figure 10.3 simulates meta-analyses of 10 trials with true heterogeneity but no real moderators, and tests five random study-level characteristics in each.


Code
dredge_once <- function(k = 10, n_mods = 5, tau2 = 0.1) {
  vi <- runif(k, 0.02, 0.2)
  yi <- rnorm(k, log(0.8), sqrt(tau2 + vi))           # no moderator affects yi
  X  <- matrix(rnorm(k * n_mods), k)
  p  <- map(seq_len(n_mods), \(j) {
    c(z    = rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ X[, j], method = "REML", control = ctl)$QMp,
      knha = rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ X[, j], method = "REML", test = "knha", control = ctl)$QMp)
  }) |> do.call(what = rbind)
  c(z_one = unname(p[1, "z"] < 0.05), knha_one = unname(p[1, "knha"] < 0.05),
    z_any = any(p[, "z"] < 0.05), knha_any = any(p[, "knha"] < 0.05))
}
set.seed(10)
dredge <- replicate(1000, tryCatch(dredge_once(), error = \(e) rep(NA, 4))) |>
  rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE)




Code
tibble::tibble(test = rep(c("Default (z)", "Knapp-Hartung"), 2),
               scope = rep(c("One pre-specified moderator", "Best of five moderators"), each = 2),
               p = dredge[c("z_one", "knha_one", "z_any", "knha_any")]) |>
  mutate(scope = factor(scope, levels = c("One pre-specified moderator", "Best of five moderators"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(p, scope, fill = test)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * p)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey60", "#041E42"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.45)) +
  labs(x = "False-positive rate", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 10.3: Probability of at least one ‘significant’ moderator (P < 0.05) when none is real. 1000 simulated meta-analyses of 10 trials with τ² = 0.1; default (z) and Knapp-Hartung tests.





With one pre-specified moderator, the Knapp-Hartung test keeps close to its nominal 5% error rate (7%) while the default test exceeds it (8%). Choosing the best of five moderators gives a “significant” result in 24% of meta-analyses with the Knapp-Hartung test and 32% with the default: no adjustment of the test can correct for the selection. The Cochrane Handbook advises that meta-regression should generally not be considered with fewer than ten studies, and that the characteristics examined be pre-specified in the protocol, few in number and with a scientific rationale (5).

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
10.2 When pooling misleads: Simpson’s paradox
Section 9.6.3 showed that adding the 2×2 tables of different trials into one table breaks randomisation and can reverse the direction of an effect. The mistake has been made in print: a 1999 meta-analysis of male circumcision and HIV that pooled raw counts found circumcised men at higher risk, while a within-study analysis of the same studies showed the opposite (Section 6.4) (6,7).
The same paradox has an ecological form that matters for meta-regression and for comparisons across countries. Figure 10.4 simulates countries in two regions. Within each region, countries with more circumcision have less HIV. But the region with more circumcision also has more HIV for other reasons, so a regression across all countries points the wrong way.


Code
set.seed(42)
eco <- tibble::tibble(
  region = rep(c("Region A: high circumcision, high HIV",
                 "Region B: low circumcision, low HIV"), each = 12),
  circ   = c(runif(12, 0.70, 0.95), runif(12, 0.10, 0.35))) |>
  mutate(hiv = if_else(startsWith(region, "Region A"), 0.40, 0.12) - 0.15 * circ +
           rnorm(n(), 0, 0.015))
b_all    <- coef(lm(hiv ~ circ, data = eco))[["circ"]]
b_within <- coef(lm(hiv ~ circ + region, data = eco))[["circ"]]

ggplot(eco, aes(circ, hiv)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = region), size = 2.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = region), method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x, colour = "#B22222",
              linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#041E42"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Circumcision prevalence (country)", y = "HIV prevalence (country)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")








Figure 10.4: Ecological Simpson’s paradox (simulated data). Solid lines: within each region, more circumcision goes with less HIV. Dashed line: ignoring region, the association reverses.





Within regions the slope is -0.15 (protective); across all countries it is +0.28 (apparently harmful). Region is a confounder of the between-country comparison, related both to circumcision and to HIV. Studies in a meta-regression are like these countries: they differ in many ways at once, and an association across studies can reverse the association within them. The remedies are the same as for any confounded comparison: compare within strata where possible (within-study comparisons, individual patient data), and treat across-study associations as hypotheses, not findings.

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
10.3 Method sensitivity
Section 9.5 showed a conclusion that depended on the choice of estimator and interval. A pre-specified primary method, with a set of alternatives as sensitivity analyses, is the defence against both fragility and “method shopping”, in which analyses are tried until one gives the desired answer.
The data below are simulated: nine hypothetical trials of continuous labour support (by a doula, nurse or midwife) with epidural use as the outcome. The clinical question is borrowed from a real Cochrane topic, but the counts are invented for teaching.


Code
cb <- data.frame(study = paste("Trial", 1:9),
                 ai  = c(10, 18, 22, 13, 40, 25,  8, 30, 15),   # epidurals, support
                 n1i = c(55, 80, 95, 60, 135, 110, 45, 120, 70),
                 ci  = c(22, 30, 35, 18, 55, 38, 15, 48, 24),   # epidurals, usual care
                 n2i = c(50, 75, 90, 58, 130, 105, 42, 118, 68))
cb_rr <- escalc("RR", ai = ai, n1i = n1i, ci = ci, n2i = n2i, data = cb, slab = study)

fits <- list(
  "Equal effects (inverse variance)" = rma(yi, vi, data = cb_rr, method = "EE"),
  "Random effects, DL, Wald"         = rma(yi, vi, data = cb_rr, method = "DL"),
  "Random effects, REML, Wald"       = rma(yi, vi, data = cb_rr, method = "REML"),
  "Random effects, REML, HKSJ"       = rma(yi, vi, data = cb_rr, method = "REML", test = "knha"),
  "Random effects, REML, HKSJ (ad hoc)" = rma(yi, vi, data = cb_rr, method = "REML", test = "adhoc"),
  "Mantel-Haenszel"                  = rma.mh(measure = "RR", ai = ai, n1i = n1i, ci = ci,
                                              n2i = n2i, data = cb))
cb_tab <- imap_dfr(fits, \(m, nm) tibble::tibble(
  Method = nm, RR = exp(m$b[1]), lo = exp(m$ci.lb), hi = exp(m$ci.ub)))
cb_tab |>
  mutate(`RR (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", RR, lo, hi),
         `CI width (log scale)` = sprintf("%.3f", log(hi) - log(lo))) |>
  select(Method, `RR (95% CI)`, `CI width (log scale)`) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")










Method
RR (95% CI)
CI width (log scale)




Equal effects (inverse variance)
0.61 (0.52 to 0.71)
0.313


Random effects, DL, Wald
0.61 (0.52 to 0.71)
0.313


Random effects, REML, Wald
0.61 (0.52 to 0.71)
0.313


Random effects, REML, HKSJ
0.61 (0.55 to 0.68)
0.214


Random effects, REML, HKSJ (ad hoc)
0.61 (0.51 to 0.73)
0.368


Mantel-Haenszel
0.61 (0.52 to 0.71)

Every method reaches the same conclusion, a reduction in epidural use of about a third, so this conclusion is robust to the method. Two features of the table are worth understanding.
Four estimates are identical. Cochran’s Q is 2.7 on 8 degrees of freedom, less than its expectation under homogeneity, so every estimator returns \(\hat\tau^2 = 0\), the random-effects weights equal the fixed-effect weights, and the models coincide. Mantel-Haenszel, with slightly different weights, is almost the same.
The HKSJ interval is narrower than the Wald interval. The HKSJ variance is rescaled by roughly Q/(k − 1) = 0.34. When the trials agree more closely than chance predicts, that factor is below 1, and the shrinkage of the standard error (by a factor of 0.58) outweighs the widening from the t multiplier (2.31 instead of 1.96). The net result is an interval 0.68 times as wide as the Wald interval, the anomaly described in Section 9.3.2. Real data this homogeneous are unusual (simulated data, and data that have been tidied, are more often too neat), but the anomaly also occurs with real data when there are few studies. The ad hoc version, which never lets the HKSJ variance fall below the Wald variance, restores the Wald interval here.
When methods disagree, which is most likely with few studies, high heterogeneity, rare events or unbalanced arms, report them all and explain the difference. Sensitivity analyses are a test of robustness, not a menu from which to choose the most favourable result.

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
10.4 Influence and cumulative analyses

10.4.1 Leave-one-out
A leave-one-out analysis repeats the meta-analysis \(k\) times, omitting each study in turn. If omitting a single study changes the estimate substantially, or moves it across a decision threshold, the conclusion rests on that study, which then deserves scrutiny: is it larger, older, at higher risk of bias, or from a different population?


Code
loo <- leave1out(m_bcg, transf = exp)
forest(loo$estimate, ci.lb = loo$ci.lb, ci.ub = loo$ci.ub, slab = loo$slab,
       refline = exp(m_bcg$b[1]), header = c("Trial omitted", "RR [95% CI]"),
       xlab = "Pooled risk ratio with one trial omitted")








Figure 10.5: Leave-one-out analysis of the BCG trials (REML, HKSJ). Each row is the pooled risk ratio with that trial omitted. Dashed line: the pooled risk ratio from all 13 trials.





The estimates range only from 0.45 to 0.53: no single trial drives the average. influence(m_bcg) adds formal diagnostics, such as studentised residuals and Cook’s distances, that flag outlying or influential studies. Robust average, unexplained spread: the leave-one-out analysis shows that the mean effect is stable, but says nothing about the heterogeneity, which is what makes the BCG average hard to apply.


10.4.2 Cumulative meta-analysis
A cumulative meta-analysis adds studies one at a time, usually in order of publication, and shows the pooled estimate as it would have been after each one. It answers two questions: when did the evidence first become convincing, and was the answer available before the field acted on it? The classic example is the cumulative meta-analysis by (8) of 33 trials of intravenous streptokinase after myocardial infarction, which are distributed with metafor as dat.lau1992.


Code
lau   <- dat.lau1992
m_lau <- rma(measure = "OR", ai = ai, n1i = n1i, ci = ci, n2i = n2i, data = lau,
             method = "EE", slab = paste(trial, year))
cum_lau <- cumul(m_lau)
n_cum   <- cumsum(lau$n1i + lau$n2i)
k_lau   <- length(cum_lau$estimate)
sig     <- cum_lau$ci.ub < 0                 # cumulative CI excludes OR = 1
first_sig <- max(which(!sig)) + 1            # significant from here on




Code
forest(cum_lau, atransf = exp, at = log(c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4)),
       xlim = c(-7.5, 4.5), ilab = n_cum, ilab.xpos = -2.6, cex = 0.75,
       header = c("Trial added", "Cumulative OR [95% CI]"),
       xlab = "Cumulative pooled odds ratio for death")
text(-2.6, k_lau + 2, "Patients", font = 2, cex = 0.75)








Figure 10.6: Cumulative fixed-effect meta-analysis of 33 trials of intravenous streptokinase for acute myocardial infarction (mortality), adding trials in order of publication. Data from Lau et al. (1992), as distributed with metafor.





The cumulative estimate first excluded no effect after 4 trials, and did so consistently from 1973 onward. At that point, after 8 trials and 2,432 patients, the cumulative odds ratio was 0.74 (0.60 to 0.93), close to the 0.74 (0.59 to 0.92) that Lau and colleagues reported. The 25 later trials, which enrolled another 34,542 patients through 1988, including the two mega-trials GISSI and ISIS-2, narrowed the interval but hardly moved the estimate (final OR 0.77). Lau and colleagues argued that a cumulative meta-analysis could have established the benefit well before the large trials were done.
That conclusion needs the same appraisal as any other. The early trials were small, varied in their comparators and their methods, and would now be judged at high risk of bias; a cumulative estimate can only be as trustworthy as the trials it accumulates. Repeated looks at accumulating evidence also inflate the chance of a false-positive result, the multiplicity problem that affects interim analyses of a single trial; trial sequential analysis and Bayesian updating are two responses. And a cumulative estimate that drifts as studies accumulate signals heterogeneity, or small early studies that overstated the effect.

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
10.5 The fragility index
The fragility index of a trial is the smallest number of patients whose outcome would have to change, from non-event to event in the arm with fewer events, to turn a statistically significant result (by Fisher’s exact test) into a non-significant one (9). In 399 trials in high-impact journals Walsh and colleagues found a median fragility index of 8, and a quarter of trials had an index of 3 or less.


Code
p_trial <- function(e1, n1, e0, n0)
  fisher.test(matrix(c(e1, n1 - e1, e0, n0 - e0), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))$p.value

fragility <- function(e1, n1, e0, n0) {
  k <- 0
  while (p_trial(e1, n1, e0, n0) < 0.05) {   # add events to the arm with fewer events
    if (e1 / n1 < e0 / n0) e1 <- e1 + 1 else e0 <- e0 + 1
    k <- k + 1
  }
  k
}
c(p = p_trial(30, 1000, 50, 1000), fragility_index = fragility(30, 1000, 50, 1000))


              p fragility_index 
     0.02956235      2.00000000 


A trial of 2000 patients with 30 events among 1000 treated and 50 among 1000 controls has P = 0.030, a “significant” 40% reduction. Its fragility index is 2: had 2 of the 2000 patients had a different outcome, it would have been reported as showing no significant difference.
A small fragility index is not evidence that a result is wrong. Figure 10.7 simulates 2000 trials of a drug that truly reduces risk from 10% to 7% (RR 0.70), with 500 patients per arm.


Code
set.seed(629)
sims <- tibble::tibble(e1 = rbinom(2000, 500, 0.07), e0 = rbinom(2000, 500, 0.10)) |>
  mutate(rr  = e1 / e0,
         p   = map2_dbl(e1, e0, \(a, b) p_trial(a, 500, b, 500)),
         sig = p < 0.05 & e1 < e0)
sig_trials <- sims |> filter(sig) |>
  mutate(fi = map2_dbl(e1, e0, \(a, b) fragility(a, 500, b, 500)))




Code
p1 <- ggplot(sims, aes(rr, fill = sig)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.70, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "#041E42"),
                    labels = c("Not significant", "P < 0.05"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Observed risk ratio", y = "Trials") + theme(legend.position = "top")
p2 <- ggplot(sig_trials, aes(fi)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#041E42") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5.5, colour = "#B22222", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Fragility index (patients)", y = "Significant trials")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)








Figure 10.7: Two thousand simulated trials of a drug with a true risk ratio of 0.70 (500 patients per arm, control risk 10%). Left: observed risk ratios; navy trials reached P < 0.05. Right: fragility indices of the significant trials.





Although every trial tests the same effective drug, only 35% reach P < 0.05, which is the trials’ power; the rest would be reported as “no significant difference”. Of the significant trials, 54% have a fragility index of 5 or less (median 5). The fragility index re-expresses how close a P value is to 0.05, in units of patients. For a result near the threshold, a small index is the expected finding, not in itself a warning sign, and the deeper lesson is the one of Section 9.1.1: dichotomising results at P = 0.05 makes them look more different than they are. The idea has been extended to meta-analyses, many of whose significant results are similarly fragile (10).

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
10.6 A sensitivity checklist
Sensitivity analyses should be pre-specified in the protocol and all reported. A finding that survives them is robust; one that depends on a single choice is fragile, and should be described as such.



Table 10.1: Pre-specified sensitivity analyses.









Domain
Analyses




Model
Fixed vs random effects; τ² estimator (REML, PM, DL); Wald vs HKSJ interval


Studies
Omit studies at high risk of bias; leave-one-out; omit studies with high attrition or unregistered protocols


Data
Intention-to-treat vs per-protocol; handling of zero cells (Mantel-Haenszel, continuity corrections, exact methods); imputed standard deviations


Outcomes
Narrower vs broader definitions; different time points; components of composite outcomes


Small-study effects
Fixed vs random effects comparison; funnel plot and related methods (Chapter 15)

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
10.7 Common pitfalls



Table 10.2: Common pitfalls in meta-analysis.










Pitfall
What goes wrong
Detection or remedy




Pooling incompatible studies
The summary applies to no real population
Check PICO before pooling; stratify; consider not pooling


Ignoring heterogeneity
A single estimate is presented as if all studies agreed
Report Q, I², τ² and a prediction interval; explore sources


Trusting I² with few studies
I² is imprecise: 3% (0% to 50%) for the six heparin trials of Section 9.5
Report confidence intervals for I² and τ² (confint())


No prediction interval
The interval for the average hides the variation in true effects
predict(); addpred = TRUE in forest()


DerSimonian-Laird and Wald intervals with few studies
τ² underestimated; intervals too narrow
REML or PM; HKSJ guarded by the ad hoc rule


Adding 2×2 tables across studies
Simpson’s paradox; randomisation broken
Pool within-study effects (inverse variance, Mantel-Haenszel, Peto)


No zero-cell sensitivity analysis
Safety conclusions depend on an arbitrary correction
Mantel-Haenszel or exact methods as primary; alternatives as sensitivity


Post hoc moderators
False-positive effect modifiers
Pre-specify; few moderators; Knapp-Hartung tests


Reading meta-regression causally
Study-level confounding; ecological fallacy
Treat as hypothesis-generating; individual patient data


Method shopping
The reported analysis is the most favourable of several
Pre-specify the primary analysis; report all sensitivity analyses


Vote counting
“Not significant” read as “no effect”
Pool effect sizes

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
10.8 Beyond pairwise comparisons
Everything so far compares two interventions. Decisions usually involve several: four antiplatelet strategies, five antidepressants. Network meta-analysis combines direct evidence (trials of A against B) with indirect evidence (trials of A against C and of B against C). If A against C gives RR 0.70 and B against C gives RR 0.85, the indirect estimate of A against B is 0.70/0.85 ≈ 0.82, a comparison never made in any trial. The method rests on transitivity: the trials in different parts of the network must be similar enough, in the distribution of effect modifiers such as latitude for BCG, that the indirect comparison is fair. Whether this holds is a clinical question before it is a statistical one. Later chapters develop network meta-analysis in full.

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
Key points

Heterogeneity should be explained if possible, not just reported. Meta-regression relates effect sizes to study-level characteristics.
R² is the share of τ² explained; residual I² compares what is left with sampling error. Both can be large at once.
A moderator modifies the treatment effect; it is not a confounder of a randomised comparison. But study-level covariates are not randomised across studies, so meta-regression associations are observational and can be confounded.
Pre-specify a few plausible moderators, use Knapp-Hartung tests, and treat post hoc findings as hypotheses.
Aggregating across studies or countries can reverse an association (Simpson’s paradox); compare within studies.
Check robustness to the method, to individual studies (leave-one-out) and over time (cumulative meta-analysis), and report all pre-specified sensitivity analyses.
A small fragility index is expected for results near P = 0.05, even when the treatment works; it is a reminder not to dichotomise evidence.

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness
text:
Exercises

Fit the BCG meta-regression with method = "DL" and with method = "ML". How do τ²_res, R² and the slope change?
Add the moderator alloc to the latitude model. Does it explain additional heterogeneity? How many degrees of freedom are left?
Rerun dredge-sim with 20 trials and with 5 trials. How do the false-positive rates change for the default and Knapp-Hartung tests?
In childbirth, change Trial 5 to 70 epidurals among 135 with support. Recompute the method comparison table. Which methods now disagree?
Run influence(m_bcg) and plot() it. Which trials, if any, are flagged as influential, and why?
Compute the fragility index of the pooled heparin trials of Section 9.5 treated as a single 2×2 table. Why is this the wrong calculation for a meta-analysis? (See (10).)

title: 10  Heterogeneity and Robustness

Further reading

title: 11  P Values and Surprise
text:
11.1 What a P value is
The last two chapters kept running into P values. The heparin meta-analysis of Section 9.5 turned on an interval that just included 1; the fragility index of Section 10.5 re-expressed a P value near 0.05 as a handful of patients; vote counting (Section 9.1.1) failed because it treated P > 0.05 as “no effect”. This chapter steps back to the P value itself: what it measures, how noisy it is, and what to report instead. The arguments are not new (1,2), but they are still widely ignored, and simulation makes them hard to dismiss.
A P value is the probability, computed under the null hypothesis and under all the other assumptions of the statistical model, that a test statistic would be at least as extreme as the one observed. For an estimate with a normal sampling distribution, the statistic is \(z = \text{estimate}/SE\) and the two-sided P value is \(2\{1 - \Phi(|z|)\}\), the shaded tails of Figure 11.1.
Code
tibble::tibble(z = seq(-4, 4, by = 0.01), d = dnorm(z)) |>
  ggplot(aes(z, d)) +
  geom_area(data = \(x) filter(x, z <= -1.96), fill = "#56B4E9") +
  geom_area(data = \(x) filter(x, z >= 1.96), fill = "#56B4E9") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = c(-2.9, 2.9), y = 0.08, label = "2.5%", colour = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = "z = estimate / SE", y = "Density under the null")








Figure 11.1: The standard normal distribution of z under the null hypothesis. The shaded tails beyond ±1.96 hold 5% of the probability.
Three points in the definition are routinely forgotten. The P value is computed assuming the null is true, so it cannot be the probability that the null is true. It depends on the whole model (no bias, correct distribution, no selective reporting), so a small P value may indicate a problem with any of these rather than a real effect. And it says nothing about the size of an effect: a trivial effect estimated precisely and a large effect estimated imprecisely can have the same P value (Section 13.1 returns to this). (1) list 25 common misinterpretations; most come from forgetting one of these three points.

title: 11  P Values and Surprise
section: 11.2 How noisy is a P value?
text:
11.2 How noisy is a P value?
Consider an experiment whose true effect is two standard errors from zero, so that \(z \sim N(2, 1)\). If the same experiment were repeated ten times, what would be the range of the ten P values?

0.02 to 0.05
0.002 to 0.05
0.0002 to 0.05
0.0002 to 0.5

When I asked this question of 17 clinicians, 4 chose the right answer; among 706 epidemiology graduate students, 153 did. The most popular answers were the narrow ranges, 1 and 2. One line of R gives the answer.


Code
set.seed(123)
p_ten <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(rnorm(10, mean = 2, sd = 1))))
round(p_ten, 4)


 [1] 0.1500 0.0768 0.0004 0.0384 0.0332 0.0002 0.0139 0.4624 0.1891 0.1201


The ten values run from 0.0002 to 0.46: answer 4. When I put the question to a large language model it gave answer 1 with a confident explanation, accepted the simulation when shown it, and gave the same wrong answer a week later; intuition, human or machine, is a poor guide here, and a simulation is a good one. (The example was prompted by a post on Andrew Gelman’s blog in October 2024.)
Figure 11.2 shows why. The z statistic varies, as it must, by about ±1 around its true value of 2. But the P value is a steeply nonlinear function of z: a step from z = 0 to z = 1 lowers P by 0.68, while the same step from 2 to 3 lowers it by only 0.04. Modest, symmetric variation in z becomes variation in P over three orders of magnitude.


Code
marks <- tibble::tibble(z = 0:3, p = 2 * pnorm(-z))
p_left <- tibble::tibble(z = seq(0, 4, 0.01), p = 2 * pnorm(-z)) |>
  ggplot(aes(z, p)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#B22222") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_point(data = marks, colour = "#B22222", size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", p)), nudge_x = 0.28, nudge_y = 0.04, size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = "z = estimate / SE", y = "Two-sided P value")
set.seed(2024)
z_rep <- rnorm(2000, 2, 1)
p_right <- tibble::tibble(p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_rep))) |>
  ggplot(aes(p, fill = p < 0.05)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, boundary = 0.05) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#B22222") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1e-4, 1e-3, 0.01, 0.05, 0.2, 1),
                labels = c("0.0001", "0.001", "0.01", "0.05", "0.2", "1")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#041E42", `FALSE` = "grey65"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "P value (log scale)", y = "Replications")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_left, p_right)








Figure 11.2: Left: the two-sided P value as a function of z. Right: P values from 2000 replications of a study whose true z is 2 (power about 50%), on a log scale.





Only 51% of the replications reach P < 0.05. For a study with this power, whether it is reported as “significant” or “not significant” is close to a coin toss, even though the effect is real and identical in every replication. This is the mechanism behind the vote-counting failure of Section 9.1.1 and the fragile trials of Section 10.5.

11.2.1 P values under the null are uniform
When the null hypothesis is true, a test at level α rejects with probability α, whatever α is: \(\Pr(P < \alpha) = \alpha\). That is the definition of a uniform distribution on (0, 1). Under the null, a P value of 0.8 is as likely as one of 0.08, and a P value of 0.04 occurs one time in 25.


Code
set.seed(1234)
p_t   <- replicate(10000, t.test(rnorm(100), rnorm(100))$p.value)
p_bin <- replicate(10000, binom.test(rbinom(1, 100, 0.2), 100, p = 0.2)$p.value)
tibble::tibble(p = c(p_t, p_bin),
               test = rep(c("t test (continuous)", "Exact binomial test (discrete)"), each = 10000)) |>
  mutate(test = factor(test, levels = unique(test))) |>
  ggplot(aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), fill = "#041E42", colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 500, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#B22222") +
  facet_wrap(~ test) +
  labs(x = "P value", y = "Count")








Figure 11.3: P values from 10 000 two-sample t tests (left) and 10 000 exact binomial tests (right), all with the null hypothesis true.





For the t test the histogram is flat at the expected 500 per bin. The exact binomial test is discrete, so its P values take only certain values and the histogram is lumpy; such tests are conservative, with \(\Pr(P < \alpha) \le \alpha\) (here 0.045 at α = 0.05). Uniformity under the null is what makes an excess of P values just below 0.05 in a literature suspicious, a point taken up with publication bias in Section 15.6.

title: 11  P Values and Surprise
text:
11.3 Surprise: S values
A P value is hard to grasp because it lives on a compressed, nonlinear scale. (3) recommend re-expressing it as an S value (Shannon information, or surprisal):
\[S = -\log_2 P .\]
S is the number of bits of information against the null hypothesis, and it has a concrete calibration: S bits is as surprising as seeing S heads in a row from a coin assumed fair. P = 0.05 gives S = 4.3, between four and five heads in a row; P = 0.005 gives 7.6. A small S means only that the data are not surprising under the hypothesis tested; it does not mean that hypothesis is true.

11.3.1 No significant difference: the STICH trial
The STICH trial randomised 1212 patients with ischaemic left ventricular dysfunction to coronary bypass surgery or medical therapy. Death occurred in 41% of the medical-therapy group and 36% of the surgical group (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.04, P = 0.12), and the authors concluded that there was “no significant difference” in all-cause mortality (4). S = \(-\log_2 0.12 \approx 3\) bits: as surprising as three heads in a row. Three heads would not convince anyone that a coin is biased; equally, so little information should not convince anyone that the null is true.
Testing only the null wastes most of the information in the estimate. The same calculation can be done for every possible hazard ratio, giving a compatibility curve (or P value function): the P value, or S value, for each hypothesised effect.


Code
s_curve <- function(hr, lo, hi, hr_test) {
  se <- (log(hi) - log(lo)) / (2 * 1.96)               # SE of log HR from the 95% CI
  p  <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(log(hr_test) - log(hr)) / se)
  tibble::tibble(hr_test, p, s = -log2(p))
}
stich <- s_curve(0.86, 0.72, 1.04, exp(seq(log(0.6), log(1.25), length.out = 400)))
s_at  <- s_curve(0.86, 0.72, 1.04, c(0.75, 1))
s_at

p
s

0.1445819
2.790041


1.00

Code
pts <- s_at |> mutate(lab = sprintf("HR %.2f\nP = %.2f, S = %.1f", hr_test, p, s))
p_curve <- ggplot(stich, aes(hr_test, p)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = pts, colour = "#B22222", size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.6, 0.75, 0.86, 1, 1.2)) +
  labs(x = "Hypothesised hazard ratio", y = "P value")
s_plot <- ggplot(stich, aes(hr_test, s)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_point(data = pts, colour = "#B22222", size = 2.5) +
  geom_label(data = pts, aes(y = 6.6, label = lab), size = 3.1, lineheight = 0.9, label.size = 0) +
  geom_segment(data = pts, aes(xend = hr_test, y = 5.9, yend = s + 0.3), colour = "grey50") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.6, 0.75, 0.86, 1, 1.2)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 8)) +
  labs(x = "Hypothesised hazard ratio", y = "S value (bits)")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_curve, s_plot)








Figure 11.4: Compatibility curves for STICH (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.04). Left: P value for each hypothesised hazard ratio; the interval at P = 0.05 is the 95% confidence interval. Right: the same as S values (bits of information against each hazard ratio).





The data carry 3.2 bits of information against the null (HR = 1) and 2.8 bits against a clinically important 25% reduction in mortality (HR = 0.75). The trial is thus slightly more incompatible with no effect than with an important benefit. Yet “no significant difference” is routinely read as support for the first and rejection of the second. The compatibility curve shows what the single test hides: the data are most compatible with a modest benefit, and a wide range of effects, from substantial benefit to slight harm, remains reasonably compatible with them. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

title: 11  P Values and Surprise
text:
11.4 Intuition about randomness
S values calibrate surprise against runs of heads, so they help only if our sense of what random sequences look like is sound. It is not. Figure 11.5 shows 200 tosses of a fair coin and 200 draws from a process that switches between 0 and 1 with probability 0.7.


Code
set.seed(629)
n <- 200
coin   <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                                    # independent fair tosses
switch <- (rbinom(1, 1, 0.5) + cumsum(c(0, rbinom(n - 1, 1, 0.7)))) %% 2   # 70% switching
runs <- tibble::tibble(Sequence = c("Fair coin", "70% switching"),
                       switches = c(sum(diff(coin) != 0), sum(diff(switch) != 0)),
                       longest_run = c(max(rle(coin)$lengths), max(rle(switch)$lengths)))




Code
tibble::tibble(value = c(coin, switch),
               seq = rep(c("A", "B"), each = n), i = rep(seq_len(n) - 1, 2)) |>
  mutate(row = i %/% 50, col = i %% 50) |>
  ggplot(aes(col, row, fill = factor(value))) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey85", "#041E42"), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~ seq, ncol = 1, labeller = as_labeller(c(A = "Sequence A", B = "Sequence B"))) +
  theme_void() + theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))








Figure 11.5: Two binary sequences of 200 draws, read left to right in rows of 50. Which is random?





Most people choose B as random, because A has long runs and looks “clumpy”. A is the fair coin. Its longest run is 7, and it switches value 102 times in 199 opportunities; B switches 137 times and its longest run is only 5. Genuine randomness produces runs that look like patterns; sequences that alternate “nicely” are structured.
How long must one wait for a run? The expected number of tosses of a fair coin before seeing n heads in a row is \(2^{n+1} - 2\): 30 tosses for four heads, 126 for six, 2046 for ten. In a large literature, or a large table of subgroup analyses, runs as surprising as P < 0.01 (about seven heads) turn up regularly by chance. This is part of why selective reporting and multiple testing produce so many false positives (Section 10.1.6).

title: 11  P Values and Surprise
section: 11.5 Simpson’s paradox is a causal question
text:
11.5 Simpson’s paradox is a causal question
Section 9.6.3 and Section 10.2 showed that pooling across strata can reverse an association, and that comparisons should usually be made within strata. “Usually” matters: whether to stratify is a causal question, and the same numbers can call for different answers (5). Table 11.1 shows 700 patients, 350 given a drug and 350 not; the numbers are from a well-known study of treatments for kidney stones (6), used by Pearl and colleagues to make this point.


Code
sp <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Subgroup,    ~drug_rec, ~drug_n, ~none_rec, ~none_n,
  "Stratum 1",        81,      87,      234,     270,
  "Stratum 2",       192,     263,       55,      80)
sp <- bind_rows(sp, summarise(sp, Subgroup = "All patients", across(-Subgroup, sum)))
sp |>
  transmute(Subgroup,
            Drug    = sprintf("%d/%d (%.0f%%)", drug_rec, drug_n, 100 * drug_rec / drug_n),
            `No drug` = sprintf("%d/%d (%.0f%%)", none_rec, none_n, 100 * none_rec / none_n)) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")




Table 11.1: Recovery with and without a drug, overall and by subgroup.






Subgroup
Drug
No drug




Stratum 1
81/87 (93%)
234/270 (87%)


Stratum 2
192/263 (73%)
55/80 (69%)


All patients
273/350 (78%)
289/350 (83%)








In each stratum the drug group does better; overall it does worse. Should we believe the strata or the total? The table cannot say. Consider two stories that produce exactly these numbers.

The strata are sex, and women (stratum 2) both have a worse prognosis and are more likely to take the drug. Sex is a confounder: it affects both treatment and outcome. The stratified comparison is the right one, and the drug helps.
The strata are blood pressure measured after treatment, and the drug affects recovery partly through its effect on blood pressure. Blood pressure is now a mediator, on the causal path from drug to recovery. Stratifying on it removes part of the drug’s effect and compares patients who are no longer comparable, so the overall comparison is the right one, and the drug does harm.



Code
dag_plot <- function(edges, nodes, title) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_curve(data = edges, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), curvature = edges$curv[1],
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed"), colour = "#041E42") +
    geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = lab), fill = "#F4F6F8", size = 3.8) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.4, 2.4), ylim = c(-0.4, 1.3)) +
    labs(title = title) + theme_void() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))
}
n1 <- tibble::tibble(x = c(0, 2, 1), y = c(0, 0, 1), lab = c("Drug", "Recovery", "Sex"))
e1 <- tibble::tibble(x = c(0.25, 0.9, 1.1), y = c(0, 0.85, 0.85), xend = c(1.65, 0.15, 1.85),
                     yend = c(0, 0.12, 0.12), curv = 0)
n2 <- tibble::tibble(x = c(0, 2, 1), y = c(0, 0, 1), lab = c("Drug", "Recovery", "Blood\npressure"))
e2 <- tibble::tibble(x = c(0.25, 0.15, 1.1), y = c(0, 0.12, 0.8), xend = c(1.65, 0.8, 1.85),
                     yend = c(0, 0.85, 0.12), curv = 0)
patchwork::wrap_plots(dag_plot(e1, n1, "Confounder: stratify"),
                      dag_plot(e2, n2, "Mediator: do not stratify"))








Figure 11.6: Two causal structures consistent with the same 2×2 tables. Left: the stratifying variable is a confounder; adjust for it. Right: it is a mediator; adjusting for it blocks part of the effect.





There is no paradox once the causal structure is stated, and no rule based on the numbers alone can choose between the analyses. For meta-analysis, the practical consequence is the one reached in Section 10.2: within-study comparisons protect randomisation, and across-study associations must be interpreted with the causal structure in mind.

title: 11  P Values and Surprise
text:
11.6 What to report instead
None of this means P values must be banned. It means that a dichotomy at 0.05 should not carry the weight it is given.



Table 11.2: Replacing dichotomous significance.









Instead of
Report




“Significant” or “not significant”
The estimate and its confidence interval, read over its whole width


P < 0.05
The exact P value, or its S value, as one measure of compatibility with one hypothesis


A test of the null alone
A compatibility curve, or intervals compared with a clinically important difference (Section 9.4.2)


“No effect” when P > 0.05
Which effects the data rule out, and which they do not


A P value as the probability that the null is true
A posterior probability from a model that states its prior (Chapter 12, Chapter 13)






What clinicians usually want to know is the probability that an effect is large enough to matter. A P value cannot answer that; a posterior distribution can, and the next two chapters develop the Bayesian approach that provides it.

title: 11  P Values and Surprise
text:
Key points

A P value is the probability of data at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null hypothesis and the whole model. It is not the probability that the null is true, and it says nothing about effect size.
P values are very noisy: identical studies with a real effect and 50% power give P values spread over three orders of magnitude.
Under the null, P values are uniformly distributed (exactly for continuous tests, conservatively for discrete ones).
S values (\(-\log_2 P\)) express evidence against a hypothesis in bits, calibrated by runs of heads from a fair coin; P = 0.05 is about 4 bits.
Compatibility curves show the evidence about every effect size, not just the null. “Not significant” is not “no effect”, as STICH shows.
Human intuition about randomness is poor: real randomness produces runs.
Whether to stratify is a causal question; the same tables can require different analyses.

title: 11  P Values and Surprise
text:
Exercises

Repeat ten-pvalues with true z = 3 and true z = 1. How does the spread of P values change? What proportion of replications reach P < 0.05 in each case?
Draw the compatibility curve for the published heparin meta-analysis of Section 9.5 (OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.02). How many bits of information does it provide against OR = 1, and against OR = 0.67?
Show by simulation that the expected number of tosses to see five heads in a row is 62.
Construct a 2×2×2 table in which the drug helps in both strata and overall, but with a much larger effect in one stratum. Is there a Simpson’s paradox?
Read the abstract of a recent trial that reported “no significant difference”. Compute the S value against the null and against an effect you would consider clinically important.

title: 12  Bias and a Bridge to Bayes
text:
12.1 A bias that the checklists miss
The previous chapters supplied a toolkit: models, heterogeneity, sensitivity analyses and an honest reading of P values. This chapter applies it to two real problems. The first is a meta-analysis that passes every standard check and is probably wrong, because the trials share a bias that no checklist detects. The second compares frequentist and Bayesian analyses of the same data, which give almost the same numbers but answer different questions. Along the way the chapter introduces the first Bayesian models of the book; Chapter 13 develops them.
Should patients with severe but asymptomatic aortic stenosis have their valve replaced early, surgically (SAVR) or by catheter (TAVR), rather than under clinical surveillance until symptoms appear? Four randomised trials have compared the strategies (1–4). Several meta-analyses published in 2025 pooled them, rated them at low risk of bias, and concluded that early replacement reduces a composite of death and unplanned hospitalisation, and calls to change guidelines followed. This section follows a re-analysis that asked whether that conclusion is credible (5).
Code
avr <- tibble::tribble(
  ~study,       ~treat,              ~n_int, ~n_cs, ~fu_yr, ~xover12, ~hr,  ~lo,  ~hi,
  "RECOVERY",   "SAVR",                  73,    72,   6.2,      9,   0.09, 0.01, 0.67,
  "AVATAR",     "SAVR",                  78,    79,   5.2,     12,   0.46, 0.23, 0.90,
  "EVOLVED",    "SAVR 75%, TAVR 25%",   113,   111,   3.5,     31,   0.79, 0.44, 1.43,
  "EARLY TAVR", "TAVR",                 455,   446,   3.8,    208,   0.50, 0.40, 0.63) |>
  mutate(yi = log(hr), sei = (log(hi) - log(lo)) / (2 * 1.96))   # log HR and SE from the 95% CI

avr |>
  transmute(Trial = study, `Early replacement` = treat, `n (early / surveillance)` = paste(n_int, "/", n_cs),
            `Median follow-up (years)` = fu_yr,
            `Surveillance patients replaced in year 1` = sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", xover12, 100 * xover12 / n_cs),
            `Published HR (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", hr, lo, hi)) |>
  kable(align = "llcccc", caption = "Four trials of early valve replacement versus surveillance in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis.")

title: 12  Bias and a Bridge to Bayes
text:
12.1.1 Step 1: the conventional meta-analysis


Code
m_avr <- rma(yi, sei = sei, data = avr, slab = study, method = "REML", test = "knha")




Code
forest(m_avr, atransf = exp, at = log(c(0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2)), header = c("Trial", "HR [95% CI]"),
       xlab = "Hazard ratio, early replacement vs surveillance")








Figure 12.1: Conventional random-effects meta-analysis of the four trials (REML, Hartung-Knapp interval).





The pooled hazard ratio is 0.52 (0.34 to 0.78): early replacement roughly halves the risk of the composite outcome. τ² is estimated as zero, so there is no statistical heterogeneity, the effects all point the same way, and the trials were rated at low risk of bias with RoB 2. Every check in Chapter 5, Chapter 9 and Chapter 10 is passed.


12.1.2 Step 2: a signature of bias
The red flag is in the crossover column of the table. A surveillance patient “crosses over” by having the valve replaced, usually after an unplanned hospitalisation, which is itself a primary-outcome event.


Code
xo   <- escalc(measure = "PLO", xi = xover12, ni = n_cs, data = avr, slab = study)  # logit of a proportion
m_xo <- rma(yi, vi, data = xo, method = "REML", subset = study != "EARLY TAVR")      # the three surgical trials
xo_surg <- predict(m_xo, transf = transf.ilogit)


In the three surgical trials about 18% (95% CI 11% to 30%) of surveillance patients had their valve replaced within a year. In EARLY TAVR it was 47%, although every patient had been confirmed asymptomatic by an exercise test at entry. Why would half of them need a valve within a year?
In an unblinded trial, four influences push in the same direction. Surveillance patients know they have severe, untreated disease and are more likely to report symptoms and seek care. Investigators know who is untreated and are more likely to attribute a symptom to the valve and admit the patient. Treated patients feel “fixed” and are less likely to consult, and their physicians less likely to blame the heart. Each increases unplanned hospitalisations in the surveillance arm relative to the treated arm: performance bias that manufactures a benefit. A less invasive procedure lowers the threshold to intervene, which fits the much higher crossover rate with TAVR. Meta-epidemiological studies confirm that unblinded trials with subjective outcomes exaggerate treatment effects (6,7).
The point is subtle. The early-replacement arm receives its valve at randomisation, as the intervention. The surveillance arm receives the same valve a few weeks or months later, often preceded by a hospitalisation that counts as an outcome. The composite outcome thus partly measures how quickly patients and clinicians chose to intervene in the control arm, which is exactly what knowledge of the allocation influences.


12.1.3 Step 3: a landmark analysis on reconstructed data
If the benefit is real, it should persist, or grow, after the first year, as untreated disease progresses. If it is produced by early crossovers, it should be confined to the first year. A landmark analysis tests this by restarting the clock at one year among patients still event-free. That needs individual patient data, which the trialists did not share; they were reconstructed from the published Kaplan-Meier curves with the algorithm of (8), which recovers event and censoring times from the digitised curves and the numbers at risk.


Code
ipd <- readRDS("data/ch12/dat_all_km.rds") |>                # reconstructed IPD, 1427 patients
  mutate(time  = if_else(study == "AVATAR", time / 12, time), # AVATAR digitised in months
         trt   = as.integer(group != "Clinical Surveillance"),
         study = recode(study, EARLY = "EARLY TAVR"))

cox_hr <- function(d) {                                      # log HR and its SE for one trial
  f <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ trt, data = d)
  tibble::tibble(yi = unname(coef(f)), sei = sqrt(vcov(f)[1, 1]))
}
yr1 <- ipd |>                                                # events in year 1 only
  mutate(event = if_else(time > 1, 0, event), time = pmin(time, 1)) |>
  filter(study != "RECOVERY") |>                             # 2 events in year 1: no estimate
  group_by(study) |> group_modify(\(d, k) cox_hr(d)) |> ungroup()
lmk <- ipd |>                                                # landmark: from year 1 onwards
  filter(time > 1) |> mutate(time = time - 1) |>
  group_by(study) |> group_modify(\(d, k) cox_hr(d)) |> ungroup()




Code
km <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ trt, data = filter(ipd, study == "EARLY TAVR"))
tibble::tibble(time = km$time, inc = 1 - km$surv,
               arm = rep(c("Surveillance", "Early TAVR"), km$strata)) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, inc, colour = arm)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Early TAVR" = "#041E42", Surveillance = "#B22222"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Years from randomisation", y = "Cumulative incidence") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 12.2: EARLY TAVR, reconstructed data: cumulative incidence of the primary outcome. The vertical line marks the one-year landmark.







Code

tibble::tibble(Trial = avr$study) |>
  left_join(tibble::tibble(Trial = yr1$study, `Year 1` = hr_txt(yr1)), by = "Trial") |>
  left_join(tibble::tibble(Trial = lmk$study, `After year 1 (landmark)` = hr_txt(lmk)), by = "Trial") |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) tidyr::replace_na(x, "too few events"))) |>
  kable(align = "lcc")

In EARLY TAVR, which dominates the pooled estimate, the whole benefit falls in the first year (HR 0.24 (0.17 to 0.35)), exactly when the crossovers happen; after the landmark the curves run in parallel (HR 1.03 (0.75 to 1.41)). The smaller surgical trials behave differently, with estimates after year 1 that still favour early surgery but are imprecise. Pooled after the landmark, the frequentist estimate is 0.55 (0.13 to 2.26), compatible with anything from a large benefit to substantial harm. Reconstructed data are approximations: they reproduce the published curves, not the original records, and small differences from the published estimates are expected.

title: 12  Bias and a Bridge to Bayes
text:
12.2 A first Bayesian model
Before re-analysing these data, we need the simplest Bayesian model. Bayes’ theorem says that the posterior distribution of a parameter is proportional to the likelihood of the data times the prior distribution of the parameter:
\[p(\theta \mid \text{data}) \propto p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\, p(\theta).\]
If a trial’s estimate is normally distributed around the true effect, \(\hat\theta \sim N(\theta, SE^2)\), and the prior is also normal, \(\theta \sim N(m_0, s_0^2)\), the posterior is again normal, with
\[\text{posterior precision} = \frac{1}{s_0^2} + \frac{1}{SE^2}, \qquad \text{posterior mean} = \frac{m_0/s_0^2 + \hat\theta/SE^2}{1/s_0^2 + 1/SE^2}.\]
The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the estimate, exactly like the inverse-variance weighting of a fixed-effect meta-analysis (Section 9.2), with the prior acting as one more “study”.


Code
update_normal <- function(m0, s0, est, se) {
  prec <- 1 / s0^2 + 1 / se^2
  c(mean = (m0 / s0^2 + est / se^2) / prec, sd = sqrt(1 / prec))
}
update_normal(m0 = 0, s0 = 1.5, est = log(0.50), se = 0.20)   # vague prior: the data dominate


      mean         sd 
-0.6810398  0.1982456 


Code
update_normal(m0 = 0, s0 = 0.20, est = log(0.50), se = 0.20)  # sceptical prior as precise as the data


      mean         sd 
-0.3465736  0.1414214 


With a vague prior, N(0, 1.5²) on the log hazard ratio, the posterior mean is almost the estimate. With a sceptical prior as precise as the data, the posterior lies halfway between the null and the estimate.

12.2.1 The Bayesian random-effects model
For several studies, the Bayesian version of the random-effects model of Section 9.3 has the same two levels, plus priors:
\[\hat\theta_i \sim N(\theta_i, SE_i^2), \qquad \theta_i \sim N(\mu, \tau^2), \qquad \mu \sim p(\mu), \quad \tau \sim p(\tau).\]
Integrating out the study effects gives \(\hat\theta_i \sim N(\mu, SE_i^2 + \tau^2)\), so the posterior depends on just two unknowns, μ and τ. With two unknowns, the posterior can be computed directly on a grid: evaluate prior × likelihood at every combination of μ and τ, normalise, and sample combinations in proportion to their posterior probability. Each sampled (μ, τ) pair also gives a draw of the true effect in a new study, \(\theta_{\text{new}} \sim N(\mu, \tau^2)\), the Bayesian prediction.


Code
bayes_nn <- function(yi, sei, mu_mean = 0, mu_sd = 1.5,
                     tau_prior = \(t) 2 * dt(t, df = 3),      # half-t(3) on tau, scale 1
                     mu_range = c(-4, 3), tau_max = 4, grid = 400, n_draws = 40000) {
  g  <- expand.grid(mu = seq(mu_range[1], mu_range[2], length.out = grid),
                    tau = seq(0, tau_max, length.out = grid))
  lp <- dnorm(g$mu, mu_mean, mu_sd, log = TRUE) + log(tau_prior(g$tau))   # log prior
  for (i in seq_along(yi))                                                # + log likelihood
    lp <- lp + dnorm(yi[i], g$mu, sqrt(sei[i]^2 + g$tau^2), log = TRUE)
  s  <- g[sample(nrow(g), n_draws, replace = TRUE, prob = exp(lp - max(lp))), ]
  dm <- diff(mu_range) / (grid - 1); dt_ <- tau_max / (grid - 1)          # jitter within a cell
  s$mu  <- s$mu + runif(n_draws, -dm / 2, dm / 2)
  s$tau <- abs(s$tau + runif(n_draws, -dt_ / 2, dt_ / 2))
  tibble::tibble(mu = s$mu, tau = s$tau, new = rnorm(n_draws, s$mu, s$tau))
}


A grid is exact up to its resolution, transparent, and fast for two parameters. It does not scale: ten parameters on a grid of 400 values each would need 40010 evaluations. General-purpose software therefore uses Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). In R the most convenient interface is brms, which writes and runs a Stan model from one formula (9). The same model, with the priors used in the published re-analysis, is:


Code
library(brms)
pri <- c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = Intercept),     # mu, log HR
         prior(student_t(3, 0, 1), class = sd))        # tau; brms truncates sd priors at zero
fit_pub <- brm(yi | se(sei) ~ 1 + (1 | study), data = avr, prior = pri,
               iter = 6000, warmup = 1000, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99), seed = 2026)
fit_lmk <- update(fit_pub, newdata = lmk, seed = 2026)


The formula reads: yi is observed with known standard error sei; there is an overall mean (1) and study-specific deviations ((1 | study)) with standard deviation τ. Both approaches give the same posterior, to within simulation error; here we use the grid, and Chapter 13 uses brms for a model the grid cannot handle.


12.2.2 Step 4: the Bayesian re-analysis


Code
set.seed(2026)
post_avr <- bind_rows(
  bayes_nn(avr$yi, avr$sei) |> mutate(analysis = "Published HRs"),
  bayes_nn(lmk$yi, lmk$sei) |> mutate(analysis = "One-year landmark")) |>
  mutate(analysis = factor(analysis, levels = c("Published HRs", "One-year landmark")))
q_txt <- \(x) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(median(x)), exp(quantile(x, 0.025)), exp(quantile(x, 0.975)))
avr_tab <- post_avr |>

            `P(HR < 1)` = sprintf("%.2f", mean(mu < 0)), `P(HR < 0.9)` = sprintf("%.2f", mean(mu < log(0.9))),
            `τ, median` = sprintf("%.2f", median(tau)))

  geom_density(alpha = 0.55, colour = NA, adjust = 1.5) +

These results reproduce the published re-analysis, which reported 0.52 (0.25 to 0.97) for the published hazard ratios and 0.59 (0.20 to 1.40) for the landmark (5). Removing the early, unblinding-prone period moves the posterior towards 1 and widens it: the probability of a reduction of at least 10% falls from 0.97 to 0.87, and the next trial could show anything from a large benefit to harm. The evidence is compatible with benefit but is not conclusive: hypothesis-generating rather than guideline-changing.


12.2.3 Why the frequentist and Bayesian results differ


Code
f_z  <- rma(yi, sei = sei, data = lmk, method = "REML")
f_hk <- rma(yi, sei = sei, data = lmk, method = "REML", test = "knha")
pl   <- filter(post_avr, analysis == "One-year landmark")
fmt3 <- \(m, l, u) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(m), exp(l), exp(u))
tibble::tibble(
  Analysis = c("REML, Wald interval", "REML, Hartung-Knapp interval", "Bayesian, median and 95% credible interval"),
  `τ` = c(sprintf("%.2f (point estimate)", sqrt(f_z$tau2)), sprintf("%.2f (point estimate)", sqrt(f_hk$tau2)),
          sprintf("posterior median %.2f", median(pl$tau))),
  `Pooled HR` = c(fmt3(f_z$b[1], f_z$ci.lb, f_z$ci.ub), fmt3(f_hk$b[1], f_hk$ci.lb, f_hk$ci.ub),
                  fmt3(median(pl$mu), quantile(pl$mu, 0.025), quantile(pl$mu, 0.975)))) |>
  kable(align = "llc")




Table 12.2: Landmark analysis: frequentist and Bayesian summaries of the same four estimates.











Analysis
τ
Pooled HR




REML, Wald interval
0.58 (point estimate)
0.55 (0.27 to 1.11)


REML, Hartung-Knapp interval
0.58 (point estimate)
0.55 (0.13 to 2.26)


Bayesian, median and 95% credible interval
posterior median 0.64
0.60 (0.21 to 1.34)








With only four trials, three things drive the differences.

The width. The Wald interval plugs in \(\hat\tau\) as if known and is the narrowest. The Hartung-Knapp interval multiplies by a t quantile with 3 degrees of freedom (3.18 rather than 1.96) and is very wide. The Bayesian interval, which averages over the uncertainty in τ, lies between them.
The priors carry information. Four trials barely identify τ (the REML Q-profile 95% interval is 0.15 to 4.52). The half-t prior on τ and the N(0, 1.5²) prior on μ rule out implausibly large values. With so few trials the prior matters: a strength if it is justified, a risk if it is not.
The point estimate. The frequentist estimate weights the trials with one value of τ. The Bayesian estimate averages over all plausible values of τ, each giving different weights, and reports the posterior median, pulled slightly towards no effect by a prior centred there.



12.2.4 Lessons
Every statistical step in this case was standard. What changed the conclusion was asking whether the pattern of events made clinical sense: patients confirmed asymptomatic at entry, half of whom needed a valve within a year; crossovers that began with an outcome event; curves that ran in parallel after the first year, when a real benefit of treating a progressive disease should persist or grow; and an unblinded design. No statistical test flagged the problem.

Risk-of-bias tools are necessary, not sufficient. They cannot codify every trial-specific mechanism of bias.
Look for the signature of a suspected bias in the data: here, the crossover rate and its timing.
Heterogeneity can hide in time. A hazard ratio over the whole follow-up averaged a large early effect with no late effect.
Unavailable data can sometimes be reconstructed, from published Kaplan-Meier curves.
Correct for bias with design-based analyses (landmark or time-varying effects, objective outcomes such as all-cause mortality, restriction to blinded trials), stratification or meta-regression on the bias marker, or explicit bias modelling with an empirical prior for the bias (10), always as sensitivity analyses reported alongside the naive estimate.
Report probabilities of meaningful benefit, not just significance.

Meta-analysis is a scientific judgement supported by statistics, not a statistical procedure applied to whatever trials exist.

section: 12.3 Do the two frameworks give the same answer?
text:
12.3 Do the two frameworks give the same answer?
(11) meta-analysed 12 epidemiological studies of blood lead and children’s IQ, once with a frequentist and once with a Bayesian random-effects model. The effect is the change in IQ points per unit increase in the natural logarithm of blood lead (µg/dL). Their pooled estimates were almost identical, which raises a fair question: why bother with Bayes?


Code
lead <- tibble::tribble(        # harmonised regression coefficients and SEs, Sell et al., Table 2
  ~study,                     ~yi,   ~sei,
  "Bauer 2020",              -0.10,  0.87,
  "Crump 2013",              -3.31,  0.63,
  "Dantzer 2020",            -5.71,  1.61,
  "Desrochers-Couture 2018",  0.02,  0.06,
  "Earl 2016",               -5.86,  2.22,
  "Hong 2015",               -3.14,  1.37,
  "Lee 2021",                -3.83,  2.25,
  "Lucchini 2019",           -1.10,  0.84,
  "Lucchini 2012",           -3.48,  1.48,
  "Menezes-Filho 2018",      -3.74,  1.29,
  "Roy 2013",                -4.70,  1.66,
  "Schnaas 2006",             0.17,  0.81)
m_lead_ee <- rma(yi, sei = sei, data = lead, method = "EE")


One study, Desrochers-Couture 2018, is 15 to 40 times more precise than the others and reports essentially no effect; most of the rest show losses of 3 to 6 IQ points. A fixed-effect analysis would give it 97% of the weight and a pooled estimate of -0.05. How much the true effects vary, τ, is therefore the central question.

12.3.1 Frequentist and Bayesian fits


Code
m_lead  <- rma(yi, sei = sei, data = lead, slab = study, method = "REML", test = "knha")
pr_lead <- predict(m_lead)
ci_lead <- confint(m_lead)

set.seed(2026)
post_lead <- bayes_nn(lead$yi, lead$sei, mu_mean = -1, mu_sd = 2,    # the paper's priors
                      tau_prior = \(t) 2 * dnorm(t, 0, 2),          # half-normal(0, 2) on tau
                      mu_range = c(-10, 6), tau_max = 10, grid = 500)




Code
fmt <- \(m, l, u) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", m, l, u)
tibble::tibble(
  Quantity = c("Pooled effect μ", "τ²", "95% prediction interval, new study"),
  Frequentist = c(fmt(m_lead$b[1], m_lead$ci.lb, m_lead$ci.ub),
                  fmt(m_lead$tau2, ci_lead$random["tau^2", "ci.lb"], ci_lead$random["tau^2", "ci.ub"]),
                  sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", pr_lead$pi.lb, pr_lead$pi.ub)),
  Bayesian = c(fmt(median(post_lead$mu), quantile(post_lead$mu, 0.025), quantile(post_lead$mu, 0.975)),
               fmt(median(post_lead$tau^2), quantile(post_lead$tau^2, 0.025), quantile(post_lead$tau^2, 0.975)),
               sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", quantile(post_lead$new, 0.025), quantile(post_lead$new, 0.975)))) |>
  kable(align = "lcc")




Table 12.3: Blood lead and IQ: frequentist (REML, Hartung-Knapp) and Bayesian (posterior median, 95% credible interval) results.











Quantity
Frequentist
Bayesian




Pooled effect μ
-2.45 (-3.82 to -1.08)
-2.26 (-3.57 to -1.07)


τ²
3.32 (0.99 to 11.66)
3.26 (1.04 to 9.80)


95% prediction interval, new study
-6.68 to 1.79
-6.42 to 1.81








The numbers agree closely, and the grid reproduces the published results (frequentist −2.45, 95% CI −3.82 to −1.08; Bayesian −2.28, 95% CrI −3.54 to −1.04). That is expected: the likelihood is the same, the priors are weak, and 12 studies with I² of about 85% identify τ reasonably well. One difference in the τ² row deserves attention. The frequentist confidence interval for τ² is reported but not used: the weights, the interval for μ and the prediction interval are all computed as if τ² were known to equal \(\hat\tau^2\). In the Bayesian analysis every draw of μ comes with its own τ, so the uncertainty about heterogeneity flows into every interval.


12.3.2 Same numbers, different meaning
The frequentist 95% confidence interval is a statement about a procedure: if the whole study-and-analysis process were repeated many times, 95% of the intervals would cover the fixed, unknown μ. This particular interval either covers μ or does not, and all values inside it are treated alike. The Bayesian 95% credible interval is a statement about μ: given the model, the priors and the data, there is a 95% probability that μ lies within it. The posterior also ranks values (those near the median are much more plausible than those at the edges), and any probability a decision-maker needs can be read from it directly.


Code
tibble::tibble(
  Question = c("Is lead harmful at all?  P(μ < 0)",
               "Loss of more than 1 IQ point per log unit?  P(μ < −1)",
               "Loss of more than 2 IQ points?  P(μ < −2)",
               "Loss of more than 3 IQ points?  P(μ < −3)",
               "Would a new study's true effect be harmful?  P(θ_new < 0)",
               "Is heterogeneity substantial?  P(τ > 1)"),
  `Posterior probability` = sprintf("%.2f", c(mean(post_lead$mu < 0), mean(post_lead$mu < -1),
                                              mean(post_lead$mu < -2), mean(post_lead$mu < -3),
                                              mean(post_lead$new < 0), mean(post_lead$tau > 1)))) |>
  kable(align = "lc")




Table 12.4: Posterior probabilities for questions a regulator might ask.










Question

Is lead harmful at all? P(μ < 0)
1.00


Loss of more than 1 IQ point per log unit? P(μ < −1)
0.98


Loss of more than 2 IQ points? P(μ < −2)
0.67


Loss of more than 3 IQ points? P(μ < −3)

Would a new study’s true effect be harmful? P(θ_new < 0)
0.88


Is heterogeneity substantial? P(τ > 1)
0.98








A regulator does not ask whether P < 0.05 but how likely an effect larger than some amount is, or what loss to plan for in a new population. Note the fifth row: although the average effect is clearly harmful, there is a 12% chance that a new study’s true effect is zero or beneficial, because the heterogeneity is large.


12.3.3 With few studies, the frameworks diverge
The lead example agrees because τ is well identified. With few studies it is not, and REML often estimates τ² = 0 even when the true heterogeneity is large (as in the heparin example of Section 9.5). Figure 12.4 simulates meta-analyses of 4, 6 and 12 studies from a population like the lead studies (μ = −2.4, τ = 1.8), and asks how often each 95% prediction interval contains the true effect in a new study.


Code
sei_pool <- lead$sei[lead$sei > 0.1]                  # SEs of the real studies, minus the outlier
one_sim <- function(k, mu = -2.4, tau = 1.8) {
  sei <- sample(sei_pool, k, replace = TRUE)
  yi  <- rnorm(k, mu + rnorm(k, 0, tau), sei)         # observed = true + sampling error
  new <- rnorm(1, mu, tau)                            # true effect in a new study
  m   <- tryCatch(rma(yi, sei = sei, method = "REML", test = "knha",
                      control = list(stepadj = 0.5, maxiter = 500)), error = \(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
  pz <- predict(update(m, test = "z")); pk <- predict(m)
  pb <- quantile(bayes_nn(yi, sei, mu_mean = -1, mu_sd = 2, tau_prior = \(t) 2 * dnorm(t, 0, 2),
                          mu_range = c(-12, 8), tau_max = 8, grid = 150, n_draws = 4000)$new,
                 c(0.025, 0.975))
  tibble::tibble(k = k, tau_zero = m$tau2 < 1e-4,
                 `Frequentist (Wald)` = new > pz$pi.lb & new < pz$pi.ub,
                 `Frequentist (Hartung-Knapp)` = new > pk$pi.lb & new < pk$pi.ub,
                 Bayesian = new > pb[1] & new < pb[2])
}
set.seed(629)
smallk <- map_dfr(rep(c(4, 6, 12), each = 600), one_sim) |>
  summarise(.by = k, tau0 = mean(tau_zero), across(c(starts_with("Freq"), Bayesian), mean))




Code
smallk |>
  pivot_longer(-c(k, tau0), names_to = "Method", values_to = "coverage") |>
  mutate(Method = factor(Method, levels = c("Frequentist (Wald)", "Frequentist (Hartung-Knapp)", "Bayesian"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(k), coverage, fill = Method)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.75), width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#E69F00", "#0072B2"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.6, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Number of studies", y = "Coverage of 95% prediction interval") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 12.4: Coverage of 95% prediction intervals for the true effect in a new study, by number of studies (600 simulated meta-analyses at each size; true μ = −2.4, τ = 1.8).





With four studies, REML set τ² to zero in 23% of the simulated meta-analyses, although the true τ is large. The Wald prediction interval then covered the next study’s true effect only 79% of the time. The Hartung-Knapp interval repaired much of this (86%), and the Bayesian interval, which averages over the uncertainty in τ, came closest to 95% (94%). As the number of studies grows, the three converge. The Bayesian result is helped here by a prior compatible with the true τ; a badly chosen prior would hurt.


12.3.4 Sensitivity to the prior on τ


Code
set.seed(1)
tau_sds <- c("Strong shrinkage, half-normal(0, 0.67)" = 0.67, "Half-normal(0, 1)" = 1,
             "Default, half-normal(0, 2)" = 2, "Weak shrinkage, half-normal(0, 6)" = 6)
imap_dfr(tau_sds, \(sd, nm) {
  p <- bayes_nn(lead$yi, lead$sei, mu_mean = 0, mu_sd = 100, tau_prior = \(t) 2 * dnorm(t, 0, sd),
                mu_range = c(-10, 6), tau_max = 10)
  tibble::tibble(`Prior on τ` = nm,
                 `μ, median (95% CrI)` = fmt(median(p$mu), quantile(p$mu, 0.025), quantile(p$mu, 0.975)),
                 `τ, median` = sprintf("%.2f", median(p$tau)),
                 `95% prediction, new study` = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", quantile(p$new, 0.025), quantile(p$new, 0.975)))
}) |> kable(align = "lccc")




Table 12.5: Blood lead and IQ: sensitivity of the posterior to the prior on τ (the prior on μ is essentially flat, N(0, 100²)).
