With 12 studies the data dominate; only a prior that strongly shrinks τ changes μ noticeably, by pulling the imprecise studies, which report the largest losses, towards the mean. With three to five studies the prior on τ matters far more, which is exactly when it should be chosen carefully, for example from the empirical distributions of (12).


12.3.5 Why Bayes is worth the bother

Interpretation. A credible interval is a probability statement about the effect; a confidence interval is a statement about a procedure.
Decisions. The probability that an effect exceeds a threshold, expected losses and burden-of-disease simulations follow directly from the posterior.
Uncertainty in τ is propagated, not plugged in. This matters most with few studies, where frequentist \(\hat\tau\) is often zero and prediction intervals are overconfident.
Assumptions are explicit. Priors are stated, and their influence can be tested.

When the frameworks agree numerically, as here, that is expected rather than evidence that they are equivalent. The Bayesian result answers the question decision-makers actually ask.

title: 12  Bias and a Bridge to Bayes
text:
Key points

A meta-analysis can pass every standard check and still be biased. Look for the mechanism of bias specific to the trials, and for its signature in the data.
Unblinded trials with outcomes that depend on decisions, such as unplanned hospitalisation, are vulnerable to performance bias; crossovers that begin with an outcome event are a warning sign.
Landmark analyses on reconstructed individual patient data can test whether an effect survives removal of the period most prone to bias.
A normal prior and a normal likelihood give a normal posterior whose mean is a precision-weighted average; the Bayesian random-effects model adds priors on μ and τ.
With two parameters, the posterior can be computed exactly on a grid; brms fits the same model, and more complex ones, by MCMC.
Frequentist and Bayesian results agree when τ is well identified and priors are weak; they diverge with few studies, where the Bayesian prediction interval is better calibrated if the prior is reasonable.
Report posterior probabilities of clinically meaningful effects, and check sensitivity to the prior on τ.

title: 12  Bias and a Bridge to Bayes
text:
Exercises

Re-run the Bayesian analysis of the published AVR hazard ratios with a sceptical prior on μ, N(0, 0.35²). How much does P(HR < 0.9) change?
Fit a meta-regression of the published log hazard ratios on the year-1 crossover proportion. With four trials, what can and cannot be concluded?
Using the reconstructed data, estimate a time-varying hazard ratio for EARLY TAVR with coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ trt + tt(trt), tt = function(x, t, ...) x * log(t)). Does it support the landmark analysis?
In the lead example, omit Desrochers-Couture 2018. How do the frequentist and Bayesian estimates of μ and τ change?
Extend smallk-sim to a true τ of 0.5. Which method’s prediction intervals now have the best coverage?

title: 13  Bayesian Meta-Analysis
text:
13.1 Why Bayesian?
Chapter 12 introduced the Bayesian random-effects model and showed that, with enough studies and weak priors, it gives numbers close to a frequentist analysis while answering different questions. This chapter develops the approach: why the questions it answers matter, how to choose priors, and how a Bayesian meta-analysis resolves a controversy in which the same evidence was read as showing both that a treatment works and that it does not.
A frequentist meta-analysis answers the question “is the average effect different from zero?”. Clinicians, guideline panels and patients ask different questions: how probable is it that the treatment helps, how probable is a benefit large enough to matter, and what should I expect in my patients? A posterior distribution answers these directly. Two examples show what the P value hides.
Code
z <- qnorm(1 - 0.03 / 2)
trl <- tibble::tibble(trial = c("Trial 1: 25 000 patients, RR 0.97", "Trial 2: 400 patients, RR 0.72"),
                      rr = c(0.97, 0.72)) |>
  mutate(se = abs(log(rr)) / z, p_imp = pnorm((log(0.95) - log(rr)) / se))
curves <- trl |>
  crossing(x = seq(log(0.4), log(1.4), length.out = 600)) |>
  mutate(dens = dnorm(x, log(rr), se)) |>
  group_by(trial) |> mutate(dens = dens / max(dens)) |> ungroup()
ggplot(curves, aes(exp(x), dens)) +
  geom_area(data = \(d) filter(d, exp(x) < 0.95), fill = "#B22222", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text(data = trl, aes(x = 1.03, y = 0.85, label = sprintf("P = 0.03\nP(RR < 0.95) = %.2f", p_imp)),
            hjust = 0, size = 3.6, colour = "#B22222") +
  facet_wrap(~ trial) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.7, 0.95, 1.2)) +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio (log scale)", y = "Relative likelihood")








Figure 13.1: Two trials with P = 0.03. With a flat prior, the shaded area is the probability of a clinically important effect (RR < 0.95).
Both trials are “significant” at P = 0.03. Trial 1 estimates precisely an effect too small to matter; Trial 2 estimates imprecisely an effect that is probably important. The P value cannot distinguish them; the probability of a clinically important effect can.
Code
trl2 <- tibble::tibble(trial = c("Trial A: 900 patients, HR 0.93", "Trial B: 4400 patients, HR 0.97"),
                       hr = c(0.93, 0.97), se = c(0.0675, 0.03)) |>
  mutate(p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(log(hr)) / se), p_imp = pnorm((log(0.9) - log(hr)) / se))
curves2 <- trl2 |>
  crossing(x = seq(log(0.55), log(1.35), length.out = 600)) |>
  mutate(dens = dnorm(x, log(hr), se)) |>
  group_by(trial) |> mutate(dens = dens / max(dens)) |> ungroup()
ggplot(curves2, aes(exp(x), dens)) +
  geom_area(data = \(d) filter(d, exp(x) < 0.9), fill = "#B22222", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.9, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text(data = trl2, aes(x = 0.57, y = 0.85, label = sprintf("P = %.2f\nP(HR < 0.9) = %.3f", p, p_imp)),
            hjust = 0, size = 3.6, colour = "#B22222") +
  facet_wrap(~ trial) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.6, 0.8, 0.9, 1, 1.2)) +
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio (log scale)", y = "Relative likelihood")








Figure 13.2: Two trials with P ≈ 0.3. The shaded area is the probability of an important benefit (HR < 0.9), with a flat prior.
Both are “not significant” and would usually be reported identically, as showing no benefit. Trial A is too small to tell: an important benefit still has a probability of about 31%. Only Trial B, with its narrow interval, makes an important benefit unlikely. The conclusion comes from the posterior, or at least from the whole interval, not from the P value.
The move from statistical output to clinical action is itself a skill: asking not only “is there an effect?” but “what should I do, given this evidence and what I knew before?”. Bayesian analysis does not make that judgement, but it makes its ingredients explicit and gives it the right inputs: probabilities of effects large enough to matter, a prediction for new patients, and a clear statement of what was assumed.

title: 13  Bayesian Meta-Analysis
text:
13.2 Prior, likelihood and posterior
\[\text{posterior} \propto \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior}\]
The prior describes what was believed about the effect before the new evidence, the likelihood what the new data say, and the posterior what is believed after combining them. With a normal prior and a normal likelihood the posterior is normal, with precision equal to the sum of the two precisions and mean equal to their precision-weighted average (Section 12.2). Figure 13.3 shows the update for a pooled RR of 0.90 with a standard error of 0.05 on the log scale, under two priors.


Code
y <- -0.10; s <- 0.05
pri <- tibble::tibble(prior = factor(c("Weakly informative N(0, 0.5²)", "Sceptical N(0, 0.05²)"),
                                     levels = c("Weakly informative N(0, 0.5²)", "Sceptical N(0, 0.05²)")),
                      m0 = 0, s0 = c(0.5, 0.05)) |>
  mutate(prec = 1 / s0^2 + 1 / s^2, pm = (m0 / s0^2 + y / s^2) / prec, ps = sqrt(1 / prec),
         p_ben = pnorm(0, pm, ps))
pri |>
  crossing(x = seq(-0.45, 0.25, length.out = 500)) |>
  mutate(Prior = dnorm(x, m0, s0), Likelihood = dnorm(x, y, s), Posterior = dnorm(x, pm, ps)) |>
  pivot_longer(Prior:Posterior, names_to = "curve") |>
  group_by(prior, curve) |> mutate(value = value / max(value)) |> ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(exp(x), value, colour = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_text(data = pri, aes(x = 0.68, y = 1.08, label = sprintf("P(RR < 1) = %.2f", p_ben)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, size = 3.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ prior) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Likelihood = "grey50", Prior = "#E69F00", Posterior = "#041E42"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Likelihood = "dashed", Prior = "dotted", Posterior = "solid"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1, 1.1, 1.2)) +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio (log scale)", y = "Scaled density") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 13.3: Prior, likelihood and posterior for a pooled log RR of −0.10 (RR 0.90, SE 0.05), under a weakly informative and a sceptical prior. Curves scaled to the same height.





A weak prior lets the data speak. A sceptical prior as precise as the data pulls the estimate halfway to the null. Showing both is the point: it makes explicit how much a conclusion depends on prior belief.

13.2.1 Choosing priors for the effect
Four kinds of prior are useful for the mean effect μ (1,2).


Code
lv <- c("Weakly informative\nN(0, 0.5²)", "Sceptical\nN(0, 0.1²)", "Enthusiastic\nN(−0.3, 0.3²)",
        "Empirical\nN(−0.18, 0.12²)")
tibble::tibble(type = factor(lv, levels = lv), m = c(0, 0, -0.3, -0.18), s = c(0.5, 0.1, 0.3, 0.12)) |>
  crossing(x = seq(log(0.25), log(2.5), length.out = 400)) |>
  mutate(d = dnorm(x, m, s)) |>
  ggplot(aes(exp(x), d)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~ type, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio (log scale)", y = "Prior density") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())








Figure 13.4: Four kinds of prior for a log risk ratio, shown on the risk ratio scale.






Weakly informative: centred on no effect and wide. The usual primary analysis; the data dominate.
Sceptical: concentrated near the null. Does the evidence convince a doubter?
Enthusiastic: centred on a benefit suggested by mechanism or early trials. Does the evidence dissuade a believer?
Empirical: derived from earlier trials or an earlier meta-analysis. The most defensible informative prior when good precedent exists, provided the earlier evidence is relevant to the question.

Reporting results under several such priors, a community of priors, shows whether a conclusion is robust to reasonable differences in prior belief. The usual objection, that priors are subjective, has a usual answer: every analysis makes assumptions (the model, the distributions, the treatment of heterogeneity), and a Bayesian analysis states one more of them openly. (3) suggest replacing the debate about “objective” and “subjective” with the virtues an analysis should have: transparency, consensus, impartiality, correspondence to observable reality, awareness of multiple perspectives and of context, and investigation of stability.


13.2.2 Priors for τ
The prior on τ matters most. With few studies, τ is barely identified (Section 12.3.3), and a frequentist estimate of zero is common. A prior that gives most of its weight to small and moderate heterogeneity, but allows large values, stabilises the estimate and carries its uncertainty into the results. Half-normal and half-t distributions are common choices. (4) and (5) derived empirical predictive distributions for τ² from thousands of Cochrane meta-analyses, by outcome type and type of comparison; these are the natural choice when a defensible informative prior is needed.


13.2.3 Prediction and shrinkage
Two outputs of a Bayesian random-effects model have no simple frequentist counterpart. The posterior predictive distribution for the true effect in a new trial, \(\theta_{\text{new}} \sim N(\mu, \tau^2)\) averaged over the posterior of μ and τ, includes the uncertainty in both, not only sampling variability around fixed estimates. It is usually, though not always, wider than the frequentist prediction interval, because the frequentist interval treats \(\hat\tau\) as known. And the posterior for each trial’s own effect θi is shrunk towards the mean: small, noisy trials move most, large trials barely move, and the amount of shrinkage is set by τ, which the model learns from the data.

title: 13  Bayesian Meta-Analysis
text:
13.3 Colchicine after coronary events
Low-dose colchicine, an old anti-inflammatory drug, has been tested for the secondary prevention of cardiovascular events. The evidence offers an instructive sequence: an early meta-analysis that seemed conclusive, a large trial that found nothing, and meta-analyses that again found benefit (6).

13.3.1 The 2022 meta-analysis
(7) pooled seven trials of colchicine in patients with coronary disease undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (six of them after an acute coronary syndrome) and reported a risk ratio for major adverse cardiovascular events of 0.73 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.87; P = 0.0003), with I² = 6%. The trials ranged from 30-day studies to COLCOT, a trial of 4745 patients followed for a median of 22.6 months (8); their outcome definitions differed, and the pooled MACE did not include myocardial infarction.


Code
colch <- tibble::tribble(          # events / patients from the published forest plot
  ~study,           ~ev_col, ~n_col, ~ev_pbo, ~n_pbo,
  "CISR",                 1,     30,       8,     60,
  "COLCHICINE-PCI",      24,    206,      25,    194,
  "COLCOT",             131,   2366,     170,   2379,
  "COPS",                24,    396,      41,    399,
  "Deftereos 2013",      16,    100,      32,     96,
  "LoDoCo-MI",            0,    119,       2,    118,
  "O'Keefe 1992",        41,    130,      25,     67)
dat <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = ev_col, n1i = n_col, ci = ev_pbo, n2i = n_pbo,
              data = colch, slab = study)                 # 0.5 added to cells of LoDoCo-MI
m_dl <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "DL")            # as published
m_hk <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "REML", test = "knha")
pr_dl <- predict(m_dl, transf = exp)
f_rr <- \(m) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(m$b[1]), exp(m$ci.lb), exp(m$ci.ub))
tibble::tibble(Method = c("DerSimonian-Laird, Wald (as published)", "REML, Hartung-Knapp"),
               `RR (95% CI)` = c(f_rr(m_dl), f_rr(m_hk)),
               `95% prediction interval` = c(sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", pr_dl$pi.lb, pr_dl$pi.ub),
                                             sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", predict(m_hk, transf = exp)$pi.lb,
                                                     predict(m_hk, transf = exp)$pi.ub)),
               P = sprintf("%.4f", c(m_dl$pval, m_hk$pval)),
               `τ²` = sprintf("%.4f", c(m_dl$tau2, m_hk$tau2))) |>
  kable(align = "lcccc", caption = "The 2022 colchicine meta-analysis, reproduced.")



The 2022 colchicine meta-analysis, reproduced.

DerSimonian-Laird reproduces the published result. With REML and a Hartung-Knapp interval the interval widens and P rises to 0.010: seven trials, one of which (COLCOT) carries half the weight. REML estimates τ² = 0, so the frequentist prediction interval collapses onto the confidence interval, leaving no room for a new trial in a different population to differ. The published analysis reported no prediction interval at all; the DerSimonian-Laird one, 0.59 to 0.90, would have suggested that any new trial would show benefit.


13.3.2 The same seven trials, Bayesian
The grid function of Section 12.2.1 fits the normal-normal model exactly. Here the prior on μ is N(0, 1) on the log RR scale (95% of prior mass on RRs between 0.14 and 7), and the prior on τ is half-normal with scale 0.5 (median 0.34; 95% of mass below 0.98).


Code
bayes_nn <- function(yi, sei, mu_mean = 0, mu_sd = 1, tau_prior = \(t) 2 * dnorm(t, 0, 0.5),
                     mu_range = c(-3, 2), tau_max = 2.5, grid = 400, n_draws = 40000) {
  g  <- expand.grid(mu = seq(mu_range[1], mu_range[2], length.out = grid),
                    tau = seq(0, tau_max, length.out = grid))
  lp <- dnorm(g$mu, mu_mean, mu_sd, log = TRUE) + log(tau_prior(g$tau))
  for (i in seq_along(yi)) lp <- lp + dnorm(yi[i], g$mu, sqrt(sei[i]^2 + g$tau^2), log = TRUE)
  s  <- g[sample(nrow(g), n_draws, replace = TRUE, prob = exp(lp - max(lp))), ]
  dm <- diff(mu_range) / (grid - 1); dt_ <- tau_max / (grid - 1)
  s$mu  <- s$mu + runif(n_draws, -dm / 2, dm / 2)
  s$tau <- abs(s$tau + runif(n_draws, -dt_ / 2, dt_ / 2))
  tibble::tibble(mu = s$mu, tau = s$tau, new = rnorm(n_draws, s$mu, s$tau))
}
set.seed(2025)
post_c <- bayes_nn(dat$yi, sqrt(dat$vi))
q3 <- \(x) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(median(x)), exp(quantile(x, 0.025)), exp(quantile(x, 0.975)))




Code
# The same model with bayesmeta, which integrates numerically rather than on a grid
library(bayesmeta)
bma <- bayesmeta(dat, mu.prior.mean = 0, mu.prior.sd = 1,
                 tau.prior = \(tau) dhalfnormal(tau, scale = 0.5))
bma$summary; bma$pposterior(mu = log(0.85))


The posterior median RR is 0.72 (0.52 to 0.91), close to the frequentist estimate, and the posterior probability that colchicine reduces risk by at least 15% is high, 0.93. The difference is in the prediction: the 95% interval for the true effect in a new trial is 0.37 to 1.21, which, unlike the frequentist prediction interval, reaches past 1. Seven trials that agree with one another cannot rule out that a trial in a different population would find no benefit. bayesmeta gives the same posterior by numerical integration (9).


Code
p_mu <- ggplot(post_c, aes(exp(mu))) +
  geom_density(fill = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.5, colour = "#041E42", adjust = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.85, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.7, 0.85, 1, 1.2), limits = c(0.4, 1.3)) +
  labs(x = "Mean RR, colchicine vs control (log scale)", y = "Posterior density",
       title = sprintf("μ: P(RR < 0.85) = %.2f", mean(post_c$mu < log(0.85))))
p_tau <- ggplot(post_c, aes(tau)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#B22222", alpha = 0.35, colour = "#B22222", adjust = 1.5) +
  stat_function(fun = \(t) 2 * dnorm(t, 0, 0.5), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.5)) +
  labs(x = "τ (between-trial SD of the log RR)", y = "Density",
       title = "τ: posterior (shaded) and prior (dashed)")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_mu, p_tau)








Figure 13.5: Seven trials in the 2022 meta-analysis: posterior for the mean risk ratio (left; shaded area RR < 0.85) and prior and posterior for τ (right).





The seven trials shift belief about τ towards small values, but leave a long tail: τ = 0, the frequentist estimate, is plausible, but so is appreciable heterogeneity. The frequentist analysis plugs in one value; the Bayesian analysis averages over all of them, which is why its prediction is wider.


Code
shrink <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(dat)), \(i) {
  v <- dat$vi[i]; t2 <- pmax(post_c$tau^2, 1e-8)
  prec  <- 1 / v + 1 / t2
  theta <- rnorm(nrow(post_c), (dat$yi[i] / v + post_c$mu / t2) / prec, sqrt(1 / prec))
  tibble::tibble(study = dat$study[i], type = c("Observed", "Shrunken"),
                 est = c(dat$yi[i], median(theta)),
                 lo  = c(dat$yi[i] - 1.96 * sqrt(v), quantile(theta, 0.025)),
                 hi  = c(dat$yi[i] + 1.96 * sqrt(v), quantile(theta, 0.975)))
}) |>
  mutate(study = factor(study, levels = rev(dat$study)))
ggplot(shrink, aes(exp(est), study, colour = type, shape = type)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(median(post_c$mu)), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = exp(lo), xmax = exp(hi)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.55)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Observed = "grey50", Shrunken = "#041E42"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Observed = 1, Shrunken = 16), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 13.6: Observed risk ratios (open circles, 95% CI) and Bayesian shrunken estimates of each trial’s true effect (filled, 95% credible interval). The dashed line is the posterior median of μ.





The small trials, with very wide intervals, are pulled most of the way to the mean; COLCOT, the largest, barely moves. Shrinkage trades a small bias towards the ensemble for a large reduction in variance, and gives better estimates of each trial’s true effect than the trial alone.


13.3.3 A large trial finds nothing
The CLEAR trial randomised 7062 patients after myocardial infarction at 104 centres in 14 countries to colchicine or placebo. Over a median follow-up of 3 years, the primary outcome (cardiovascular death, recurrent myocardial infarction, stroke or ischaemia-driven revascularisation) occurred in 322 of 3528 patients given colchicine (9.1%) and 327 of 3534 given placebo (9.3%): HR 0.99 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.16), P = 0.93 (10). The authors concluded that colchicine “did not reduce the incidence of the composite primary outcome”. They acknowledged COLCOT, with a similar population and outcome, HR 0.77 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.96), as the most comparable earlier trial, but offered no quantitative synthesis of the two.
Within months, several meta-analyses that included CLEAR concluded that colchicine is beneficial. The largest, by a collaboration that included the CLEAR investigators, pooled nine trials of 30 659 patients with coronary disease or stroke in a fixed-effect model and reported that colchicine reduced cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke by 12% (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.95) (11); another reported a 25% reduction in a broader composite (12). Read as dichotomies, these are contradictory: the treatment does not work, and the treatment works. Both statements are made from largely the same evidence, about somewhat different populations and outcomes. A Bayesian analysis asks a better question: how should CLEAR change what we believed before it?


13.3.4 Updating with a community of priors
Three priors describe three reasonable states of belief before CLEAR. All are normal on the log scale, with mean log(estimate) and standard deviation (log upper − log lower)/(2 × 1.96).

Vague, N(0, 2²): let CLEAR speak for itself.
COLCOT, N(−0.26, 0.12²): the trial the CLEAR investigators themselves named as most comparable.
Earlier meta-analysis, N(−0.31, 0.09²): the 2022 pooled estimate. Its trials were smaller, shorter and in a somewhat different population, and its outcome excluded infarction; whether it is exchangeable with CLEAR is a clinical judgement, which is exactly why it is one prior among several rather than the only one.

CLEAR’s result enters as a normal likelihood for the log hazard ratio. Because the priors and the likelihood are all normal, the update is the conjugate calculation of Section 12.2.


Code
y_cl <- log(0.99); s_cl <- (log(1.16) - log(0.85)) / (2 * 1.96)
post_cl <- tibble::tibble(
  Prior = factor(c("Vague", "COLCOT", "Earlier meta-analysis"),
                 levels = c("Vague", "COLCOT", "Earlier meta-analysis")),
  m0 = c(0, log(0.77), log(0.73)),
  s0 = c(2, (log(0.96) - log(0.61)) / 3.92, (log(0.87) - log(0.61)) / 3.92)) |>
  mutate(prec = 1 / s0^2 + 1 / s_cl^2,
         pm = (m0 / s0^2 + y_cl / s_cl^2) / prec, ps = sqrt(1 / prec))
post_cl |>
  transmute(Prior,
            `Prior HR (95%)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(m0), exp(m0 - 1.96 * s0), exp(m0 + 1.96 * s0)),
            `Posterior HR (95% CrI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(pm), exp(pm - 1.96 * ps), exp(pm + 1.96 * ps)),
            `P(HR < 1)` = sprintf("%.2f", pnorm(0, pm, ps)),
            `P(HR < 0.90)` = sprintf("%.2f", pnorm(log(0.90), pm, ps)),
            `P(HR < 0.85)` = sprintf("%.2f", pnorm(log(0.85), pm, ps)),
            `P(HR < 0.80)` = sprintf("%.2f", pnorm(log(0.80), pm, ps))) |>
  kable(align = "lcccccc", caption = "Posterior after CLEAR under three priors (normal approximation).")

  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey60") +

Figure 13.7: Prior (dotted) and posterior (solid) distributions of the hazard ratio after CLEAR, under three priors. The dashed line is the CLEAR likelihood.





With the vague prior the posterior is CLEAR’s own result, and the probability of any benefit is about one half. With the COLCOT prior it is 92%, and with the earlier meta-analysis 99%. But under every prior the probability of a reduction of 15% or more is modest, at most 37%. CLEAR has made a large benefit unlikely without eliminating a modest one. That is a statement both the trialists and the meta-analysts could accept, and neither “no effect” nor “a 12% reduction” conveys it.
The normal approximation is adequate for a trial this large. With small trials or rare events, the counts can be modelled directly with a binomial likelihood. brms fits such a model; the grid cannot, because each trial adds a baseline-risk parameter.


Code
library(brms)
arms <- tibble::tibble(study = "CLEAR", treat = c(1, 0), r = c(322, 327), n = c(3528, 3534))
priors <- list(vague  = prior(normal(0, 2), class = b),          # log OR for treat
               colcot = prior(normal(-0.26, 0.12), class = b),
               meta   = prior(normal(-0.31, 0.09), class = b))
fit_vague <- brm(r | trials(n) ~ 1 + treat, family = binomial(), data = arms,
                 prior = priors$vague, seed = 2025)
fit_colcot <- update(fit_vague, prior = priors$colcot)          # Stan recompiles for a new prior
fit_meta   <- update(fit_vague, prior = priors$meta)


This model works on the odds ratio scale for cumulative incidence, which with 9% event rates is close to the hazard ratio; with several trials, add (1 | study) for study-specific baselines and treatment effects.


13.3.5 Adding CLEAR to the trials
Using earlier evidence as a prior treats it as exchangeable with the new trial up to the uncertainty in the prior. The alternative is to put CLEAR into the random-effects model as an eighth trial, so that its disagreement with the others is treated as heterogeneity.


Code
dat8 <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = ev_col, n1i = n_col, ci = ev_pbo, n2i = n_pbo, slab = study,
               data = bind_rows(colch, tibble::tibble(study = "CLEAR", ev_col = 322, n_col = 3528,
                                                      ev_pbo = 327, n_pbo = 3534)))
set.seed(2025)
post_c8 <- bayes_nn(dat8$yi, sqrt(dat8$vi))
pr8 <- predict(rma(yi, vi, data = dat8, method = "REML"), transf = exp)
pr7 <- predict(rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "REML"), transf = exp)
pi_txt <- \(x) sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", exp(quantile(x, 0.025)), exp(quantile(x, 0.975)))
tibble::tibble(Evidence = c("2022 meta-analysis, 7 trials", "7 trials + CLEAR"),
               `Mean RR, Bayesian (95% CrI)` = c(q3(post_c$mu), q3(post_c8$mu)),
               `τ, posterior median` = sprintf("%.2f", c(median(post_c$tau), median(post_c8$tau))),
               `New trial, frequentist (REML)` = c(sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", pr7$pi.lb, pr7$pi.ub),
                                                   sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", pr8$pi.lb, pr8$pi.ub)),
               `New trial, Bayesian` = c(pi_txt(post_c$new), pi_txt(post_c8$new))) |>
  kable(align = "lcccc", caption = "Before and after adding CLEAR as an eighth trial.")

CLEAR is by far the largest trial, but in a random-effects model it pulls the mean less than it would in a fixed-effect analysis, and because it disagrees with the earlier trials it raises the estimated heterogeneity, which widens the prediction for a new trial. Which analysis is preferable depends on a judgement the data cannot make: whether CLEAR’s population, timing of treatment and outcome make it one more draw from the same distribution as the earlier trials, or a different and more relevant question. Prediction intervals quoted for “the colchicine evidence” therefore need a statement of which trials, which model and which prior on τ produced them; intervals from different evidence sets or models cannot be compared.


13.3.6 From posterior to decision
A posterior becomes a decision through thresholds chosen before seeing the results. Suppose a relative reduction of less than 5% is too small to justify a daily drug with gastrointestinal side effects (a region of practical equivalence), a reduction of 15% or more is clearly worthwhile, and the range between is a grey zone in which the choice depends on the patient.


Code
post_cl |>
  mutate(`Important benefit (HR < 0.85)` = pnorm(log(0.85), pm, ps),
         `Grey zone (0.85 to 0.95)` = pnorm(log(0.95), pm, ps) - pnorm(log(0.85), pm, ps),
         `Little or none (HR ≥ 0.95)` = 1 - pnorm(log(0.95), pm, ps)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(starts_with("Important"), starts_with("Grey"), starts_with("Little")),
               names_to = "Region", values_to = "p") |>
  mutate(Region = factor(Region, levels = c("Little or none (HR ≥ 0.95)", "Grey zone (0.85 to 0.95)",
                                            "Important benefit (HR < 0.85)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(p, Prior, fill = Region)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(p > 0.06, sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * p), "")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#B22222", "#E69F00", "#2E7D32"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Posterior probability after CLEAR", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 13.8: Posterior probability after CLEAR of little or no benefit (HR ≥ 0.95), a grey zone (0.85 to 0.95) and important benefit (HR < 0.85), under three priors.





If most of the mass lies in the first region, recommend against; in the last, recommend for; spread across them, share the decision with the patient or seek more evidence. Whatever the prior, most of the mass now lies outside “important benefit”. A reasonable conclusion is that colchicine provides at most a modest benefit after myocardial infarction: the evidence does not support a strong recommendation, but neither does it rule out benefit for some patients, and a discussion of the uncertainty (and of the side effects) is appropriate.


13.3.7 Sensitivity beyond the prior on μ
With seven trials the data say little about τ, so its prior matters, mainly for the prediction.


Code
set.seed(7)
tau_priors <- list(`Half-normal(0.1)` = \(t) 2 * dnorm(t, 0, 0.1),
                   `Half-normal(0.5)` = \(t) 2 * dnorm(t, 0, 0.5),
                   `Half-normal(1)`   = \(t) 2 * dnorm(t, 0, 1),
                   `Half-Cauchy(0.5)` = \(t) 2 * dcauchy(t, 0, 0.5))
imap_dfr(tau_priors, \(pr, nm) {
  p <- bayes_nn(dat$yi, sqrt(dat$vi), tau_prior = pr)
  tibble::tibble(`Prior on τ` = nm, `RR (95% CrI)` = q3(p$mu),
                 `New trial (95%)` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", exp(quantile(p$new, 0.025)), exp(quantile(p$new, 0.975))),
                 `P(RR < 0.85)` = sprintf("%.2f", mean(p$mu < log(0.85))))
}) |> kable(align = "lccc")

The mean barely changes, but the prediction for a new trial ranges from narrow to very wide, depending on how much heterogeneity the prior allows. A leave-one-out analysis (Section 10.4.1) can be run the same way, by refitting the model without each trial in turn; it checks robustness within the evidence, but cannot reveal that the evidence base as a whole is unrepresentative. Every trial in the 2022 meta-analysis pointed the same way; the much larger CLEAR did not.

title: 13  Bayesian Meta-Analysis
text:
13.4 A Bayesian workflow



Table 13.2: A Bayesian workflow for a clinical meta-analysis.









Step
Content




1. Ask the clinical question
Not “does it work?” but “how probable is a benefit large enough to change practice?”


2. Pre-specify thresholds
What counts as important benefit, and what as practically no effect


3. Choose and justify priors
Weakly informative primary analysis; sceptical, enthusiastic or empirical alternatives; a defensible prior on τ


4. Fit the model
Grid or bayesmeta for the normal-normal model; brms for binomial data, covariates or complex structures; check convergence (R̂, effective sample size)


5. Report the posterior
Median and 95% credible interval, the prediction for a new trial, and the probability of each pre-specified region


6. Test sensitivity
Community of priors for μ and τ; leave-one-out; risk of bias


7. State the clinical conclusion
For example: “under a vague prior the probability of a reduction of at least 15% is X%; under the COLCOT prior, Y%”






A meta-analysis is only as reliable as the studies in it. Several meta-analyses agreeing does not make a conclusion correct if they share the same trials and the same assumptions, and the clinical questions (crossovers, blinding, the timing and definition of outcomes) matter as much as the statistical ones. What the Bayesian approach adds is a transparent way to combine evidence with what was known before, and to express the result in the probabilities that decisions need.

title: 13  Bayesian Meta-Analysis
text:
Key points

A posterior distribution answers the questions clinicians ask: the probability of benefit, of an important benefit, and the expected effect in a new setting.
Two “significant” results can have very different clinical meaning, and two “non-significant” ones very different implications; the whole distribution, not the P value, tells them apart.
Choose priors openly and report a community of priors (weakly informative, sceptical, enthusiastic, empirical). The prior on τ matters most with few studies; empirical distributions are available.
The Bayesian prediction for a new trial includes the uncertainty in μ and τ; shrinkage gives better estimates of each trial’s effect.
Updating an earlier body of evidence with a new trial reconciles results that dichotomous reporting presents as contradictory, as for colchicine and CLEAR.
Pre-specified thresholds turn a posterior into a decision.

title: 13  Bayesian Meta-Analysis
text:
Exercises

Using the conjugate update, find the standard deviation of a sceptical prior centred on HR = 1 that leaves P(HR < 0.9) after CLEAR below 5%.
Refit the seven trials of the 2022 meta-analysis with a Turner empirical prior for τ² appropriate to a semi-objective outcome comparing a drug with placebo (see (5)). How do the prediction interval and P(RR < 0.85) change?
Compare the eight-trial random-effects analysis with the analysis that uses the 2022 meta-analysis as a prior for CLEAR. Why do they give different posteriors for the mean? Which better reflects the differences between the trials?
Repeat the shrinkage plot with a half-normal(0.1) prior on τ. Which trials move, and why?
Write a one-paragraph summary of the colchicine evidence for a patient, using posterior probabilities rather than P values.

title: 14  Missing Data
text:
14.1 The scale of the problem
Every meta-analysis has missing data. Whole studies may be unpublished, outcomes may be measured but not reported, summary statistics may be incomplete, and within each trial some participants’ outcomes are never observed. This chapter deals mainly with the last two: missing participants and missing summary statistics. Missing studies, the subject of publication bias, are taken up in Chapter 15.
In a review of 77 trials published in the BMJ, JAMA, Lancet and NEJM in the second half of 2013, 95% reported some missing outcome data, with a median of 9% of participants missing (range 0% to 70%). The primary analysis used complete cases in 45%, simple imputation such as last observation carried forward in 27%, model-based methods in 19% and multiple imputation in 8%; only 35% reported a sensitivity analysis (1). In a review of 235 trials with a statistically significant binary outcome in five leading journals (median loss to follow-up 6%), 0% to 33% of results were no longer significant under plausible assumptions about the participants lost (2).
For the meta-analyst the problem compounds. A trial reports a number analysed, rarely the mechanism of missingness, and sometimes not even the method used to handle it. Different trials use different methods, and pooling them combines estimates that may answer slightly different questions, weighted by size rather than by data quality.
Missing study-level data mainly limit which questions can be asked; a subgroup analysis restricted to the trials that chose to report the subgroup is itself open to selective reporting. Missing participants bias the answers.

title: 14  Missing Data
text:
14.2 Mechanisms of missingness
Three mechanisms, defined by Rubin, describe how the probability that an outcome is missing relates to the data.

Missing completely at random (MCAR). Missingness depends on neither observed nor unobserved data: \(P(\text{missing} \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) = P(\text{missing})\). The complete cases are a random subsample, and analysing them is unbiased, with some loss of precision. A dropped laboratory sample is the classic example; in trials, MCAR is rare.
Missing at random (MAR). Missingness depends only on observed data: \(P(\text{missing} \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) = P(\text{missing} \mid Y_{obs})\). Older or sicker patients may drop out more, but given their age and baseline severity, dropout is random. Analyses that condition on the variables that predict missingness (multiple imputation, mixed models) are valid.
Missing not at random (MNAR). Missingness depends on the unobserved outcome itself, even after conditioning on everything observed. Patients who are not improving stop attending; patients with adverse effects withdraw. No analysis of the observed data alone is guaranteed valid.

The distinction between MAR and MNAR cannot be tested from the data, because it concerns values that were never observed. Figure 14.1 simulates the same 2000 patients under each mechanism.


Code
set.seed(42)
n <- 2000
baseline <- rnorm(n)                                        # observed for everyone
y <- 0.7 * baseline + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(1 - 0.7^2))          # final outcome (higher = worse)
miss <- list(MCAR = rbinom(n, 1, 0.30),                     # a coin flip
             MAR  = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + 1.5 * baseline)),  # depends on observed baseline
             MNAR = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + 1.5 * y)))         # depends on the outcome itself
est <- imap_dfr(miss, \(m, nm) {
  obs <- m == 0
  fit <- lm(y ~ baseline, subset = obs)
  tibble::tibble(Mechanism = nm, pct = 100 * mean(m),
                 `True mean (everyone)` = mean(y), `Mean of observed only` = mean(y[obs]),
                 `Baseline-adjusted estimate` = mean(predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(baseline))))
}) |> mutate(Mechanism = factor(Mechanism, c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR")))
lines <- est |> select(-pct) |>
  pivot_longer(-Mechanism, names_to = "Estimate", values_to = "x") |>
  mutate(Estimate = factor(Estimate, c("True mean (everyone)", "Mean of observed only",
                                       "Baseline-adjusted estimate")))
lab <- est |> mutate(label = sprintf("%.0f%% missing\nbias, observed: %+.2f\nbias, adjusted: %+.2f", pct,
                                     `Mean of observed only` - `True mean (everyone)`,
                                     `Baseline-adjusted estimate` - `True mean (everyone)`))
imap_dfr(miss, \(m, nm) tibble::tibble(Mechanism = nm, y = y,
                                       Status = ifelse(m == 1, "Missing", "Observed"))) |>
  mutate(Status = factor(Status, c("Observed", "Missing")),
         Mechanism = factor(Mechanism, c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(y)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = Status), bins = 35, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(data = lines, aes(xintercept = x, colour = Estimate, linetype = Estimate), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_label(data = lab, aes(x = -2.5, y = Inf, label = label), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             hjust = 0, vjust = 1.1, size = 3, fill = "white", label.size = 0, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.5))) +
  facet_wrap(~ Mechanism) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Observed = "#041E42", Missing = "#B22222"), name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "#E69F00", "#2E7D32"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dotted", "dashed"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-2.5, 2.5)) +
  labs(x = "Final outcome (higher = worse)", y = "Patients") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical")








Figure 14.1: The same 2000 simulated patients under three missingness mechanisms. Bars: observed (navy) and missing (red) outcomes, stacked. Lines: the true mean of everyone (black), the mean of the observed (orange, dotted) and an estimate adjusted for the observed baseline value (green, dashed).





Under MCAR the observed mean is unbiased. Under MAR the patients who were sicker at baseline drop out, so the observed mean looks too good; because baseline is observed, adjusting for it removes the bias. Under MNAR, dropout depends on the outcome itself, and adjustment for baseline helps only partly.
In most drug trials MNAR is plausible: patients who are not improving stop treatment, patients with adverse effects withdraw, and deteriorating patients become too ill to attend. Yet trials’ primary analyses almost always assume MCAR or MAR. The recommended practice is a primary analysis under a plausible MAR assumption plus sensitivity analyses that explore departures towards MNAR (3). If dropout differs between arms for reasons related to the outcome, the comparison of completers is no longer randomised, and the bias can favour either arm. The STRIDE trial assessed in Chapter 5 is an example: about 15% of participants were missing at 52 weeks, more in the placebo arm, and placebo patients who were not improving plausibly left more often.
No analysis can recover information that was never collected. Trial features that reduce missing data (follow-up continued after treatment is stopped, flexible dosing, rescue medication built into the protocol, outcomes less prone to missingness) point to a lower risk of bias in RoB 2 domain 3. Some designs reduce missing data at a price: run-in periods and randomised withdrawal designs exclude, before randomisation, patients who cannot tolerate or adhere to the drug, so that harms are underestimated and the results apply to a selected group, an issue of indirectness rather than risk of bias.

title: 14  Missing Data
text:
14.3 Handling methods and their assumptions
Every method for handling missing outcomes is an assumption about what those outcomes would have been. Knowing which assumption each trial made tells the meta-analyst which trials may be biased, and in which direction.



Table 14.2: Methods for missing outcome data (adapted from Egger, Higgins and Davey Smith, Systematic Reviews in Health Research, 3rd ed., Table 11.1).











Method
Assumption
Consequence
Use in meta-analysis




Complete case (available case)
MCAR, or MAR given the covariates in the model
Unbiased under MCAR; biased under MNAR
The usual primary analysis; a starting point


Last observation carried forward (LOCF)
Outcome frozen at dropout
Biased, often towards the null; CIs too narrow
Common in trials; accept with caution


Baseline observation carried forward (BOCF)
Dropouts return to baseline
Erases any improvement among dropouts
Some regulatory analyses


Worst or best case
All missing had the worst (best) outcome
Bounds, not estimates
Extreme sensitivity check


Single imputation (mean, regression)
MAR
SEs too small
Not as primary analysis


Multiple imputation
MAR
Valid under MAR with a good imputation model
Needs individual data; prefer the trial’s MI estimate


Likelihood-based (mixed models)
MAR
Valid under MAR
Needs individual data; prefer the trial’s estimate


IMOR, δ-adjustment (pattern mixture)
Specified departure from MAR
Quantifies sensitivity to MNAR
Recommended sensitivity analysis with aggregate data







14.3.1 One simulated trial, three mechanisms
To see these assumptions at work, we simulate a trial of a depression-type score (higher is worse), measured at baseline and three follow-up visits in 150 patients per arm. Both arms improve; by visit 3 the active arm has improved 6 points more (true effect −6). Patients drop out with the same rule in both arms: under MCAR, 10% of those remaining at each visit by chance; under MAR, with a probability that rises with lack of improvement at the previous (observed) visit; under MNAR, with lack of improvement at the current (unobserved) visit. Under MAR and MNAR the placebo arm, with more non-improvers, loses more patients. Each scenario is simulated 150 times, and each simulated trial is analysed six ways, all adjusting for baseline.


Code
sim_trial <- function(n = 150, mech = "MCAR", effect = -6) {
  trt <- rep(0:1, each = n)
  u   <- rnorm(2 * n, 0, 4)                                   # patient level
  s   <- rnorm(2 * n, 0, 6)                                   # patient response
  Y   <- sapply(0:3, \(t) 30 + u + (-3 + trt * effect / 3 + s / 3) * t + rnorm(2 * n, 0, 4))
  R   <- matrix(TRUE, 2 * n, 4)                               # TRUE = observed
  for (t in 2:4) {
    worse_prev <- Y[, t - 1] - Y[, 1] + 3 * (t - 2)           # lack of improvement, previous visit
    worse_now  <- Y[, t]     - Y[, 1] + 3 * (t - 1)           # ... current visit (unseen if missing)
    lp <- switch(mech, MCAR = rep(-2.2, 2 * n),               # plogis(-2.2) = 10% per visit
                 MAR = -2.2 + 0.3 * worse_prev, MNAR = -2.2 + 0.3 * worse_now)
    R[, t] <- R[, t - 1] & rbinom(2 * n, 1, plogis(lp)) == 0  # monotone dropout
  }
  Yobs <- Y; Yobs[!R] <- NA
  list(Y = Y, Yobs = Yobs, trt = trt)
}
coefse <- function(fit, term = "trt") {
  s <- if (inherits(fit, "gls")) summary(fit)$tTable else summary(fit)$coefficients
  c(est = s[term, 1], se = s[term, 2])
}
analyse <- function(d) {
  Yo <- d$Yobs; trt <- d$trt; y0 <- Yo[, 1]; y3 <- Yo[, 4]
  last <- apply(Yo, 1, \(r) tail(na.omit(r), 1))
  out <- list(
    `No missing data` = coefse(lm(d$Y[, 4] ~ trt + y0)),     # benchmark, before dropout
    `Complete case`   = coefse(lm(y3 ~ trt + y0)),
    LOCF              = coefse(lm(last ~ trt + y0)),
    BOCF              = coefse(lm(ifelse(is.na(y3), y0, y3) ~ trt + y0)),
    `Mean imputation` = coefse(lm(ifelse(is.na(y3), ave(y3, trt, FUN = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)), y3) ~ trt + y0)))
  imp <- mice(data.frame(trt, y0, y1 = Yo[, 2], y2 = Yo[, 3], y3), m = 5, method = "norm", printFlag = FALSE)
  pm  <- summary(pool(with(imp, lm(y3 ~ trt + y0))))
  out$`Multiple imputation` <- c(est = pm$estimate[2], se = pm$std.error[2])
  N    <- length(trt)
  long <- tibble::tibble(id = rep(1:N, 3), trt = rep(trt, 3), y0 = rep(y0, 3),
                         visit = factor(rep(1:3, each = N)), y = c(Yo[, 2:4])) |> filter(!is.na(y))
  mm <- gls(y ~ visit * trt + visit * y0, data = long,           # mixed model for repeated measures
            correlation = corSymm(form = ~ as.integer(visit) | id),
            weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | visit))
  V  <- vcov(mm)[c("trt", "visit3:trt"), c("trt", "visit3:trt")]
  out$`Mixed model (MMRM)` <- c(est = sum(coef(mm)[c("trt", "visit3:trt")]), se = sqrt(sum(V)))
  bind_rows(out, .id = "method")
}
set.seed(629)
sims <- map_dfr(c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR"), \(m) map_dfr(1:150, \(r) {
  d <- sim_trial(mech = m)
  analyse(d) |> mutate(mech = m, miss_pbo = mean(is.na(d$Yobs[d$trt == 0, 4])),
                       miss_act = mean(is.na(d$Yobs[d$trt == 1, 4])))
}))
sim_summary <- sims |>
  mutate(mech = factor(mech, c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR")),
         method = factor(method, c("No missing data", "Complete case", "LOCF", "BOCF",
                                   "Mean imputation", "Multiple imputation", "Mixed model (MMRM)"))) |>
  group_by(mech, method) |>
  summarise(est_mean = mean(est), lo = mean(est - 1.96 * se), hi = mean(est + 1.96 * se),
            coverage = mean(abs(est + 6) < 1.96 * se),
            miss_pbo = mean(miss_pbo), miss_act = mean(miss_act), .groups = "drop")
miss_rates <- sim_summary |> distinct(mech, miss_pbo, miss_act)




Code
sim_summary |>
  mutate(method = forcats::fct_rev(method), cov_lab = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * coverage)) |>
  ggplot(aes(est_mean, method, colour = mech)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -6, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, group = forcats::fct_rev(mech)),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.7)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 1.8, label = cov_lab, group = forcats::fct_rev(mech)), size = 3.3,
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-9, 2.3)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(MCAR = "#2E7D32", MAR = "#E69F00", MNAR = "#B22222"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Estimated treatment effect (true = −6)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 14.2: Six analyses of 150 simulated trials under each mechanism (true effect −6, dashed line). Point: average estimate; bar: a typical single trial’s 95% CI. Percentages at right: coverage, the proportion of trials whose 95% CI contains −6.





At visit 3 the placebo arm lost about 43% of patients under MNAR, the active arm about 26%. Reading Figure 14.2 method by method:

Complete case is unbiased under MCAR, at the cost of precision. Under MAR and MNAR the placebo arm loses more of its non-improvers, so its completers look better than the arm as a whole, and the benefit is understated. Complete-case analysis assumes that the missing patients in each arm would have done, on average, like the observed patients in that arm.
LOCF and BOCF are biased towards the null even under MCAR, not because patients improve, but because the gap between the arms widens over time and the dropouts are frozen at an earlier visit, or at baseline, when the arms had separated less. Under MAR and MNAR they land nearer the truth than complete case, because their pull towards the null happens to offset the placebo arm’s selective losses: luck, not validity. A “conservative” method is conservative only for one direction of one comparison; in a non-inferiority trial, bias towards the null favours the new drug.
Mean imputation has about the same bias as complete case, but treats imputed values as data, so its intervals are too narrow.
Multiple imputation and the mixed model (MMRM) are close to unbiased under MCAR and MAR, and give nearly the same answers. Under MNAR both are biased in the same way: the information that would correct them was never measured.

Figure 14.3 illustrates why LOCF misleads for a condition that changes over time.


Code
set.seed(99)
true_traj <- function(t) 50 + 8 * t - 0.5 * t^2
obs4 <- true_traj(0:4) + rnorm(5, 0, 4)
tibble::tibble(time = c(0:4, 4:12, 0:12),
               value = c(obs4, rep(last(obs4), 9), true_traj(0:12) + rnorm(13, 0, 4)),
               type = c(rep("Observed (dropout at week 4)", 5), rep("LOCF imputation", 9),
                        rep("True trajectory (if followed)", 13))) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, value, colour = type, linetype = type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#B22222", "#041E42", "#E69F00"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid", "solid"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Outcome score") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 14.3: A single patient who drops out at week 4. LOCF freezes the outcome at the last observed value; the true trajectory continues to change.





For the meta-analyst the practical lessons are to prefer a trial’s multiple-imputation or mixed-model estimate to its LOCF estimate when both are reported; to avoid mixing LOCF, BOCF and MMRM estimates without at least a sensitivity analysis by method; and to remember that neither MI nor MMRM removes the need to examine departures from MAR.


14.3.2 Worst and best cases
For a binary outcome the missing participants can be assigned the most extreme outcomes. Consider one trial in which the outcome is an adverse event (RR < 1 favours treatment): 12 events among 55 analysed of 63 randomised to treatment, and 22 among 55 analysed of 60 controls. Because this is an illustration, we also know that 4 of the 8 treatment dropouts and 2 of the 5 control dropouts had the event.


Code
rr <- function(et, nt, ec, nc) {
  e <- escalc("RR", ai = et, n1i = nt, ci = ec, n2i = nc)
  x <- exp(e$yi + c(0, -1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(e$vi))
  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", x[1], x[2], x[3])
}
tibble::tibble(
  Scenario = c("Truth: everyone counted", "Complete case", "Missing = no event",
               "Worst case for treatment", "Best case for treatment"),
  `RR (95% CI)` = c(rr(12 + 4, 63, 22 + 2, 60), rr(12, 55, 22, 55), rr(12, 63, 22, 60),
                    rr(12 + 8, 63, 22, 60), rr(12, 63, 22 + 5, 60))) |>
  kable(align = "lc")





Scenario
RR (95% CI)




Truth: everyone counted

Complete case

Missing = no event

The truth lies between the bounds, as it must. Complete case overstates the benefit, because the treatment dropouts had the event more often (4 of 8) than the treatment completers (12 of 55). Bounds are usually too wide to be informative, which is why GRADE recommends plausible worst cases rather than extreme ones (Section 14.6).

title: 14  Missing Data
text:
14.4 Missing summary statistics
Continuous outcomes need a mean and an SD (or SE) for each arm, but papers often report only means with P values, confidence intervals, or medians and ranges. This is missing summary information, not missing participants, and much of it can be recovered (4).

From a 95% confidence interval for a mean: \(SE = (\text{upper} - \text{lower})/(2 \times 1.96)\), using \(t_{n-1}\) in place of 1.96 for small samples, and \(SD = SE\sqrt{n}\).
From a t statistic or exact P value for a difference: \(SE_{\text{diff}} = |\bar X_1 - \bar X_2|/t\), and \(SD = SE_{\text{diff}}/\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}\).
When nothing can be calculated: ask the authors; otherwise borrow an SD from other studies in the review, which performs reasonably well empirically (5). For a mean difference a larger imputed SD only down-weights the study; for a standardised mean difference it shrinks the effect towards zero. If most studies lack SDs, do not impute; and always show the effect of removing the imputed studies.



Code
md <- 5.0; p <- 0.03; n1 <- n2 <- 40                    # "MD 5.0 points, p = 0.03, 40 per arm"
t_val <- qt(1 - p / 2, df = n1 + n2 - 2)
se_md <- md / t_val
round(c(t = t_val, SE = se_md, SD = se_md / sqrt(1 / n1 + 1 / n2)), 2)


    t    SE    SD 
 2.21  2.26 10.12 


Only exact P values can be inverted; “P < 0.05” cannot. P values are rounded (0.03 could be 0.025 to 0.035), so check the sensitivity of the recovered SD. If the trial used ANCOVA or a mixed model, the recovered SD is a residual SD, smaller than the raw SD, and should not be mixed with raw SDs in a standardised mean difference.

14.4.1 Change scores and the unknown correlation
To pool change from baseline, each arm needs the SD of the change, which many trials do not report:
\[SD_{\text{change}} = \sqrt{SD_{\text{base}}^2 + SD_{\text{final}}^2 - 2\,r\,SD_{\text{base}}\,SD_{\text{final}}},\]
where r is the correlation between baseline and final values, almost never reported. It can be estimated from studies that report all three SDs and borrowed for those that do not, but it is an assumption about missing data and should be varied. Consider a small trial of fluoxetine and nortriptyline in children with depression (20 per arm), reporting the Children’s Depression Inventory as 28.9 (SD 8.4) → 17.9 (8.1) with fluoxetine and 28.4 (8.7) → 25.8 (8.6) with nortriptyline.


Code
sd_change <- \(sb, sf, r) sqrt(sb^2 + sf^2 - 2 * r * sb * sf)
diff_change <- (28.9 - 17.9) - (28.4 - 25.8)
tibble::tibble(r = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.97)) |>
  mutate(`SD change, fluoxetine` = sd_change(8.4, 8.1, r),
         `SD change, nortriptyline` = sd_change(8.7, 8.6, r),
         `Pooled SD` = sqrt((`SD change, fluoxetine`^2 + `SD change, nortriptyline`^2) / 2),
         `Change-score SMD` = diff_change / `Pooled SD`) |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = "ccccc")

14.4.2 Medians, quartiles and ranges
If the outcome is roughly normal, quartiles and extremes carry information about the mean and SD. In a normal distribution the interquartile range spans 1.35 SD, so \(SD \approx IQR/1.35\) in large samples. The range depends on sample size: in a sample of 10 it spans about 3 SD, in a sample of 1000 about 6.5. (6) proposed the first formulas; (7) replaced fixed divisors with ones that change with n; (8) improved the estimate of the mean.

title: 14  Missing Data
section: 14.5 Binary outcomes: the informative missingness odds ratio
text:
14.5 Binary outcomes: the informative missingness odds ratio
For binary outcomes, a sensitivity analysis that works with aggregate data is the informative missingness odds ratio (IMOR) (10,11). Within one arm, it compares the odds of the outcome among the missing with the odds among the observed:
\[IMOR = \frac{\text{odds of success among the missing}}{\text{odds of success among the observed}} .\]
IMOR = 1 is complete-case analysis; IMOR < 1 means the missing did worse; IMOR = 0 means every missing participant failed; and IMOR → ∞ means every missing participant succeeded. IMOR cannot be estimated from the data; it is a sensitivity parameter chosen by clinical judgement. For example, if an arm has 40 improved, 20 not improved and 40 missing (odds 2), and a clinician thinks that 10 of the 40 missing would have improved (odds 1/3), the IMOR is 1/6.

14.5.1 The haloperidol meta-analysis
Seventeen placebo-controlled trials of haloperidol in schizophrenia, with clinical improvement as the outcome (RR > 1 favours haloperidol), are a standard worked example for missing binary outcomes (11). Two trials, Beasley 1996 and Selman 1976, lost many patients, more on placebo; and in schizophrenia trials, patients who leave are plausibly those not improving.


Code
haloperidol <- tibble::tribble(   # improved, not improved, missing; haloperidol (H) and placebo (P)
  ~study, ~rH, ~fH, ~mH, ~rP, ~fP, ~mP,
  "Arvanitis 1997", 25, 25, 2, 18, 33, 0,   "Beasley 1996", 29, 18, 22, 20, 14, 34,
  "Bechelli 1983", 12, 17, 1,  2, 28, 1,    "Borison 1992",  3,  9,  0,  0, 12,  0,
  "Chouinard 1993", 10, 11, 0, 3, 19, 0,    "Durost 1964",  11,  8,  0,  1, 14,  0,
  "Garry 1962",  7, 18, 1,  4, 21, 1,       "Howard 1974",   8,  9,  0,  3, 10,  0,
  "Marder 1994", 19, 45, 2, 14, 50, 2,      "Nishikawa 1982", 1, 9,  0,  0, 10,  0,
  "Nishikawa 1984", 11, 23, 3, 0, 13, 0,    "Reschke 1974", 20,  9,  0,  2,  9,  0,
  "Selman 1976", 17,  1, 11, 7,  4, 18,     "Serafetinides 1972", 4, 10, 0, 0, 13, 1,
  "Simpson 1967",  2, 14, 0, 0,  7, 1,      "Spencer 1992", 11,  1,  0,  1, 11,  0,
  "Vichaiya 1971", 9, 20, 1, 0, 29, 1)

14.5.2 Applying the IMOR
For each arm of each study: compute the observed risk p among the n analysed and the proportion missing π; convert the chosen IMOR into a risk among the missing, \(p_m = IMOR \cdot p/(IMOR \cdot p + 1 - p)\); and compute the risk for everyone randomised, \(p^* = (1-\pi)p + \pi p_m\). The variance of \(p^*\), by the delta method, has terms for sampling error in p, sampling error in π (zero when IMOR = 1), and, if the IMOR is uncertain, uncertainty in the IMOR itself. The adjusted log RRs are then pooled as usual. Adding guessed events to the 2×2 table and analysing them as if observed is wrong: trials with many missing participants would then look more precise, when they are less certain.


Code
adj_arm <- function(r, f, m, imor, sd_log = 0, cc = 0) {    # one arm (Higgins, White & Wood 2008)
  N  <- r + f + m; pi <- m / N                               # randomised; proportion missing
  n  <- r + f + 2 * cc; p <- (r + cc) / n                    # analysed; observed risk
  pm <- imor * p / (imor * p + 1 - p)                        # risk among the missing
  ps <- (1 - pi) * p + pi * pm                               # risk among everyone randomised
  dp <- (1 - pi) + pi * imor / (imor * p + 1 - p)^2          # d ps / d p
  v  <- dp^2 * p * (1 - p) / n +                             # 1. sampling error in p
        (pm - p)^2 * pi * (1 - pi) / N +                     # 2. sampling error in pi
        (pi * pm * (1 - pm))^2 * sd_log^2                    # 3. uncertainty in log IMOR
  tibble::tibble(ps, v)
}
imor_ma <- function(d, imorH, imorP = imorH, sd_log = 0) {   # pooled log RR, common effect
  cc <- ifelse(with(d, rH * fH * rP * fP) == 0, 0.5, 0)
  h  <- with(d, adj_arm(rH, fH, mH, imorH, sd_log, cc))
  pl <- with(d, adj_arm(rP, fP, mP, imorP, sd_log, cc))
  rma(yi = log(h$ps / pl$ps), vi = h$v / h$ps^2 + pl$v / pl$ps^2, method = "EE")
}
scen <- list(`Complete case (IMOR = 1)` = imor_ma(haloperidol, 1),
             `Missing did worse (IMOR = 0.5)` = imor_ma(haloperidol, 0.5),
             `All missing failed (IMOR = 0)` = imor_ma(haloperidol, 0),
             `Missing did better (IMOR = 2)` = imor_ma(haloperidol, 2),

             `Best case for haloperidol` = imor_ma(haloperidol, 1e6, 0))

14.5.3 Tipping points and uncertain IMORs
Patients may leave the two arms for different reasons, so the IMOR can differ by arm. Figure 14.4 maps the pooled RR over a grid of IMORs for each arm and marks where the 95% CI first includes 1: a tipping-point analysis.


Code
imor_brk <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 10, 20)
grid_df <- expand.grid(dH = seq(-3, 3, by = 0.2), dP = seq(-3, 3, by = 0.2)) |>
  mutate(fit = map2(dH, dP, \(a, b) imor_ma(haloperidol, exp(a), exp(b))),
         RR = map_dbl(fit, \(f) exp(f$b[1])), lo = map_dbl(fit, \(f) exp(f$ci.lb))) |>
  select(-fit)
ggplot(grid_df, aes(dH, dP)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = RR)) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = lo), breaks = 1, colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, shape = 18, size = 5, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Pooled RR", trans = "log", breaks = c(1, 1.25, 1.5, 2)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = log(imor_brk), labels = imor_brk) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = log(imor_brk), labels = imor_brk) +
  labs(x = "IMOR, haloperidol arm (log scale)", y = "IMOR, placebo arm (log scale)") +
  coord_fixed()








Figure 14.4: Pooled RR over IMORs from 0.05 to 20 in each arm. Inside the dashed contour (top left) the 95% CI includes 1. The diamond marks complete-case analysis.





Significance is lost only in the top-left corner, where missing haloperidol patients did much worse and missing placebo patients much better than the observed. Whether that is plausible is a clinical question, which is the point: the analysis converts a vague worry about missing data into a specific assumption that can be judged.
Rather than a single IMOR, our belief can be described by a distribution. Suppose, for these trials, a log IMOR centred on log(0.7) with SD 0.35: missing patients probably did somewhat worse than those observed, but not all failed. The uncertainty can enter analytically, through the variance term above, or by simulation, drawing an IMOR for each arm, re-running the meta-analysis, and pooling the results.


Code
set.seed(629)
draws <- map_dbl(1:2000, \(i) {
  f <- imor_ma(haloperidol, exp(rnorm(1, -0.35, 0.35)), exp(rnorm(1, -0.35, 0.35)))
  rnorm(1, f$b[1], f$se)
})
an <- imor_ma(haloperidol, exp(-0.35), sd_log = 0.35)
tibble::tibble(Analysis = c("Complete case", "Uncertain IMOR, analytic", "Uncertain IMOR, simulation"),
               `Pooled RR (95% interval)` = c(fmt_rr(aca), fmt_rr(an),
                 sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(median(draws)), exp(quantile(draws, 0.025)),
                         exp(quantile(draws, 0.975)))),
               `Weight: Beasley` = sprintf("%.0f%%", c(weights(aca)[2], weights(an)[2], NA))) |>
  mutate(`Weight: Beasley` = replace(`Weight: Beasley`, 3, "")) |>
  kable(align = "lcc")

title: 14  Missing Data
text:
14.6 What reviewers should do
The Cochrane Handbook recommends contacting investigators for missing data, stating the assumptions behind whatever method is used, assessing risk of bias due to missing outcome data, running sensitivity analyses over reasonable changes in those assumptions, and discussing the potential impact of missing data on the findings (12). Single imputation treated as observed data is not recommended; complete-case analysis is acceptable as a starting point; methods that allow for the uncertainty (multiple imputation, IMOR with its variance) are preferred.
For each arm of each study, extract the number randomised, the number analysed and at what time, the number missing and the reasons, the method used to handle missing data, and whether the primary analysis was intention-to-treat. The CONSORT flow diagram is the primary source, and RoB 2 domain 3 is judged for each outcome.
GRADE guidance 17 (13) starts from the complete-case meta-analysis and re-analyses under plausible worst-case assumptions: for binary outcomes, that participants with missing data in the intervention arms had higher event rates than those followed, by factors such as 1.5 to 5; for continuous outcomes, imputed means taken from other studies in the review. If the conclusion is robust to the most extreme plausible assumptions, do not rate down for risk of bias; if it is not, rate down. Applied to 100 meta-analyses with a significant result, plausible assumptions of this kind moved 6% to 22% across the null (14).
There is no sensible threshold for an acceptable proportion missing: the impact depends on the event rate and on how different the missing are, not only on how many there are. If 900 of 1000 patients are followed with 2% mortality and the 100 missing had 20% mortality, the true mortality is 3.8%, nearly double what was observed.

title: 14  Missing Data
text:
Key points

Missing data are the rule. Distinguish missing studies, outcomes, summary statistics, participants and study-level data; each has its own tools.
MCAR, MAR and MNAR describe how missingness relates to the data; MAR cannot be verified, and MNAR is often plausible in clinical trials.
Complete-case analysis assumes the missing resemble the observed in each arm; LOCF and BOCF make implausible assumptions and can bias in either direction; multiple imputation and mixed models are valid under MAR but not MNAR.
Missing SDs can often be recovered from intervals, exact P values or quartiles; change-score SDs depend on an unknown correlation, which should be varied.
The IMOR framework turns assumptions about missing participants into explicit sensitivity analyses, including different assumptions by arm, tipping points and uncertain IMORs.
Extract numbers randomised, analysed and missing, with reasons, per arm; judge RoB 2 domain 3; and follow GRADE guidance 17.

title: 14  Missing Data
text:
Exercises

In missing-sim, make dropout depend on improvement in the active arm only (for example, side effects among responders). How does the direction of the complete-case bias change?
Recompute the change-score SMD of Table 14.3 with r = 0.6 for one arm and 0.9 for the other.
Using imor_ma(), find the smallest common IMOR (the same in both arms) at which the haloperidol result loses significance, if any.
Re-run the uncertain-IMOR analysis with SD 0.7 for log IMOR. What happens to the weight of Beasley 1996?
For a meta-analysis you know, extract the numbers randomised, analysed and missing per arm, and apply the GRADE 17 plausible worst case with a relative event rate of 2 among the missing.
