title: 15  Publication Bias
text:
15.1 The problem
Chapter 14 dealt with participants missing from studies. This chapter deals with studies missing from the literature. When the chance that a study is published depends on its result, the published studies are a biased sample, and a meta-analysis of them is biased however well it is done. No statistical method can recover data that were never released, so the first defence is searching (Chapter 2): registers, regulatory documents and clinical study reports. The methods in this chapter detect the signature of missing studies and estimate how much they might matter.
Several related biases push in the same direction. Publication bias: studies with significant or “positive” results are more likely to be published at all. Time-lag bias: positive studies are published faster, so early meta-analyses over-represent them. Language and location bias: negative results are more often published in non-English journals or the grey literature. Selective outcome reporting: studies are published, but unfavourable outcomes are omitted (RoB 2 domain 5). All of them make the published literature look more favourable than the evidence.
Code
set.seed(1)
n_st <- 200; true_effect <- 0.15
study_se <- runif(n_st, 0.05, 0.40)
observed <- rnorm(n_st, true_effect, study_se)
p_value  <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(observed / study_se))
published <- rbinom(n_st, 1, ifelse(p_value < 0.05, 0.95, 0.30)) == 1
df_pub <- tibble::tibble(observed, study_se, status = ifelse(published, "Published", "Unpublished"))
p1 <- ggplot(df_pub, aes(observed, 1 / study_se, colour = status)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_effect, colour = "#2E7D32", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Published = "#041E42", Unpublished = "#B22222"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Observed log OR", y = "Precision (1/SE)", title = "All 200 studies") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p2 <- ggplot(filter(df_pub, status == "Published"), aes(observed, 1 / study_se)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#041E42", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_effect, colour = "#2E7D32", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(observed[published]), colour = "#B22222") +
  labs(x = "Observed log OR", y = NULL, title = "Published studies only")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)








Figure 15.1: Two hundred simulated studies of a small true effect (log OR 0.15, dashed green line). Significant studies are published with probability 0.95, others with probability 0.30. Left: all studies, with the unpublished in red. Right: the published studies alone, whose mean (red line) overstates the truth.

title: 15  Publication Bias
text:
15.1.1 How large is it?
The clearest evidence comes from comparisons of published literatures with complete regulatory records. (1) obtained the US Food and Drug Administration reviews of 74 registered trials of 12 antidepressants. Of the 38 trials the FDA judged positive, 37 were published. Of the 36 judged negative or questionable, 22 were not published, 11 were published in a way that conveyed a positive result, and only 3 were published as not positive. In the journals, 94% of the trials appeared positive; in the FDA’s analysis, 51% were. The published literature overstated the standardised mean difference by 32% on average (0.41 against 0.31), from 11% to 69% for individual drugs.
Other cases show the consequences for decisions.

Rosiglitazone. A Cochrane review of the 18 published trials in 2007 could say nothing about cardiovascular safety. Two months later, a meta-analysis of 42 trials, 26 of them unpublished and obtained from the manufacturer’s register, reported an increase in myocardial infarction, OR 1.43 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.98) (2). The analysis was debated (Section 9.6.4), but the debate was possible only because the unpublished data had become available.
Reboxetine. When the manufacturer’s unpublished data were obtained, data from 74% of the patients in the trials had never been published. The published trial suggested a large benefit; with all trials the benefit was small and uncertain, and more patients on reboxetine than on placebo withdrew because of adverse events (3). The published record overstated benefit and hid harm.
Oseltamivir. Reviewers who obtained the full clinical study reports found that the drug shortened symptoms in adults by less than a day but did not reduce hospital admissions, a less favourable picture than the published trials had supported for national stockpiling (4).

Of 677 completed trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov between 2000 and 2007, only 46% had been published in a journal (5). Even published trials are incompletely reported: information is lost at every step from protocol and clinical study report to journal article (6), and Chalmers and Glasziou estimated that, through poor design, non-publication and poor reporting, up to 85% of research investment is wasted (7). The ROB-ME tool assesses the risk of bias due to missing evidence in a synthesis (8).

title: 15  Publication Bias
text:
15.2 Detecting small-study effects

15.2.1 The funnel plot
A funnel plot shows each study’s effect against its precision (usually its standard error, plotted with the most precise studies at the top). Without bias, small studies scatter widely and symmetrically around the pooled effect, large studies narrowly, forming an inverted funnel. If small studies with unfavourable results are missing, one corner of the funnel is empty.


Code
set.seed(42)
se_f <- runif(30, 0.05, 0.50)
y_f  <- rnorm(30, 0.3, se_f)
fun_df <- bind_rows(tibble::tibble(y = y_f, se = se_f, data = "No bias"),
                    tibble::tibble(y = y_f, se = se_f, data = "Small negative studies missing") |>
                      filter(!(y < 0 & se > 0.25)))
pools <- fun_df |> summarise(.by = data, pool = weighted.mean(y, 1 / se^2))
cones <- pools |> crossing(se = seq(0, 0.5, length.out = 50)) |>
  mutate(lo = pool - 1.96 * se, hi = pool + 1.96 * se)
ggplot(fun_df, aes(y, se)) +
  geom_line(data = cones, aes(lo, se), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(data = cones, aes(hi, se), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(colour = "#041E42", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(data = pools, aes(xintercept = pool), colour = "#B22222") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  facet_wrap(~ data) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Effect size", y = "Standard error")








Figure 15.2: Simulated funnel plots of 30 studies with a true effect of 0.3. Left: all studies. Right: small studies (SE > 0.25) with negative results suppressed. Red line: inverse-variance pooled estimate.





Funnel plots need care. With fewer than about 10 studies they are uninterpretable (9). And asymmetry shows only that smaller studies report different effects, a small-study effect; publication bias is one cause, but others include genuine differences (small trials often enrol higher-risk patients or deliver the intervention more intensively), poorer methods in small trials, artefacts of the effect measure, and chance. Contour-enhanced funnel plots, which shade the regions of statistical significance, help distinguish asymmetry caused by missing non-significant studies from other causes.


15.2.2 Tests for asymmetry
Egger’s test regresses the standardised effect on precision (equivalently, the effect on its standard error); an intercept away from zero indicates asymmetry. Because the tests have little power, a threshold of P < 0.10 is often used. For odds ratios, Egger’s test has inflated false-positive rates, because the log odds ratio and its standard error are correlated; Peters’ test, which regresses the effect on the inverse of the total sample size, and Harbord’s test are preferred for binary outcomes. Begg’s rank correlation test has lower power.


Code
bcg   <- escalc("RR", ai = tpos, n1i = tpos + tneg, ci = cpos, n2i = cpos + cneg, data = dat.bcg)
m_bcg <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg, method = "REML")
eg <- regtest(m_bcg, model = "lm", predictor = "sei")      # Egger
bg <- ranktest(m_bcg)                                      # Begg
pt <- regtest(m_bcg, model = "lm", predictor = "ninv")     # Peters: effect on 1/n
pt_wrong <- regtest(m_bcg, model = "lm", predictor = "ni") # a common error: effect on n
round(c(Egger = eg$pval, Begg = bg$pval, Peters = pt$pval, `Peters on n (wrong)` = pt_wrong$pval), 3)


              Egger                Begg              Peters Peters on n (wrong) 
              0.189               0.952               0.175               0.001 


The three tests agree that the 13 BCG trials show no detectable asymmetry. Regressing on n rather than 1/n gives a spurious signal: the trials range from 262 to more than 176 000 participants, and on the n scale the single huge trial acts as a lever. “No asymmetry” is not “no bias”: with 13 heterogeneous trials (I² over 90%, largely explained by latitude, Section 10.1) these tests have little power, and heterogeneity can create or hide asymmetry on its own.


15.2.3 Trim-and-fill
Trim-and-fill estimates how many studies are missing from the sparse side of the funnel, imputes their mirror images, and recomputes the pooled estimate (10).


Code
tf <- trimfill(m_bcg)
funnel(tf, xlab = "Log risk ratio (BCG vs control)")








Figure 15.3: Trim-and-fill applied to the BCG trials. Filled points would be imputed studies.





Here trim-and-fill imputes 1 missing study, and the RR moves from 0.49 to 0.52 (0.37 to 0.74). Trim-and-fill is easy to explain but is a sensitivity analysis, not a correction: it assumes that the asymmetry is entirely due to missing studies and that those studies mirror the observed ones. It is misleading when heterogeneity causes the asymmetry, and in simulations it usually corrects too little (11).

title: 15  Publication Bias
text:
15.3 Correcting for small-study effects: PET-PEESE
PET-PEESE treats the small-study pattern as a regression and extrapolates it to a study of infinite size (12). The precision-effect test (PET) fits a weighted meta-regression of each study’s effect on its standard error:
\[\hat\theta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 SE_i .\]
The slope β₁ is the small-study effect (essentially Egger’s test). The intercept β₀ is the predicted effect of a study with SE = 0, which would always be published and has no small-study quirks: the effect with the small-study pattern removed. When there is a true effect, a straight line over-corrects, so the precision-effect estimate with standard error (PEESE) uses \(SE_i^2\) instead. The conventional two-step rule reports the PEESE intercept if the PET intercept differs significantly from zero, and the PET intercept otherwise.


Code
set.seed(42)
se_i <- runif(25, 0.08, 0.45)
yi   <- rnorm(25, 0.20, se_i)                      # true effect 0.20
pub  <- !(yi < 0.05 & se_i > 0.25)                 # small, disappointing trials stay in the drawer
d_pp <- tibble::tibble(yi = yi[pub], sei = se_i[pub], vi = sei^2)
m_naive <- rma(yi, vi, data = d_pp)
m_pet   <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ sei, data = d_pp)
m_peese <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ vi, data = d_pp)
p_pet   <- coef(summary(m_pet))["intrcpt", "pval"]




Code
b_pet <- coef(m_pet); b_peese <- coef(m_peese)
ggplot(d_pp, aes(sei, yi)) +
  geom_function(fun = \(x) b_pet[1] + b_pet[2] * x, xlim = c(0, 0.45), colour = "#B22222", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_function(fun = \(x) b_peese[1] + b_peese[2] * x^2, xlim = c(0, 0.45), colour = "#E69F00", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.20, colour = "#2E7D32", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = m_naive$b[1], colour = "grey50", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(colour = "#041E42", size = 2.3) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = c(b_pet[1], b_peese[1]), size = 3.5, colour = c("#B22222", "#E69F00")) +
  labs(x = "Standard error (larger = smaller study)", y = "Observed effect")








Figure 15.4: PET (red, straight line in SE) and PEESE (orange, curve in SE²) fitted to the published trials and extrapolated to SE = 0. Green dashed: the true effect (0.20); grey dotted: naive pooled estimate.





Of 25 trials, 20 were published, and the naive pooled estimate, 0.31, overstates the truth by 54%. The PET slope is 1.05, a clear small-study effect. The PET intercept, 0.11 (P = 0.29), is not significantly different from zero, so the two-step rule would report it and conclude that the data are consistent with no effect. That is wrong here; the PEESE intercept, 0.22, is close to the truth. With few studies PET has little power, and its straight line over-corrects when a real effect exists. PET-PEESE is a sensitivity analysis, not an oracle, and like every funnel-based method it cannot tell publication bias from other causes of small-study effects.

title: 15  Publication Bias
text:
15.4 Two simulated literatures
PET-PEESE was tested above on a small literature. To test the remaining methods we need larger literatures whose truth we know. Each of the two below runs 150 trials with 15 to 120 patients per arm; the outcome is a standardised mean difference with true value 0.30 in one literature and 0 in the other, with slight heterogeneity. Every trial significant in favour of treatment is published, and 15% of the rest: a non-significant trial is about 6.7 times less likely to be published.


Code
make_lit <- function(delta, k_all = 150, seed = 629) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n     <- round(runif(k_all, 15, 120))                    # patients per arm
  sei   <- sqrt(2 / n)                                     # approximate SE of an SMD
  theta <- delta + rnorm(k_all, 0, 0.05)                   # each trial's true effect
  yi    <- rnorm(k_all, theta, sei)
  p     <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(yi / sei))
  sig   <- p < 0.05 & yi > 0
  keep  <- sample(which(!sig), round(0.15 * sum(!sig)))    # 15% of the rest are published
  all   <- data.frame(yi, sei, vi = sei^2, z = yi / sei, p, theta,
                      published = sig | seq_len(k_all) %in% keep)
  structure(all[all$published, ], all = all)
}
lit  <- make_lit(0.30)
lit0 <- make_lit(0)
naive  <- rma(yi, vi, data = lit)
naive0 <- rma(yi, vi, data = lit0)


Of the trials with a true SMD of 0.30, 80 are published, and the naive pooled estimate is 0.41, about 36% too high. With no true effect, only 27 trials are published and the naive estimate is 0.03: with no effect, few trials reach significance, so selection removes most of the evidence rather than creating a large false effect.

title: 15  Publication Bias
text:
15.5 Selection models
Funnel-plot methods see only a pattern. A selection model writes down a model of the publication process, the probability \(w(p)\) that a study with P value p is published, and estimates it together with the pooled effect (13):
\[L(\mu, \tau^2, w) = \prod_{i=1}^k \frac{f(y_i \mid \mu, \tau^2)\, w(p_i)}{\int f(y \mid \mu, \tau^2)\, w(p(y))\, dy} .\]
The denominator, the probability that any study is published, normalises the likelihood for the selected sample. In the step-function model of Vevea and Hedges, one-sided P values are divided into bands (for example 0 to 0.025, 0.025 to 0.05, 0.05 to 0.10, 0.10 to 0.50, 0.50 to 1); the first band has weight 1 and the others are estimated. A one-sided P of 0.025 is a two-sided P of 0.05 in the favourable direction. metafor fits these models with selmodel(); weightr is an alternative.


Code
m_ml <- rma(yi, vi, data = lit, method = "ML")
p_one <- pnorm(lit$yi / lit$sei, lower.tail = FALSE)            # one-sided P values
table(cut(p_one, c(0, 0.025, 0.05, 0.10, 0.50, 1)))               # published studies per band



   (0,0.025] (0.025,0.05]   (0.05,0.1]    (0.1,0.5]      (0.5,1] 
          68            2            3            4            3 


Code
sel  <- selmodel(m_ml, type = "stepfun", steps = c(0.025, 0.05, 0.10, 0.50))
sel3 <- selmodel(m_ml, type = "stepfun", steps = 0.025)           # one cut-point: "3PSM"
tibble::tibble(Model = c("Naive (ML)", "Step function, four cut-points", "Step function, one cut-point (3PSM)"),
               `Pooled SMD (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)",
                                               c(m_ml$b[1], sel$b[1], sel3$b[1]),
                                               c(m_ml$ci.lb, sel$ci.lb, sel3$ci.lb),
                                               c(m_ml$ci.ub, sel$ci.ub, sel3$ci.ub)),
               `Relative publication weights` = c("", paste(sprintf("%.2f", sel$delta), collapse = ", "),
                                                  paste(sprintf("%.2f", sel3$delta), collapse = ", ")),
               `LRT for selection, P` = c("", format.pval(sel$LRTp, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
                                          format.pval(sel3$LRTp, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))) |>
  kable(align = "lccc")











Model
Pooled SMD (95% CI)
Relative publication weights
LRT for selection, P




Naive (ML)

<0.001

Allowing for selection moves the estimate from 0.41 towards the truth of 0.30, and the estimated weights recover the selection built into the simulation: studies that were not significant were published about 0.09 times as often as significant ones (the true value is 0.15). The bands between 0.025 and 0.50 contain only a handful of studies, so their individual weights are imprecise.
Selection models are data-hungry: every band needs studies in it (selmodel() stops with an error if a band is empty, as it would for the 20 published trials of the PET-PEESE example), and with modest numbers of studies it is better to use few cut-points (a single cut at 0.025, the “three-parameter selection model”), or fix the weights at plausible values and report how the estimate changes (14).

title: 15  Publication Bias
section: 15.6 The distribution of significant P values
text:
15.6 The distribution of significant P values
A different family of methods looks not at effects versus precision but at the shape of the statistically significant P values. Under the null hypothesis, P values are uniform (Section 11.2.1), so among significant results each 0.01-wide slice from 0 to 0.05 is equally likely: a flat p-curve. With a real effect, small P values are more likely: a right-skewed curve, more so as power increases. With no effect but P-hacking (adding participants, dropping outliers or switching outcomes until P dips below 0.05), results bunch just below 0.05: a left-skewed curve (15).


Code
set.seed(42)
p_null <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(rnorm(20000)))
p_true <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(rnorm(20000, 2.8, 1)))
p_hack <- replicate(4000, {
  x <- rnorm(70); y <- rnorm(70)
  for (n in seq(20, 70, by = 10)) {
    p <- t.test(x[1:n], y[1:n], var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
    if (p < 0.05) break
  }
  p
})
tibble::tibble(p = c(p_null, p_true, p_hack),
               scenario = rep(c("No effect", "Real effect, 80% power", "No effect + p-hacking"),
                              c(20000, 20000, 4000))) |>
  filter(p < 0.05) |>
  mutate(bin = cut(p, seq(0, 0.05, 0.01), labels = c(".01", ".02", ".03", ".04", ".05")),
         scenario = factor(scenario, c("No effect", "Real effect, 80% power", "No effect + p-hacking"))) |>
  count(scenario, bin) |>
  mutate(.by = scenario, pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(bin, pct, group = scenario)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#041E42") + geom_point(colour = "#041E42") +
  facet_wrap(~ scenario) +
  labs(x = "P value bin (significant results only)", y = "% of significant results")








Figure 15.5: Distribution of significant P values in 0.01 bins. No effect: flat. A real effect with 80% power: right-skewed. No effect plus optional stopping (start with 20 per arm, add 10 up to five times until P < 0.05): left-skewed. Dashed line: 20% per bin.





Publication bias filters which significant studies are seen, but it cannot make a null effect produce right-skewed P values. A right-skewed curve is therefore evidence that the literature contains a real effect.

15.6.1 P-curve
P-curve keeps only the significant results and asks whether their P values are right-skewed. Each significant P value is converted to a “pp-value”, its probability under the null given significance (\(p/0.05\)), and the pp-values are combined with Stouffer’s method; a significant result indicates evidential value. A second test asks whether the curve is flatter than one produced by studies with only 33% power, which would suggest the evidence is too weak to trust.


Code
pcurve_tests <- function(d) {
  s   <- subset(d, p < 0.05 & yi > 0)
  z   <- s$yi / s$sei
  pp0 <- s$p / 0.05                                         # uniform under no effect
  ncp <- qnorm(0.975) - qnorm(2 / 3)                        # z-shift giving 33% power
  pp33 <- (pnorm(z, ncp, lower.tail = FALSE) + pnorm(-z, ncp)) / (1 / 3)  # uniform under 33% power
  Z_rs <- sum(qnorm(pp0)) / sqrt(nrow(s))
  Z_fl <- sum(qnorm(pmin(pp33, 1 - 1e-12))) / sqrt(nrow(s))
  c(k_significant = nrow(s), `share P < 0.025` = mean(s$p < 0.025),
    `right-skew test P` = pnorm(Z_rs), `flatness (33% power) test P` = pnorm(Z_fl, lower.tail = FALSE))
}
round(rbind(`True SMD 0.30` = pcurve_tests(lit), `True SMD 0` = pcurve_tests(lit0)), 3)


              k_significant share P < 0.025 right-skew test P
True SMD 0.30            68           0.735             0.000
True SMD 0                5           0.600             0.453
              flatness (33% power) test P
True SMD 0.30                       0.941
True SMD 0                          0.116


With a real effect the curve is strongly right-skewed and not flatter than a 33%-power literature; with no effect it is not right-skewed. P-curve tests for evidential value but does not give a good corrected estimate, needs several independent significant results, and is misleading if the studies test different hypotheses (15). dmetar::pcurve() and the online p-curve app implement the full method.


15.6.2 P-uniform
P-uniform turns the same idea into an estimate (16,17). For a candidate effect δ, compute each significant study’s conditional P value: the probability, given δ and given that the study was significant, of a result at least as large as the one observed. At the true δ these conditional P values are uniform. If δ is too small, the observed effects look surprisingly large and the conditional P values pile up near 0; if δ is too large, they pile up near 1. P-uniform finds the δ at which they look uniform, here using the simple criterion that their sum equals its expectation, k/2.


Code
puniform_simple <- function(d) {
  s <- subset(d, p < 0.05 & yi > 0)
  crit <- qnorm(0.975) * s$sei                             # smallest significant effect
  cond_p <- \(delta) pnorm((s$yi - delta) / s$sei, lower.tail = FALSE) /
                     pnorm((crit - delta) / s$sei, lower.tail = FALSE)
  k <- nrow(s); half_w <- qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(k / 12)      # normal approximation to Irwin-Hall
  f <- \(delta, target) sum(cond_p(delta)) - target
  c(estimate = uniroot(f, c(-2, 2), target = k / 2)$root,
    lower = uniroot(f, c(-2, 2), target = k / 2 - half_w)$root,
    upper = uniroot(f, c(-2, 2), target = k / 2 + half_w)$root)
}
round(rbind(`True SMD 0.30` = puniform_simple(lit), `True SMD 0` = puniform_simple(lit0)), 2)


              estimate lower upper
True SMD 0.30     0.30  0.22  0.36
True SMD 0        0.06 -1.76  0.38


The corrected estimates are close to the truth. P-uniform uses only significant studies and assumes homogeneous effects; with large heterogeneity it overestimates. The puniform package implements the exact method and p-uniform*, an extension that uses all studies and allows heterogeneity:


Code

puniform(yi = lit$yi, vi = lit$vi, side = "right", method = "P")

    3.2639   <.001

    0.4072    0.0184   22.1055   <.001    0.3711    0.4433   71.8838    0.7022

Z-curve applies related ideas to whole literatures, estimating the average power of the studies from their significant z statistics, and from that the expected rates of discovery and replication (18). It is designed for large, heterogeneous literatures rather than single meta-analyses (package zcurve).

title: 15  Publication Bias
section: 15.7 How much selection would it take?
text:
15.7 How much selection would it take?
Instead of estimating the selection, (19) ask how severe it would have to be to explain away the result. Suppose that affirmative studies (significant and favouring treatment) are η times more likely to be published than non-affirmative ones. Each non-affirmative study then stands for η studies in the full literature, and a corrected estimate up-weights non-affirmative studies by η. The question is how large η must be to bring the estimate to zero. A simple fixed-effect version of the calculation:


Code
eta_fit <- function(d, eta) {
  aff <- d$p < 0.05 & d$yi > 0
  w   <- ifelse(aff, 1, eta) / d$vi
  est <- sum(w * d$yi) / sum(w)
  se  <- sqrt(sum(w^2 * d$vi)) / sum(w)
  c(eta = eta, est = est, lo = est - 1.96 * se, hi = est + 1.96 * se)
}
etas <- c(1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6.7, 10, 20, 50, 200)
sens <- map_dfr(etas, \(e) eta_fit(lit, e))
ggplot(sens, aes(eta, est)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#041E42", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(colour = "#041E42", linewidth = 1) + geom_point(colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.30, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#2E7D32") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1 / 0.15, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#B22222") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 2, 4, 10, 50, 200)) +
  labs(x = "Selection ratio η (log scale)", y = "Corrected pooled SMD (95% CI)")








Figure 15.6: Corrected pooled SMD as the assumed selection ratio η increases (fixed-effect version: non-affirmative studies up-weighted by η). Green dashed: the truth (0.30). Red dotted: the selection ratio used in the simulation (6.7).





At the true selection ratio the corrected estimate is close to 0.30, and no plausible η brings it to zero, because the non-affirmative published studies themselves point to a positive effect. When the corrected estimate stays away from zero for any plausible degree of selection, publication bias alone cannot explain the result. The PublicationBias package implements the method with robust random-effects estimation and reports the η needed to reduce the estimate to zero or to any chosen value.

title: 15  Publication Bias
text:
15.8 Robust Bayesian meta-analysis
Each method so far assumes one model of bias, and simulations show that every method fails in some realistic scenario (11). Robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA) averages over models instead of choosing one (20,21). It fits models that cross three questions (is there an effect? do the effects vary? is there publication bias, modelled by several selection models and by PET and PEESE?) and weights each model by how well it predicts the data. The output includes Bayes factors for the presence of an effect, of heterogeneity and of bias, and a model-averaged estimate whose uncertainty includes the uncertainty about which model is right.


Code
library(RoBMA)                     # requires JAGS
fit1 <- RoBMA(d = lit$yi, se = lit$sei, algorithm = "ss", seed = 1)
summary(fit1)

(Estimated publication weights omega correspond to one-sided p-values.)


A well-known test case is a series of experiments that claimed evidence of precognition (22). A naive meta-analysis finds a small, highly significant effect; RoBMA, allowing for publication bias, finds the evidence weak (the data are in the package as Bem2011). RoBMA is computationally heavier, depends on its priors, and like every method cannot recover studies whose results were never released.

title: 15  Publication Bias
text:
15.9 Putting it together


Code
pet_l   <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ sei, data = lit)
peese_l <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ vi,  data = lit)
pp_l    <- if (coef(summary(pet_l))["intrcpt", "pval"] < 0.10) peese_l else pet_l
sel_l   <- selmodel(rma(yi, vi, data = lit, method = "ML"), type = "stepfun", steps = 0.025)
tf_l    <- trimfill(naive)
pu_l    <- puniform_simple(lit)
eta_l   <- eta_fit(lit, 1 / 0.15)
tibble::tribble(
  ~method,                               ~est,          ~lo,              ~hi,
  "Naive random effects",                naive$b[1],    naive$ci.lb,      naive$ci.ub,
  "Trim-and-fill",                       tf_l$b[1],     tf_l$ci.lb,       tf_l$ci.ub,
  "PET-PEESE (two-step)",                pp_l$b[1],     pp_l$ci.lb[1],    pp_l$ci.ub[1],
  "Selection model (3PSM)",              sel_l$b[1],    sel_l$ci.lb[1],   sel_l$ci.ub[1],
  "p-uniform (simple)",                  pu_l[1],       pu_l[2],          pu_l[3],
  "Selection ratio η = 6.7 (fixed effect)", eta_l["est"], eta_l["lo"],   eta_l["hi"]) |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = rev(method))) |>
  ggplot(aes(est, method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.30, colour = "#2E7D32", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), colour = "#041E42") +
  labs(x = "Estimated SMD (95% interval)", y = NULL)








Figure 15.7: Several methods applied to the same published literature (true SMD 0.30, green dashed line).

A practical sequence: search registers and regulatory sources first; draw a funnel plot if there are at least 10 studies; test for asymmetry with a test suited to the outcome; then, as sensitivity analyses, apply at least two correction methods that make different assumptions (a regression method and a selection model, or RoBMA). If corrected estimates differ meaningfully from the naive one, rate down the certainty of evidence for publication bias.

15.9.1 Does correction work?
The antidepressant trials offer a rare test, because the FDA records provide the complete evidence. (23) used only the published papers, fitted a regression line to the funnel plot and extrapolated it to a study of infinite size. Their adjusted estimate (0.29, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.35) was close to the FDA value (0.31), while the naive estimate from the journals was 0.41. It worked here because the bias came mainly from selective publication of small negative trials, there were many trials, and the true effects were similar. With few studies, high heterogeneity, or small studies that are genuinely different, corrections can be badly wrong, and usually there is no FDA record to check them against. Corrected estimates show how sensitive a naive result is to publication bias; they do not replace it.

title: 15  Publication Bias
text:
Key points

Publication, time-lag, language and outcome-reporting biases all make the published literature look more favourable; the antidepressant, rosiglitazone and reboxetine cases show the consequences.
Searching registers, regulatory documents and clinical study reports is the main defence; statistical methods cannot recover unreleased data.
A funnel plot shows small-study effects, which have causes other than publication bias; interpret it only with at least 10 studies, and use Peters’ or Harbord’s test for odds ratios.
Trim-and-fill corrects too little and is misleading with heterogeneity; PET-PEESE and selection models make explicit, different assumptions and are better treated as sensitivity analyses.
The shape of significant P values tests for evidential value (p-curve) and supports a corrected estimate (p-uniform).
Ask how much selection would be needed to explain a result away; use RoBMA, or several methods, to reflect uncertainty about the bias model.

title: 15  Publication Bias
text:
Exercises

Re-run lit-sim with heterogeneity SD 0.20 instead of 0.05. How do PET-PEESE, the selection model and p-uniform perform?
Draw a contour-enhanced funnel plot of the BCG trials with funnel(m_bcg, level = c(90, 95, 99), shade = c("white", "grey80", "grey60"), refline = 0). Where do the trials fall?
Fit the three-parameter selection model to lit with the weight for non-significant studies fixed at 0.5, 0.25 and 0.10 (selmodel(..., delta = c(1, w))). How sensitive is the estimate?
Compute the p-curve tests for the published studies of lit0 after adding five “p-hacked” studies with P values between 0.04 and 0.05.
Find a meta-analysis in your field and compare its pooled estimate with PET-PEESE and a three-parameter selection model.

title: 16  Individual Participant Data
text:
16.1 What aggregate data cannot do
So far the unit of analysis has been the study: one effect estimate and its standard error per study. An individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis obtains the original records for each participant and re-analyses them together. It is often called the gold standard of evidence synthesis (1,2), because it removes several limitations of aggregate data at once. It is also slow, expensive, and dependent on others’ willingness, and legal ability, to share.
With aggregate data the reviewer must accept each study’s choices: its outcome definition, its covariates, its analysis, its subgroups. IPD allows
The third point deserves an example. Whether treatment benefit depends on a patient characteristic is the question clinicians most often ask of a meta-analysis. With aggregate data the only route is meta-regression on the study’s average characteristic (Section 10.1), which has two weaknesses: studies usually differ little in their averages, and a between-study association is open to ecological bias. With IPD, the interaction can be estimated within each study and then pooled (4).
Code
set.seed(42)
trials <- tibble::tibble(study = paste("Trial", 1:6), n = c(150, 220, 120, 300, 180, 160),
                         mean_age = c(63, 66, 64, 68, 65, 67), base = c(50, 55, 48, 62, 45, 52))
true_benefit <- \(age) 4 + 0.4 * (age - 65)
ipd_age <- trials |>
  rowwise() |>
  reframe(study = study, age = rnorm(n, mean_age, 10), trt = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
          y = base - 0.2 * (age - 65) - trt * true_benefit(age) + rnorm(n, 0, 12)) |>
  mutate(.by = study, age_c = age - mean(age))
ad <- ipd_age |>                                           # one benefit per trial
  summarise(.by = study, mean_age = mean(age),
            yi = mean(y[trt == 0]) - mean(y[trt == 1]),
            vi = var(y[trt == 1]) / sum(trt == 1) + var(y[trt == 0]) / sum(trt == 0))
mr <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ I(mean_age - 65), data = ad)
grid <- tibble::tibble(age = 40:90)
ad_line <- as.data.frame(predict(mr, newmods = grid$age - 65)) |> bind_cols(grid)
# IPD: trial-specific intercepts and age slopes; interaction from within-trial (centred) age
fit_age <- lm(y ~ study + study:age_c + trt + trt:age_c, data = ipd_age)
ctr <- mean(trials$mean_age)
X <- cbind(1, grid$age - ctr)
b <- -coef(fit_age)[c("trt", "age_c:trt")]                 # benefit = minus the effect on y
V <- vcov(fit_age)[c("trt", "age_c:trt"), c("trt", "age_c:trt")]
ipd_line <- grid |> mutate(pred = drop(X %*% b), se = sqrt(rowSums((X %*% V) * X)),
                           ci.lb = pred - 1.96 * se, ci.ub = pred + 1.96 * se)
bands <- ipd_age |>
  mutate(band = cut(age, c(-Inf, 50, 60, 70, 80, Inf))) |>
  group_by(band) |>
  group_modify(\(d, k) { m <- lm(y ~ study + trt, data = d)
    tibble::tibble(age = median(d$age), est = -coef(m)[["trt"]], se = sqrt(vcov(m)["trt", "trt"])) }) |>
  ungroup()
slope_ad  <- coef(summary(mr))[2, ]
slope_ipd <- c(b[2], -rev(confint(fit_age)["age_c:trt", ]))
panel <- function(line, pts, x, title) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_ribbon(data = line, aes(age, ymin = ci.lb, ymax = ci.ub), fill = "#041E42", alpha = 0.15) +
    geom_line(data = line, aes(age, pred), colour = "#041E42", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_function(fun = true_benefit, colour = "#2E7D32", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_pointrange(data = pts, aes(.data[[x]], est, ymin = est - 1.96 * se, ymax = est + 1.96 * se),
                    colour = "#B22222", size = 0.3) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 90), ylim = c(-12, 16)) +
    labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Benefit (control − treated)", title = title)
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  panel(ad_line, mutate(ad, est = yi, se = sqrt(vi)), "mean_age",
        sprintf("Aggregate data: slope %.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", slope_ad["estimate"], slope_ad["ci.lb"], slope_ad["ci.ub"])),
  panel(ipd_line, bands, "age",
        sprintf("IPD: slope %.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", slope_ipd[1], slope_ipd[2], slope_ipd[3])))








Figure 16.1: Six simulated trials in which the benefit grows with age (green dashed line: 4 units at age 65, 0.4 units per year). Left: aggregate data, one point per trial at its mean age, with a meta-regression. Right: IPD from the same patients, with the age interaction estimated within trials; points are age-band estimates.
The trials’ mean ages span only five years, so the aggregate-data meta-regression has almost nothing to learn from and its slope is hopelessly imprecise. The same 1130 patients span 50 years of age, and comparing older and younger patients within each trial recovers the interaction precisely. Centring age within each trial keeps between-trial differences in mean age, which could be confounded by anything else that differs between trials, out of the interaction estimate.

title: 16  Individual Participant Data
16  Individual Participant Data
text:
16.2 The NSAID collaboration
A real project shows the practical side. By 2006 the selective COX-2 inhibitor rofecoxib had been withdrawn for cardiovascular harm, but the risks of other NSAIDs in everyday use (intermittent, low-dose, switching between drugs) were uncertain. Randomised trials were too small and too selected to answer questions about the onset of risk, dose and duration, while observational studies in prescription databases had defined exposure in incompatible ways. A Bayesian IPD meta-analysis set out to answer them (5).

16.2.1 Data access
Of 82 studies whose full texts were screened, 15 were eligible. Seven were excluded because their definition of exposed time precluded valid pooling of patient-level data, and access to IPD could not be obtained for four more; four studies, each from a different database, were included: the Quebec RAMQ cohort (233,816 people, 21,256 cases of myocardial infarction), Finland (172,219; 33,309), the UK General Practice Research Database (17,561; 3,643) and Saskatchewan (23,167; 3,252), in all 446,763 people with 61,460 cases (5). The obstacles were not scientific: investigators who were willing to share were not legally permitted to transfer anonymised data across borders, and the project took years of ethics approvals and data-sharing agreements. Missing IPD threatens an IPD meta-analysis in the same way that missing studies threaten any review (Chapter 15): data that are available may differ systematically from data that are not. Before committing to an IPD meta-analysis, assess the feasibility of access, and plan for the possibility that some studies can be included only as aggregate data.


16.2.2 Harmonisation
Harmonisation creates comparable variables from datasets collected independently. It is a series of scientific judgements rather than a technical step. In the NSAID project:

outcome: myocardial infarction was ascertained from hospital discharge diagnoses, national registers, general-practice records or insurance claims, each validated, but differently;
exposure: dose and duration were derived from pill strength, number of pills and days supplied in some databases, and from prescription records in others;
timing: the window defining “current use” differed between databases and had to be made common;
confounders: comorbidities came from diagnoses in some databases and from drug-dispensing algorithms in others, and some covariates were unavailable in some databases.

The common exposure definition combined drug, recency, duration and dose: non-use in the preceding year (reference), past use, recent use, and five categories of current use (any dose for 1 to 7 days; low or high dose for 8 to 30 days; low or high dose for more than 30 days), with drug-specific dose thresholds (for example 200 mg/day for celecoxib, 100 mg/day for diclofenac, 1200 mg/day for ibuprofen and 750 mg/day for naproxen).
An essential check is to reproduce each study’s published results from the harmonised data before pooling. If the original estimate cannot be reproduced, either the harmonisation or the original analysis is wrong, and the reviewer does not yet understand the data well enough to pool them.

title: 16  Individual Participant Data
text:
16.3 One-stage and two-stage analyses
A two-stage IPD meta-analysis fits the same model within each study, extracts the estimate and its standard error, and pools them with the methods of Chapter 9. A one-stage analysis fits a single model to all participants, with study as a stratifying or random effect. To compare them, we simulate four observational studies of an exposure and a binary outcome, loosely modelled on the NSAID databases but much smaller.


Code
sim_study <- function(n, log_or, id, shift = 0) {
  age   <- rnorm(n, 68, 10)
  chd   <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2 + 0.04 * age))
  nsaid <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.30)
  mi    <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-3 + log_or * nsaid + 0.04 * age + 0.5 * chd + shift))
  data.frame(study = id, mi, nsaid, age = age - 68, chd)
}
set.seed(42)
studies <- bind_rows(sim_study(6000, log(1.48), "RAMQ", 0.10),
                     sim_study(4500, log(1.55), "Finland", -0.10),
                     sim_study(450, log(1.40), "GPRD", 0),
                     sim_study(580, log(1.52), "Saskatchewan", 0.05))
# Two-stage: the same logistic model in each study, then a random-effects meta-analysis
stage1 <- studies |>
  group_by(study) |>
  group_modify(\(d, k) { m <- glm(mi ~ nsaid + age + chd, family = binomial, data = d)
    tibble::tibble(yi = coef(m)[["nsaid"]], vi = vcov(m)["nsaid", "nsaid"]) }) |>
  ungroup()
two <- rma(yi, vi, data = stage1, method = "REML")
# One-stage: one model; study-specific intercepts and covariate effects, random exposure effect
one <- glmer(mi ~ 0 + study + study:age + study:chd + nsaid + (0 + nsaid | study),
             family = binomial, data = studies, control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
b1 <- fixef(one)[["nsaid"]]; se1 <- sqrt(vcov(one)["nsaid", "nsaid"])
tibble::tibble(Analysis = c("Two-stage (REML)", "One-stage (glmer)"),
               `Pooled OR (95% CI)` = c(sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(two$b[1]), exp(two$ci.lb), exp(two$ci.ub)),
                                        sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(b1), exp(b1 - 1.96 * se1), exp(b1 + 1.96 * se1))),
               τ = c(sqrt(two$tau2), attr(VarCorr(one)$study, "stddev"))) |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = "lcc")





Analysis

Two-stage (REML)
1.49 (1.37 to 1.62)

The two approaches agree here, as they usually do when studies are large, events are common, the same model is fitted in every study and heterogeneity is small (6). They differ when studies are small or events rare (two-stage analyses rely on approximately normal study estimates; one-stage analyses use the exact likelihood), when there are few studies (the estimate of τ depends on the method), when the one-stage model makes different assumptions (a common intercept or common covariate effects across studies, which should generally be avoided), when interactions mix within- and between-study information, and when some exposure categories are absent from some studies. Pre-specify the approach, report the other as a sensitivity analysis, and if they disagree, find out why.

title: 16  Individual Participant Data
text:
16.4 A Bayesian hierarchical IPD model
The NSAID analysis used a one-stage Bayesian hierarchical model (5). Within each database the odds of myocardial infarction were modelled by (conditional) logistic regression on the exposure categories and confounders; the log odds ratio for exposure category k in study j was drawn from a common distribution,
\[\beta_{kj} \sim N(\theta_k, \tau_k^2),\]
with a vague prior on each pooled log odds ratio \(\theta_k\) and a half-normal prior on each between-study SD \(\tau_k\), varied in sensitivity analyses.
With four studies, τ is barely identified by the data, and Section 12.3.3 showed what that does to frequentist intervals. The Bayesian model averages over the plausible values of τ rather than plugging in one estimate, and it adds several things a two-stage frequentist analysis cannot easily provide: exact likelihoods for sparse exposure cells; borrowing strength, so that a category with few or no participants in one database is still estimated, shrunk towards the others; joint modelling of dozens of related drug, dose and duration categories; and direct probability statements.


Code
nsaid <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Drug, ~Category, ~or, ~lo, ~hi, ~p1, ~p15,
  "Celecoxib", "Any dose, 1–7 days", 1.24, 0.91, 1.82, 92.4, 12.1,
  "Celecoxib", "> 200 mg/day, 8–30 days", 1.23, 0.78, 1.80, 85.8, 12.5,
  "Diclofenac", "Any dose, 1–7 days", 1.50, 1.06, 2.04, 98.6, 50.1,
  "Diclofenac", "> 100 mg/day, > 30 days", 1.48, 1.08, 1.95, 98.8, 45.6,
  "Ibuprofen", "Any dose, 1–7 days", 1.48, 1.00, 2.26, 97.3, 47.1,
  "Ibuprofen", "> 1200 mg/day, 8–30 days", 1.75, 1.00, 2.93, 97.5, 70.8,
  "Naproxen", "Any dose, 1–7 days", 1.53, 1.07, 2.33, 98.8, 54.9,
  "Naproxen", "> 750 mg/day, 8–30 days", 1.76, 1.14, 2.65, 99.2, 77.2,
  "Rofecoxib", "Any dose, 1–7 days", 1.58, 1.07, 2.17, 98.8, 63.6,
  "Rofecoxib", "> 25 mg/day, 8–30 days", 2.65, 1.46, 4.67, 99.8, 96.9)

  transmute(Drug, Category, `OR (95% CrI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", or, lo, hi),
            `P(OR > 1)` = sprintf("%.1f%%", p1), `P(OR > 1.5)` = sprintf("%.1f%%", p15)) |>

Every NSAID, naproxen included, was associated with increased risk, beginning in the first week of use and greater at higher doses; risk with use beyond a month did not appear to exceed that with shorter use. These are observational estimates, open to residual confounding, but the questions of timing and dose could not have been answered from the published aggregate data, which used incompatible exposure categories.
The posterior probabilities answer questions a P value cannot: how likely is it that the odds ratio exceeds 1, or exceeds a threshold that would matter clinically? Figure 16.2 plots the whole curve, here approximated from each credible interval by a normal distribution on the log scale.


Code

  filter(Category == "Any dose, 1–7 days") |>
  mutate(m = log(or), s = (log(hi) - log(lo)) / (2 * 1.96)) |>
  crossing(threshold = seq(0.8, 2.5, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(prob = 100 * pnorm(log(threshold), m, s, lower.tail = FALSE)) |>

  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.8, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 2.5)) +

Figure 16.2: Approximate posterior probability that the odds ratio for 1 to 7 days of use at any dose exceeds each threshold (normal approximation on the log scale, from the published 95% credible intervals).





The same patient-level data supported analyses beyond the meta-analysis. In the RAMQ cohort, with dose recorded for every day of follow-up, weighted cumulative exposure models suggested that doses taken up to about three weeks earlier still contributed to current risk for rofecoxib, ibuprofen and naproxen, and up to 75 days for diclofenac, and that the risk with celecoxib appeared only after more than a month of continuous use (7). An analysis of additive interaction found that cardioprotective aspirin did not attenuate the risk with any NSAID, but could not demonstrate consistent interactions with cardiovascular comorbidities (8): interactions need far more data than main effects, even with hundreds of thousands of patients.

title: 16  Individual Participant Data
section: 16.5 IPD without the data: reconstruction from Kaplan-Meier curves
text:
16.5 IPD without the data: reconstruction from Kaplan-Meier curves
Often the IPD cannot be obtained. For time-to-event outcomes, a published Kaplan-Meier curve with its numbers at risk contains most of the information needed to rebuild an approximate patient-level dataset (9,10). Section 12.1.3 used such reconstructed data for four trials of early aortic valve replacement. Here we go through the steps for one of them, EARLY TAVR, in which 901 patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis were randomised to early transcatheter replacement or clinical surveillance; the primary outcome (death, stroke or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation) had a hazard ratio of 0.50 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.63) (11).

16.5.1 Step 1: digitise, and check the digitisation
A tool such as WebPlotDigitizer turns the published figure into coordinates: calibrate both axes, trace each curve, and export (time, cumulative incidence) pairs. The numbers at risk are copied by hand. A digitised curve must start at zero and can never decrease; any digitised value printed on the figure is a check.


Code
read_digitised <- function(file) {
  read.csv(file, header = FALSE, col.names = c("time", "cuminc")) |>
    bind_rows(tibble::tibble(time = 0, cuminc = 0)) |>
    arrange(time) |>
    mutate(cuminc = cummax(pmax(cuminc, 0)))                 # never negative, never decreasing
}
dig_tavr <- read_digitised("data/ch16/early_tavr_int.csv")
dig_cs   <- read_digitised("data/ch16/early_tavr_cs.csv")
at <- \(d, t) approx(d$time, d$cuminc, xout = t, rule = 2, ties = max)$y
tibble::tibble(Arm = rep(c("TAVR", "Surveillance"), each = 2), Year = c(2, 5, 2, 5),
               `Printed (%)` = c(17.7, 35.1, 37.5, 51.2),
               `Digitised (%)` = c(at(dig_tavr, c(2, 5)), at(dig_cs, c(2, 5)))) |>
  kable(digits = 1, align = "lccc")

16.5.2 Step 2: reconstruct event and censoring times
Between two times with known numbers at risk, the number leaving the risk set is known, and the digitised curve gives the conditional risk of an event in the interval. The simple actuarial version below splits those leaving into events and censorings, assuming censoring spread evenly through the interval, and places their times at random within it. The algorithm of (9), implemented in IPDfromKM (10), does the same at every digitised step and is more accurate; the simple version is enough to show the idea.


Code
t_risk    <- 0:5
risk_tavr <- c(455, 390, 363, 285, 142, 103)                 # numbers at risk, from the figure
risk_cs   <- c(446, 305, 266, 187, 117, 46)
reconstruct_ipd <- function(dig, at_risk, t_risk, arm) {
  out <- map(seq_len(length(t_risk) - 1), \(i) {
    a <- t_risk[i]; b <- t_risk[i + 1]
    ci <- at(dig, c(a, b)) / 100
    leaving <- at_risk[i] - at_risk[i + 1]
    p <- 1 - (1 - ci[2]) / (1 - ci[1])                       # risk in (a, b], given event-free at a
    events <- min(round((at_risk[i] - leaving / 2) * p / (1 - p / 2)), leaving)
    tibble::tibble(time = runif(leaving, a, b), event = rep(c(1, 0), c(events, leaving - events)))
  })
  bind_rows(out, tibble::tibble(time = last(t_risk), event = rep(0, last(at_risk)))) |>
    mutate(arm = arm)
}
make_ipd <- \() bind_rows(reconstruct_ipd(dig_tavr, risk_tavr, t_risk, "TAVR"),
                          reconstruct_ipd(dig_cs, risk_cs, t_risk, "Surveillance")) |>
  mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Surveillance", "TAVR")))
set.seed(2026)
ipd <- make_ipd()




16.5.3 Step 3: validate


Code
km <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ arm, data = ipd)
km_df <- tibble::tibble(time = km$time, cuminc = 100 * (1 - km$surv),
                        arm = rep(c("Surveillance", "TAVR"), km$strata))
bind_rows(mutate(dig_tavr, arm = "TAVR"), mutate(dig_cs, arm = "Surveillance")) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, cuminc, colour = arm)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_step(data = km_df, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Surveillance = "#E69F00", TAVR = "#041E42"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Years since randomisation", y = "Cumulative incidence (%)") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Code
hr_txt <- function(fit) { x <- exp(c(coef(fit), confint(fit))); sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", x[1], x[2], x[3]) }

16.5.4 Step 4: analyse what the paper did not report
With patient-level data, the hazard ratio can be split by period. The surveillance arm was unblinded and almost half of it received a valve within the first year, usually through an unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation that counted as a primary event (Section 12.1.2).


Code
yr1 <- ipd |> mutate(event = event * (time <= 1), time = pmin(time, 1))
lmk <- ipd |> filter(time > 1) |> mutate(time = time - 1)        # event-free at 1 year; clock restarted
rmst_diff <- function(data, horizon) {
  tab <- summary(survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ arm, data = data), rmean = horizon)$table
  d <- unname(diff(tab[, "rmean"])); se <- sqrt(sum(tab[, "se(rmean)"]^2))
  sprintf("%.1f (%.1f to %.1f)", 12 * d, 12 * (d - 1.96 * se), 12 * (d + 1.96 * se))
}
tibble::tibble(Period = c("Whole follow-up (5 years)", "Year 1 only", "After year 1 (landmark, 4 years)"),
               `HR (95% CI)` = c(hr_txt(cox_full), hr_txt(coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ arm, yr1)),
                                 hr_txt(coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ arm, lmk))),
               `RMST difference, months (95% CI)` = c(rmst_diff(ipd, 5), rmst_diff(ipd, 1), rmst_diff(lmk, 4))) |>
  kable(align = "lcc")

Most of the benefit falls in the first year, when the crossovers happen; after the landmark the hazard ratio is much closer to 1 and its confidence interval includes 1. Restricted mean survival time (RMST), the average event-free time up to a horizon, avoids the proportional hazards assumption and is easy to explain, but it is a different summary of the same data, not a correction for bias: an event in year 1 removes event-free time from every later year, so an early gap produced by unblinding is carried forward to the horizon. Restricting it to patients event-free at one year asks how much event-free time early TAVR adds after the crossover year. Landmark analyses condition on surviving to the landmark, so the groups compared are no longer exactly the randomised groups, and the landmark time must be chosen before looking at the curves.
Reconstructed IPD allow time-varying effects, landmark analyses, absolute measures at any time, the same model in every trial of a meta-analysis, and one-stage pooling (for example a Cox model with strata(trial)). They contain only what was plotted: no covariates, so no patient-level subgroups or adjustment. They are not a substitute for real IPD.

title: 16  Individual Participant Data
section: 16.6 When is an IPD meta-analysis worth it?
text:
16.6 When is an IPD meta-analysis worth it?



Table 16.4: When to undertake an IPD meta-analysis.










Question
Favours IPD
If not, consider




Is the question about patient-level characteristics or subgroups?
Interactions must be estimated within studies
Aggregate-data meta-regression, interpreted cautiously


Do studies define outcomes or exposures differently?
Harmonisation needs raw data
Aggregate data, with sensitivity analyses by definition


Is a time-to-event or time-varying analysis needed?
Aggregate summaries cannot provide it
Reconstruction from published curves


Are outcomes rare, studies few or categories sparse?
One-stage or Bayesian models with exact likelihoods
Bayesian aggregate-data meta-analysis with an informative prior for τ


Is data access legally and practically feasible?
Custodians agree; legal frameworks allow transfer or federated analysis
Aggregate data now; IPD later


Are funding and years of coordination available?
Infrastructure in place
Aggregate data, with IPD from a subset of studies






If IPD are obtained for only some studies, check whether the studies with and without IPD differ, and consider combining IPD with aggregate data for the rest. Report IPD meta-analyses following PRISMA-IPD (12), including the number of studies and participants for which IPD were sought and obtained.

title: 16  Individual Participant Data
text:
Key points

IPD meta-analysis allows consistent definitions, the same analysis in every study, patient-level interactions and time-to-event analyses; it is the most reliable way to answer who benefits most.
Estimate patient-level interactions within studies; aggregate-data meta-regression on study averages is imprecise and open to ecological bias.
Data access is the main obstacle, and missing IPD can bias the result; harmonisation is a set of scientific judgements, and reproducing each study’s published results is mandatory.
One-stage and two-stage analyses usually agree with large studies and common events; they differ with sparse data, few studies, interactions and differing model assumptions.
Bayesian hierarchical models handle few studies and sparse categories, borrow strength, and give direct probability statements.
Approximate IPD can be reconstructed from published Kaplan-Meier curves and numbers at risk, permitting landmark, RMST and consistent re-analyses, but without covariates.

title: 16  Individual Participant Data
text:
Exercises

In fig-ad-vs-ipd, make the trials’ mean ages range from 45 to 80 instead of 63 to 68. How does the precision of the aggregate-data slope change? Then add a between-trial confounder correlated with mean age, and compare the two slopes again.
In one-two-stage, reduce each study to one tenth of its size. When do the one-stage and two-stage estimates diverge?
Repeat the landmark analysis of EARLY TAVR with landmarks at 6 months and 2 years.
Using the posterior approximation of Figure 16.2, compute the probability that the odds ratio for naproxen at more than 750 mg/day for 8 to 30 days exceeds 1.25.
Reconstruct a Kaplan-Meier curve from a trial in your own field, validate it against every printed number, and compare its hazard ratios before and after a pre-specified landmark.

title: 17  Network Meta-Analysis
text:
17.1 A prerequisite: trustworthy trials and honest models
Clinicians rarely choose between two treatments. After an acute coronary syndrome, a patient receives aspirin and one of three P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel, ticagrelor or prasugrel), and the trials compare them two at a time. Network meta-analysis combines all of these comparisons, direct and indirect, into one coherent set of estimates. It is also where every earlier chapter’s warnings apply at once: the answer depends on which trials are included, how trustworthy they are, and what the model assumes about heterogeneity. This chapter uses the antiplatelet story throughout, starting with the trial that made ticagrelor a guideline favourite.
The PLATO trial randomised 18,624 patients with an acute coronary syndrome, at 862 centres in 43 countries, to ticagrelor or clopidogrel. At 12 months the primary outcome (vascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke) had occurred in 9.8% of patients on ticagrelor and 11.7% on clopidogrel, HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.77 to 0.92) (1). Questions were raised about the trial’s conduct and adjudication (2), and in the United States, where ticagrelor appeared harmful, the result was not reproduced. No fraud has been shown, but the episode raises a question that every meta-analysis must face: how much should the regions of one trial, or the trials of one review, be assumed to share?
The answer is a modelling choice, and modelling choices matter. When 73 research teams were given the same data to test the same social-science hypothesis, 58% of their 1,253 models had a confidence interval including zero, 17% found a significant effect in one direction and 25% in the other (3).

title: 17  Network Meta-Analysis
text:
17.1.1 Complete, no and partial pooling
The FDA’s review of PLATO reported events by region. Treating the six regions as six “studies” gives three ways to analyse the same trial.


Code
plato <- tibble::tibble(
  Region = c("US", "Eastern Europe", "Western Europe", "Asia", "Latin America", "Other"),
  tic_O = c(84, 299, 240, 90, 91, 60),   tic_N = c(707, 3820, 2725, 819, 621, 641),
  clo_O = c(67, 394, 281, 114, 104, 54), clo_N = c(706, 3825, 2704, 812, 615, 628)) |>
  mutate(yi  = log((tic_O / tic_N) / (clo_O / clo_N)),                # log RR, ticagrelor vs clopidogrel
         sei = sqrt(1 / tic_O - 1 / tic_N + 1 / clo_O - 1 / clo_N))
pool_mh <- rma.mh(measure = "RR", ai = tic_O, n1i = tic_N, ci = clo_O, n2i = clo_N, data = plato)
fmt3 <- \(x) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", x[1], x[2], x[3])



Complete pooling (“lumping”) assumes one identical effect in every region: RR 0.85 (0.78 to 0.92), essentially the published result.
No pooling (“splitting”) analyses each region alone: in the US, 1,413 patients, RR 1.25 (0.92 to 1.70), suggesting harm.
Partial pooling treats the regions as different but related: \(y_j \sim N(\theta_j, s_j^2)\), \(\theta_j \sim N(\mu, \tau^2)\), the random-effects model of Chapter 9 applied within one trial. Each region’s estimate is shrunk towards \(\mu\) by the factor \(\lambda_j = \tau^2/(\tau^2 + s_j^2)\), small noisy regions more than large ones, and \(\tau\) is learned from the data.

With six regions, τ is poorly determined, so the Bayesian version, which averages over its uncertainty rather than plugging in one estimate, is the natural choice (Section 12.2.1). The model is fitted below on a grid, with priors \(\mu \sim N(0, 1)\) and \(\tau \sim\) half-\(N(0, 0.5)\) on the log RR scale; the equivalent brms code is shown after it.


Code
nn_grid <- function(yi, sei, mu_sd = 1, tau_sd = 0.5, grid = 300, n_draws = 40000) {
  g  <- expand.grid(mu = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = grid), tau = seq(0, 1.5, length.out = grid))
  lp <- dnorm(g$mu, 0, mu_sd, log = TRUE) + dnorm(g$tau, 0, tau_sd, log = TRUE)
  for (i in seq_along(yi)) lp <- lp + dnorm(yi[i], g$mu, sqrt(sei[i]^2 + g$tau^2), log = TRUE)
  s <- g[sample(nrow(g), n_draws, replace = TRUE, prob = exp(lp - max(lp))), ]
  s$mu  <- s$mu + runif(n_draws, -1.5, 1.5) / (grid - 1)          # jitter within a grid cell
  s$tau <- abs(s$tau + runif(n_draws, -0.75, 0.75) / (grid - 1))
  # each region's true effect, given mu and tau (normal-normal conditional posterior)
  theta <- sapply(seq_along(yi), \(j) {
    w <- s$tau^2 / (s$tau^2 + sei[j]^2)
    rnorm(n_draws, w * yi[j] + (1 - w) * s$mu, sqrt(w) * sei[j])
  })
  list(mu = s$mu, tau = s$tau, new = rnorm(n_draws, s$mu, s$tau), theta = theta)
}
set.seed(629)
pp <- nn_grid(plato$yi, plato$sei)
q3 <- \(x) exp(quantile(x, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975)))




Code
library(brms)                               # the same model by MCMC
priors <- c(prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept), prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = sd))
fit_plato <- brm(yi | se(sei) ~ 1 + (1 | Region), data = plato, prior = priors,
                 chains = 4, iter = 4000, seed = 629, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99))




Code
fp <- bind_rows(
  plato |> transmute(Region, Analysis = "Observed (no pooling)",
                     est = exp(yi), lo = exp(yi - 1.96 * sei), hi = exp(yi + 1.96 * sei)),
  map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(plato)), \(j) {
    q <- q3(pp$theta[, j])
    tibble::tibble(Region = plato$Region[j], Analysis = "Partial pooling (Bayesian)",
                   est = q[1], lo = q[2], hi = q[3]) }),
  tibble::tibble(Region = "Overall",
                 Analysis = c("Complete pooling", "Partial pooling (Bayesian)", "Prediction, new region"),
                 est = c(exp(pool_mh$b), q3(pp$mu)[1], q3(pp$new)[1]),
                 lo  = c(exp(pool_mh$ci.lb), q3(pp$mu)[2], q3(pp$new)[2]),
                 hi  = c(exp(pool_mh$ci.ub), q3(pp$mu)[3], q3(pp$new)[3]))) |>
  mutate(Region = factor(Region, levels = rev(c(plato$Region, "Overall"))),
         Analysis = factor(Analysis, levels = c("Observed (no pooling)", "Partial pooling (Bayesian)",
                                                "Complete pooling", "Prediction, new region")))
ggplot(fp, aes(est, Region, colour = Analysis, shape = Analysis)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.7, 0.85, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#041E42", "#B22222", "grey45", "#E69F00"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 15, 17, 18), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio, ticagrelor vs clopidogrel (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2), shape = guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 17.1: PLATO by region: observed risk ratios (no pooling), Bayesian partially pooled estimates, and overall estimates under complete pooling, partial pooling, and for a new region.





The US estimate is pulled from 1.25 towards the others (1.02), while Eastern Europe, the largest region, barely moves. The overall estimate, RR 0.88 (0.74 to 1.10), is less certain than complete pooling suggests, and for a new region (a confirmatory North American trial, say) the prediction runs from 0.56 to 1.45: from clear benefit to harm. The posterior probability that ticagrelor reduces risk at all is 90%, and that it reduces it by at least 10% is 61%. A hierarchical re-analysis with somewhat different priors reached a similar conclusion (4). A conclusion that changes materially with a reasonable change of model is not robust, whatever the P value under any one model.


17.1.2 A new trial, designed with the prior evidence
That uncertainty justified a new trial. TC4 randomised 1,005 patients with an acute coronary syndrome at one Montreal hospital to ticagrelor or clopidogrel, by two-month time clusters, with 12-month outcomes taken from Quebec’s administrative health databases: a pragmatic, registry-based design that cost about $300 per patient and lost no one to follow-up (5). It was designed and analysed as a Bayesian trial, with a community of priors (Chapter 13): a vague prior, a “focused” primary prior from the North American PLATO patients, an “enthusiastic” prior from all of PLATO, a modified enthusiastic prior allowing for regional heterogeneity, and a summary prior from a network meta-analysis.


Code
tibble::tribble(
  ~Prior,                    ~`RR (95% CrI)`,       ~`P(benefit)`, ~`P(equivalence)`, ~`P(harm)`,
  "Vague",                   "0.95 (0.67 to 1.35)", "37%", "42%", "21%",
  "Focused (primary)",       "1.12 (0.91 to 1.39)", "2%",  "41%", "57%",
  "Enthusiastic",            "0.85 (0.78 to 0.93)", "89%", "11%", "0%",
  "Modified enthusiastic",   "1.03 (0.73 to 1.44)", "22%", "35%", "43%",
  "Summary (earlier NMA)",   "0.99 (0.69 to 1.38)", "30%", "44%", "26%") |>
  kable(align = "lcccc")

title: 17  Network Meta-Analysis
text:
17.2 Why network meta-analysis
The data used in the rest of this chapter come from a Bayesian network meta-analysis of the three drugs: 20 randomised trials with 77,714 patients, restricted to trials at low risk of bias with at least six months’ follow-up (6). Three separate pairwise meta-analyses answer three separate questions, each from part of the evidence.


Code
dp <- read_csv("data/ch17/direct_pairwise.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dp |>
  mutate(label = factor(sprintf("%s (%d RCTs, %s patients)", comparison, trials, format(patients, big.mark = ",")),
                        levels = rev(sprintf("%s (%d RCTs, %s patients)", comparison, trials,
                                             format(patients, big.mark = ","))))) |>
  ggplot(aes(median_HR, label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo95_HR, xmax = hi95_HR), colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", median_HR, lo95_HR, hi95_HR)), vjust = -1, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1, 1.1, 1.2)) +
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio for MACE (log scale)", y = NULL)








Figure 17.2: Direct evidence only: Bayesian pairwise meta-analyses of the head-to-head trials (hazard ratio for MACE; T = ticagrelor, P = prasugrel, C = clopidogrel).





Prasugrel versus ticagrelor can also be estimated indirectly, through their common comparator clopidogrel, without using the five head-to-head trials. On the log scale the indirect estimate is a difference (7):
\[\hat\theta^{\,ind}_{PT} = \hat\theta_{PC} - \hat\theta_{TC}, \qquad \text{Var}(\hat\theta^{\,ind}_{PT}) = \text{Var}(\hat\theta_{PC}) + \text{Var}(\hat\theta_{TC}).\]


Code
se_ci <- \(lo, hi) (log(hi) - log(lo)) / (2 * 1.96)               # SE from a 95% interval
d_tc <- filter(dp, comparison == "T vs C"); d_pc <- filter(dp, comparison == "P vs C")
ind  <- log(d_pc$median_HR) - log(d_tc$median_HR)
se_ind <- sqrt(se_ci(d_pc$lo95_HR, d_pc$hi95_HR)^2 + se_ci(d_tc$lo95_HR, d_tc$hi95_HR)^2)
fmt3(exp(ind + c(0, -1.96, 1.96) * se_ind))


[1] "0.94 (0.70 to 1.27)"


The indirect estimate is much less precise than either of its parts, because the uncertainties of two comparisons add. A network meta-analysis combines direct and indirect evidence for every comparison in one model, so that the three estimates are coherent (P vs T equals P vs C divided by T vs C) and every trial contributes to every comparison it informs.

  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x1, y1, xend = x2, yend = y2, linewidth = trials), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_label(data = edges, aes((x1 + x2) / 2, (y1 + y2) / 2,
                               label = paste0(trials, " RCTs\n", format(N, big.mark = ","), " pts")),
             size = 3.5, label.size = 0, lineheight = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y, size = n), shape = 21, fill = "#E69F00", colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y + ifelse(y > 0, 0.32, -0.32),
                              label = paste0(drug, "\nn = ", format(n, big.mark = ","))),
            fontface = "bold", size = 3.8, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_linewidth(range = c(2, 6), guide = "none") +
  scale_size(range = c(10, 20), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1.5, 1.5), ylim = c(-0.95, 1.45)) +
  theme_void()








Figure 17.3: The DAPT network: nodes sized by patients randomised, edges by number of trials.





Nodes are treatments; edges are comparisons with direct randomised evidence. Every pair here has direct evidence, so the network is a closed loop and direct and indirect estimates can be compared. A star network, in which every treatment is compared only with placebo, has no loops: indirect comparisons are then entirely dependent on the transitivity assumption and cannot be checked.

title: 17  Network Meta-Analysis
text:
17.4 Transitivity and consistency
Transitivity is the clinical assumption behind every indirect comparison: the trials of T versus C and those of P versus C must be similar in their distribution of effect modifiers, characteristics that change the size of the relative effect. Equivalently, every patient in the network could in principle have been randomised to any of the treatments. In the DAPT network, TREAT (patients given fibrinolysis) and TRILOGY ACS (medically managed patients, without PCI) differ from the PCI trials; SWITCH-SWEDEHEART enrolled unselected registry patients; prasugrel is dose-reduced in older and lighter patients. Transitivity cannot be tested statistically. Tabulate effect modifiers by comparison, and run sensitivity analyses that restrict the network to similar trials.
Consistency is its statistical counterpart: where direct and indirect evidence exist for the same comparison, they should agree. Node-splitting estimates the comparison separately from the direct trials and from the rest of the network, and examines their difference (8).


Code
ns <- read_csv("data/ch17/nodesplit_PT.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(estimate = factor(estimate, levels = rev(c("direct", "indirect", "network", "ratio_direct_indirect")),
                           labels = rev(c("Direct (5 P vs T trials)", "Indirect (15 C-controlled trials)",
                                          "Network (all 20 trials)", "Ratio direct / indirect"))))
ggplot(ns, aes(median_HR, estimate)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.90, xmax = 1.11, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#4393C3", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo95_HR, xmax = hi95_HR, colour = grepl("Ratio", estimate)), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#041E42", "#B22222")) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.6, 0.8, 0.9, 1, 1.11, 1.3)) +
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio, prasugrel vs ticagrelor (log scale)", y = NULL)








Figure 17.4: Node-splitting for prasugrel vs ticagrelor (MACE): direct, indirect and network estimates, and the ratio of direct to indirect. Shaded band: hazard ratios of 0.90 to 1.11.





The direct trials favour prasugrel more than the indirect route, which inherits the near-null ticagrelor-versus-clopidogrel result. Their ratio, 0.86 (0.59 to 1.22), is compatible with consistency but also with substantial inconsistency: with five direct trials, the check has little power. When direct and indirect evidence clearly disagree, investigate which trials or populations differ; do not simply average incompatible sources (Chapter 18 shows what happens when this is not done).

title: 17  Network Meta-Analysis
text:
17.5 Models for network meta-analysis

17.5.1 An arm-based model on the hazard scale
The DAPT trials report events \(r_{ij}\) among \(n_{ij}\) patients in arm \(j\) of trial \(i\), over follow-up times \(t_i\) from 6 to 30 months. A binomial model with a complementary log-log link and a follow-up offset puts all trials on a common hazard scale (9):
\[r_{ij} \sim \text{Binomial}(n_{ij}, \pi_{ij}), \qquad \text{cloglog}(\pi_{ij}) = \mu_i + \beta_j + u_{ij} + \log t_i ,\]
where \(\mu_i\) is trial \(i\)’s baseline (clopidogrel) log hazard, \(\beta_j\) the network log hazard ratio of drug \(j\) versus clopidogrel (\(\beta_C = 0\)), and \(u_{ij}\) the trial-specific deviation, with between-trial SDs \(\tau_T\) and \(\tau_P\). If the hazard λ is constant, \(\pi = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}\), so \(\log(-\log(1 - \pi)) = \log \lambda + \log t\): differences on this scale are log hazard ratios. Odds ratios would exaggerate the hazard ratios here, because events are common and follow-up varies. Prasugrel versus ticagrelor is \(\exp(\beta_P - \beta_T)\), so all three comparisons come from one posterior.
The model was fitted with brms and Stan, with priors \(\beta_j \sim N(0, 0.5^2)\), \(\tau \sim\) half-\(N(0, 0.5)\) and an LKJ(1) prior on the correlation of the deviations. The code is below; it takes several minutes to run, so the chapter uses the saved posterior draws.


Code
library(brms)
eff <- read_csv("data/ch17/switch_effective_counts.csv") |> filter(outcome == "MACE")
dat <- mace |>                                     # SWITCH-SWEDEHEART enters as effective counts
  mutate(r = case_when(study == "SWITCH-SWEDEHEART" & treat == "T" ~ eff$r0,
                       study == "SWITCH-SWEDEHEART" & treat == "P" ~ eff$r1, TRUE ~ r),
         n = case_when(study == "SWITCH-SWEDEHEART" & treat == "T" ~ eff$n0,
                       study == "SWITCH-SWEDEHEART" & treat == "P" ~ eff$n1, TRUE ~ n),
         treat = factor(treat, levels = c("C", "T", "P")), log_time = log(time_yr),
         r_cc = ifelse(r == 0, 1, r), n_cc = ifelse(r == 0, n + 1, n))   # zero-event arms
priors <- c(prior(normal(-2, 1), class = Intercept), prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = b),
            prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = sd))
fit_re <- brm(r_cc | trials(n_cc) ~ treat + offset(log_time) + (treat | study), data = dat,
              family = binomial(link = "cloglog"), prior = priors,
              chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 20260529)
fit_fe <- update(fit_re, formula. = ~ treat + offset(log_time) + (1 | study))


In brms, (treat | study) gives trial-specific baselines and trial-specific treatment deviations; (1 | study) gives baselines only, the fixed-effect NMA. (Here the trial baselines also have a common distribution; a strictly contrast-based NMA would make them fixed.)


17.5.2 Fixed versus random effects


Code
draws <- read_csv("data/ch17/posterior_draws.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(logHR_PT = logHR_PC - logHR_TC)
rope_lo <- log(0.90); rope_hi <- log(1.11)
pct <- \(p) ifelse(p < 0.005, "<1%", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * p))
summ <- \(x) tibble::tibble(HR = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(median(x)), exp(quantile(x, 0.025)),
                                         exp(quantile(x, 0.975))),
                            pben = mean(x < rope_lo), prope = mean(x >= rope_lo & x <= rope_hi),
                            pharm = mean(x > rope_hi))
long <- draws |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("logHR"), names_to = "comp", values_to = "lh", names_prefix = "logHR_") |>
  mutate(comp = factor(comp, levels = c("TC", "PC", "PT"), labels = c("T vs C", "P vs C", "P vs T")))
res <- long |> group_by(model, comp) |> reframe(summ(lh))
tau_re <- draws |> filter(model == "MACE_RE")

The fixed-effect NMA makes all three comparisons “significant”: a confident hierarchy of prasugrel over ticagrelor over clopidogrel. Once heterogeneity is acknowledged, every interval widens to include values close to no effect. The between-trial SDs are themselves uncertain, τT = 0.14 (0.02 to 0.37) and τP = 0.10 (0.01 to 0.34), and the Bayesian model carries that uncertainty into every comparison. Leave-one-out cross-validation preferred the random-effects model in the original analysis (6), but a clinical judgement that trials from different decades, countries and populations are unlikely to share one identical effect should come first.
A frequentist version of the same model can be fitted with lme4 as a check (trials with no events at all are dropped, since they carry no information about the relative effect):


Code
eff  <- read_csv("data/ch17/switch_effective_counts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dfq <- mace |>
  mutate(r = case_when(study == "SWITCH-SWEDEHEART" & treat == "T" ~ eff$r0[1],
                       study == "SWITCH-SWEDEHEART" & treat == "P" ~ eff$r1[1], TRUE ~ r),
         n = case_when(study == "SWITCH-SWEDEHEART" & treat == "T" ~ eff$n0[1],
                       study == "SWITCH-SWEDEHEART" & treat == "P" ~ eff$n1[1], TRUE ~ n),
         isT = as.numeric(treat == "T"), isP = as.numeric(treat == "P"), lt = log(time_yr)) |>
  filter(.by = study, sum(r) > 0)
f_fe <- glm(cbind(r, n - r) ~ 0 + factor(study) + isT + isP + offset(lt),
            family = binomial("cloglog"), data = dfq)
f_re <- glmer(cbind(r, n - r) ~ 0 + factor(study) + isT + isP + (0 + isT + isP || study) + offset(lt),
              family = binomial("cloglog"), data = dfq, control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
hr_row <- \(b, se) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", exp(b), exp(b - 1.96 * se), exp(b + 1.96 * se))
tibble::tibble(
  Model = c("Fixed effect (glm)", "Random effects (glmer, ML)"),
  `T vs C` = c(hr_row(coef(f_fe)["isT"], sqrt(vcov(f_fe)["isT", "isT"])),
               hr_row(fixef(f_re)["isT"], sqrt(vcov(f_re)["isT", "isT"]))),
  `P vs C` = c(hr_row(coef(f_fe)["isP"], sqrt(vcov(f_fe)["isP", "isP"])),
               hr_row(fixef(f_re)["isP"], sqrt(vcov(f_re)["isP", "isP"]))),
  `τ (T, P)` = c("0, 0", paste(sprintf("%.2f", attr(VarCorr(f_re)$study, "stddev")),
                               sprintf("%.2f", attr(VarCorr(f_re)$study.1, "stddev")), sep = ", "))) |>
  kable(align = "lccc")
