title: 17  Network Meta-Analysis
section: 17.6 Trials that are not individually randomised
text:
17.6 Trials that are not individually randomised
SWITCH-SWEDEHEART randomised seven Swedish regions, in three clusters, to switch at staggered times from a default ticagrelor policy to a default prasugrel policy: a stepped-wedge cluster trial of 17,095 patients undergoing PCI for an acute coronary syndrome (10). At one year the primary outcome (death, myocardial infarction or stroke) occurred in 11.1% under the prasugrel policy and 11.8% under the ticagrelor policy, adjusted OR 0.90 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.06); major bleeding was lower with prasugrel, OR 0.80 (0.64 to 0.99).
Entering the crude counts in an arm-based NMA would be wrong for two reasons. Every cluster started on ticagrelor and ended on prasugrel, so calendar time is confounded with treatment and the effect is identified only after adjusting for time. And patients within a cluster are correlated, so treating 17,095 patients as independent overstates the trial’s precision. The fix is to convert the adjusted estimate into effective counts: keep the observed ticagrelor-arm risk, set the prasugrel-arm risk so that the odds ratio equals the adjusted OR, and shrink both arms by a common factor so that the binomial standard error matches the adjusted one, a generalisation of the effective-sample-size method for cluster trials (11).


Code
adj_to_counts <- function(r0, n0, n1, or, lo, hi) {
  p0 <- r0 / n0                                       # observed control-arm risk, kept
  p1 <- p0 / (1 - p0) * or / (1 + p0 / (1 - p0) * or) # treated-arm risk implied by the adjusted OR
  se_adj <- (log(hi) - log(lo)) / (2 * qnorm(0.975))  # SE implied by the adjusted CI
  k <- (1 / (n0 * p0 * (1 - p0)) + 1 / (n1 * p1 * (1 - p1))) / se_adj^2
  N0 <- round(k * n0); N1 <- round(k * n1)
  tibble::tibble(r0 = round(N0 * p0), n0 = N0, r1 = round(N1 * p1), n1 = N1, design_effect = 1 / k)
}
sw <- bind_rows(MACE     = adj_to_counts(1113, 9444, 7651, 0.90, 0.77, 1.06),
                Bleeding = adj_to_counts(413, 9444, 7651, 0.80, 0.64, 0.99), .id = "Outcome")

Ticagrelor and clopidogrel are probably equivalent for MACE (79% probability), with probable excess bleeding on ticagrelor (89%). Eligibility rules set before any statistics (risk of bias, minimum follow-up, the population, which time point of PRAGUE-18 to use) shape the network. Before comparing the conclusions of two NMAs, compare their trial lists. The Bayesian NMA also differs in its model (random effects with uncertainty in τ propagated, a hazard rather than odds scale), its handling of SWITCH-SWEDEHEART, and its reporting: probabilities of meaningful differences rather than rankings.

title: 17  Network Meta-Analysis
text:
17.8 Treatment rankings
Many NMAs summarise results by ranking. SUCRA, the surface under the cumulative ranking curve, rescales each treatment’s mean rank to between 0 (always worst) and 1 (always best), \(\text{SUCRA}_k = (K - \bar r_k)/(K - 1)\) (13); the P-score is its frequentist analogue, computed from point estimates and standard errors (14).


Code
rk <- draws |> filter(model == "MACE_RE") |>
  transmute(draw, Clopidogrel = 0, Ticagrelor = logHR_TC, Prasugrel = logHR_PC) |>
  pivot_longer(-draw, names_to = "drug", values_to = "lh") |>
  mutate(.by = draw, rank = rank(lh))
rank_tab <- rk |> summarise(.by = drug, `P(best)` = mean(rank == 1), `Mean rank` = mean(rank),
                            SUCRA = (3 - mean(rank)) / 2) |> arrange(`Mean rank`)
kable(rank_tab, digits = 2, col.names = c("Treatment", "P(best)", "Mean rank", "SUCRA"))

Prasugrel ranks first in 88% of draws, which sounds decisive. Yet the probability that it beats ticagrelor by a clinically meaningful margin is 51%. Rankings discard the size of the differences: a tiny, clinically irrelevant advantage that is consistent across draws earns a near-certain top rank, and a treatment can be the best of a weak field. Report effect sizes with credible intervals and the probabilities of meaningful benefit, equivalence and harm; if rankings are shown, show them as secondary, with their uncertainty.

title: 17  Network Meta-Analysis
text:
17.9 Appraising a network meta-analysis



Table 17.7: Appraising a network meta-analysis.










Domain
What to check

title: 17  Network Meta-Analysis
text:
Key points

The statistical model is not neutral: complete, no and partial pooling of the same trial lead to different conclusions, and partial pooling with honest uncertainty in τ is usually the defensible compromise.
NMA combines direct and indirect evidence into coherent estimates for every comparison; an indirect estimate is a difference on the log scale, with the variances added.
Transitivity (similar distributions of effect modifiers) is a clinical judgement; consistency, its statistical counterpart, is checked by node-splitting, which has little power with few direct trials.
Fixed-effect NMAs can create confident hierarchies that disappear when heterogeneity is acknowledged; a frequentist random-effects NMA with τ estimated at zero has the same problem.
Cluster and stepped-wedge trials must enter with their adjusted estimates and true information content.
Report probabilities of clinically meaningful benefit, equivalence and harm, and absolute effects, rather than rankings; compare trial lists before comparing NMAs.

title: 17  Network Meta-Analysis
text:
Exercises

Refit the PLATO hierarchical model with τ ~ half-N(0, 0.25) and half-N(0, 1). How do the US estimate and the prediction for a new region change?
From Figure 17.2, compute the indirect estimate of ticagrelor versus clopidogrel through prasugrel and compare it with the direct estimate.

Recompute SWITCH-SWEDEHEART’s effective counts if the adjusted 95% CI for MACE had been 0.70 to 1.15. What is the design effect?
Re-run freq-check with the crude SWITCH-SWEDEHEART counts. How do the P vs C and P vs T estimates change?

title: 18  Network Meta-Analysis in Practice
text:
18.1 The paper
Chapter 17 introduced the tools of network meta-analysis. This chapter applies them, and the tools of earlier chapters, to one influential NMA. (1) combined 71 trials (9,510 children and adolescents with depressive disorders) of 16 antidepressants, seven psychotherapies and five combinations, and concluded that “fluoxetine (alone or in combination with CBT) seems to be the best choice” for acute treatment. With an earlier NMA restricted to antidepressants (2), it underpins guideline recommendations of fluoxetine as first-line medication. In 2026 a re-appraisal traced a discrepancy between these NMAs and a Cochrane NMA (3) to a single 40-patient trial (4). The question for this chapter is whether the checks in this book, all available in 2016, would have found the problem earlier.
Zhou and colleagues estimated, for each treatment, the standardised mean difference (SMD) in change of depressive symptoms against pill placebo, with a Bayesian random-effects NMA, a common heterogeneity variance across comparisons, rankings by SUCRA, and certainty rated with CINeMA (5). Every rating scale scores higher for more depression, so changes are negative and an SMD below zero favours the treatment. They reported significant global inconsistency in the efficacy network, rated most comparisons “very low” confidence, and noted that the loop formed by fluoxetine, nortriptyline and pill placebo was inconsistent; neither its cause nor an analysis without the trials that created it was reported.
Code
published <- tibble::tribble(                         # Zhou et al., Figure 4A (SMD vs pill placebo)
  ~treat, ~smd, ~lo, ~hi,
  "Fluoxetine+CBT", -0.73, -1.39, -0.07, "Fluoxetine", -0.51, -0.84, -0.18,
  "Nortriptyline", 1.14, 0.46, 1.81, "WL", 0.99, 0.18, 1.79)

title: 18  Network Meta-Analysis in Practice
text:
18.2 Can it be reproduced?
The authors shared arm-level data (mean change, SD and number for each arm of 70 trials in the efficacy network), to their credit. The analysis model can be written as an arm-level NMA: each arm’s mean change is divided by its trial’s pooled SD, and the model fits every arm with a fixed trial intercept, so that treatment differences are formed within trials:
\[y_{ik} = \mu_i + d_{t(ik)} + u_{ik}, \qquad u_{ik} \sim N(0, \tau^2/2),\]
with arm-level variances \(1/n_{ik}\). This is the model behind the SMD link of the gemtc package used by both Lancet NMAs. In metafor it is a multilevel model with trial as a fixed factor and arm as a random effect. The helper functions below are adapted from the code that (4) made public.


Code
arm_data <- function(arms, ref) {
  arms |>
    mutate(.by = study, sd_pool = sqrt(sum((n - 1) * sd^2) / (sum(n) - n()))) |>
    mutate(y = mean / sd_pool, v = 1 / n, se = sqrt(v),
           trt = gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]", "", treat),
           trt = relevel(factor(trt), gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]", "", ref)),
           study = factor(study), arm = paste(study, trt))
}
nma_freq <- \(ad) rma.mv(y, v, mods = ~ 0 + study + trt, random = ~ 1 | arm, data = ad)
nma_tau  <- \(fit) sqrt(2 * fit$sigma2)
nma_effects <- function(fit, ad) {                # each treatment vs the reference, with 95% PI
  b <- coef(fit); keep <- startsWith(names(b), "trt"); tau2 <- 2 * fit$sigma2
  tibble::tibble(trt = sub("^trt", "", names(b)[keep]), est = b[keep],
                 se = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[keep]) |>
    mutate(lo = est - 1.96 * se, hi = est + 1.96 * se,
           pi_lo = est - 1.96 * sqrt(se^2 + tau2), pi_hi = est + 1.96 * sqrt(se^2 + tau2)) |>
    left_join(distinct(ad, trt = as.character(trt), treat), by = "trt")
}
nma_contrast <- function(fit, A, B) {             # network estimate of A vs B
  b <- coef(fit); cv <- setNames(rep(0, length(b)), names(b))
  if (paste0("trt", A) %in% names(b)) cv[paste0("trt", A)] <- 1
  if (paste0("trt", B) %in% names(b)) cv[paste0("trt", B)] <- -1
  c(est = sum(cv * b), var = as.numeric(t(cv) %*% vcov(fit) %*% cv))
}
node_split <- function(ad, fit, A, B) {           # direct vs back-calculated indirect evidence
  A <- gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]", "", A); B <- gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]", "", B)
  dd <- ad |> filter(.by = study, all(c(A, B) %in% trt)) |> filter(trt %in% c(A, B)) |>
    mutate(trt = relevel(droplevels(trt), B), study = droplevels(study))
  form <- if (nlevels(dd$study) > 1) ~ 0 + study + trt else ~ trt
  fd   <- rma.mv(y, v, mods = form, random = ~ 1 | arm, data = dd, sigma2 = fit$sigma2)
  dir  <- coef(fd)[[paste0("trt", A)]]; vdir <- vcov(fd)[paste0("trt", A), paste0("trt", A)]
  net  <- nma_contrast(fit, A, B)
  vind <- 1 / (1 / net[["var"]] - 1 / vdir)
  ind  <- (net[["est"]] / net[["var"]] - dir / vdir) * vind
  tibble::tibble(comparison = paste(A, "vs", B), k_direct = n_distinct(dd$study),
                 direct = dir, se_dir = sqrt(vdir), indirect = ind, se_ind = sqrt(vind),
                 network = net[["est"]], p = 2 * pnorm(-abs((dir - ind) / sqrt(vdir + vind))))
}




Code
arms_posted <- read_csv("data/ch18/zhou_arms_posted.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)   # as posted
arms        <- read_csv("data/ch18/zhou_arms.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)          # corrected
ad_posted <- arm_data(arms_posted, "Pill-PBO"); f_posted <- nma_freq(ad_posted)
ad1 <- arm_data(arms, "Pill-PBO");              f1 <- nma_freq(ad1)
fx <- \(f, ad) with(filter(nma_effects(f, ad), treat == "Fluoxetine"), fmt_ci(est, lo, hi))
audit <- full_join(select(arms_posted, study, treat, m_post = mean, n_post = n),
                   select(arms, study, treat, m_corr = mean, n_corr = n), by = c("study", "treat")) |>
  summarise(.by = study, bad = any(abs(m_post - m_corr) > 0.01 | n_post != n_corr, na.rm = TRUE),
            pbo = any(treat == "Pill-PBO"))


Analysed exactly as posted, the data give fluoxetine versus placebo an SMD of -0.08 (-0.42 to 0.27), not the published −0.51 (−0.84 to −0.18). Comparing the posted file with a version in which every arm assignment was checked against the trial reports (4) shows why: 37 of 70 trials have results attached to the wrong arm, including 33 of the 33 trials with a pill-placebo arm. Means, SDs and numbers move together, a systematic ordering error in the shared file rather than random typing errors. With the corrected data the published estimates are reproduced.


Code
draws <- read_csv("data/ch18/zhou_draws.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
d_full <- filter(draws, fit == "zhou_full")
bq <- function(d, t, pred = FALSE) {
  x <- d[[paste0("b_trt", gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]", "", t))]]
  if (pred) { set.seed(629); x <- x + rnorm(length(x), 0, sqrt(2) * d$sd_arm__Intercept) }
  fmt_ci(median(x), quantile(x, 0.025), quantile(x, 0.975))
}
e1 <- nma_effects(f1, ad1)
published |>
  transmute(Treatment = treat, Published = fmt_ci(smd, lo, hi),
            `Frequentist (metafor)` = map_chr(treat, \(t) with(filter(e1, treat == t), fmt_ci(est, lo, hi))),
            `Bayesian (brms)` = map_chr(treat, \(t) bq(d_full, t)),
            `95% prediction interval (brms)` = map_chr(treat, \(t) bq(d_full, t, pred = TRUE))) |>
  kable(align = "lcccc")

The Bayesian fits were run with brms on the course data; the chapter reads their saved posterior draws, so it does not need Stan to render. The model is:


Code
library(brms)
nma_priors <- c(prior(normal(0, 10), class = b), prior(normal(0, 1), class = sd))
b1 <- brm(y | se(se) ~ 0 + study + trt + (1 | arm), data = ad1, prior = nma_priors,
          chains = 4, iter = 3000, warmup = 1000, seed = 629, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95))


The estimated heterogeneity is large: τ = 0.49 SD units, about the size of fluoxetine’s whole effect. The paper reported credible intervals only; the prediction interval in Table 18.1, for the effect of fluoxetine in a new trial, runs from a large benefit to a moderate harm.
So the problems that follow are not coding errors. The posting error did not affect the authors’ own analysis; it made the analysis irreproducible for everyone else, and nobody (authors, reviewers or editors) checked that the shared file reproduced the paper (Section 1.1.3).

18.2.1 Arm-level or contrast-level?
The same data can be analysed at the contrast level: compute each trial’s SMD and its variance with escalc(), then pool the contrasts. The large-sample variance of an SMD is
\[\text{Var}(d) \approx \frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2} + \frac{d^2}{2(n_1 + n_2)} .\]
The last term is negligible for ordinary effects, but not for an extreme one. The arm-level model omits it, so a trial with an extreme SMD is treated as more precise than it is.


Code
make_contrasts <- function(arms) {             # each arm vs its trial's first arm
  arms |>
    mutate(.by = study, ref = first(treat), mref = first(mean), sref = first(sd),
           nref = first(n), N = sum(n), k = row_number()) |>
    filter(k > 1) |>
    escalc(measure = "SMD", m1i = mean, sd1i = sd, n1i = n, m2i = mref, sd2i = sref, n2i = nref, data = _)
}
contr <- make_contrasts(arms)
att_c <- filter(contr, study == "Attari 2006")
tau2_a <- 2 * f1$sigma2
c(SMD = att_c$yi, `variance, arm-level` = 1 / 20 + 1 / 20, `variance, contrast-level` = att_c$vi,
  `weight ratio, arm vs contrast` = (1 / (0.10 + tau2_a)) / (1 / (att_c$vi + tau2_a))) |> round(2)


                          SMD           variance, arm-level 
                         4.24                          0.10 
     variance, contrast-level weight ratio, arm vs contrast 
                         0.32                          1.66 


One trial stands out: Attari 2006, a 40-patient trial of fluoxetine against nortriptyline (6), with an SMD of 4.24 in favour of fluoxetine. Its variance is three times larger than the arm-level model assumes, and even after adding between-trial heterogeneity, it receives 1.7 times more weight in the arm-level model. It is the only trial comparing fluoxetine with nortriptyline, so it alone forms that side of the inconsistent loop. When a result depends on a technical modelling detail, look for the observation that makes the detail matter.

title: 18  Network Meta-Analysis in Practice
text:
18.3 Applying the checks
The checks below were each taught in an earlier chapter. Zhou et al. ran one of them (node-splitting) but did not follow up on what it showed.

18.3.1 Prediction intervals


Code
pw <- arms |>
  filter(.by = study, all(c("Fluoxetine", "Pill-PBO") %in% treat)) |>
  reframe(.by = study,
          m1 = mean[treat == "Fluoxetine"], s1 = sd[treat == "Fluoxetine"], n1 = n[treat == "Fluoxetine"],
          m2 = mean[treat == "Pill-PBO"], s2 = sd[treat == "Pill-PBO"], n2 = n[treat == "Pill-PBO"]) |>
  escalc(measure = "SMD", m1i = m1, sd1i = s1, n1i = n1, m2i = m2, sd2i = s2, n2i = n2, data = _)
pw_fit <- rma(yi, vi, data = pw, method = "REML", test = "knha"); pw_pr <- predict(pw_fit)
bind_rows(
  as.data.frame(pw) |> transmute(label = study, est = yi, lo = yi - 1.96 * sqrt(vi), hi = yi + 1.96 * sqrt(vi), type = "Trial"),
  tibble::tibble(label = c("Pooled (95% CI)", "95% prediction interval"), est = pw_pr$pred,
                 lo = c(pw_pr$ci.lb, pw_pr$pi.lb), hi = c(pw_pr$ci.ub, pw_pr$pi.ub), type = c("Pooled", "PI"))) |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(unique(label)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(est, label, colour = type)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.35, xmax = 0.35, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey90") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Trial = "#041E42", Pooled = "#041E42", PI = "#B22222"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "SMD, fluoxetine vs placebo (< 0 favours fluoxetine)", y = NULL)








Figure 18.1: Pairwise meta-analysis of the nine fluoxetine-placebo trials (direct evidence only; HKSJ confidence interval). Grey band: ±0.35 SD. Red: 95% prediction interval.





The direct evidence gives an SMD of -0.25 (-0.48 to -0.01), about half the network estimate, with a prediction interval of -0.83 to 0.34. The ±0.35 SD band is the margin of clinical equivalence pre-specified by (3) (±5 points on the CDRS-R, whose SD is about 14.5).


18.3.2 Consistency

map_dfr(loop, \(x) node_split(ad1, f1, x[1], x[2])) |>
  transmute(Comparison = comparison, `Direct trials` = k_direct,
            Direct = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", direct, se_dir), Indirect = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", indirect, se_ind),
            Network = sprintf("%.2f", network), `P (direct = indirect)` = fmt_p(p)) |>

  scale_y_reverse() + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#041E42", `TRUE` = "#B22222"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Trial-level SMD", y = "Standard error")








Figure 18.3: Every within-trial comparison in the network (each arm vs its trial’s first arm), by SMD and standard error. The sign reflects only which arm is listed first.





Looking at the data would have found it. So would a leave-one-trial-out analysis (Section 10.4.1), which drops each trial in turn with no suspect in mind:


Code
loo <- map_dfr(levels(ad1$study), \(s) {
  d <- filter(ad1, study != s) |> mutate(study = droplevels(study), trt = droplevels(trt))
  if (!all(c("Fluoxetine", "PillPBO") %in% d$trt)) return(NULL)
  f <- nma_freq(d); e <- nma_contrast(f, "Fluoxetine", "PillPBO")
  tibble::tibble(omitted = s, est = e[["est"]], tau = nma_tau(f),
                 p_incons = node_split(d, f, "Fluoxetine", "Pill-PBO")$p)
})
others <- filter(loo, omitted != "Attari 2006"); att <- filter(loo, omitted == "Attari 2006")


Omitting any of the other 69 trials leaves the fluoxetine estimate between -0.57 and -0.44, τ between 0.44 and 0.50, and the inconsistency P below 0.001. Omitting Attari 2006 moves fluoxetine to -0.29, halves τ to 0.26, and removes the inconsistency (P = 0.19).


18.3.4 Is the trial trustworthy?
An outlier this extreme should prompt a trustworthiness assessment before the trial enters a synthesis. Lyus and colleagues applied the INSPECT-SR tool and found serious concerns (4): a single site, no ethics approval statement, registration or protocol; dropouts “replaced by new cases”; a reported P value that does not match the reported data; and change scores whose standard deviations (2.6 and 0.8 points on a 54-point scale) are implausibly small for a trial in which half of the fluoxetine group still met criteria for major depression. The authors, journal and publisher did not respond to queries.
The change-score SDs can be checked against the baseline and week-8 data that the trial reports, using the formula of Section 14.4.1:


Code
att <- list(bF = 28.9, sbF = 8.4, eF = 17.9, seF = 8.1,      # CDI, mean (SD), 20 per arm
            bN = 28.4, sbN = 8.7, eN = 25.8, seN = 8.6)
sd_change <- \(sb, se, r) sqrt(sb^2 + se^2 - 2 * r * sb * se)
tibble::tibble(r = seq(0, 0.99, 0.01)) |>
  mutate(smd = ((att$bF - att$eF) - (att$bN - att$eN)) /
               sqrt((sd_change(att$sbF, att$seF, r)^2 + sd_change(att$sbN, att$seN, r)^2) / 2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(r, smd)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 4.24, colour = "#B22222", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.02, y = 4.45, hjust = 0, colour = "#B22222", label = "SMD used in the NMAs") +
  labs(x = "Assumed pre-post correlation r", y = "Implied change-score SMD")








Figure 18.4: Attari 2006: the change-score SMD implied by the reported baseline and week-8 means and SDs, for each assumed pre-post correlation r. Only r ≈ 0.97 reproduces the SMD that entered both Lancet NMAs.





For depression scales, pre-post correlations are usually moderate, roughly 0.3 to 0.7, which gives an SMD around 1. An ANCOVA-type SMD, the week-8 difference adjusted for baseline and divided by the week-8 SD, barely depends on r:


Code
anc_attari <- function(r) {                         # nortriptyline vs fluoxetine, ANCOVA-type SMD
  sd_e <- sqrt((att$seF^2 + att$seN^2) / 2); sd_b <- sqrt((att$sbF^2 + att$sbN^2) / 2)
  d <- ((att$eN - att$eF) - r * sd_e / sd_b * (att$bN - att$bF)) / sd_e
  c(d = d, v = (2 / 20) * (1 - r^2) + d^2 / 80)
}
sapply(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7), anc_attari) |> round(2)


  [,1] [,2] [,3]
d 0.96 0.97 0.99
v 0.10 0.09 0.06


Attari’s own binary outcome tells the same story. Response (no longer meeting criteria for major depression at week 8) was 10/20 on fluoxetine and 2/20 on nortriptyline. Converted to the SMD scale with \(d = \ln(OR)\sqrt 3/\pi\) (7), that is about 1.2, a quarter of the 4.24 used in the NMAs, and its fragility index (Section 10.5) is small:


Code
fragility_index <- function(e1, n1, e2, n2, alpha = 0.05) {
  p <- \(a, c) fisher.test(matrix(c(a, n1 - a, c, n2 - c), 2))$p.value
  if (p(e1, e2) >= alpha) return(NA_integer_)
  k <- 0
  while (p(e1, e2) < alpha) { if (e1 / n1 < e2 / n2) e1 <- e1 + 1 else e2 <- e2 + 1; k <- k + 1 }
  k
}
fragility_index(10, 20, 2, 20)


[1] 2




18.3.5 Sensitivity analysis
Having diagnosed the problem, we compare two reasonable responses: correcting the trial (ANCOVA-type SMD with r = 0.5) and excluding it.


Code
ad2 <- arm_data(filter(arms, study != "Attari 2006"), "Pill-PBO"); f2 <- nma_freq(ad2)
ad3 <- ad1; a <- anc_attari(0.5)
ad3$y[ad3$arm == "Attari 2006 Fluoxetine"] <- 0
ad3$y[ad3$arm == "Attari 2006 Nortriptyline"] <- a[["d"]]
ad3$v[ad3$study == "Attari 2006"] <- a[["v"]] / 2; ad3$se <- sqrt(ad3$v)
f3 <- nma_freq(ad3)
sens <- list(`All trials (as published)` = list(f = f1, ad = ad1), `Attari corrected (ANCOVA)` = list(f = f3, ad = ad3),
             `Attari excluded` = list(f = f2, ad = ad2))
imap_dfr(sens, \(s, nm) {
  e <- nma_effects(s$f, s$ad); g <- \(t) with(filter(e, treat == t), fmt_ci(est, lo, hi))
  ef <- filter(e, treat == "Fluoxetine")
  tibble::tibble(Analysis = nm, Fluoxetine = g("Fluoxetine"), `Fluoxetine 95% PI` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", ef$pi_lo, ef$pi_hi),
                 Nortriptyline = g("Nortriptyline"), τ = sprintf("%.2f", nma_tau(s$f)),
                 `Inconsistency P` = fmt_p(node_split(s$ad, s$f, "Fluoxetine", "Pill-PBO")$p))
}) |> kable(align = "lccccc")

18.3.6 Is the effect clinically important?

18.3.7 What rankings hide


Code
sucra <- function(d) {
  m <- as.matrix(select(d, starts_with("b_trt"))); colnames(m) <- sub("^b_trt", "", colnames(m))
  m <- cbind(PillPBO = 0, m); rk <- t(apply(m, 1, rank))
  tibble::tibble(trt = colnames(m), SUCRA = (ncol(m) - colMeans(rk)) / (ncol(m) - 1),
                 rank_ci = apply(rk, 2, \(r) sprintf("%d to %d", as.integer(quantile(r, 0.025)), as.integer(quantile(r, 0.975)))))
}
drugs <- c("Fluoxetine", "Duloxetine", "Venlafaxine", "Mirtazapine", "Sertraline", "Paroxetine", "Escitalopram", "Citalopram")

title: 18  Network Meta-Analysis in Practice
text:
18.4 The re-appraisal
Lyus and colleagues re-analysed the datasets of all three NMAs (4). The two Lancet NMAs included Attari 2006; the Cochrane NMA, restricted to newer-generation antidepressants, excluded it by design.


Code
cip <- read_csv("data/ch18/cipriani_arms.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
het <- read_csv("data/ch18/hetrick_arms.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cip_arms <- filter(cip, !is.na(mean)) |> select(study, treat, mean, sd, n)
adc1 <- arm_data(cip_arms, "Placebo"); fc1 <- nma_freq(adc1)
adc2 <- arm_data(filter(cip_arms, study != "Attari 2006"), "Placebo"); fc2 <- nma_freq(adc2)
adh  <- arm_data(het, "Placebo"); fh <- nma_freq(adh)
tibble::tribble(~NMA, ~Analysis, ~fit, ~ad,
  "Cipriani 2016", "All trials", fc1, adc1, "Cipriani 2016", "Attari excluded", fc2, adc2,
  "Zhou 2020", "All trials", f1, ad1, "Zhou 2020", "Attari excluded", f2, ad2,
  "Hetrick 2021", "No Attari (by design)", fh, adh) |>
  mutate(`Fluoxetine vs placebo` = map2_chr(fit, ad, fx),
         `Inconsistency P` = map2_chr(fit, ad, \(f, a) {
           ref <- levels(a$trt)[1]; fmt_p(node_split(a, f, "Fluoxetine", ref)$p) })) |>
  select(-fit, -ad) |> kable(align = "llcc")

One trial explains the discrepancy. Without it, all three NMAs agree that fluoxetine’s advantage over placebo is about 0.2 to 0.3 SD, about 3 to 4 points on the CDRS-R, largely inside the pre-specified margin of clinical equivalence. The Cochrane NMA, independently, had reached the same conclusion in 2021 (3). The direct evidence on response, the outcome patients notice, tells the same story:


Code
resp <- cip |>
  filter(.by = study, all(c("Fluoxetine", "Placebo") %in% treat)) |>
  filter(treat %in% c("Fluoxetine", "Placebo"), !is.na(responders)) |>
  reframe(.by = study, ai = responders[treat == "Fluoxetine"], n1i = responders_n[treat == "Fluoxetine"],
          ci = responders[treat == "Placebo"], n2i = responders_n[treat == "Placebo"])
rr <- rma(measure = "RR", ai = ai, n1i = n1i, ci = ci, n2i = n2i, data = resp, method = "REML", test = "knha")
predict(rr, transf = exp)



   pred  ci.lb  ci.ub  pi.lb  pi.ub 
 1.3107 0.9772 1.7580 0.6595 2.6050 


In the placebo-controlled fluoxetine trials, response was more frequent on fluoxetine, but the pooled risk ratio’s confidence interval (HKSJ) includes 1 and its prediction interval is wide.

title: 18  Network Meta-Analysis in Practice
text:
18.5 From NMA to guideline
Would the guideline recommendation of fluoxetine as first-line medication have survived these checks? The certainty of evidence was already “very low” for most comparisons in both Lancet NMAs, the efficacy network showed significant inconsistency, and the prediction interval for fluoxetine included harm. Every one of the checks applied here (reproduce the analysis, report prediction intervals, investigate inconsistency rather than average over it, plot the data, leave one trial out, assess the trustworthiness of influential trials, and ask whether an effect is clinically important rather than merely non-zero) was available when the first NMA was published. A modest benefit of fluoxetine remains plausible; a recommendation resting on its ranking as “the best choice” does not.
The general lessons:

Reproduce before you trust. Shared data are only useful if someone checks that they reproduce the paper.
Inconsistency is a signal to investigate. A network estimate that blends incompatible direct and indirect evidence summarises nothing.
One small trial can dominate a network when it closes a loop, when its effect is extreme, and when the model underweights its uncertainty.
Check trustworthiness, not only risk of bias. Risk-of-bias tools assume the data are genuine.
Correct where possible, and show both. Report analyses with the trial corrected and excluded, and examine every conclusion, not only the headline estimate.

title: 18  Network Meta-Analysis in Practice
text:
Key points

The shared data of an influential NMA did not reproduce it; with corrected arm assignments, the published estimates were reproduced exactly.
Arm-level SMD models omit the \(d^2/2N\) term of the SMD variance and so overweight trials with extreme effects.
A single 40-patient trial with an implausible SMD of 4.2, created by implausibly small change-score SDs, caused the network’s inconsistency, much of its heterogeneity and much of fluoxetine’s apparent effect.
Prediction intervals, node-splitting, outlier plots, leave-one-out analysis, trustworthiness assessment and fragility would each have flagged the problem.
Corrected or excluded, the trial’s removal brings three NMAs into agreement on a small effect, largely within the margin of clinical equivalence.
Rankings and “significant” network estimates did not convey this; posterior probabilities of clinically important effects do.

title: 18  Network Meta-Analysis in Practice
text:
Exercises

Re-run tbl-nma-sens with the ANCOVA correction at r = 0.3 and r = 0.7. Which conclusions change?
Fit the contrast-level NMA (escalc() SMDs, then rma.mv() with the multi-arm covariance) and compare the fluoxetine estimate with the arm-level result, with and without Attari 2006.
Use node_split() for every comparison in the network with at least two direct trials. Are there other inconsistent loops?
From zhou_draws.csv, compute the probability that fluoxetine + CBT is better than fluoxetine alone by more than 0.2 SD, with and without Attari 2006.
Draft a two-sentence recommendation on fluoxetine for adolescent depression, with a certainty rating, from the analysis without Attari 2006.

title: 19  Systematic Reviews of Observational Studies
text:
19.1 Pooling does not remove confounding
Many questions can only be answered with observational studies: harms too rare or too delayed for trials, exposures that cannot be randomised, and populations that trials exclude. Systematic reviews of such studies follow the same steps as reviews of trials, but the central threat is different. A trial’s randomisation protects against confounding; in an observational study, confounding is the default. Chapter 5 and Section 7.2 introduced ROBINS-I, healthy-user, immortal-time and selection biases, and target trial emulation. This chapter is about what happens when such studies are combined.
Code
set.seed(42)
k  <- 8
lr <- rnorm(k, log(1.0) - 0.25, 0.08)        # truth RR = 1; shared bias of about -0.25 on the log scale
se <- runif(k, 0.06, 0.18)
pooled <- rma(lr, sei = se, method = "REML")
tibble::tibble(label = c(paste("Study", 1:k), "Pooled"), rr = exp(c(lr, pooled$b)),
               lo = exp(c(lr - 1.96 * se, pooled$ci.lb)), hi = exp(c(lr + 1.96 * se, pooled$ci.ub)),
               type = c(rep("Study", k), "Pooled")) |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(label))) |>
  ggplot(aes(rr, label, colour = type)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "#2E7D32", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, shape = type)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Study = "#041E42", Pooled = "#B22222"), guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Study = 16, Pooled = 18), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio (truth = 1)", y = NULL)








Figure 19.1: Eight simulated studies of an exposure with no effect, all sharing the same healthy-user bias (about 22% apparent protection). The pooled estimate is precise, consistent and wrong.
When every study shares the same bias, pooling narrows the interval around the wrong answer. The studies agree with each other, so I² is low (here 0%): low heterogeneity is not evidence of validity. Healthy-user bias, confounding by indication, sick-stopper bias and immortal time (Section 7.2) are typically shared by most studies of a question, and pooling adds problems of its own:
The practical rule is to assess each study with ROBINS-I (1), exclude results at critical risk of bias, and present results by risk of bias rather than as a single pooled estimate (2,3).

title: 19  Systematic Reviews of Observational Studies
text:
studies adjust for different confounders, so the “same” estimate means different things in different studies;
odds ratios, risk ratios and hazard ratios are mixed;
what none of the studies measured stays confounded, however many studies are pooled.



19.1.1 Mixing odds ratios and risk ratios
Suppose a treatment reduces risk by 30% (RR = 0.70) in every population. When the outcome is rare, the odds ratio is about the same; when it is common, the odds ratio is more extreme.


Code
tibble::tibble(p0 = seq(0.01, 0.5, 0.005)) |>
  mutate(p1 = 0.70 * p0, or = (p1 / (1 - p1)) / (p0 / (1 - p0))) |>
  ggplot(aes(p0, or)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.70, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_line(colour = "#B22222", linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.72, hjust = 1, label = "risk ratio = 0.70", colour = "#041E42") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.52, hjust = 1, label = "odds ratio", colour = "#B22222") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Baseline risk", y = "Effect")








Figure 19.2: The odds ratio corresponding to a constant risk ratio of 0.70, as baseline risk increases.





Pooling odds ratios from low- and high-risk populations creates spurious heterogeneity and an estimate that matches neither. When outcomes are common, convert odds ratios to risk ratios using each study’s baseline risk (Chapter 8).

title: 19  Systematic Reviews of Observational Studies
text:
19.2 The E-value
Adjusted estimates from observational studies remain open to unmeasured confounding. The E-value asks how strongly an unmeasured confounder would have to be associated with both the exposure and the outcome, on the risk-ratio scale and beyond the measured confounders, to explain away the observed association (4):
\[E = RR + \sqrt{RR \times (RR - 1)}, \qquad \text{using } 1/RR \text{ when } RR < 1 .\]
An E-value close to 1 means a weak confounder could explain the result; around 2, a confounder doubling both the exposure and the outcome would suffice; 4 or more requires a very strong confounder. Report it for the point estimate and for the confidence limit closest to the null.


Code
evalue_rr <- \(rr) { rr <- ifelse(rr < 1, 1 / rr, rr); rr + sqrt(rr * (rr - 1)) }
ev <- evalue_rr(0.78); ev_ci <- evalue_rr(0.85)          # an illustrative pooled HR 0.78 (0.72 to 0.85)
round(c(`E-value, estimate` = ev, `E-value, CI limit` = ev_ci), 2)


E-value, estimate E-value, CI limit 
             1.88              1.63 


The E-value is the symmetric solution of a more general bound. A confounder that is \(RR_{EU}\) times more common among the exposed and raises the outcome risk \(RR_{UD}\) times can bias a risk ratio by at most \(B = RR_{EU}RR_{UD}/(RR_{EU} + RR_{UD} - 1)\) (5). Setting \(B\) equal to the observed RR traces every combination just strong enough to explain the association away.


Code
rr_obs <- 1 / 0.78
tibble::tibble(rr_EU = seq(rr_obs + 0.01, 4, 0.005)) |>
  mutate(rr_UD = rr_obs * (rr_EU - 1) / (rr_EU - rr_obs)) |>
  filter(rr_UD <= 4) |>
  ggplot(aes(rr_EU, rr_UD)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = rr_UD, ymax = 4), fill = "#B22222", alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1565C0", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 1.5, xmax = 2, ymin = 1.5, ymax = 2, fill = NA, colour = "grey30", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("point", x = ev, y = ev, colour = "#B22222", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = ev, y = ev, hjust = -0.15, label = sprintf("E-value = %.2f", ev), colour = "#B22222") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.2, y = 3.4, label = "could explain\nthe association", colour = "#B22222") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1, 4), ylim = c(1, 4)) +
  labs(x = "Confounder-exposure association (RR)", y = "Confounder-outcome association (RR)")








Figure 19.3: Combinations of confounder-exposure and confounder-outcome associations strong enough to explain away an observed HR of 0.78 (on and above the curve). Red point: the E-value. Dashed box: a plausible range for healthy-user bias.





The E-value does not say that confounding is present; it says how strong it would have to be. Whether that is plausible requires subject knowledge. Here, people who take preventive drugs also exercise more, smoke less and see doctors more often, and a confounder of the strength in the dashed box would explain much of the association.

title: 19  Systematic Reviews of Observational Studies
section: 19.3 A worked example: statins in primary prevention
text:
19.3 A worked example: statins in primary prevention
For all-cause mortality, randomised trials of statins in primary prevention show about a 10% relative reduction, RR 0.89 (95% CI 0.85 to 0.93) (6). Systematic reviews of observational studies report more: HR 0.86 (0.79 to 0.93) in ten studies of adults aged 65 or more without cardiovascular disease, with the certainty rated very low (7), and HR 0.72 (0.68 to 0.76), with I² of 95%, in 54 propensity-matched studies of mixed populations (8). The usual suspects are healthy users, prevalent users (survivors of early treatment), immortal time, and patients who stop statins when they become frail.
What should a careful review of the observational evidence do? Ten simulated studies, built to resemble a typical review (none is real), illustrate.


Code
studies <- tibble::tribble(
  ~study, ~hr,  ~se,  ~robins,
  "A", 0.76, 0.07, "Moderate", "B", 0.94, 0.06, "Serious",  "C", 0.73, 0.08, "Serious",
  "D", 0.84, 0.07, "Critical", "E", 0.97, 0.08, "Moderate", "F", 0.79, 0.06, "Serious",
  "G", 0.69, 0.09, "Critical", "H", 0.87, 0.05, "Moderate", "I", 0.75, 0.07, "Serious",
  "J", 0.90, 0.06, "Serious") |>
  mutate(robins = factor(robins, levels = c("Moderate", "Serious", "Critical")), label = paste("Study", study))
res     <- rma(yi = log(hr), sei = se, data = studies, slab = label, method = "REML")
res_mod <- rma(yi = log(hr), sei = se, data = studies, subset = robins == "Moderate", method = "REML")
res_nc  <- rma(yi = log(hr), sei = se, data = studies, subset = robins != "Critical", method = "REML")




Code
rob_col <- c(Moderate = "#2E7D32", Serious = "#E07B00", Critical = "#B22222")
fp <- forest(res, atransf = exp, refline = 0, at = log(c(0.5, 0.7, 1, 1.4)), colout = rob_col[studies$robins],
             ilab = as.character(studies$robins), ylim = c(-3, res$k + 3), mlab = "All studies (REML)",
             header = c("Study (simulated)", "HR [95% CI]"), xlab = "Hazard ratio, all-cause mortality")
text(fp$ilab.xpos, res$k + 2, "ROBINS-I", font = 2, cex = fp$cex)
addpoly(res_mod, row = -2, atransf = exp, col = rob_col["Moderate"], mlab = "Moderate risk of bias only")








Figure 19.4: Ten simulated observational studies of statins and all-cause mortality, coloured by ROBINS-I rating, with pooled estimates for all studies and for moderate-risk studies only.







Code
studies$rob <- as.numeric(studies$robins)                       # 1 Moderate, 2 Serious, 3 Critical
mr <- rma(yi = log(hr), sei = se, mods = ~ rob, data = studies, method = "REML", test = "knha")
sub_hr <- sapply(levels(studies$robins), \(r)
  exp(coef(rma(yi = log(hr), sei = se, data = studies, subset = robins == r, method = "REML"))))


All ten studies give HR 0.82; excluding the critical-risk studies, as ROBINS-I guidance requires, 0.84; the moderate-risk studies alone, 0.86, closer to the trials. Pooled within each category, the HR is 0.86 (moderate), 0.82 (serious) and 0.77 (critical): the more biased the studies, the larger the apparent benefit, itself a signal of bias. A meta-regression on the ROBINS-I score gives a ratio of HRs of 0.95 (0.84 to 1.07) per category; with ten studies it can neither confirm nor exclude the gradient (Section 10.1).

19.3.1 Should the studies be pooled at all?



Table 19.1: A sequence of decisions before pooling observational studies (after (2) and (3)).










Question
If no
If yes




Are populations, exposures, comparators and outcomes similar enough to combine?
Narrative synthesis
Continue


Are any results at critical risk of bias (ROBINS-I)?
Continue
Exclude them from the synthesis


Are all remaining results at low or moderate risk?
Pool with caution; sensitivity analysis excluding serious risk
Pool as the primary analysis


Is the E-value large relative to plausible unmeasured confounders?
Confounding cannot be excluded; say so
Report the pooled estimate with its E-value


Does the result agree with randomised evidence, where it exists?
Prefer the trials; report and explain the discordance
Report the pooled estimate






For statins in primary prevention, the observational estimates are large, precise and “significant”; an unmeasured confounder of plausible strength could explain them; the effect shrinks in the better studies; certainty starts low and is rated down for risk of bias; and the trials show a smaller effect. This is not an argument against statins. It is an argument for using the right evidence for the decision.

title: 19  Systematic Reviews of Observational Studies
text:
19.4 Dose-response meta-analysis
Most observational studies report results for several categories of exposure, not just “exposed” versus “unexposed”. Collapsing them to a binary contrast throws information away, and different studies’ cut-offs give different answers even when the underlying dose-response curve is the same.


Code
f_true <- \(d) exp(-0.04 * d + 0.0012 * d^2)
thr <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
binary <- sapply(thr, \(t) mean(f_true(seq(t, 50, 5))))
ggplot(tibble::tibble(d = seq(0, 50, 0.5)), aes(d, f_true(d))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = "#041E42", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_segment(data = tibble::tibble(thr, binary), aes(x = thr, xend = 50, y = binary, yend = binary,
                                                       colour = factor(thr)), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = tibble::tibble(thr, binary), aes(x = 51, y = binary, colour = factor(thr),
            label = sprintf("exposed = >= %d g/day: RR %.2f", thr, binary)), hjust = 0, size = 3.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#B22222", "#E07B00", "#2E7D32", "#1565C0"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 85), breaks = seq(0, 50, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Dose (g/day)", y = "Risk ratio")








Figure 19.5: A hypothetical J-shaped dose-response curve (navy), and the ‘exposed vs unexposed’ risk ratio obtained when four studies define exposure with different cut-offs (coloured lines).





Dose-response meta-analysis uses every category of every study in two steps (9,10):

Within each study, fit a curve through the log RRs against dose. The RRs share one reference group, so they are correlated; the method of (11) reconstructs these correlations from the reported cases and totals, so that the shared reference is not counted several times.
Across studies, pool the study-specific curves with a (multivariate) random-effects meta-analysis.

The shape of the curve must be chosen: linear (one slope), quadratic (one symmetric bend), a restricted cubic spline (a smooth curve that bends where the data say and is linear beyond its outer knots), or a fully flexible Gaussian process. Pre-specify the main shape in the protocol.

19.4.1 Alcohol and cardiovascular disease

Two pairs of these “studies” (Malarcher and Vliegenthart) are wine and beer results from the same study, so the six analyses come from four independent studies. Entered separately, a shared reference group is counted twice, and the pooled interval is too narrow.


Code
knots <- quantile(alcohol_cvd$dose, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
rr20 <- function(d) {
  m <- dosresmeta(logrr ~ rcs(dose, knots), id = id, type = type, cases = cases, n = n, se = se,
                  data = d, method = "reml")
  p <- predict(m, newdata = data.frame(dose = c(0, 20)), xref = 0, expo = TRUE)[2, ]
  tibble::tibble(Studies = length(unique(d$id)), `RR at 20 g/day (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", p$pred, p$ci.lb, p$ci.ub))
}
bind_rows(`All six, as if independent` = rr20(alcohol_cvd),
          `One per study: wine` = rr20(subset(alcohol_cvd, !id %in% c(4, 6))),
          `One per study: beer` = rr20(subset(alcohol_cvd, !id %in% c(3, 5))), .id = "Data used") |>
  kable(align = "lcc")

Before pooling, check what the units of the meta-analysis are: one estimate per study, ideally for total alcohol, chosen by a pre-specified rule, with the alternatives as sensitivity analyses.


Code
fit_dr <- \(f) dosresmeta(f, id = id, type = type, cases = cases, n = n, se = se, data = alcohol_cvd, method = "reml")
m_lin  <- fit_dr(logrr ~ dose)
m_quad <- fit_dr(logrr ~ dose + I(dose^2))
m_rcs  <- fit_dr(logrr ~ rcs(dose, knots))
grid   <- data.frame(dose = seq(0, 75, 0.5))
curve_of <- function(m, label) {
  p <- predict(m, newdata = grid, xref = 0, expo = TRUE)
  tibble::tibble(dose = grid$dose, est = p$pred, lo = p$ci.lb, hi = p$ci.ub, model = label)
}
p_quad <- waldtest(Sigma = vcov(m_quad), b = coef(m_quad), Terms = 2)$chitest["P"]
p_rcs  <- waldtest(Sigma = vcov(m_rcs), b = coef(m_rcs), Terms = 2)$chitest["P"]


A Gaussian process (GP) places a prior directly on smooth curves, with no knots to choose. With normal likelihoods it can be computed in closed form: the curve \(g(d) = f(d) - f(0)\) has a squared-exponential covariance, the within-study covariances are the same Greenland-Longnecker matrices that dosresmeta uses, between-study heterogeneity enters as a random slope, and the hyperparameters are averaged over a grid weighted by prior times marginal likelihood.


Code
nr <- subset(alcohol_cvd, dose > 0); y <- nr$logrr; dd <- nr$dose
V  <- as.matrix(Matrix::bdiag(m_lin$Slist))                     # within-study (G-L) covariances
kfun <- \(a, b, s, l) s^2 * exp(-outer(a, b, "-")^2 / (2 * l^2))
kt   <- \(a, b, s, l) kfun(a, b, s, l) - kfun(a, 0, s, l) %*% t(rep(1, length(b))) -
                      rep(1, length(a)) %*% kfun(0, b, s, l) + s^2   # covariance of f(d) - f(0)
slope_cov <- outer(nr$id, nr$id, "==") * outer(dd, dd)          # random slope per study
hyp <- expand.grid(s = seq(0.05, 1.5, length.out = 30), l = seq(5, 80, length.out = 30),
                   tau = c(0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03))
logpost <- apply(hyp, 1, \(h) {
  S <- kt(dd, dd, h["s"], h["l"]) + V + h["tau"]^2 * slope_cov
  -0.5 * (as.numeric(determinant(S)$modulus) + sum(y * solve(S, y))) +
    dnorm(h["s"], 0, 0.5, log = TRUE) + dgamma(1 / h["l"], 3, 50, log = TRUE) - 2 * log(h["l"]) +
    dnorm(h["tau"], 0, 0.02, log = TRUE)
})
set.seed(2026)
gp_draws <- t(sapply(sample(nrow(hyp), 2000, replace = TRUE, prob = exp(logpost - max(logpost))), \(i) {
  h  <- unlist(hyp[i, ]); S <- kt(dd, dd, h["s"], h["l"]) + V + h["tau"]^2 * slope_cov
  Ks <- kt(grid$dose, dd, h["s"], h["l"])
  C  <- kt(grid$dose, grid$dose, h["s"], h["l"]) - Ks %*% solve(S, t(Ks))
  e  <- eigen((C + t(C)) / 2, symmetric = TRUE)
  as.numeric(Ks %*% solve(S, y) + e$vectors %*% (sqrt(pmax(e$values, 0)) * rnorm(nrow(grid))))
}))
gp_q <- apply(exp(gp_draws), 2, quantile, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))
gp_curve <- tibble::tibble(dose = grid$dose, est = gp_q[1, ], lo = gp_q[2, ], hi = gp_q[3, ], model = "Gaussian process")




Code
curves <- bind_rows(curve_of(m_lin, "Linear"), curve_of(m_quad, "Quadratic"),
                    curve_of(m_rcs, "Restricted cubic spline"), gp_curve) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("Linear", "Quadratic", "Restricted cubic spline", "Gaussian process")))
ggplot(curves, aes(dose)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = mutate(nr, rr = exp(logrr)), aes(dose, rr), colour = "grey60", size = 1.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#041E42", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(aes(y = est), colour = "#041E42", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.25, 4)) +
  labs(x = "Alcohol (g/day)", y = "RR vs non-drinkers (log scale)")








Figure 19.6: Alcohol and cardiovascular disease: four pooled dose-response curves (line and 95% interval). Grey points: study-specific RRs.





The linear model cannot bend, so it cannot show a J-curve. The quadratic and spline curves dip to a minimum around 18 g/day (RR about 0.72) and then rise; the Gaussian process, which is not forced into any shape, shows a shallower dip (minimum RR about 0.81) and no clear rise. All agree on modestly lower risk at 10 to 20 g/day; above about 30 g/day the data are sparse, and at 60 g/day the spline’s interval is 0.38 to 6.94. Tests of non-linearity give P = 0.12 (quadratic) and 0.06 (spline): suggestive, not conclusive. Conclusions about shape should not hinge on one functional form.


19.4.2 Is the J-curve real?
The wider evidence shows why a consistent, dose-dependent association can still be confounded. In 84 cohort studies, drinkers had a lower incidence of coronary heart disease than non-drinkers, RR 0.71 (0.66 to 0.77) (12). But “non-drinkers” include people who stopped because they were ill (“sick quitters”), and moderate drinkers differ from abstainers in income and health; after adjusting for abstainer bias and study quality, low-volume drinkers had no lower mortality than lifetime abstainers, RR 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) (13). Mendelian randomisation compares groups whose drinking differs because of genetic variants fixed at conception, so these biases cannot operate: carriers of a variant that reduces drinking had lower coronary risk, OR 0.90 (0.84 to 0.96) (14), and in 500,000 Chinese adults genetically predicted drinking increased the risk of stroke and showed no protection against myocardial infarction (15). The dose-response meta-analysis described the shape of the association correctly; it could not say whether the shape was causal.
GRADE allows observational evidence to be rated up for a large effect, a dose-response gradient, or when all plausible confounding would reduce the effect (Chapter 6). Each is a trap: large effects rarely survive honest adjustment (check the E-value); gradients can be confounded, as the alcohol J-curve shows; and confounding that would reduce an apparent benefit is rarely demonstrable. Upgrading needs evidence that the effect is not confounded, such as a Mendelian randomisation study, a natural experiment or a trial, not only a consistent, dose-dependent association.


19.4.3 A second example: coffee and mortality
The coffee_mort data hold 22 dose-response tables from cohort studies of coffee and all-cause mortality, the worked example of the dose-response chapter in (16), re-analysing (17). Some studies use 0.5 or 2 cups/day, not 0, as the reference. A linear model gives one slope per study (log RR per cup/day), which can be pooled like any effect size:


Code
data(coffee_mort)
cf_fit <- \(f, d = coffee_mort) dosresmeta(f, id = id, type = type, cases = cases, n = n, se = se, data = d, method = "reml")
cf_lin <- cf_fit(logrr ~ dose)
cf_slopes <- coffee_mort |> distinct(id, author, gender) |> arrange(id) |>
  mutate(bi = unname(cf_lin$bi[, 1]), vi = unlist(cf_lin$Si))      # Si holds variances
cf_re <- rma(yi = bi, vi = vi, data = cf_slopes, method = "REML", slab = paste0(author, " (", gender, ")"))
forest(cf_re, atransf = exp, at = log(c(0.6, 0.8, 1, 1.2)), addpred = TRUE, cex = 0.75,
       header = c("Study (sex)", "RR per cup/day [95% CI]"), xlab = "RR per additional cup/day")
cf_pr <- predict(cf_re, transf = exp)








Figure 19.7: Coffee and all-cause mortality: study-specific linear slopes (RR per additional cup/day) and the random-effects pooled slope with its 95% prediction interval.





The pooled slope, RR 0.97 (0.96 to 0.98) per cup/day with a prediction interval of 0.93 to 1.00, assumes every extra cup has the same effect, the first or the eighth. A spline lets the data decide:


Code
cf_knots <- quantile(coffee_mort$dose, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
cf_rcs   <- cf_fit(logrr ~ rcs(dose, cf_knots))
cf_kl    <- cf_fit(logrr ~ rcs(dose, cf_knots), subset(coffee_mort, id == 3))   # one study alone
cf_wald  <- \(m) waldtest(Sigma = vcov(m), b = coef(m), Terms = 2)$chitest
cf_grid  <- data.frame(dose = seq(0, 8, 0.1))
cf_curve <- \(m, label) { p <- predict(m, newdata = cf_grid, xref = 0, expo = TRUE)
  tibble::tibble(dose = cf_grid$dose, est = p$pred, lo = p$ci.lb, hi = p$ci.ub, model = label) }
cfc <- bind_rows(cf_curve(cf_lin, "Linear"), cf_curve(cf_rcs, "Restricted cubic spline"))
ggplot(cfc, aes(dose)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#041E42", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(aes(y = est), colour = "#041E42", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) + scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1, 1.1)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.6, 1.15)) + labs(x = "Coffee (cups/day)", y = "RR of death vs 0 cups/day")
cf_at <- \(m, d) with(filter(cfc, model == m, abs(dose - d) < 1e-8), sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", est, lo, hi))








Figure 19.8: Coffee and all-cause mortality: linear and restricted cubic spline dose-response curves (knots at the quartiles of dose).





The linear model keeps promising more benefit with every cup (RR 0.77 (0.71 to 0.83) at 8 cups/day). The spline shows risk falling up to 3 or 4 cups/day (0.83 (0.79 to 0.86)) and then flattening (0.84 (0.79 to 0.88) at 8). One study alone (Klatsky 1993) cannot see the shape (test of non-linearity P = 0.54, absence of evidence rather than evidence of a straight line); all 22 tables can (P < 0.0001).
Again, the curve describes an association. Heavy coffee drinkers smoke and drink more, which pushes the right-hand end of the curve up; people who become ill cut down, which makes the zero-cup reference look worse. A flat plateau could be a real effect or a spurious early benefit and residual harm partly cancelling. Genetically predicted coffee intake was not associated with mortality (18), although caffeine-metabolism genes make coffee a difficult instrument. And every curve is informative only where there are data: the top category is usually open-ended, so “no evidence of harm up to 8 cups” is not “no harm”.

title: 19  Systematic Reviews of Observational Studies
text:
Key points

Pooling studies that share a bias gives a precise wrong answer; low heterogeneity is not evidence of validity.
Assess each study with ROBINS-I, exclude critical-risk results, and present results by risk of bias; a larger effect in more biased studies is itself a signal of bias.
Odds ratios exaggerate risk ratios when outcomes are common; do not pool them indiscriminately.
The E-value states how strong unmeasured confounding would have to be to explain an association; judging its plausibility needs subject knowledge.
Compare observational results with randomised evidence where it exists, and prefer the trials when they disagree.
Dose-response meta-analysis uses every exposure category; its shape depends on the model, so use flexible models and check the units of analysis.
A dose-response gradient can be confounded; Mendelian randomisation, natural experiments or trials are needed before rating observational evidence up.

title: 19  Systematic Reviews of Observational Studies
text:
Exercises

Compute E-values for the statin example using all ten studies and the moderate-risk studies only. How do they compare with the plausible healthy-user range?
In statin-studies, make the critical-risk studies show smaller benefits than the moderate-risk studies. What would that pattern suggest?
Refit the alcohol spline with knots at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of dose. Does the nadir move?
Fit the quadratic model to the coffee data and compare its predictions at 8 cups/day with the spline.
Find a systematic review of observational studies in your field. Does it present results by risk of bias, report an E-value, and compare with trials?

title: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models
text:
20.1 The threshold problem
A review of an intervention asks whether a treatment works, and answers with one effect measure. A review of a diagnostic test asks how well the test separates people who have the target condition from those who do not. That needs two numbers, sensitivity and specificity, which are not independent: every test that produces a measurement must be turned into “positive” or “negative” at some threshold, and moving the threshold trades one for the other. This chapter develops the methods for diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) reviews, using high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) to rule out acute myocardial infarction (MI) as the running example, and then turns to reviews of prediction models, which raise related problems.
Code
set.seed(42)
trop_d  <- rlnorm(1000, 3.0, 0.6)          # MI
trop_nd <- rlnorm(1000, 1.8, 0.5)          # no MI
ops <- tibble::tibble(t = c(5, 14, 40)) |>
  mutate(sens = map_dbl(t, \(x) mean(trop_d >= x)), fpr = map_dbl(t, \(x) mean(trop_nd >= x)),
         lab = sprintf("%g ng/L\nsens %.2f, spec %.2f", t, sens, 1 - fpr))
roc <- tibble::tibble(t = sort(unique(c(0, trop_d, trop_nd, Inf)))) |>
  mutate(sens = map_dbl(t, \(x) mean(trop_d >= x)), fpr = map_dbl(t, \(x) mean(trop_nd >= x)))
p1 <- tibble::tibble(trop = c(trop_d, trop_nd), group = rep(c("MI", "No MI"), each = 1000)) |>
  ggplot(aes(trop, fill = group)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ops$t, linetype = c(2, 1, 3)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 120)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(MI = "#B22222", `No MI` = "#041E42"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Troponin (ng/L)", y = "Patients") + theme(legend.position = "top")
p2 <- ggplot(roc, aes(fpr, sens)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_path(colour = "#041E42", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = ops, colour = c("#2E7D32", "#E69F00", "#B22222"), size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = ops, aes(label = lab), hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1, size = 3, lineheight = 0.9) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "1 − specificity (false-positive rate)", y = "Sensitivity")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)








Figure 20.1: Simulated troponin concentrations in 1000 patients with MI and 1000 without (left), and the ROC curve traced by moving the threshold (right). Each marked point is one threshold.
A low threshold detects almost every MI but labels many patients without MI as positive; a high threshold does the reverse. Studies that use different thresholds report different pairs of sensitivity and specificity for the same test. A review that pools sensitivities and specificities separately averages operating points that no study used, and finds “heterogeneity” that is largely the threshold.

title: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models
section: 20.2 From the 2×2 table to clinical decisions
text:
20.2 From the 2×2 table to clinical decisions
Each study contributes a 2×2 table of test result against the reference standard: true positives (TP), false negatives (FN), false positives (FP) and true negatives (TN).



Table 20.1: Measures of diagnostic accuracy.










Measure
Formula
Meaning




Sensitivity
TP / (TP + FN)
Probability of a positive test in people with the condition; high sensitivity rules out


Specificity
TN / (TN + FP)
Probability of a negative test in people without it; high specificity rules in


Positive likelihood ratio, LR+
sens / (1 − spec)
Factor by which a positive test multiplies the odds of the condition


Negative likelihood ratio, LR−
(1 − sens) / spec
Factor by which a negative test multiplies the odds


Diagnostic odds ratio, DOR
(TP × TN) / (FP × FN) = LR+ / LR−
A single measure of discrimination


Positive and negative predictive values
TP / (TP + FP), TN / (TN + FN)
Depend on prevalence; not to be pooled across populations






Likelihood ratios link a test result to a patient. On the odds scale, Bayes’ theorem is a multiplication: post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR.


Code
post <- \(p, lr) { o <- p / (1 - p) * lr; o / (1 + o) }
lr_pos <- 0.98 / 0.25; lr_neg <- 0.02 / 0.75
tibble::tibble(`Pre-test probability` = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.40)) |>
  mutate(`After a positive test` = post(`Pre-test probability`, lr_pos),
         `After a negative test` = post(`Pre-test probability`, lr_neg),
         across(everything(), \(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x))) |>
  kable(align = "ccc")




Table 20.2: Post-test probabilities for a test with sensitivity 0.98 and specificity 0.75, at three pre-test probabilities.






Pre-test probability
After a positive test
After a negative test




5.0%
17.1%
0.1%


15.0%
40.9%
0.5%


40.0%
72.3%
1.7%








With LR− = 0.027, a negative test lowers a 15% pre-test probability to 0.5%, low enough for a rule-out strategy; with LR+ = 3.9, a positive test raises it only to 41%. A test can be excellent for ruling out and poor for ruling in. Predictive values change with prevalence, so a review should pool sensitivity and specificity (or likelihood ratios) and apply them to the prevalence of the target setting.

title: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models
text:
20.3 Risk of bias: QUADAS-2
QUADAS-2 assesses diagnostic accuracy studies in four domains, each with signalling questions and a judgement of low, high or unclear risk of bias; the first three also have a judgement of applicability to the review question (1). The domains are not added into a score.



Table 20.3: QUADAS-2 domains.









Domain
Risk-of-bias questions




1. Patient selection
Consecutive or random sample? Case-control design avoided? Inappropriate exclusions avoided?


2. Index test
Interpreted without knowledge of the reference standard? Threshold pre-specified?


3. Reference standard
Likely to classify the target condition correctly? Interpreted without knowledge of the index test?


4. Flow and timing
Appropriate interval between tests? Same reference standard for everyone? All patients analysed?






Two designs are especially misleading. A case-control (“two-gate”) design compares clearly diseased patients with healthy volunteers and exaggerates accuracy (Section 20.5). Partial or differential verification, in which not everyone receives the same reference standard, biases sensitivity and specificity in predictable directions:


Code
tp <- 135; fn <- 15; fp <- 170; tn <- 680; v <- 0.25
tibble::tibble(Verification = c("Full", "Partial: unverified patients excluded",
                                "Differential: unverified negatives assumed MI-free"),
               TP = tp, FN = c(fn, v * fn, v * fn), FP = fp, TN = c(tn, v * tn, tn + (1 - v) * fn)) |>
  mutate(Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN), Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = "lcccccc")

title: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models
text:
20.4 The bivariate model
Each study gives two correlated estimates. The bivariate random-effects model treats each study’s logit sensitivity and logit false-positive rate (FPR = 1 − specificity) as drawn from a bivariate normal distribution, with within-study binomial variation (3):
\[\begin{pmatrix} \text{logit sens}_i \\ \text{logit FPR}_i \end{pmatrix} \sim N\left(\begin{pmatrix} \mu_{sens} \\ \mu_{FPR} \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_{sens}^2 & \rho\,\sigma_{sens}\sigma_{FPR} \\ \rho\,\sigma_{sens}\sigma_{FPR} & \sigma_{FPR}^2 \end{pmatrix}\right).\]
Five parameters: two means (the summary operating point), two between-study SDs and a correlation. A positive correlation between logit sensitivity and logit FPR is the threshold effect: studies with a low threshold have high sensitivity and a high FPR.
To see what the model recovers, we simulate 14 studies of hs-cTn, each with 400 to 2500 emergency department patients and an MI prevalence of 8% to 20%, using thresholds of 3, 5, 7 or 9 ng/L. At 5 ng/L the true sensitivity is 0.97 and the true FPR 0.21; each 1 ng/L increase in threshold lowers logit sensitivity by 0.30 and logit FPR by 0.18; and studies differ randomly beyond that.


Code
set.seed(2026)
k <- 14
cut  <- sample(c(3, 5, 7, 9), k, replace = TRUE)
n    <- round(runif(k, 400, 2500)); prev <- runif(k, 0.08, 0.20)
u    <- MASS::mvrnorm(k, c(0, 0), matrix(c(0.30, 0.05, 0.05, 0.12), 2))
lsens <- qlogis(0.97) - 0.30 * (cut - 5) + u[, 1]
lfpr  <- qlogis(0.21) - 0.18 * (cut - 5) + u[, 2]
dis <- rbinom(k, n, prev)
TP <- rbinom(k, dis, plogis(lsens)); FN <- dis - TP
FP <- rbinom(k, n - dis, plogis(lfpr)); TN <- n - dis - FP
dta <- data.frame(study = paste0("S", 1:k), cut, TP, FN, FP, TN)
fit <- reitsma(dta)                                    # bivariate model, REML
sm  <- summary(fit)$coefficients
tibble::tibble(Parameter = c("Sensitivity", "Specificity", "SD logit sensitivity", "SD logit FPR", "Correlation ρ"),
               Estimate = c(sprintf("%.3f (%.3f to %.3f)", sm[3, 1], sm[3, 5], sm[3, 6]),
                            sprintf("%.3f (%.3f to %.3f)", 1 - sm[4, 1], 1 - sm[4, 6], 1 - sm[4, 5]),
                            sprintf("%.2f", sqrt(fit$Psi[1, 1])), sprintf("%.2f", sqrt(fit$Psi[2, 2])),
                            sprintf("%.2f", cov2cor(fit$Psi)[1, 2]))) |>
  kable(align = "lc")





Parameter
Estimate




Sensitivity
0.949 (0.918 to 0.969)


Specificity
0.822 (0.788 to 0.852)


SD logit sensitivity
0.83


SD logit FPR
0.40


Correlation ρ
0.57





The summary point averages studies that used thresholds from 3 to 9 ng/L, a threshold nobody uses. The positive correlation is the threshold effect; the between-study SDs include it.

20.4.1 The summary ROC curve


Code
mu  <- coef(fit)[1, ]; V <- vcov(fit); Psi <- fit$Psi
sw  <- \(m) m[2:1, 2:1]                                # order (FPR, sens)
conf <- as.data.frame(plogis(ellipse::ellipse(sw(V), centre = mu[2:1], level = 0.95)))
pred <- as.data.frame(plogis(ellipse::ellipse(sw(Psi + V), centre = mu[2:1], level = 0.95)))
names(conf) <- names(pred) <- c("fpr", "sens")
srocc <- as.data.frame(sroc(fit, fpr = seq(0.01, 0.6, length.out = 300))); names(srocc) <- c("fpr", "sens")
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = pred, aes(fpr, sens), fill = NA, colour = "#041E42", linetype = 2) +
  geom_polygon(data = conf, aes(fpr, sens), fill = "#041E42", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = srocc, aes(fpr, sens), colour = "#B22222", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = dta, aes(FP / (FP + TN), TP / (TP + FN), colour = factor(cut)), size = 2.5) +
  annotate("point", x = plogis(mu[2]), y = plogis(mu[1]), shape = 18, size = 5, colour = "#B22222") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#009E73", "#E69F00", "#B22222"), name = "Threshold (ng/L)") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.6), ylim = c(0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "1 − specificity", y = "Sensitivity")








Figure 20.2: The bivariate model for 14 simulated hs-cTn studies: study estimates (points, coloured by threshold), summary point (diamond), 95% confidence region (shaded), 95% prediction region (dashed) and summary ROC curve (red).





The summary ROC (SROC) curve shows the trade-off between sensitivity and FPR as the threshold changes; its area is 0.93. The confidence region shows how well the average operating point is known; the prediction region, which adds between-study variation, shows where a new study is likely to fall, and is much larger. Studies spread along the curve, ordered by their thresholds.


20.4.2 HSROC parameters
The hierarchical summary ROC (HSROC) model describes the same studies as points on one curve: each study has an accuracy (Λ, the log DOR in the middle of the curve), a threshold or positivity parameter (Θ), and the curve has a shape (β, which allows the DOR to change along the curve) (4). Without covariates, the bivariate and HSROC models are the same model in different parameterisations, and the HSROC parameters are functions of the bivariate ones (5):


Code
sA <- sqrt(Psi[1, 1]); sB <- sqrt(Psi[2, 2]); sAB <- -Psi[1, 2]   # A = sensitivity, B = specificity
muA <- mu[[1]]; muB <- -mu[[2]]; r <- sB / sA
hs <- c(beta = log(r), Lambda = sqrt(r) * muA + sqrt(1 / r) * muB,
        Theta = (sqrt(r) * muA - sqrt(1 / r) * muB) / 2,
        sd_accuracy = sqrt(2 * (sA * sB + sAB)), sd_threshold = sqrt((sA * sB - sAB) / 2))
round(hs, 2)


        beta       Lambda        Theta  sd_accuracy sd_threshold 
       -0.73         4.24        -0.08         0.54         0.51 


Λ = 4.24 corresponds to a DOR of about 69 in the middle of the curve. β = -0.73 is away from 0, so the DOR changes with the threshold, and the SD of accuracy is similar to the SD of threshold: not all of the heterogeneity is threshold variation.


20.4.3 What the summary means clinically


Code
s_sum <- plogis(mu[[1]]); f_sum <- plogis(mu[[2]])
lrn <- (1 - s_sum) / (1 - f_sum)


At the summary point, LR− = 0.062, and a negative test lowers a 15% pre-test probability to 1.1%. Safe discharge after a rule-out test usually requires a miss rate below about 1%, so the average operating point is not good enough on its own. But the average is the wrong question: the rule-out decision needs accuracy at the low threshold actually used, which the next section estimates.
In the real evidence, all studies used one rule. A collaborative meta-analysis of 11 cohorts and 9241 patients evaluated a single hs-cTnT below the limit of detection (5 ng/L) combined with a non-ischaemic ECG: 30.6% of patients were classified as low risk, 0.5% of them had an MI, and the pooled sensitivity was 98.7% (95% CI 96.6% to 99.5%) (6). With one threshold there is no threshold effect to model, which is why the simulation is used here to illustrate the bivariate model.

title: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models
text:
20.5 Heterogeneity in diagnostic accuracy
Three sources of heterogeneity are specific to diagnostic studies.

Threshold variation, already seen. Report the SROC curve, and accuracy at clinically relevant thresholds.
Spectrum. Sensitivity is higher in patients with severe or established disease than in patients with early or mild disease; specificity is higher in healthy volunteers than in symptomatic patients without the disease. A case-control study that enrols both extremes overestimates both. The same assay at the same threshold has different accuracy in a tertiary centre and in an emergency department.
Verification (Section 20.3).

Adding a covariate to the bivariate model gives a bivariate meta-regression. With the threshold as covariate:


Code
fit_cut <- reitsma(dta, formula = cbind(tsens, tfpr) ~ cut)
b <- coef(fit_cut)
tibble::tibble(`Threshold (ng/L)` = c(3, 5, 7, 9)) |>
  mutate(Sensitivity = plogis(b[1, 1] + b[2, 1] * `Threshold (ng/L)`),
         Specificity = 1 - plogis(b[1, 2] + b[2, 2] * `Threshold (ng/L)`)) |>
  kable(digits = 3, align = "ccc")





Threshold (ng/L)
Sensitivity
Specificity




3
0.978
0.764


5
0.962
0.806


7
0.934
0.843


9
0.889
0.874





The between-study SD of logit sensitivity falls from 0.83 to 0.54 once the threshold is in the model: much of the heterogeneity was the threshold. At 3 ng/L, sensitivity is about 0.978, which is what a rule-out decision needs. The usual cautions of meta-regression apply (Section 10.1). Comparing two tests is best done with studies that applied both tests to the same patients; comparisons across separate sets of studies are confounded by everything else that differs (7).

title: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models
text:
20.6 GRADE for diagnostic evidence
GRADE rates the certainty of accuracy estimates with the usual domains (risk of bias judged with QUADAS-2, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision and publication bias). Cross-sectional accuracy studies of consecutive patients with full verification start at high certainty for accuracy (8). Imprecision is judged against the decision: for rule-out, whether the lower limit of sensitivity still gives an acceptable miss rate.
Accuracy is only the first link of a chain. A test improves outcomes only if its result changes management and the change helps patients. That needs evidence on test-and-treat strategies. In the High-STEACS stepped-wedge cluster trial, ten Scottish hospitals introduced a high-sensitivity troponin I assay in random order (48,282 patients). The assay reclassified 1771 patients as having myocardial injury or infarction, but among them MI or cardiovascular death at one year was not reduced, 15% before and 12% after implementation, adjusted OR 1.10 (95% CI 0.75 to 1.61) (9). More accurate diagnosis does not automatically mean better outcomes; its main value may lie elsewhere, for example in faster safe discharge, which needs its own evaluation.
crumbs: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models

title: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models
text:
20.7 Reviews of prediction models
A prediction model estimates an individual’s probability of a diagnosis or a future outcome from several predictors, for example the 10-year risk of a cardiovascular event from age, sex, smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes. Reviews of prediction models face their own versions of the problems above.

CHARMS structures data extraction: data source, participants, outcome, predictors, sample size and events, missing data, model development, and performance measures (10).
PROBAST assesses risk of bias in four domains (participants, predictors, outcome, analysis); the analysis domain is the one most often at high risk, through too few events per predictor, no internal validation, or no assessment of calibration (11).
TRIPOD is a reporting guideline for primary studies, not a quality tool; reviews are reported with TRIPOD-SRMA (12).

Performance has two parts. Discrimination, usually the C-statistic (the probability that a randomly chosen person with the outcome has a higher predicted risk than one without), measures ranking. Calibration, measured by the observed-to-expected (O:E) ratio and the calibration slope, measures whether predicted risks are right. A model can discriminate well and still predict risks that are systematically too high, which is what matters for decisions based on absolute risk (13).
Apparent performance, measured in the data used to develop a model, is optimistic. Internal validation (bootstrapping or cross-validation) estimates the optimism; only external validation in new patients shows whether a model transports (14). A meta-analysis of performance should pool external validations of one model and never mix in apparent performance from development studies.

20.7.1 Pooling C-statistics
Nine hypothetical external validations of one cardiovascular risk model report C-statistics in hospital clinics, community practices and primary care. The C-statistic is a bounded probability, so it is pooled on the logit scale, with its standard error converted by the delta method, and with random effects, because performance depends on case-mix and setting (15).


Code
val <- tibble::tribble(~study, ~auc, ~se, ~setting,
  "Cohort A", 0.77, 0.02, "Hospital", "Cohort B", 0.70, 0.03, "Community", "Cohort C", 0.80, 0.02, "Hospital",
  "Cohort D", 0.70, 0.03, "Primary care", "Cohort E", 0.67, 0.03, "Community", "Cohort F", 0.75, 0.02, "Hospital",
  "Cohort G", 0.73, 0.03, "Community", "Cohort H", 0.68, 0.02, "Primary care", "Cohort I", 0.79, 0.02, "Hospital") |>
  mutate(yi = qlogis(auc), sei = se / (auc * (1 - auc)))      # logit C and delta-method SE
res <- rma(yi, sei = sei, data = val, method = "REML", test = "knha", slab = study)
pr  <- predict(res, transf = plogis)
set_col <- c(Hospital = "#041E42", Community = "#2E7D32", `Primary care` = "#B22222")
metafor::forest(res, transf = plogis, refline = NA, addpred = TRUE, at = seq(0.5, 0.9, 0.1),
                colout = set_col[val$setting], ilab = val$setting, ilab.lab = "Setting",
                header = c("Validation", "C [95% CI]"), mlab = "Random effects (REML, HKSJ)", xlab = "C-statistic")








Figure 20.3: Nine simulated external validations of one risk model: C-statistics pooled on the logit scale (REML, Hartung-Knapp), with the 95% prediction interval. Colour: setting.





The pooled C-statistic is 0.74 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.77), adequate on average, but the prediction interval, 0.62 to 0.83, shows that in a new setting the model may discriminate well or barely adequately. Validations in hospitals do better than those in community and primary care, consistent with more heterogeneous case-mix in hospital populations (in these simulated data). Calibration is not shown because, as is common, it was not reported consistently; it usually varies far more between settings than discrimination, and a model should be recalibrated locally before use.
With few validations, τ is poorly estimated, and a Bayesian random-effects model with a weakly informative prior on τ (for example half-Student-t with scale 0.5 on the logit C scale) gives more honest prediction intervals and direct probabilities such as P(C > 0.70 in a new setting) (15):


Code
library(brms)
fit_b <- brm(yi | se(sei) ~ 1 + (1 | study), data = val, seed = 629,
             prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2), class = Intercept), prior(student_t(3, 0, 0.5), class = sd)))
d <- as_draws_df(fit_b)
c_new <- plogis(d$b_Intercept + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, d$sd_study__Intercept))
quantile(c_new, c(0.025, 0.975)); mean(c_new > 0.70)

title: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models
text:
Key points

Sensitivity and specificity are paired and depend on the threshold; analyse them jointly with the bivariate (or equivalent HSROC) model.
Pool sensitivity and specificity, not predictive values; translate them with likelihood ratios to the pre-test probability of the target setting.
Assess studies with QUADAS-2; case-control designs and partial or differential verification bias accuracy.
Report the summary point with its confidence and prediction regions and the SROC curve, and accuracy at the threshold used in practice.
Threshold, spectrum and verification explain much diagnostic heterogeneity; bivariate meta-regression can quantify the threshold effect.
Accuracy does not guarantee better outcomes; recommendations need evidence about test-and-treat strategies.
For prediction models, pool external validations only, on the logit (C-statistic) or log (O:E) scale, with random effects and prediction intervals; calibration matters as much as discrimination.
crumbs: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models

title: 20  Diagnostic Accuracy and Prediction Models
text:
Exercises

Re-run dta-sim with all 14 studies at 5 ng/L. What happens to the correlation ρ and to the SROC curve?
Pool sensitivity and specificity separately with rma() on the logit scale and compare the result with reitsma().
Using the meta-regression, find the threshold at which the post-test probability after a negative test, at 15% pre-test probability, falls below 1%.
Add setting as a moderator to the C-statistic meta-analysis. How much of τ² does it explain?
Choose a published DTA review and check whether it reports a prediction region, accuracy at a specific threshold, and QUADAS-2 judgements by domain.

14. Steyerberg EW, Harrell FE. Prediction models need appropriate internal, internal-external, and external validation. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. 2016;69:245–7. 


15. Debray TPA, Damen JAAG, Riley RD, et al. A framework for meta-analysis of prediction model studies with binary and time-to-event outcomes. Statistical Methods in Medical Research. 2019;28(9):2768–86.
