title: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial
text:
21.1 Cochrane reviews
This chapter covers three evidence situations. In the first, many trials have been synthesised, often by Cochrane. In the second, trials keep arriving and the review must keep up. In the third, there is only one trial, and its result is surprising. The common thread is that every conclusion combines new data with what was already known, explicitly or not; the last part of the chapter shows how to do it explicitly.
Cochrane, founded in 1993 and named after Archie Cochrane, publishes systematic reviews in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews and maintains CENTRAL, the largest register of controlled trials (Chapter 2). A Cochrane review starts from a peer-reviewed, published protocol; searches extensively, including trial registries and unpublished sources; screens and extracts in duplicate; assesses risk of bias with RoB 2 or ROBINS-I and certainty with GRADE; accepts no commercial funding for individual reviews; and is meant to be updated. For 30 years reviews were produced by topic-based Cochrane Review Groups. UK government (NIHR) funding of those groups ended in March 2023, and Cochrane moved to a central editorial service.
Does the label help? Jørgensen and colleagues matched 24 Cochrane reviews with other meta-analyses of the same two drugs (1). The Cochrane reviews had higher methodological quality (median score 7 vs 3 on a 7-point scale). All seven industry-supported reviews that stated conclusions recommended the experimental drug without reservation, and none of the matched Cochrane reviews did; yet the pooled effect estimates were similar on average. The difference lay in how the same numbers were turned into conclusions.
The label is not a guarantee. Reviews go out of date: in a survival analysis of 100 reviews, the median time until new evidence changed, or should have changed, the conclusions was 5.5 years, and 7% were already out of date when published (2). And the appraisal tools of earlier chapters still apply, whoever wrote the review: AMSTAR 2 for the review (Section 7.2), and the search date and GRADE certainty for each outcome (3). Three well-known cases show different ways a careful review can still mislead.
crumbs: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial

title: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial
text:
Oseltamivir (Tamiflu): incomplete data. Early reviews relied on manufacturers’ summaries of mostly unpublished trials. Once full clinical study reports were obtained, the 2014 review found no clear reduction in hospital admission or complications (4) (Chapter 15). A sound method applied to incomplete data still misleads.
Masks: misread conclusions. The 2023 review of physical interventions against respiratory viruses (5) was widely reported as showing that “masks don’t work”. Cochrane’s Editor-in-Chief issued a statement calling that interpretation inaccurate: the review had found the effect of promoting mask wearing inconclusive. “No clear evidence of an effect” is not “evidence of no effect”.
Mammography: disputed judgements. The Cochrane review of screening judged several large trials inadequately randomised and concluded that benefits were smaller, and over-diagnosis larger, than generally believed (6). Screening experts disputed those risk-of-bias judgements. Inclusion and risk-of-bias decisions are judgements, and they can drive the conclusion.
crumbs: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial

title: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial
text:
21.2 Living systematic reviews
A living systematic review is continually updated: searches run regularly and new trials are added as they appear (7). Many were published during the COVID-19 pandemic, some updated monthly. They are worth their cost when the question is a priority, new trials are appearing, and those trials could change the conclusion.
Re-testing at p < 0.05 after each new trial is repeated significance testing, and the chance of a false “significant” result somewhere along the way is well above 5%. Even with a treatment that works, the conclusion can flip back and forth:


Code
set.seed(42)
true_or  <- 0.75; n_trials <- 12
trial_n  <- sample(80:400, n_trials)
trial_se <- sqrt(4 / trial_n)                       # approximate SE of a log OR
trial_y  <- rnorm(n_trials, log(true_or), 0.25)     # observed log ORs
cumulative <- map_dfr(1:n_trials, function(k) {
  m <- rma(trial_y[1:k], sei = trial_se[1:k], method = "EE")
  tibble::tibble(update = k, pooled = exp(coef(m)), lo = exp(m$ci.lb), hi = exp(m$ci.ub),
                 sig = m$ci.ub < 0)
})
ggplot(cumulative, aes(update, pooled, colour = sig)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = true_or, linetype = 3, colour = "#041E42") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 12, y = true_or - 0.04, label = "true OR = 0.75", hjust = 1, colour = "#041E42") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#de2d26", `TRUE` = clr_post),
                      labels = c("CI includes 1", "CI excludes 1"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  labs(x = "Update (trials included so far)", y = "Pooled OR (95% CI)") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 21.1: A simulated living review: 12 trials of a treatment with a true OR of 0.75, pooled (common effect) after each new trial. Whether the 95% CI excludes 1 changes from one update to the next.





Stopping at the first update whose interval excludes 1, or declaring “no effect” while it includes 1, would both be premature. There are two remedies. Trial sequential analysis, borrowed from interim monitoring of trials, uses stricter significance boundaries until enough information has accumulated. Bayesian updating treats today’s posterior as tomorrow’s prior and reports at each update the probability of a meaningful effect, which is a statement about the strength of evidence rather than about crossing a threshold. The rest of this chapter applies the same logic, prior plus new data gives posterior, to a single trial.

title: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial
section: 21.3 Only one trial: the DECAF example
text:
21.3 Only one trial: the DECAF example
Caffeine has long been regarded as proarrhythmic, and patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) are often told to avoid coffee. In the DECAF trial, 200 coffee drinkers with persistent AF or flutter who were having cardioversion were randomised to continue caffeinated coffee (about one cup a day) or to abstain from all caffeine for six months (8). The trial was open label. Recurrence of AF or flutter occurred in 47 of 100 patients who continued coffee and 64 of 100 who abstained: hazard ratio (HR) 0.61 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.89), p = 0.01. The result was widely reported as showing that coffee protects against AF.
It was surprising for three reasons. It contradicted clinical belief. The prior evidence suggested no large effect either way: a crossover trial in 100 ambulatory adults found no increase in atrial ectopy on caffeinated days (rate ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.20) (9), and a meta-analysis of observational studies found no association with incident AF (pooled RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.09) (10). And the trial was designed to detect the opposite: 80% power for a 41% relative reduction in recurrence with abstinence, from 50% to 29.5%. The paper does not state which arm was expected to do better, but the power calculation, the population (coffee drinkers randomised to abstinence) and the clinical tradition all point to abstinence. An undeclared direction is one of the researcher degrees of freedom that let a result be interpreted after the data are seen (11).
How should a single surprising trial change what we believe? A meta-analysis combines several sources of evidence weighted by their precision. With one trial, the other source is external evidence, written as a prior distribution. We take three approaches: a frequentist critique of the design, a prior based on the trial’s own design, and an empirical prior based on thousands of trials.


Code
HR <- 0.61; CI_lo <- 0.42; CI_hi <- 0.89
y_obs <- log(HR)                                        # observed log HR, coffee vs abstinence
se    <- (log(CI_hi) - log(CI_lo)) / (2 * qnorm(0.975))  # its standard error
z_obs <- y_obs / se
round(c(log_HR = y_obs, se = se, se_from_events = sqrt(1 / 47 + 1 / 64), z = z_obs), 3)


        log_HR             se se_from_events              z 
        -0.494          0.192          0.192         -2.580 


The standard error from the confidence interval agrees with the approximation \(\text{Var}(\log HR) \approx 1/E_1 + 1/E_2\) from the 47 and 64 events. With equal arms, \(s^2 \approx 4/E\), so the precision of a trial is set by its number of events, here about 109.
crumbs: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial

title: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial
section: 21.4 Frequentist design critique: Type S and Type M errors
text:
21.4 Frequentist design critique: Type S and Type M errors
Suppose the truth is a realistic, still worthwhile 15% relative reduction (50% to 42.5%, a risk difference of 7.5 percentage points) and we run many DECAF-sized trials.


Code
set.seed(629)
p0 <- 0.50; p1 <- 0.425; n <- 100
sims <- tibble::tibble(e0 = rbinom(1e4, n, p0), e1 = rbinom(1e4, n, p1)) |>
  mutate(rd  = (e1 - e0) / n,
         se  = sqrt(e1 / n * (1 - e1 / n) / n + e0 / n * (1 - e0 / n) / n),
         sig = abs(rd / se) > 1.96)
ggplot(sims, aes(rd, fill = sig)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01, colour = "white", boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = p1 - p0, linewidth = 1, colour = clr_post) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -0.17, linetype = 2, colour = clr_lik, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = clr_sig),
                    labels = c("p > 0.05", "p < 0.05"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Observed risk difference", y = "Simulated trials") + theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 21.2: Risk differences in 10,000 simulated trials with 100 patients per arm and a true difference of −7.5 percentage points (green line). Trials reaching p < 0.05 are in purple; DECAF’s observed difference is the dashed line.





With 100 patients per arm, the standard error of a risk difference is about 0.07, so the true effect is only about 1.1 standard errors from zero. A trial reaches significance only when chance adds almost another standard error in the right direction, which happens in 20% of trials: that is the power. The significant trials are, by construction, those in which chance exaggerated the effect; their average absolute difference is 17.3 percentage points, about 2.3 times the truth. This is the winner’s curse (12).
Gelman and Carlin named the two errors that follow from low power (13). Among results that reach significance, a Type S (sign) error is an estimate in the wrong direction, and a Type M (magnitude) error, or exaggeration ratio, is the expected ratio of the estimate to the true effect. Both depend only on the ratio of the true effect to the standard error, and they can be calculated without simulation:


Code
retrodesign <- function(A, s, alpha = 0.05, n.sims = 1e5) {
  z     <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)
  p.hi  <- 1 - pnorm(z - A / s)              # significant, correct sign
  p.lo  <- pnorm(-z - A / s)                 # significant, wrong sign
  power <- p.hi + p.lo
  est   <- A + s * rnorm(n.sims)             # replicate estimates
  sig   <- abs(est) > s * z
  c(power = power, type_s = p.lo / power, type_m = mean(abs(est[sig])) / A)
}
s_design <- sqrt(0.5 * 0.5 / 100 + 0.425 * 0.575 / 100)
set.seed(1)
retro <- rbind(`Design: RD 20.5%`    = retrodesign(0.205, s_design),
               `Realistic: RD 7.5%`  = retrodesign(0.075, s_design))
round(retro, 2)


                   power type_s type_m
Design: RD 20.5%    0.83   0.00   1.11
Realistic: RD 7.5%  0.19   0.01   2.35


DECAF had 80% power only for an absolute reduction of 20.5 percentage points, larger than almost any cardiovascular intervention achieves. For a realistic 7.5-point difference its power was about 19%, and a significant result would on average overstate the effect 2.3-fold. DECAF’s observed difference of 17 points is therefore quite compatible with a true effect less than half that size.

title: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial
section: 21.5 Combining the trial with a prior
text:
21.5 Combining the trial with a prior

21.5.1 Normal prior and normal likelihood: a two-study meta-analysis
With the trial summarised as \(\hat\theta \sim N(\theta, s^2)\) on the log-HR scale and a prior \(\theta \sim N(m_0, s_0^2)\), the posterior is normal with
\[\frac{1}{s_1^2} = \frac{1}{s_0^2} + \frac{1}{s^2}, \qquad m_1 = s_1^2\left(\frac{m_0}{s_0^2} + \frac{\hat\theta}{s^2}\right),\]
a precision-weighted average: exactly a common-effect meta-analysis with the prior as a second “study” (Chapter 13).
What prior? The investigators’ own design assumptions are a ready-made, pre-specified choice. They assumed 50% recurrence with coffee and 29.5% with abstinence. On the log odds ratio scale, coffee versus abstinence, that is \(\log\{(0.5/0.5)/(0.295/0.705)\} = 0.871\): centred on harm from coffee. The SD is a judgement. With \(s_0 = 0.5\), the prior’s 95% range for the ratio is 0.90 to 6.37, the prior probability that coffee is beneficial is 4.1%, and, inverting \(s^2 \approx 4/E\), the prior carries the information of a trial with about 16 events (14).


Code
m0 <- 0.871; s0 <- 0.5
w0 <- 1 / s0^2; w <- 1 / se^2
m1 <- (w0 * m0 + w * y_obs) / (w0 + w); s1 <- sqrt(1 / (w0 + w))
ma <- rma(yi = c(m0, y_obs), sei = c(s0, se), method = "EE")     # the same, as a meta-analysis
rbind(closed_form = exp(c(m1, m1 - 1.96 * s1, m1 + 1.96 * s1)),
      rma         = exp(c(ma$b, ma$ci.lb, ma$ci.ub))) |> round(2) |> `colnames<-`(c("HR", "lower", "upper"))


              HR lower upper
closed_form 0.73  0.51  1.03
rma         0.73  0.51  1.03


Code
setNames(round(pnorm(log(c(1, 0.9, 0.8)), m1, s1), 2), c("P(HR<1)", "P(HR<0.9)", "P(HR<0.8)"))


  P(HR<1) P(HR<0.9) P(HR<0.8) 
     0.96      0.88      0.70 




Code
th <- seq(-1.3, 2.4, length.out = 800)
dd <- bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(th, d = dnorm(th, m0, s0),    what = "Prior (design: abstinence better)"),
  tibble::tibble(th, d = dnorm(th, y_obs, se), what = "Likelihood (DECAF)"),
  tibble::tibble(th, d = dnorm(th, m1, s1),    what = "Posterior")) |>
  mutate(what = factor(what, levels = unique(what)))
ggplot(dd, aes(th, d, colour = what)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(dd, what == "Posterior", th < log(0.9)), aes(th, d),
            fill = clr_post, alpha = 0.25, colour = NA, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(clr_prior, clr_lik, clr_post), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = log(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2.5, 5, 10)),
                     labels = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2.5, 5, 10)) +
  labs(x = "HR, coffee vs abstinence (log scale)", y = "Density") + theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 21.3: Design prior (centred on harm from coffee), DECAF likelihood, and posterior for the HR of coffee versus abstinence. Shaded: P(HR < 0.9).





The trial is about 7 times as precise as the prior, so the posterior, HR 0.73 (95% CrI 0.51 to 1.03), lies close to the data. Benefit remains probable, P(HR < 1) = 0.96, but the evidence is more modest than p = 0.01 suggests.


21.5.2 The absolute scale
Patients and clinicians think in absolute risks. A binomial model for the two arms puts a prior on the logit risk with coffee, \(a \sim N(0, 1.5^2)\) (centred on the design’s 50%, with a 95% range of 5% to 95%), and the same design prior on the log odds ratio for abstinence versus coffee, \(b \sim N(-0.871, 0.5^2)\). The risk difference, coffee minus abstinence, is \(\text{plogis}(a) - \text{plogis}(a + b)\). With two parameters there is no closed form, so the model is fitted with brms:


Code
library(brms)
decaf <- tibble::tibble(abst = c(0, 1), events = c(47, 64), n = c(100, 100))
pri_rd <- c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = b, coef = Intercept),
            prior(normal(-0.871, 0.5), class = b, coef = abst))
fit_rd <- brm(events | trials(n) ~ 0 + Intercept + abst, data = decaf, family = binomial,
              prior = pri_rd, chains = 4, iter = 6000, warmup = 1000, seed = 2026)
draws <- as_draws_df(fit_rd)[, c("b_Intercept", "b_abst")]


The 20,000 posterior draws from that fit are stored with the book:


Code
draws <- read.csv("data/ch21/decaf_rd_draws.csv")
rd <- plogis(draws$b_Intercept) - plogis(draws$b_Intercept + draws$b_abst)
round(100 * c(mean = mean(rd), quantile(rd, c(0.025, 0.975))), 1)


 mean  2.5% 97.5% 
 -7.7 -19.2   4.1 


Code
round(c(`P(RD < 0)` = mean(rd < 0), `P(RD < -2%)` = mean(rd < -0.02)), 2)


  P(RD < 0) P(RD < -2%) 
       0.90        0.83 


The trial alone gives a risk difference of −17 percentage points (95% CI −31 to −3). With the design prior it is -7.7 points (95% CrI -19.2 to +4.1). The probability of any benefit from coffee is 0.90; of a benefit of at least 2 points (a number needed to treat of 50 or fewer), 0.83. As a frequentist cross-check, dividing −17 by the Type M ratio for a realistic effect gives about -7.2 points, similar to the Bayesian estimate. Both rest on an assumption about plausible effect sizes: the Type M correction states it as a true effect, the Bayesian analysis as a prior.


21.5.3 How much does the prior matter?


Code
post_norm <- function(m0, s0) {
  w0 <- 1 / s0^2; m <- (w0 * m0 + w * y_obs) / (w0 + w); s <- sqrt(1 / (w0 + w))
  tibble::tibble(post_hr = exp(m), post_lo = exp(m - 1.96 * s), post_hi = exp(m + 1.96 * s),
                 p1 = pnorm(0, m, s), p08 = pnorm(log(0.8), m, s))
}
hr_design <- log(1 - 0.295) / log(1 - 0.50)        # abstinence vs coffee, proportional hazards
sens <- tibble::tibble(
  Prior = c("1. Vague: N(0, 10²)", "2. Sceptical: N(0, 0.5²)",
            sprintf("3. Design as an HR: N(%.3f, 0.5²)", log(1 / hr_design)),
            "4. Design as an OR: N(0.871, 0.5²)", "5. Design, held firmly: N(0.871, 0.25²)"),
  m0 = c(0, 0, log(1 / hr_design), 0.871, 0.871), s0 = c(10, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.25)) |>
  mutate(prior_p1 = pnorm(0, m0, s0), post = map2(m0, s0, post_norm)) |> unnest(post)
sens |>
  transmute(Prior, `Prior P(HR < 1)` = sprintf("%.2f", prior_p1),
            `Posterior HR (95% CrI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", post_hr, post_lo, post_hi),
            `P(HR < 1)` = sprintf("%.2f", p1), `P(HR < 0.8)` = sprintf("%.2f", p08)) |>
  kable(align = "lcccc")

A vague prior recovers the trial. A sceptical prior centred on no effect pulls the estimate to 0.65. The two versions of the design prior, which give coffee little prior chance of benefit, leave a posterior that still favours coffee; only a firmly held design prior removes the benefit (P(HR < 1) = 0.47). The probability of a large benefit, P(HR < 0.8), is the quantity most sensitive to the prior, ranging from 0.92 to 0.06. A single trial should be reported with its posterior under a range of defensible priors.

title: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial
section: 21.6 An empirical Bayes prior from Cochrane trials
text:
21.6 An empirical Bayes prior from Cochrane trials
A trial-specific prior needs subject-matter judgement. An alternative asks what effects trials usually find. To compare trials of different outcomes and sizes, work on the signal-to-noise ratio scale: SNR = θ/s, and the observed \(z = \hat\theta / s \sim N(\text{SNR}, 1)\). For DECAF, z = -2.58.
Van Zwet and colleagues fitted the z-values of 23,551 RCTs from the Cochrane Database as a mixture of four normal distributions centred at 0 (15). Since each observed z is the true SNR plus noise with SD 1, the SD of the true SNRs in each component is \(\sqrt{\text{SD}_z^2 - 1}\). Most trials have small true effects; a few have large ones. One consequence is that the median power of a Cochrane trial against its own true effect is only about 13%, far below the 80% to 90% assumed at the design stage (16).
The posterior for DECAF’s SNR reweights each mixture component by how well it predicts the observed z, and then shrinks z within each component by \(B_k = s_k^2/(s_k^2 + 1)\), the normal-normal shrinkage of Section 21.5.1.


Code
sd_z  <- c(1.17, 1.74, 2.38, 5.73); p_mix <- c(0.32, 0.31, 0.30, 0.07)
sd_snr <- sqrt(sd_z^2 - 1)                         # remove the unit noise
post_w <- p_mix * dnorm(z_obs, 0, sd_z); post_w <- post_w / sum(post_w)
Bk <- sd_snr^2 / (sd_snr^2 + 1)
set.seed(2026); N <- 2e5
comp   <- sample.int(4, N, TRUE, post_w)
snr_EB <- rnorm(N, Bk[comp] * z_obs, sqrt(Bk[comp]))
hr_EB  <- exp(snr_EB * se)                         # back to the HR scale
rbind(prior_weight = p_mix, sd_true_snr = sd_snr, posterior_weight = post_w, shrinkage_B = Bk) |>
  round(2) |> `colnames<-`(paste0("k=", 1:4))


                  k=1  k=2  k=3  k=4
prior_weight     0.32 0.31 0.30 0.07
sd_true_snr      0.61 1.42 2.16 5.64
posterior_weight 0.15 0.36 0.43 0.07
shrinkage_B      0.27 0.67 0.82 0.97


Code
round(c(HR = median(hr_EB), quantile(hr_EB, c(0.025, 0.975)),
        `P(HR<1)` = mean(hr_EB < 1), `P(HR<0.8)` = mean(hr_EB < 0.8)), 2)


       HR      2.5%     97.5%   P(HR<1) P(HR<0.8) 
     0.71      0.49      1.00      0.98      0.72 


The observed z of -2.58 is shrunk to -1.79, which corresponds to p ≈ 0.07. The HR becomes 0.71 (95% CrI 0.49 to 1.00): benefit is still probable, P(HR < 1) = 0.98, but a large benefit is far from certain. This prior says nothing about coffee. Its posterior has a frequency interpretation: among trials like DECAF that observed this z, this is how their true effects are distributed. It assumes that DECAF is exchangeable with a typical Cochrane trial.
The same machinery gives Type S, Type M and the chance that a same-size replication would be significant in the same direction, under each prior:


Code
normal_post_snr <- function(mu0, tau) {
  B <- tau^2 / (tau^2 + 1); rnorm(N, B * z_obs + (1 - B) * mu0, sqrt(B))
}
set.seed(2026)
snr <- list(`Empirical Bayes (Cochrane)` = snr_EB,
            `Vague N(0, 10²)`            = normal_post_snr(0, 10),
            `Sceptical N(0, 1²)`         = normal_post_snr(0, 1),
            `Design prior`               = normal_post_snr(0.871 / se, 0.5 / se))
imap_dfr(snr, function(s, nm) {
  z2 <- s + rnorm(length(s))
  tibble::tibble(`Prior on SNR` = nm,
                 `Posterior HR (95% CrI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", median(exp(s * se)),
                                                    quantile(exp(s * se), .025), quantile(exp(s * se), .975)),
                 `Type S` = round(mean(sign(s) != sign(z_obs)), 3),
                 `Type M` = round(median(abs(z_obs / s)), 2),
                 Replication = round(mean(z2 < -1.96), 2))
}) |> kable(align = "lcccc")

title: 21  Cochrane Reviews, Living Reviews and the Single Trial
text:
Key points

The Cochrane label signals a rigorous process, not a correct conclusion; check the search date, the completeness of the data and the GRADE certainty.
Similar effect estimates can be turned into very different conclusions.
Living reviews need methods for repeated looks; Bayesian updating, which reports the strength of evidence at each update, is a natural one.
A single trial is still a meta-analysis problem: the trial plus a prior.
With low power, significant results are exaggerated (Type M); retrospective design analysis quantifies by how much.
Report probabilities of clinically meaningful effects, on the absolute scale, under several defensible priors.
An empirical Bayes prior from many trials calibrates a surprising result without subject-matter judgement, assuming the trial is typical.

title: 22  Health Technology Assessment and Decision-Making
text:
22.1 Why HTA?
A systematic review answers the question “what is the effect of treatment X on outcome Y?”. A health technology assessment answers a different one: “should treatment X be funded for population Z at price P, compared with everything else we could do with the money?”. Bridging the two needs structured deliberation, comparisons against every relevant alternative, economic modelling, and a way to judge whether the current evidence is good enough to decide. The running example in this chapter is dapagliflozin for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), appraised by England’s National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in 2021.
Technology assessment began in the 1960s and 1970s with the recognition that technologies have social, economic and ethical consequences as well as technical ones; the US Congress created an Office of Technology Assessment in 1972. In 1978, at McGill, McGregor and Pelletier argued in the New England Journal of Medicine that costly new services for common diseases, such as coronary bypass surgery, must be evaluated for cost and outcome before they spread, and asked not only who should be treated but where, and at what volume (1). Their cost model is simple enough to reproduce: with 1976 Montreal costs, each surgical unit carried fixed costs of $18,993 a year, duplicated for every block of 400 operations, plus $733 of variable cost per operation.
Code
ops <- 5:1000
cost_per_op <- 18993 * ceiling(ops / 400) / ops + 733
ggplot(tibble::tibble(ops, cost_per_op), aes(ops, cost_per_op)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = navy) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(50, 200), linetype = 2, colour = red) +
  annotate("text", x = c(55, 205), y = 3800, hjust = 0, size = 3.3, colour = red,
           label = c("~50: cost levels off", "~200: suggested\nfor good outcomes")) +
  labs(x = "Operations per year", y = "Extra cost per operation ($)")








Figure 22.1: Extra cost per coronary bypass operation by annual volume, reproducing the cost model of McGregor and Pelletier (1978; 1976 Canadian dollars, physicians’ fees excluded).
Below about 50 operations a year the cost per operation is very high; above about 100 there is little further saving; and the outcome evidence suggested at least 200 a year. National HTA agencies followed: Sweden’s SBU in 1987, Québec’s CETS in 1988 (now INESSS), Canada’s CCOHTA in 1989 (now Canada’s Drug Agency, CDA-AMC) and NICE in 1999. McGregor also founded the first hospital-based HTA unit, at the McGill University Health Centre, a model later required for all Québec university health centres.
HTA exists because evidence is often incomplete when decisions must be made, spending correlates poorly with outcomes across and within countries, proven interventions are under-used while costs keep rising, and health care competes for money with other determinants of health. Guidelines ask whether a treatment works; HTA adds the questions guidelines usually leave out. Compared with what, which means all relevant alternatives? At what cost and opportunity cost? How certain are we, and is more certainty worth buying? For whom, and with what effect on equity?
An HTA proceeds through scoping (a PICO with several comparators and utility-weighted outcomes), a clinical systematic review, a network meta-analysis, an economic model, deliberation by a committee, and conditions such as price agreements or coverage with evidence development. A flawed review at the second step propagates through every later step: the model converts biased inputs into a precise-looking, biased ratio.

text:
22.2 The Evidence-to-Decision framework
The GRADE Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) frameworks, developed in the DECIDE project, make explicit the judgements a panel otherwise makes implicitly (2). The framework for population-level decisions, such as coverage, has 12 criteria (3).



Table 22.2: The 12 criteria of the GRADE EtD framework for population-level decisions.










Criterion
Question
Main source of evidence




1. Priority of the problem
Is the problem a priority?
Burden-of-disease data


2. Desirable effects
How large are the expected benefits?
Systematic review, with baseline risk


3. Undesirable effects
How large are the expected harms?
Systematic review, observational safety data


4. Certainty of evidence
What is the overall certainty?
GRADE assessment of the review


5. Values
Is there uncertainty or variability in how people value the outcomes?
Preference and utility studies


6. Balance of effects
Does the balance favour the intervention?
Judgement integrating 2 to 5


7. Resources required
How large are the costs?
Costing and budget-impact studies


8. Certainty of resource evidence
How certain are the costs?
Quality of cost data


9. Cost-effectiveness
Does cost-effectiveness favour the intervention?
Economic model


10. Equity
What is the effect on health equity?
Subgroup and access data


11. Acceptability
Is it acceptable to stakeholders?
Consultation


12. Feasibility
Is it feasible to implement?
Implementation studies






A systematic review informs criteria 2 to 4 directly; the rest need economic, preference and contextual evidence that a standard review does not collect. Certainty of evidence (Chapter 6) is one criterion of twelve.
Decisions need absolute effects, because the same relative effect means very different things in different populations:

title: 22  Health Technology Assessment and Decision-Making
text:
22.3 Network meta-analysis: alternatives and combinations
An HTA rarely asks whether drug A beats placebo; it asks whether A is worth funding given current care and the other options, and head-to-head trials rarely exist. Network meta-analysis (Chapter 17) supplies the missing comparisons, valid only under transitivity, which includes similar background therapy.
In its appraisal of dapagliflozin for HFrEF, NICE needed a comparison with sacubitril/valsartan, for which no trial existed. The evidence was a star-shaped network of four trials, each comparing a new drug with the control arm of its own era (4–7). With a star network there is no closed loop, so consistency cannot be checked: transitivity is a pure assumption, the usual situation in HTA submissions. The Bucher adjusted indirect comparison (8) takes the difference of two log hazard ratios against the common comparator and adds their variances. In metafor, each drug’s log HR is one coefficient of a meta-regression without intercept, and contrasts give the indirect comparisons:


Code
trials <- tibble::tribble(
  ~trial,            ~treat,          ~hr,  ~lo,  ~hi,
  "EMPHASIS-HF",     "Eplerenone",    0.63, 0.54, 0.74,
  "PARADIGM-HF",     "Sac/val",       0.80, 0.73, 0.87,
  "DAPA-HF",         "Dapagliflozin", 0.74, 0.65, 0.85,
  "EMPEROR-Reduced", "Empagliflozin", 0.75, 0.65, 0.86) |>
  mutate(loghr = log(hr), se = (log(hi) - log(lo)) / (2 * qnorm(0.975)))
nma <- rma(yi = loghr, sei = se, mods = ~ 0 + treat, data = trials, method = "EE")
names(coef(nma))                                    # Dapa, Empa, Eplerenone, Sac/val


[1] "treatDapagliflozin" "treatEmpagliflozin" "treatEplerenone"   
[4] "treatSac/val"      


Code
bd <- predict(nma, newmods = c(1, 0, 0, -1), transf = exp)      # dapagliflozin vs sac/val
round(c(HR = bd$pred, lower = bd$ci.lb, upper = bd$ci.ub), 2)


   HR lower upper 
 0.92  0.79  1.09 


The indirect HR for dapagliflozin versus sacubitril/valsartan is 0.92 (95% CI 0.79 to 1.09). NICE’s committee preferred this Bucher comparison to a matching-adjusted indirect comparison and concluded that dapagliflozin may be more effective, but that the result was uncertain, with a range that included no benefit (9). Randomisation is preserved within each trial, but the comparison between trials is only as good as their similarity, and here the control arms differed: EMPHASIS-HF patients received no mineralocorticoid antagonist, PARADIGM-HF’s control was the ACE inhibitor enalapril, and DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced added a drug to whatever patients were taking.
The more important point is that the question is rarely “A or B?”. With A as current care, B as dapagliflozin and C as sacubitril/valsartan, three different decisions are possible:

A + B versus A: add dapagliflozin to current therapy. DAPA-HF answers this directly, and NICE recommended dapagliflozin only as an add-on to optimised standard care.
B versus C: for a patient still symptomatic on an ACE inhibitor, switch to sacubitril/valsartan or add dapagliflozin. This is the Bucher comparison above.
A + B + C versus A: the value of the full regimen. Vaduganathan and colleagues estimated it by multiplying trial hazard ratios (10).



Code
combo_l  <- log(0.80) + log(0.63) + log(0.75)
combo_se <- sqrt(trials$se[2]^2 + trials$se[1]^2 + ((log(0.85) - log(0.65)) / 3.92)^2)
bind_rows(mutate(trials, type = "Each drug vs its own control"),
          tibble::tibble(treat = "ARNI + MRA + SGLT2i vs ACEi", hr = exp(combo_l),
                         lo = exp(combo_l - 1.96 * combo_se), hi = exp(combo_l + 1.96 * combo_se),
                         type = "Combination")) |>
  mutate(treat = forcats::fct_rev(forcats::fct_inorder(treat))) |>
  ggplot(aes(hr, treat, colour = type)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Combination = red, `Each drug vs its own control` = navy), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio (log scale)", y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 22.2: Each drug against its own trial’s control (navy), and the combination of sacubitril/valsartan, a mineralocorticoid antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor estimated by multiplying hazard ratios (red). Outcome: cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation.





A ranking of the four single-drug estimates (Chapter 18) would call eplerenone “best” and invite the reader to choose one drug. But the classes act on different pathways and are prescribed together; guidelines now recommend all four. Ranking add-on therapies as if they were mutually exclusive answers a question nobody is asking. The combination estimate, HR 0.38 (0.30 to 0.47), rests on strong assumptions of its own: that effects multiply (no interaction on the log scale), do not depend on background therapy, and transfer across eras; no trial randomised the full regimen. Component network meta-analysis models additive components explicitly (11).

title: 22  Health Technology Assessment and Decision-Making
text:
22.4 Economic evaluation
Economic evaluation compares the costs and consequences of alternatives. Its aim is not to save money but to get the most health from finite resources: every dollar spent on one programme is a dollar, and the health it could buy, not spent on another (12).



Table 22.4: Types of economic evaluation.










Type
Outcome measure
When used




Cost-minimisation
None: outcomes assumed equal
Equivalence established


Cost-effectiveness
Natural units (life-years, events avoided)
Interventions sharing one main outcome


Cost-utility
Quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs)
Comparisons across diseases; the HTA standard


Cost-benefit
Money
Health versus non-health investments







22.4.1 QALYs
A QALY weights each year of life by a utility between 0 (dead) and 1 (full health). Utilities come from preference-based methods, such as the time trade-off and the standard gamble, usually through a generic instrument such as the EQ-5D, whose five dimensions are converted into a utility by a country-specific value set derived from the general public. The QALY gain from a treatment is the area between two utility-over-time curves: longer life plus better quality while alive. Future costs and QALYs are discounted (3.5% a year for NICE, 1.5% for CDA-AMC).
QALYs have known limits. A QALY counts the same whoever gains it, unless modifiers are added (since 2022, NICE weights QALYs for severe conditions by 1.2 or 1.7). Instruments can be insensitive in some conditions, and carers’ burden and productivity mostly fall outside the reference case. These are reasons to interpret QALYs carefully, not to abandon a common metric.


22.4.2 The cost-effectiveness plane
For a new intervention against a comparator, the incremental cost ΔC and incremental effect ΔE place it on the cost-effectiveness plane. In the north-east quadrant (more effective, more costly) the question is whether the gain is worth the cost; in the south-east it is dominant; in the north-west it is dominated. Two equivalent rules apply at a willingness to pay of λ per QALY:
\[\text{ICER} = \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta E} < \lambda \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{NMB} = \lambda\,\Delta E - \Delta C > 0 \quad (\Delta E > 0).\]
Net monetary benefit (NMB) avoids the awkward behaviour of ratios, such as negative ICERs that mean opposite things in different quadrants, and it is the quantity used in probabilistic analysis and value of information. NICE usually accepts ICERs below £20,000 to £30,000 per QALY. CDA-AMC has no official threshold, but its recent recommendations refer to CA$50,000 per QALY. Estimates of the health actually displaced by NHS spending suggest a lower opportunity-cost threshold, about £13,000 per QALY (13).


22.4.3 A Markov model with meta-analytic inputs
A Markov model divides a cohort among mutually exclusive health states. Time advances in cycles; in each cycle patients stay or move between states with fixed transition probabilities; and each state carries a utility and a cost. Our illustrative model has three states, Stable, Post-hospitalisation (after a first heart-failure hospitalisation, with worse prognosis and quality of life) and Dead, with annual cycles over 30 years. Baseline probabilities, utilities and costs are plausible but invented; the treatment effects are DAPA-HF’s component hazard ratios, HF hospitalisation 0.70 and cardiovascular death 0.82 (6), and the drug costs £477 a year at list price (9). This is where the meta-analysis enters the model. Hazard ratios multiply rates, not probabilities, so each annual probability is converted to a rate, multiplied by the HR, and converted back.


Code
p2r <- function(p) -log(1 - p); r2p <- function(r) 1 - exp(-r)
hf_model <- function(hr_hosp = 1, hr_cvd = 1, p_hosp = .10, p_cvd = .06, p_cvd_post = .15,
                     p_oth = .03, u_stable = .78, u_post = .65, dis_hosp = .10,
                     c_stable = 1500, c_post = 2500, c_hosp = 4000, c_drug = 0,
                     cycles = 30, disc = .035) {
  ph  <- r2p(p2r(p_hosp) * hr_hosp)              # HRs act on rates
  pc  <- r2p(p2r(p_cvd) * hr_cvd)
  pcp <- r2p(p2r(p_cvd_post) * hr_cvd)
  P <- matrix(c(1 - ph - pc - p_oth, ph,              pc + p_oth,     # from Stable
                0,                   1 - pcp - p_oth, pcp + p_oth,    # from Post-hosp
                0,                   0,               1), 3, byrow = TRUE)
  s <- c(1, 0, 0); cost <- qaly <- 0
  for (t in 1:cycles) {
    hosp  <- s[1] * ph                           # hospitalised this cycle
    s_new <- as.vector(s %*% P)
    d     <- 1 / (1 + disc)^(t - 1)              # discounting
    alive <- (s[1:2] + s_new[1:2]) / 2           # half-cycle correction
    qaly  <- qaly + d * (sum(alive * c(u_stable, u_post)) - hosp * dis_hosp)
    cost  <- cost + d * (sum(alive * (c(c_stable, c_post) + c_drug)) + hosp * c_hosp)
    s <- s_new
  }
  c(cost = cost, qaly = qaly)
}
sc <- hf_model(); tx <- hf_model(hr_hosp = .70, hr_cvd = .82, c_drug = 477)
rbind(`Standard care` = sc, Dapagliflozin = tx, Difference = tx - sc) |> round(2)


                  cost qaly
Standard care 13487.08 4.61
Dapagliflozin 17970.62 5.33
Difference     4483.54 0.73


Code
icer_det <- unname((tx - sc)[1] / (tx - sc)[2])


The deterministic ICER is £6,180 per QALY, of the same order as the £7,264 preferred by NICE’s committee, whose model had nine states (four symptom levels defined by quartiles of the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire, with and without diabetes, plus death) (9). Our model is a caricature, but it shows where each meta-analytic number goes.


22.4.4 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis
Every input is uncertain, so all are sampled together. The log hazard ratios are normal with the standard errors implied by their confidence intervals (the meta-analytic output), probabilities and utilities are beta, and costs are gamma. Each of 5000 draws is one possible world, in which the model is run for both arms.


Code
set.seed(2026); n_psa <- 5000
beta_ms  <- function(n, m, s) { a <- m * (m * (1 - m) / s^2 - 1); rbeta(n, a, a * (1 - m) / m) }
gamma_ms <- function(n, m, s) rgamma(n, shape = (m / s)^2, rate = m / s^2)
pars <- tibble::tibble(
  lhr_hosp = rnorm(n_psa, log(.70), (log(.83) - log(.59)) / 3.92),   # DAPA-HF, worsening HF
  lhr_cvd  = rnorm(n_psa, log(.82), (log(.98) - log(.69)) / 3.92),   # DAPA-HF, CV death
  p_hosp = rbeta(n_psa, 50, 450), p_cvd = rbeta(n_psa, 30, 470), p_cvd_post = rbeta(n_psa, 30, 170),
  u_stable = beta_ms(n_psa, .78, .03), u_post = beta_ms(n_psa, .65, .05),
  c_hosp = gamma_ms(n_psa, 4000, 800), c_post = gamma_ms(n_psa, 2500, 500),
  c_stable = gamma_ms(n_psa, 1500, 300))
psa <- pmap_dfr(pars, function(lhr_hosp, lhr_cvd, ...) {
  a <- hf_model(...)
  b <- hf_model(hr_hosp = exp(lhr_hosp), hr_cvd = exp(lhr_cvd), c_drug = 477, ...)
  tibble::tibble(dC = b[["cost"]] - a[["cost"]], dQ = b[["qaly"]] - a[["qaly"]])
})
icer_psa <- mean(psa$dC) / mean(psa$dQ)
psa |> summarise(across(c(dC, dQ), list(mean = mean, lo = \(x) quantile(x, .025),
                                         hi = \(x) quantile(x, .975)))) |> round(2)

  labs(x = "Willingness to pay (£000 per QALY)", y = "P(cost-effective)") + ylim(0, 1)
patchwork::wrap_plots(g1, g2)








Figure 22.3: Left: 5000 PSA draws on the cost-effectiveness plane, with the £20,000/QALY line and the mean (diamond). Right: the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve, the probability that dapagliflozin is cost-effective at each threshold.





The probabilistic ICER is about £6,240 per QALY. The probability that dapagliflozin is cost-effective is 99% at £20,000 per QALY but only 7% at £5,000. The ICER is a distribution, and the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC) is its honest summary.

title: 22  Health Technology Assessment and Decision-Making
text:
22.5 The Bayesian character of HTA
Probabilistic sensitivity analysis treats parameters as random variables with distributions and propagates them by simulation: it is implicitly Bayesian, and so are the CEAC and value of information, which are probabilities about parameters. In a review of 375 UK HTA reports from 1997 to 2011, 41% used some Bayesian method, almost always implicitly through PSA; explicit Bayesian evidence synthesis, such as Bayesian network meta-analysis, was much rarer (14). Decision-makers need what a Bayesian analysis provides: direct probability statements, coherent propagation of all uncertainties with their correlations, explicit use of external evidence, and prediction of what a new study or a new population would show (15). The “two halves” of an HTA, the evidence synthesis and the economic model, are often joined badly, for example when the review reports median survival but the model needs mean survival, or when correlations between parameters are lost.

22.5.1 Is another study needed? Magnesium after myocardial infarction
By the early 1990s, 15 small to moderate trials of intravenous magnesium after acute myocardial infarction suggested a large reduction in mortality, and an influential review called magnesium an effective, safe, simple and inexpensive intervention (16). Was the ISIS-4 trial, with 58,000 patients, justified after a “significant” meta-analysis?


Code
mag <- tibble::tribble(~study, ~year, ~Ee, ~Ne, ~Ec, ~Nc,
  "Morton",1984,1,40,2,36,       "Rasmussen",1986,9,135,23,135, "Smith",1986,2,200,7,200,
  "Abraham",1987,1,48,1,46,      "Feldstedt",1988,10,150,8,148, "Shechter",1989,1,59,9,56,
  "Ceremuzynski",1989,1,25,3,23, "Bertschat",1989,0,22,1,21,    "Singh",1990,6,76,11,75,
  "Pereira",1990,1,27,7,27,      "Shechter",1991,2,89,12,80,    "Golf",1991,5,23,13,33,
  "Thogersen",1991,4,130,8,122,  "LIMIT-2",1992,90,1159,118,1157, "Shechter",1995,4,107,17,108) |>
  mutate(study = paste(study, year))
mag_es <- escalc(measure = "OR", ai = Ee, n1i = Ne, ci = Ec, n2i = Nc, data = mag) |>
  mutate(sei = sqrt(vi))
re_mag <- rma(yi, vi, data = mag_es, method = "DL")
lim <- mag$study == "LIMIT-2 1992"
re_small <- rma(yi, vi, data = mag_es[!lim, ], method = "DL")
or_limit <- exp(mag_es$yi[lim] + c(0, -1.96, 1.96) * mag_es$sei[lim])
pi_mag <- predict(re_mag, transf = exp)
round(c(OR = pi_mag$pred, lower = pi_mag$ci.lb, upper = pi_mag$ci.ub,
        PI_lower = pi_mag$pi.lb, PI_upper = pi_mag$pi.ub, I2 = re_mag$I2), 2)


      OR    lower    upper PI_lower PI_upper       I2 
    0.43     0.29     0.63     0.18     1.01    33.07 


Five reasons justified a large trial. The evidence was thin: 4,557 patients but only 377 deaths. Bigger trials showed smaller effects: the 14 small trials together gave OR 0.38 (0.26 to 0.55), whereas LIMIT-2, the only large trial (2316 patients), gave 0.74 (0.56 to 0.99), a pattern of small-study effects (Chapter 15). The effect was implausibly large for a 24-hour infusion and heterogeneous (I² = 33%), with a prediction interval for a new trial of 0.18 to 1.01. The stakes were enormous: millions of patients a year, so a small uncertainty per patient has a large total cost if the decision is wrong. And the trial was cheap at the margin, because ISIS-4 was a factorial trial that also tested captopril and oral nitrates in the same patients.
A Bayesian random-effects model (Chapter 13) gives the posterior predictive distribution for a new trial directly:


Code
library(brms)
fit_mag <- brm(yi | se(sei) ~ 1 + (1 | study), data = mag_es,
               prior = c(prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept), prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = sd)),
               control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95), seed = 629)
dr <- as_draws_df(fit_mag)[, c("b_Intercept", "sd_study__Intercept")]




Code
dr <- read.csv("data/ch22/magnesium_draws.csv")          # 4000 posterior draws from fit_mag
set.seed(629)
theta_new <- rnorm(nrow(dr), dr$b_Intercept, dr$sd_study)  # predictive: a new trial
isis <- escalc(measure = "OR", ai = 2216, n1i = 29011, ci = 2103, n2i = 29039)
isis_or <- exp(isis$yi + c(0, -1, 1) * 1.96 * sqrt(isis$vi))
tibble::tibble(`Mean effect (posterior)` = exp(dr$b_Intercept), `New trial (predictive)` = exp(theta_new)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fill = name)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .5, colour = NA) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = isis_or[2], xmax = isis_or[3], ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = red, alpha = .35) +
  annotate("text", x = isis_or[1], y = 3.5, label = "ISIS-4", colour = red, hjust = -0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(limits = c(0.1, 2.5), breaks = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(navy, orange), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio for death (log scale)", y = "Density") + theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 22.4: Magnesium after myocardial infarction: posterior for the mean effect and posterior predictive distribution for a new trial (random-effects model of the 15 trials), and the result of ISIS-4 (red band, 95% CI).





The posterior median OR is 0.46 (95% CrI 0.28 to 0.68), but the predictive OR for a new trial is 0.48 (0.15 to 1.22), and the probability that a new trial would show harm is 0.05. ISIS-4 found OR 1.06 (1.00 to 1.13) (17). The pooled mean answered “is there an effect on average in these trials?”; the decision needed “what will happen in the next setting?”. Prediction, not pooled significance, should guide decisions.

title: 22  Health Technology Assessment and Decision-Making
text:
22.6 Value of information

22.6.1 Expected value of perfect information
Each PSA draw θ is one possible world. Let \(NB_d(\theta) = \lambda \times \text{QALYs}_d(\theta) - \text{Cost}_d(\theta)\) be the net benefit of option d in that world. Deciding now, without knowing the world, we choose the option with the highest average net benefit, worth \(\max_d E_\theta[NB_d(\theta)]\). With perfect information we would choose the best option in each world, worth on average \(E_\theta[\max_d NB_d(\theta)]\). The difference is the expected value of perfect information:
\[\text{EVPI} = E_\theta\big[\max_d NB_d(\theta)\big] - \max_d E_\theta\big[NB_d(\theta)\big] \ge 0.\]
EVPI is the expected loss from deciding under current uncertainty: the average net benefit lost in the worlds where today’s best choice turns out to be wrong. It is the most that research of any kind could be worth, per patient. Multiplied by the number of patients the decision affects, it is a ceiling to compare with the cost of research (18).


Code
evpi_at <- function(lam) {
  inb <- lam * psa$dQ - psa$dC                      # incremental NB of dapagliflozin
  mean(pmax(inb, 0)) - max(mean(inb), 0)            # perfect information - decide now
}
evpi_curve <- tibble::tibble(wtp = seq(0, 30000, 250)) |> mutate(evpi = map_dbl(wtp, evpi_at))
pop <- 75000 * sum(1 / 1.035^(0:9))   # illustrative: 75,000 new patients/yr for 10 years, discounted
ev6 <- evpi_at(6000); ev20 <- evpi_at(20000)
round(c(EVPI_6000 = ev6, EVPI_20000 = ev20, patients = pop))


 EVPI_6000 EVPI_20000   patients 
       225          8     645576 




Code
ggplot(evpi_curve, aes(wtp / 1000, evpi)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = navy) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = icer_psa / 1000, linetype = 2, colour = red) +
  annotate("point", x = c(6, 20), y = c(ev6, ev20), size = 3, colour = red) +
  annotate("text", x = c(6, 20) + 0.5, y = c(ev6, ev20) + 12, hjust = 0, size = 3.4,
           label = sprintf("£%s: £%.0f", c("6,000", "20,000"), c(ev6, ev20))) +
  labs(x = "Willingness to pay (£000 per QALY)", y = "EVPI per patient (£)")








Figure 22.5: Per-patient EVPI for the dapagliflozin model at each willingness to pay. EVPI peaks near the ICER (dashed), where the two options are closest.





EVPI is highest near the ICER, where the options have nearly equal average net benefit and the best choice flips most often between worlds. At NICE’s £20,000 per QALY, EVPI is £8 per patient, or £5.0 million over the 646,000 patients affected: a trial the size of DAPA-HF (4744 patients) would have to cost less than £1,050 per participant, far below the cost of a large cardiovascular outcome trial. Decide now. At £6,000 per QALY, where the decision is close, EVPI is £225 per patient and £145 million in total; research could be justified.


22.6.2 Which uncertainty matters? EVPPI
Research is always about something specific: a trial reduces uncertainty about treatment effects, a cohort about baseline risks, a preference study about utilities. The expected value of partial perfect information (EVPPI) for a group of parameters φ is the value of learning φ exactly while the rest stay uncertain. It can be estimated directly from the PSA draws by regressing the incremental net benefit on φ with a smooth function: the fitted values estimate the expected net benefit if φ were known (19).


Code
evppi <- function(formula, lam = 6000) {
  dat <- bind_cols(pars, inb = lam * psa$dQ - psa$dC)
  g <- fitted(gam(update(formula, inb ~ .), data = dat))     # E[INB | phi]
  mean(pmax(g, 0)) - max(mean(g), 0)
}
groups <- list(`Treatment effects (HRs)` = ~ s(lhr_hosp) + s(lhr_cvd),
               `Baseline event risks`    = ~ s(p_hosp) + s(p_cvd) + s(p_cvd_post),
               `Utilities`               = ~ s(u_stable) + s(u_post),
               `Costs`                   = ~ s(c_hosp) + s(c_post) + s(c_stable))
ev <- tibble::tibble(Group = names(groups), evppi = map_dbl(groups, evppi))
ev |> arrange(desc(evppi)) |>
  mutate(`£ per patient` = round(evppi), `£ million` = round(evppi * pop / 1e6, 1),
         `% of EVPI` = round(100 * evppi / ev6),
         `Research it points to` = c(`Treatment effects (HRs)` = "Trial or updated meta-analysis",
                                     Costs = "Costing study", Utilities = "Preference study",
                                     `Baseline event risks` = "Cohort study")[Group]) |>
  select(-evppi) |> kable(align = "lcccl")

EVPPI is zero for a group whose resolution would never change the decision, however uncertain that group is, and equals EVPI for a group that accounts for all the decision uncertainty. Here the treatment effects dominate: research on them, a further trial or an updated meta-analysis, is where any research money should go. Baseline risks matter little, because their uncertainty affects both options almost equally.
A real study only reduces uncertainty. The expected value of sample information, EVSI(n), is the expected improvement in the decision from a study of size n, never larger than EVPI; the expected net gain of sampling is population EVSI minus the cost of the study, and the best design maximises it (20). The R package voi computes EVPI, EVPPI and EVSI from PSA output. Value of information separates two questions that are often conflated: should we adopt now (expected net benefit), and should we buy more evidence (is the value of information larger than the cost of research)? Statistical significance answers neither. An HTA body can adopt, reject, adopt with a requirement for research, or approve only in research, when adoption would make the needed trial impossible.

title: 22  Health Technology Assessment and Decision-Making
text:
22.7 HTA bodies
Every HTA agency asks whether a technology should be paid for, but agencies differ in what evidence counts, what decision rule they apply, and whether their advice binds.



Table 22.6: Three HTA agencies compared.











Design choice
NICE (England)
CDA-AMC (Canada)
HAS (France)




How value is judged
Cost per QALY, usually below £20,000 to £30,000; severity modifier
Cost per QALY, with recent reference to about CA$50,000; most recommendations require a price reduction
Rating of added clinical benefit (ASMR I to V) drives price; cost-effectiveness secondary


Indirect comparisons
Expected when head-to-head trials are missing
Accepted, with critical appraisal
Accepted case by case


Who must follow the advice
Binding: NHS funding within 90 days
Advisory: provinces decide (Québec through INESSS); prices negotiated by the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance
Binding for reimbursement listing


Access before full evidence
Managed access (e.g. Cancer Drugs Fund)
Limited; conditional recommendations
Early access (accès précoce), since 2021






The same drug can therefore receive different decisions. A drug slightly better than existing care at £25,000 per QALY may be recommended in England, rated as offering no meaningful improvement in France and priced no higher than the old drug, and recommended in Canada only with a price reduction.

title: 22  Health Technology Assessment and Decision-Making
section: 22.8 The complete chain: dapagliflozin and NICE TA679
text:
22.8 The complete chain: dapagliflozin and NICE TA679
The appraisal of dapagliflozin shows every step (9):

Trial. DAPA-HF randomised 4744 patients with ejection fraction 40% or less and NYHA class II to IV, on background therapy (11% on sacubitril/valsartan), to dapagliflozin or placebo added to standard care. Primary composite HR 0.74 (0.65 to 0.85) (6).
Synthesis. A meta-analysis of DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced found a consistent effect of SGLT2 inhibitors on cardiovascular death or first HF hospitalisation, HR 0.74 (0.68 to 0.82), with no difference by use of sacubitril/valsartan (21).
Indirect comparison. Bucher comparison with sacubitril/valsartan, preferred over a matching-adjusted comparison; a possible advantage for dapagliflozin, but uncertain (Section 22.3).
Model. A nine-state Markov model; DAPA-HF EQ-5D-5L values mapped to EQ-5D-3L, with a published population value replacing the best state’s utility, which the committee judged implausibly high; Gompertz survival extrapolation.
Results. Company base case £6,939 per QALY against ACE-inhibitor or ARB-based care; the committee’s preferred ICER £7,264; below £10,000 against sacubitril/valsartan-based care; and dapagliflozin dominated sacubitril/valsartan when considered as an alternative to it.
Recommendation (February 2021). Recommended for symptomatic chronic HFrEF only as an add-on to optimised standard care, started on the advice of a heart-failure specialist.

The final wording follows the trial: it tested an add-on, so the recommendation is for an add-on. A low ICER and low EVPI at the relevant threshold mean recommend now, without requiring further research.

title: 22  Health Technology Assessment and Decision-Making
text:
22.9 When critical thinking is missing

22.9.1 Drotrecogin alfa in sepsis
In 2001 the PROWESS trial of drotrecogin alfa (activated protein C) in 1690 patients with severe sepsis reported 28-day mortality of 24.7% versus 30.8%; it was stopped early for benefit, after changes to the protocol and to the drug source during the trial (22). The FDA approved the drug after a split advisory committee vote, for high-risk patients only, a subgroup. Early economic models assumed that the 28-day benefit persisted for life. In 2005 the ADDRESS trial in lower-risk patients was stopped for futility, and in 2007 a hospital-based assessment by our group pooled the evidence, found an RR of 0.93 (0.69 to 1.26) and concluded that cost-effectiveness was uncertain and further research was needed (23). In 2011 PROWESS-SHOCK found 26.4% versus 24.2% mortality, and the drug was withdrawn worldwide (24).


Code
xig <- tibble::tibble(study = c("PROWESS 2001", "ADDRESS 2005", "PROWESS-SHOCK 2012"),
                      ai = c(210, 247, 223), n1 = c(850, 1333, 846),
                      ci = c(259, 222, 202), n2 = c(840, 1307, 834))
cum <- map_dfr(1:3, function(k) {
  r <- rma(measure = "RR", ai = ai, n1i = n1, ci = ci, n2i = n2, data = xig[1:k, ],
           method = if (k == 1) "EE" else "DL")
  tibble::tibble(label = paste0("+ ", xig$study[k]), est = exp(r$b[1]), lo = exp(r$ci.lb), hi = exp(r$ci.ub))
}) |> mutate(label = forcats::fct_rev(forcats::fct_inorder(label)))
ggplot(cum, aes(est, label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), colour = navy) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.6, 0.8, 1, 1.25, 1.5)) +
  labs(x = "Relative risk of death (log scale)", y = NULL)








Figure 22.6: Cumulative meta-analysis of the three trials of drotrecogin alfa (28-day mortality, random effects after the first trial).





After two trials the pooled RR was 0.93 (0.69 to 1.26): the decision-relevant uncertainty was visible a decade before withdrawal. A single trial stopped early with mid-trial changes, a split regulatory vote, benefit concentrated in a subgroup, short-term outcomes extrapolated to a lifetime, inconsistent later evidence and a high price: every element of an HTA could have flagged the problem.


22.9.2 Ipilimumab in melanoma: extrapolation drives the ICER
In metastatic melanoma, ipilimumab improved median survival from 6.4 to 10.0 months (HR 0.68), with two-year survival of about 22% versus 14% (25). An economic claim of acceptable cost per life-year depended on assuming about a year of extra survival. Most of that gain lies beyond the trial’s follow-up, in an extrapolated tail. The illustrative reconstruction below fits mixture-cure curves to the published medians and two-year survival and then extends them under two assumptions.


Code
fit_cure <- function(med, s24) {
  f <- function(p) (p[1] + (1 - p[1]) * exp(-p[2] * med) - 0.5)^2 +
                   (p[1] + (1 - p[1]) * exp(-p[2] * 24) - s24)^2
  o <- optim(c(0.1, 0.1), f, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(0, 0.001), upper = c(0.5, 1))$par
  list(pi = o[1], lam = o[2])
}
ctl <- fit_cure(6.4, 0.137); trt <- fit_cure(10.0, 0.216)
S <- function(t, p, h_late) {
  s24 <- p$pi + (1 - p$pi) * exp(-p$lam * 24)
  ifelse(t <= 24, p$pi + (1 - p$pi) * exp(-p$lam * t), s24 * exp(-h_late * (t - 24)))
}
tt <- 0:120
curves <- bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(t = tt, arm = "Ipilimumab", A = S(tt, trt, 0.005), B = S(tt, trt, 0.06)),
  tibble::tibble(t = tt, arm = "Control",    A = S(tt, ctl, 0.005), B = S(tt, ctl, 0.06)))
gain <- function(col, upto) sum(curves[[col]][curves$arm == "Ipilimumab" & curves$t <= upto] -
                                curves[[col]][curves$arm == "Control" & curves$t <= upto])
g24 <- gain("A", 24); gA <- gain("A", 120); gB <- gain("B", 120)
curves |> pivot_longer(c(A, B), names_to = "extrap") |>
  mutate(extrap = recode(extrap, A = "2-year survivors cured (hazard 0.5%/month)",
                         B = "Disease continues (hazard 6%/month)")) |>
  ggplot(aes(t, value, colour = arm, linetype = extrap)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_vline(xintercept = 24, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = 26, y = 0.9, label = "end of\nobserved data", hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Control = "grey40", Ipilimumab = red), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Months", y = "Survival", linetype = NULL) +
  guides(linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) + theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 22.7: Illustrative survival curves calibrated to the published medians and 2-year survival of ipilimumab and control, extrapolated beyond 24 months under two assumptions about late mortality.





Within the observed 24 months the mean survival gain is 2.8 months. Over 10 years it becomes 8.8 months if two-year survivors are effectively cured, but only 4.0 months if the disease continues to kill them. The ICER is driven by an assumption the trial cannot test, which is why extrapolation should be varied in sensitivity analyses and, where possible, informed by external data.


22.9.3 Lessons
Guidelines and HTAs go wrong through conflicts of interest (63% of 95 organisations producing clinical practice guidelines reported industry funding (26)); limited training in reasoning about uncertainty and cumulating evidence; uncritical acceptance of single, early-stopped or sponsor-written trials; neglect of patients’ preferences and of costs; cognitive biases such as overconfidence and group-think; and the habit of asking “does it work?” without “is it worth it?”. The consequences are marginal therapies becoming standard care and resources diverted from effective uses. The remedies are multidisciplinary committees, appraisal anchored in a systematic review rather than a pivotal trial, patient-relevant outcomes and economics, explicit quantified uncertainty (PSA, predictive distributions, value of information), transparent processes such as the EtD framework, and reassessment when new evidence arrives.

title: 22  Health Technology Assessment and Decision-Making
text:
Key points

HTA is not just a bigger systematic review, but a flawed review poisons every downstream step.
Decisions need absolute effects for each component outcome, not only a composite relative effect.
Transitivity is an assumption about background therapy as much as about patients; star-shaped networks cannot check it.
Ranking add-on therapies as alternatives answers the wrong question; match the analysis to the decision (A + B vs A, B vs C, A + B + C vs A).
The ICER is a distribution; report the CEAC from a probabilistic sensitivity analysis, not just a point estimate.
PSA and value of information are implicitly Bayesian; explicit Bayesian synthesis adds prediction and prior information.
Prediction, not pooled significance, should guide decisions (magnesium); extrapolation can dominate the result (ipilimumab).
EVPI and EVPPI tell you whether more research is worth paying for, and which research.

title: 22  Health Technology Assessment and Decision-Making
text:
Exercises

Repeat the Bucher comparison of eplerenone with dapagliflozin. Which assumptions make it doubtful?
Change the annual drug cost in hf_model() to £1,500. What is the new deterministic ICER, and how does the CEAC change?
Halve the standard errors of the two log hazard ratios in the PSA (as if a second trial had been done) and recompute EVPI at £6,000 per QALY.
Add a fifth EVPPI group containing only lhr_cvd. How much of the treatment-effect EVPPI does cardiovascular death account for?
In the magnesium example, compute the probability that a new trial shows OR < 0.8, using the posterior predictive draws. How would you explain the difference from P(mean OR < 0.8) to a decision-maker?

title: 23  Correcting the Published Literature: A Worked Audit
text:
23.1 The claim
The earlier chapters each introduced one method. This chapter uses them together to audit a single, influential meta-analysis. The aim is not to find fault for its own sake: a result that has influenced clinical guidelines deserves the same scrutiny we would give our own work, and the audit is a template for reading any meta-analysis that announces a result “for the first time”.
In 2024, a systematic review and network meta-analysis of percutaneous revascularization strategies after myocardial infarction (MI) in patients with multivessel disease pooled 24 trials and 16,371 patients (1). In its pairwise meta-analysis, complete revascularization, treating all significant lesions, was associated with a 15% reduction in all-cause mortality compared with treating the culprit artery only: RR 0.85 (95% CI 0.74 to 0.99). The conclusions stated that complete revascularization reduces all-cause mortality, and the discussion that a statistically significant and clinically relevant reduction in mortality was demonstrated “for the first time”.
We ask five questions of it, using only the authors’ own data: the deaths and patients in each arm of the 15 trials in their mortality forest plot. We do not question which trials were included or how the data were extracted. Those are legitimate concerns, but the point here is that the conclusion is fragile even if the data are accepted as given, and a critique based on the authors’ own data cannot be dismissed as “you chose different trials”.
crumbs: 23  Correcting the Published Literature: A Worked Audit

title: 23  Correcting the Published Literature: A Worked Audit
text:
Can we reproduce the headline result, and how was the interval built?
Is the heterogeneity estimate trustworthy?
Is the prediction interval correct, and what does it say?
Which trials carry the result, and is it robust to them?
How likely is a benefit, how large is it, and what would it cost?

23.2 The data


Code
dat <- data.frame(
  study = c("Zhang 2015", "PRAGUE-13", "FIRE", "PRAMI", "DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI",
            "Politi", "CvLPRIT", "COMPARE-ACUTE", "COMPLETE", "Hamza", "Ghani",
            "Zhang 2023", "FULL REVASC", "Zhao", "HELP-AMI"),
  year  = c(2015, 2015, 2023, 2013, 2015, 2010, 2019, 2017, 2019, 2016, 2012,
            2023, 2024, 2016, 2004),
  ai    = c(13,  6, 66, 12, 15, 10,  9,  4,   96, 1, 4, 3, 76, 3, 1),   # deaths, complete
  n1i   = c(215, 106, 720, 234, 313, 130, 150, 295, 2016, 50, 79, 115, 764, 148, 52),
  ci    = c(15,  7, 93, 16, 11, 13, 15, 10,  106, 4, 0, 4, 72, 4, 0),  # deaths, culprit-only
  n2i   = c(213, 108, 725, 231, 314, 84, 146, 590, 2025, 50, 40, 114, 778, 158, 17))
# log RRs; 0.5 added only to the two trials with a zero cell, as the authors did
es <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = ai, n1i = n1i, ci = ci, n2i = n2i,
             data = dat, add = 0.5, to = "only0", slab = study)
es$sei <- sqrt(es$vi)
m_z     <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML")                    # Wald z
m_kh    <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML", test = "knha")     # HKSJ
m_adhoc <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML", test = "adhoc")    # truncated HKSJ
p_z <- predict(m_z, transf = exp); p_kh <- predict(m_kh, transf = exp)
p_ad <- predict(m_adhoc, transf = exp)
w <- setNames(weights(m_z), dat$study)
big3 <- c("FIRE", "COMPLETE", "FULL REVASC")




Code
fd <- as.data.frame(es) |>
  mutate(rr = exp(yi), lo = exp(yi - 1.96 * sei), hi = exp(yi + 1.96 * sei), wt = w,
         y = rev(seq_len(n())) + 2, counts = sprintf("%d/%d", ai, n1i), counts0 = sprintf("%d/%d", ci, n2i),

title: 23  Correcting the Published Literature: A Worked Audit
text:
23.3 Can we reproduce it?
The paper used a REML random-effects model. That fixes the point estimate, RR 0.85, but not the confidence interval, and the methods do not say how the interval was built. Section 9.3.2 described three options: the Wald interval, which treats τ² as known; the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) interval, which multiplies the standard error by \(\sqrt q\) and uses a t distribution, where \(q = \sum_i w_i (y_i - \hat\mu)^2/(k-1)\) (2,3); and a truncated HKSJ interval, which never lets q fall below 1, so that the interval is never narrower than the Wald interval (4,5).


Code
tibble::tibble(`CI method` = c("Wald z (τ treated as known)", "HKSJ", "Truncated HKSJ (q ≥ 1)"),
               `RR (95% CI)` = c(ci_t(p_z$pred, p_z$ci.lb, p_z$ci.ub), ci_t(p_kh$pred, p_kh$ci.lb, p_kh$ci.ub),
                                 ci_t(p_ad$pred, p_ad$ci.lb, p_ad$ci.ub)),
               P = f3(c(m_z$pval, m_kh$pval, m_adhoc$pval)),
               q = c("not used", f2(m_kh$s2w), sprintf("%s (truncated)", f2(m_adhoc$s2w))),
               ` ` = c("", "matches the paper", "")) |>
  kable(align = "lccll")

Only HKSJ reproduces the published result. The answer to “is q below 1?” is in the last column: \(q\) = 0.69 (m_kh$s2w in metafor). The trials agree better than their standard errors predict, so HKSJ shrinks the interval below the Wald interval; the truncated version resets q to 1. The two intervals without that property both include 1.


Code
m_ee   <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "EE")
m_mh   <- rma.mh(ai = ai, n1i = n1i, ci = ci, n2i = n2i, data = dat, measure = "RR")
m_glmm <- rma.glmm(measure = "OR", ai = ai, n1i = n1i, ci = ci, n2i = n2i, data = dat, model = "UM.FS")
many <- tibble::tibble(
  method = c("Random effects, HKSJ (published)", "Random effects, Wald z", "Random effects, truncated HKSJ",
             "Common effect, inverse variance", "Common effect, Mantel-Haenszel", "Binomial GLMM (odds ratio)"),
  est = exp(c(coef(m_kh), coef(m_z), coef(m_adhoc), coef(m_ee), coef(m_mh), coef(m_glmm))),
  lo  = exp(c(m_kh$ci.lb, m_z$ci.lb, m_adhoc$ci.lb, m_ee$ci.lb, m_mh$ci.lb, m_glmm$ci.lb)),
  hi  = exp(c(m_kh$ci.ub, m_z$ci.ub, m_adhoc$ci.ub, m_ee$ci.ub, m_mh$ci.ub, m_glmm$ci.ub)),
  p   = c(m_kh$pval, m_z$pval, m_adhoc$pval, m_ee$pval, m_mh$pval, m_glmm$pval)) |>
  mutate(method = forcats::fct_reorder(method, hi), pub = grepl("published", method),
         lab = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)  P = %.3f", est, lo, hi, p))
ggplot(many, aes(est, method, colour = pub)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 1.07, label = lab), hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(navy, red), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.68, 1.4), breaks = seq(0.7, 1.05, 0.05)) +
  labs(x = "Relative risk of death (95% CI)", y = NULL)








Figure 23.2: The pooled relative risk of death and its 95% CI under six defensible analyses of the same 15 trials. The published analysis is in red.





Every analysis gives RR ≈ 0.85; the upper limit lies between 0.99 and 1.02, and P between 0.035 and 0.074. “Significant” or “not significant” depends on a defensible but arbitrary choice: the result sits on a knife-edge. Nothing about the data changes between P = 0.035 and P = 0.074, only the formula for the interval, and the difference between “significant” and “not significant” is not itself statistically significant (6,7). A better summary of the frequentist results is that the data are compatible with relative risks from about 0.71 to about 1.02: most compatible with a modest benefit, with neither a large benefit nor no benefit excluded.

title: 23  Correcting the Published Literature: A Worked Audit
text:
23.4 Heterogeneity: “I² = 7%”
The paper reports I² = 7.1% and a non-significant Q test. How well do these data pin down the between-trial SD, τ?


Code
tau_ci <- confint(m_z)$random
est_tau2 <- sapply(c(DL = "DL", REML = "REML", PM = "PM", ML = "ML", SJ = "SJ"),
                   \(x) rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = x)$tau2)
tau_hi <- tau_ci["tau", "ci.ub"]
wi <- 1 / es$vi
s2_typ <- (m_z$k - 1) * sum(wi) / (sum(wi)^2 - sum(wi^2))   # "typical" within-trial variance
i2_of  <- \(tau2) tau2 / (tau2 + s2_typ)
round(est_tau2, 3)


   DL  REML    PM    ML    SJ 
0.000 0.007 0.000 0.001 0.091 


Code
round(tau_ci[c("tau", "I^2(%)"), ], 2)


       estimate ci.lb ci.ub
tau        0.09     0  0.33
I^2(%)     7.09     0 52.97


The estimators give τ² from 0.000 to 0.091, and the Q-profile 95% CI for τ runs from 0 to 0.33, with I² anywhere from 0% to 53%. Q has little power here, because 70% of the weight sits in three trials. A non-significant Q test is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence (8); “I² = 7%” should be read as “heterogeneity uncertain”, not “homogeneous”.
What would τ = 0.33 mean? If μ and τ were known, the true effects would follow \(\theta_i \sim N(\mu, \tau^2)\), and 95% of true RRs would lie within \(e^{\mu \pm 1.96\tau}\). This describes the spread of the true effects across settings, so it uses τ, not \(SE(\hat\mu)\), which only measures how well the average is known. Centred on RR 0.85, τ = 0.33 gives true effects from 0.45 to 1.62, from large benefit to clear harm. Over the same range of τ, I² runs from 7% (at the REML τ of 0.09) to 53%, because I² = τ²/(τ² + s²) is relative to the precision of a typical trial, here s = 0.31 (9). To judge whether effects differ enough to matter clinically, look at τ or the prediction interval, not I².
crumbs: 23  Correcting the Published Literature: A Worked Audit

title: 23  Correcting the Published Literature: A Worked Audit
text:
23.5 The prediction interval
The prediction interval (PI) estimates where the true effect in a new setting is likely to fall (Section 9.4.1). It plugs in estimates for μ and τ, so it adds \(SE(\hat\mu)^2\) to \(\hat\tau^2\) and uses a t distribution rather than 1.96 (10–12):
\[\hat\mu \pm t\,\sqrt{\hat\tau^2 + SE(\hat\mu)^2}.\]
Because the PI is centred on the same \(\hat\mu\) as the CI and adds a non-negative term, it always contains the CI. Anyone can check a published PI in seconds: does it contain the CI?
The paper printed “prediction interval −0.39 to −0.08” as text beside a forest plot drawn on the RR scale. On the RR scale that is 0.68 to 0.92. Its upper limit, 0.92, lies below the CI’s upper limit, 0.99, so it does not contain the CI, which is impossible.


Code
k <- m_z$k
pi_t <- exp(coef(m_z) + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, k - 2) * sqrt(m_z$tau2 + m_z$se^2))   # Higgins, t(k-2)
tibble::tibble(
  Interval = c("CI", "PI (HKSJ, t with k − 1 df, as metafor)", "PI (Higgins, t with k − 2 df)", "PI as published"),
  `Log scale` = c(sprintf("%.2f to %+.2f", log(p_kh$ci.lb), log(p_kh$ci.ub)),
                  sprintf("%.2f to %+.2f", log(p_kh$pi.lb), log(p_kh$pi.ub)),
                  sprintf("%.2f to %+.2f", log(pi_t[1]), log(pi_t[2])), "-0.39 to -0.08"),
  `RR scale` = c(sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", p_kh$ci.lb, p_kh$ci.ub), sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", p_kh$pi.lb, p_kh$pi.ub),
                 sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", pi_t[1], pi_t[2]), sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", exp(-0.39), exp(-0.08)))) |>
  kable(align = "lcc")




Table 23.2: Confidence and prediction intervals from the authors’ model (REML with HKSJ), on the log and RR scales.











Interval

CI

With \(\hat\tau^2\) = 0.0073 and \(SE(\hat\mu)\) = 0.069, the correct PI on the log scale is -0.39 to +0.08. The lower limits match the published one; the upper limit has lost its sign. As published, the PI says that in every new setting complete revascularization reduces mortality by 8% to 32%. Correctly computed, it says that in a new setting the effect could be anything from a 34% reduction to a 10% increase. A transcription error turns “uncertain in a new setting” into “always beneficial”.

text:
23.6 Where does the result come from?


Code
rr_of   <- \(s) exp(es$yi[dat$study == s])
no_fire <- predict(rma(yi, vi, data = es, subset = study != "FIRE"), transf = exp)
b3      <- predict(rma(yi, vi, data = es, subset = study %in% big3, method = "EE"), transf = exp)
tibble::tibble(Trial = big3, Population = c("Age ≥ 75, STEMI or NSTEMI", "STEMI", "Mostly STEMI"),
               Guidance = c("Physiology", "Angiography", "FFR"),
               RR = f2(sapply(big3, rr_of)), Weight = pct(w[big3] / 100)) |>
  kable(align = "lllcc")
